items.abstract: The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) on resource-constrained edge server clusters introduces a critical systems challenge: achieving high throughput and low latency under strict GPU memory and bandwidth limits. Current schedulers are ill-suited for this environment, as they treat requests independently, incurring two major inefficiencies. They waste compute and memory on redundant prefill computations for identical, lengthy system prompts across applications, and their phase-agnostic policies create suboptimal batches that poorly overlap compute-intensive prefills with memory-bound decodes, leading to GPU under-utilization. This paper presents ALPS, an application-aware, length-predictive scheduler for request serving for edge LLM inference. ALPS transforms the queueing layer into an intelligent orchestrator with two core techniques: (i) semantic-aware request grouping, which hashes requests by system prompt to co-locate them, reducing redundant prefill computations; and (ii) phase-aware scheduling, which uses a lightweight output token bucket predictor to estimate decode/prefill ratios and strategically reorders requests to maximize prefill-decode overlap in continuous hybrid batching. Augmented with SLO-aware preemption, ALPS is implemented as a practical scheduling layer atop vLLM. Extensive evaluations on an edge GPU testbed with diverse models and production workloads demonstrate that ALPS improves token throughput by up to 1.6× and reduces end-to-end latency by up to 2.4× compared to state-of-the-art schedulers.
items.venue: IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems

items.title: AFLoRA: Adaptive LoRA for Resource-Efficient Federated Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
items.abstract: LoRA-based federated fine-tuning allows clients to fine-tune LoRA adapters locally and aggregates updates on the server, thereby enabling the efficient adaptation of global foundation models to distributed, domain-specific data. However, existing methods assume identical and static LoRA adapters across clients, which not only limits the utilization of heterogeneous resources and adaptation to diverse data distributions, but also prevents dynamic adjustment to clients’ evolving local fine-tuning state. They also struggle to achieve precise and lightweight aggregation of LoRA matrices, hindering learning performance in resource-constrained environments. To address these issues, we propose AFLoRA, an adaptive LoRA-based resource-efficient federated fine-tuning framework. For effectively adapting to Non-IID local data while minimizing resource consumption, AFLoRA introduces diagonal-based dynamic rank assignment, which dynamically adjusts local LoRA ranks based on client resources and local adaptation state guided by a learnable diagonal matrix. It further decouples LoRA matrices updates between clients and the server to reduce overhead, and develops a zero-padding-based rank-aware aggregation mechanism to accurately integrate heterogeneous updates through lossless matrix expansion and rank-aware weighting. These mechanisms enable AFLoRA to balance resource efficiency and fine-tuning performance effectively. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AFLoRA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both LLM adaptation performance and fine-tuning efficiency in heterogeneous environments.

items.title: A System-Level Exploration of Superconducting Supercomputers for Emerging Workloads
items.abstract: Superconducting digital (SCD) technology has long carried promise for advancing large-scale computing leveraging the unique physical characteristics of superconducting materials and devices, such as low-voltage, high-frequency operation and zero-resistance interconnects. At the same time, SCD technology has also historically been beset with many scaling challenges. However, recent critical advances including improved power delivery, high integration density and availability of superconducting random-access memory prompt a fresh evaluation of SCD-based computing. In this paper, we study whether SCD systems can outperform conventional CMOS and cryo-CMOS for large-scale workloads even after accounting for full system overheads. Using a novel multilevel analytical modeling framework, our study explores performance implications of various SCD configurations across a range of architecture and technology assumptions in applications such as large language models (LLMs). The results show that, despite cooling overheads, a key benefit of recently proposed SCD technology is 9 $\boldsymbol{\times}$ × - 286 $\boldsymbol{\times}$ × better energy efficiency. By contrast, performance gains ranging between 4 $\boldsymbol{\times}$ × - 16 $\boldsymbol{\times}$ × are more limited and strongly depend on the availability of high-density, high-bandwidth on-chip memory that traditionally was not attainable. In general, the results show that recent technological advances are key to a promising scalable path forward, where our ablation studies highlight critical aspects of the maturity of SCD technology.

items.title: A Survey of Relation Extraction: From Deep Learning to Large Language Models
items.abstract: The relation extraction (RE) task aims to identify the relations between entities in texts. Structured facts extracted through RE can be effectively leveraged for various downstream tasks, including knowledge graph construction and logical reasoning. As this field has evolved over time, it has made significant progress, from deep learning to the rise of large language models (LLMs). However, deep learning-based and LLM-based methods still need to be further explored. Meanwhile, systematic surveys and comparative analysis remain insufficient. Therefore, this paper conducts a comprehensive survey of deep learning-based and LLM-based methods. Based on this, we categorize deep learning-based methods into pipeline-based and joint extraction-based methods, while LLM-based methods are classified into prompt-based and fine-tuning-based methods, providing a detailed introduction to each. In addition, drawing upon the experimental results documented in extant papers, we carry out an in-depth comparative analysis from both experimental and theoretical perspectives. Moreover, to provide valuable references for future research, we introduce several renowned open-source RE tools and explore their features and application scenarios intensively. Finally, we discuss current research challenges thoroughly and outline future research directions. We also provide a public GitHub repository containing curated resources, code links, and supplementary materials related to this survey.
items.venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering

items.title: A Resonant Capacitor-Less Parallel Resonant DC-Link Soft-Switching Inverter
items.abstract: To address the issues of reduced light-load efficiency and DC bus voltage loss in dual-resonant-circuit parallel resonant DC-link soft-switching inverter (PRDCLSI), this article proposes a resonant capacitor-less PRDCLSI. Leveraging the low turn-off loss characteristics of SiC mosfets, the resonant capacitors are eliminated to minimize the current stress of the auxiliary circuit under both light- and heavy-load conditions. An improved modulation strategy is introduced, which initiates the resonant process during the dead time to avoid prolonged existence of the DC bus zero-voltage notch. With this improved modulation strategy, no turn-off snubber capacitors are required for any switches. Furthermore, by merging redundant components, the proposed design reduces the component count by two auxiliary diodes and nine resonant capacitors, significantly lowering hardware costs. This article provides a detailed analysis of the operational modes of the resonant capacitor-less PRDCLSI under the improved modulation strategy and compares its performance with different existing schemes. Following parameter design, a 40 kHz, 5 kW experimental prototype based on SiC mosfets was built. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution maintains the advantage of a short DC bus zero-voltage notch (<1.60 μs) while achieving high-efficiency power conversion across load conditions (96.72% at 200 W and 98.25% at 5 kW).

items.title: Text-to-SQL Interface using Guardrails and Hallucination Detection
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can translate plain-English questions into SQL, which makes institutional databases usable by people who cannot write queries. In a shared system such as a college ERP, however, the generated SQL must be treated as untrusted code: it may modify data, read rows that belong to another user, or quietly answer the wrong question. This paper reports the design, deployment, and security testing of SafeSQL, a natural-language query system over a 25-table, 174- column PostgreSQL ERP schema holding about 200,000 records. SafeSQL places the LLM behind four independent layers: model-level refusal, syntax-tree (AST) blocking with sqlglot, a read-only non-owner database role, and Row-Level Security (RLS). We show that the widely used RLS pattern based on current_setting() can be defeated by generated SQL that calls set_config() from a subquery, CTE, LATERAL join, or window function, and we replace it with a session map keyed on the PostgreSQL backend process, which adds about 2.14 ms per query. We also describe five cases in which our own test infrastructure reported success for the wrong reason, and the checks we added to catch them. The system is deployed as a web application and is covered by 248 automated tests.
items.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology

items.title: Neural Palate Kueh
items.abstract: If there is one thing that you would not need nor want Artificial Intelligence (AI) to do for you, it is probably eating. Yes, more than thinking, designing, building, and even sleeping on your behalf. All work in the future including architecture work could potentially reside at the dining table. Dining as co-designing and eating as consecrating architecture. A 'tasty' architectural 'food-for-thought' and 'food-to-eat'. Neural Palate Kueh was on display at the Venice Architecture Biennale 2025 as part of the Singapore Pavilion and has since returned to Singapore for its 'Homecoming Edition' at the National Museum of Singapore. It uses the traditional Singaporean kuehs (bite-sized snack or dessert foods) to speculate on future scenarios of building-making and city-making with the analogical generativity limits (and potential creativity) of today's AI - one that could be made specific to a given culture and built environment like Singapore. It combines conditioning AI techniques such as IP-Adapters and ControlNet with the disjointedness of manual collage techniques to iteratively generate context-specific 3D urban forms from real-time dining footages and to synthesize 3D building forms with edible food. Using Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the process begins with AI's deconstruction of each kueh along three axes: conceptual underpinnings (rituals of eating and cultural symbolism), design operatives (geometric form and culinary construction), and materiality (ingredients and textures). These insights become the learnt architectural design principles of the AI models to imagine novel architectural interiors/exteriors with which perceptual associations with Singapore forms, whether buildings or food, are produced. The taxonomies of fooddining and architecture-planning now become blurred and interchangeable. The project features the outputs as 3Dprinted architectural pieces in several food scales and 3D point clouds video animations in several urban scales. Neural Palate Kueh thus proposes an experimental synesthetic AI methodology driven by architectural narrative and gastrophysics.

items.title: An Explainable Graph Attention Network for Indirect Prompt Injection Detection in RAG Systems
items.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables large language models (LLMs) to answer queries using information obtained from external documents. However, retrieved content may contain concealed commands intended to influence the model's behaviour, creating a security risk called indirect prompt injection. This research develops a GAT-based approach to identify harmful instructions in retrieved documents before they reach the language model. Each document is split into individual sentences, which are encoded using a frozen DeBERTa-v3-base model. A graph is constructed from the sentence embeddings, linking adjacent sentences and pairs with a cosine similarity score above 0.7. A two-layer Graph Attention Network (GAT), comprising approximately 0.4 million trainable parameters, processes the graph to classify the document as benign or malicious. The model was evaluated using 10,000 samples collected from financial and corporate policy documents. The dataset contains 6,400 training samples, 1,600 validation samples, and 2,000 testing samples, with equal representation of both classes. Following the addition of calibrated Gaussian noise to the input features, the model obtained 99.80% test accuracy, an F1-score of 0.998, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.996. Its 95% Wilson confidence interval for accuracy ranged from 99.49% to 99.92%. The keyword-based approach recorded an accuracy of 87.93%, but 24.1% of the malicious samples contained none of its specified trigger terms. Its performance on unseen data remains to be established through further experiments involving independently collected datasets, additional application domains, and attack techniques excluded from the original evaluation.
items.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology

items.title: WHEN CORRECT CODE IS NOT ENOUGH: ASSESSING THE PRODUCTION READINESS OF LLMGENERATED SOFTWARE
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate executable software, but functional correctness alone does not establish production readiness. This study evaluates GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna across 15 algorithmic and production-oriented tasks using five generations per model-task pair, yielding 225 generated programs plus 15 fixed references. The layered testbed combines nominal and hidden-edge-case checks, moderate and severe production-like stress, metamorphic validation, reference-normalized runtime and memory, structural quality, static analysis, implementation-strategy inspection, and generation cost. All 800 functional and 368 applicable robustness checks passed, while production-stress success fell to 95.16% for Sol, 95.60% for Terra, and 93.38% for Luna. Cross-model stress differences were not significant, but generation cost differed strongly. A Quick Sort case showed more than a 500x runtime spread among behaviorally correct implementations. The results show that production-oriented evaluation must extend beyond pass/fail correctness to include stress behavior, resources, implementation strategy, and cost
items.venue: International Journal of Software Engineering & Applications

items.title: Ripple: Coordination-Free Message Scheduling for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows at the IoT Edge
items.abstract: Distributed intelligence in IoT and edge systems increasingly runs as agentic AI: production large language model (LLM) applications execute as workflows—directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of agents and tools that exchange prompts, retrieved context, and tool outputs across end devices, edge servers, and the cloud. When many such workflows share a capacity-limited link, such as an edge gateway uplink or a regional aggregation point, that link rather than the GPU gates the communication phase, and a message that unblocks an idle agent may wait behind an unrelated bulk transfer. A dependency-aware link scheduler can mitigate this, but a scheduler that ranks messages by whole-workflow remaining work and downstream critical path requires a global, continuously updated view of every concurrent workflow, that is, a central coordinator that heterogeneous and dynamic IoT edge deployments typically lack. This paper presents Ripple, a coordination-free link scheduler in which each agent ranks only its own outgoing messages, using a local rule that prioritizes downstream criticality per unit transmission cost and applies an age credit to curb long waits. The required downstream-criticality signal is a bounded scalar initialized with the source's task descriptor, so no runtime node maintains the global graph. In an event-driven, flow-level evaluation on a shared 100 Mbps link with heavy-tailed messages (median 419 KB, 99th-percentile about 30 MB) and four DAG shapes, network waiting accounts for 46% of the mean workflow completion time (WCT) under fair sharing at offered load ρ=0.88. Ripple reduces mean and 99th-percentile WCT by 24% and 38% relative to fair sharing, and attains 9% lower mean and 27% lower tail WCT than a global-view reference heuristic while using no global state. A knowledge-horizon analysis shows that performance saturates at a one-hop view, and an ablation finds that message size and age drive most of the aggregate gain. The results use an idealized flow-level priority model; a DSCP/eBPF realization that needs no coordinator and no change to the LLM runtime is proposed but not yet evaluated.
items.venue: ACM Interational Symposium on Mobile Ad Hoc Networking and Computing

items.title: Measuring the Predictability of Beam-Level 5G Traffic: How Far Can Zero-Shot Foundation Models Go?
items.abstract: Beam-level traffic forecasting is critical for 5G resource allocation, yet the measurement properties of beam-level traffic remain poorly understood. We present a measurement-driven analysis across 2,961 time series from two public 5G datasets released by third parties. We first characterize how beam-level traffic differs from the aggregated cell-level traffic studied in prior work, identifying a sparsity-dependent predictability gradient: active beams exhibit the strongest periodicity and covariate correlations, enabling accurate forecasting, while covariate gains attenuate with sparsity until most methods converge on the sparsest beams. We then benchmark 16 model configurations, including four general-purpose Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) pre-trained without mobile-network data and one RAN-specific foundation model, across three experimental settings. A zero-shot TSFM given identical oracle covariates outperforms trained alternatives on 68-73% of beams (64% univariately), but this advantage is concentrated on active beams where periodic structure is strongest; on the sparsest beams, foundation and trained models converge to the same noise-dominated predictability floor. The dominant factor has to do with information inputs rather than the model architecture: oracle network telemetry covariates reduce error more than switching between any two general-purpose architectures, and covariate-augmented models are also more resilient to distribution shift. We interpret this benefit as an information-content upper bound: deployable pipelines that lag, extrapolate, or separately forecast the covariates recover none of the oracle gain at a one-week horizon, identifying covariate acquisition, rather than model choice, as the key open problem. Without future information, zero-shot Chronos-2 matches or beats trained univariate pipelines while requiring no training or retraining.
items.venue: ACM Interational Symposium on Mobile Ad Hoc Networking and Computing

items.title: MOSAIC: Efficient Collaborative Inference for Multi-Modal Large Language Models with Distributed Edge Computing
items.abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) enable natural language reasoning over heterogeneous sensory data, appealing to many edge AI scenarios, yet their deployment faces competing demands on latency, energy, and quality. We present MOSAIC, which adopts a component-level decomposition and distributed deployment paradigm for efficient MLLM inference at the edge, realizing three core ideas: parallel encoding, token pruning, and device-server collaboration. Specifically, for the offline stage, modality-specific encoders distilled from a unified foundation model are co-deployed with Q-Former projection on edge devices for parallel encoding, while LoRA instruction fine-tuning adapts the frozen LLM backbone to downstream tasks. For the online stage, we formulate a multi-objective optimization over latency and energy that jointly tunes token budgets, device frequencies, and quantization precision under long-term semantic accuracy constraints, achieving dynamic token pruning and device-server collaboration. We leverage Lagrangian relaxation to decompose the original problem into tractable per-slot subproblems and design an online algorithm with provable near-optimal performance and guaranteed constraint satisfaction. We implement a realistic testbed for extensive performance evaluation, which demonstrates that MOSAIC reduces latency by up to 49.8% and energy by up to 65.1% over advanced baselines while maintaining high semantic accuracy.
items.venue: ACM Interational Symposium on Mobile Ad Hoc Networking and Computing

items.title: FrozenSFL: Model-Frozen Split Federated Learning for Resource-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning over Heterogeneous Edge Devices
items.abstract: Collaborative fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) at the network edge enables privacy-preserving and personalized generative intelligence, but is constrained by the limited memory and compute resources of edge devices. Traditional approaches, such as split federated learning (SFL), partition models between devices and a server, requiring iterative exchanges of activations/gradients while the server manages multiple submodels. This leads to substantial communication overhead, high activation storage costs, and severe server-side memory pressure when scaling to massive heterogeneous devices. In this paper, we propose FrozenSFL, a resource-efficient SFL framework for collaborative fine-tuning of LLMs across heterogeneous edge devices. At its core, FrozenSFL strictly freezes device-side submodels to eliminate both deviceside backpropagation and server-to-device gradient transmission, thereby removing on-device activation storage requirements and downlink communication overhead. Building upon this design, we improve the framework in two aspects. First, we design a layerwise LoRA aggregation strategy to handle structural heterogeneity introduced by device-specific model partitioning and enable efficient server-side updates. Second, we introduce a server-side feature caching mechanism that reuses invariant features, allowing subsequent training epochs to proceed offline and reducing redundant computation and communication. We implement the FrozenSFL system as an asynchronous multi-threaded pipeline, which serves as our real-world testbed for evaluation. On the device side, forward computation and data transmission are decoupled via a producer-consumer mechanism. On the server side, a first-in-first-out scheduling strategy serializes fine-tuning tasks across devices. A hybrid memory-disk streaming mechanism further buffers incoming data and ensures stable training under network variability. Extensive evaluations with representative models, including BERT-Base (0.11B), ViT-Large (0.3B), and LLaMA-2-7B (7B), validate the effectiveness of FrozenSFL. In particular, for LLaMA-2-7B, FrozenSFL can reduce device/server VRAM footprint by up to 14%/82.7% with only 1% accuracy loss, while achieving up to 6.7× fine-tuning speedup.
items.venue: ACM Interational Symposium on Mobile Ad Hoc Networking and Computing

items.title: Demo: On-Device Agent for Personalized and Efficient Mobile Network Configuration
items.abstract: As mobile devices increasingly operate across heterogeneous access networks and diverse usage contexts, efficient network configuration requires decisions that adapt to both dynamic network conditions and individual user preferences. We demonstrate an on-device communication agent that transforms historical user network-switching behavior into personalized configuration rules. An on-device Large language model (LLM) analyzes switching records offline and generates condition-action rules capturing recurring user preferences. During real-time use, the agent retrieves matched rules locally and executes the corresponding network configuration after user confirmation, without invoking the LLM. Attendees will choose a prepared behavior trace, inspect the rule generated on the phone, and recreate its triggering context to observe an immediate network switch. The demonstration shows how separating deliberation from execution makes personalized mobile network configuration both interpretable and responsive while keeping user data and inference on the device.
items.venue: ACM Interational Symposium on Mobile Ad Hoc Networking and Computing

items.title: An Agentic AI Architecture for Zero-Touch IoT Device Onboarding and Interoperability
items.abstract: The heterogeneity of Internet of Things (IoT) devices remains a major barrier to scalable deployment, automated onboarding, and cross-platform interoperability. Device-specific protocols, software dependencies, telemetry formats, and runtime constraints often require manual configuration and ad-hoc integration logic. This paper proposes an agentic AI architecture for zero-touch IoT device onboarding, where a large language model is used as an autonomous configuration agent capable of generating device-side software, installing dependencies, validating runtime behavior, and recursively correcting failures until convergence is achieved. The proposed architecture introduces a closed-loop workflow that combines device inspection, AI-based runtime generation, remote deployment, telemetry validation, and self-correction. Interoperability is addressed through a normalized telemetry contract that abstracts device-specific behavior into a common telemetry representation. We evaluate the approach on a real IoT device by benchmarking multiple AI models under clean installation conditions in two campaigns: the original pipeline and a second pipeline assisted by a locally trained semantic context optimizer. The comparison covers convergence time, correction cycles, recursive iterations, and prompt tokens. The optimizer-assisted campaign reduced prompt redundancy and recursive recovery effort while preserving successful onboarding across all tested models. Overall, the results show that agentic AI can support zero-touch onboarding while exposing measurable differences among models in reliability, efficiency, and runtime convergence.
items.venue: ACM Interational Symposium on Mobile Ad Hoc Networking and Computing

items.title: On Evaluating Performance of LLM Inference Systems
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems has led to significant improvements in serving efficiency. However, our systematic analysis reveals that current evaluation methodologies suffer from fundamental flaws that mask critical performance issues and impede scientific progress. Through a comprehensive examination of recent systems, we identify recurring pitfalls in evaluation practices across three key dimensions: Baseline Fairness, Evaluation Setup, and Metric Design. These pitfalls are uniquely problematic for LLM inference due to its dual-phase nature combining prefill and decode operations, heterogeneous workloads, and strict temporal requirements. We demonstrate how implementation differences frequently obscure algorithmic contributions, how workload selection often fails to represent production scenarios, and how metric normalization can hide substantial performance variability that directly impacts user experience. Traditional metrics derived from the classical machine learning serving setup fail to capture the autoregressive generation characteristics essential to LLM inference, leading to misleading conclusions about system performance. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive checklist of best practices and methodological recommendations for robust LLM inference evaluations. To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we present a case study of speculative decoding evaluation - a technique whose non-uniform token generation patterns with bursts during accepted predictions and delays during verification failures fundamentally confound conventional metrics. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluation methodology that can accelerate progress in LLM inference systems by ensuring meaningful comparisons, reproducible results, and metrics that reflect real-world requirements.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing Volume 1

items.title: Memory-Decoupled Layer-Wise Fine-Tuning for Efficient On-Device LLM Adaptation
items.abstract: Federated Fine-Tuning (FFT) is essential for customizing Large Language Models (LLMs) at the edge while preserving data privacy. However, its scalability is severely constrained by the memory bottleneck. Our analysis reveals that the massive static memory footprint of LLM parameters exceeds the physical capacity of edge devices, rendering standard end-to-end training infeasible. In this paper, we propose EdgeLLM, a Cloud-Edge memory management system that democratizes efficient edge LLM adaptation via progressive layer training. Specifically, EdgeLLM re-architects the training process into a sequential pipeline: it dynamically manages the device memory hierarchy by maintaining only a minimal granular subset of layers on-chip while aggressively offloading inactive ones. To maximize system efficiency and convergence stability, EdgeLLM integrates four key components: (1) Resource Scheduler, which continuously probes device runtime memory availability to maximize resource utilization via dynamic workload mapping; (2) Training Coordinator, which bridges the semantic gap caused by offloading via virtualized context synthesis, ensuring coherent feature learning without full-graph residence; (3) Execution Planner, which optimizes the computation path by intelligently pruning redundancy and prioritizing task-critical layers for targeted adaptation; and (4) I/O Manager, which neutralizes the layer-swapping overhead through asynchronous prefetching and eviction. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that EdgeLLM effectively breaks the memory wall, unlocking participation for resource-constrained devices previously excluded from the training cohort. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, EdgeLLM delivers up to 11.86% performance improvement, accelerates model convergence by 2.08 × , and reduces communication overhead by 1.78 ×.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing Volume 1

items.title: zkTransformer: Scalable Zero-Knowledge Proofs for LLM Inference via Einsum Arithmetization and Structured Exponentiation Lookups
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed through cloud APIs; however, their inference processes are opaque and cannot be externally audited without revealing proprietary model parameters. Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) enable verifiable inference while preserving model confidentiality, but existing zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) systems remain difficult to deploy in practice due to limitations in developer usability, completeness of prover implementations, and the cost of lookup operations. We present \zkt, an end-to-end zkML framework for transformer inference that addresses these challenges while achieving high prover performance. To improve usability and correctness, we introduce \zkes, a new sumcheck-based arithmetization that lifts linear tensor operations to an AI-friendly abstraction based on Einstein summation (Einsum), enabling automatic compilation of such operations into a single Sumcheck instance without manual circuit engineering over low-level addition and multiplication gates. To reduce the cost of nonlinear operations, we further propose \zkexp, a structured lookup technique for exponentiation that eliminates the need for table-sized commitments. Together, these techniques provide a unified and model-agnostic framework for verifiable transformer inference, supporting standard architectures such as GPT-2 and LLaMA2-7B. We implement and open-source \zkt. On GPT-2, it achieves an amortized prover time of 3.4 seconds per token, representing a 5--10× speedup over state-of-the-art systems such as zkLLM and zkGPT.

items.title: zkAgent: Verifiable LLM Agent Execution via One-Shot Transcript Proofs
items.abstract: LLM-based agents, which interleave large language model inference with external tool calls, are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings. In real-world deployments, both model inference and provider-hosted tool execution occur behind provider APIs and are therefore opaque to users. This opacity creates an execution-integrity gap: a malicious provider may substitute the advertised model or fabricate tool observations to steer subsequent agent behavior. Existing zero-knowledge proof systems for LLMs prove only the Transformer computation of a single token, leaving the rest of the inference pipeline, long-form autoregressive generation, and external tool interactions outside the proof. We present zkAgent, the first SNARK system for verifiable agent execution. zkAgent proves the complete inference pipeline, from token-to-embedding lookup and positional encoding to Transformer computation and decoding. It further binds each tool observation to an authenticated execution via zkTLS or zkVM subproofs, yielding a single end-to-end proof. To scale beyond per-token proving, we introduce one-shot transcript proving : by exploiting the Transformer's causal attention mask, zkAgent proves an entire multi-step agent transcript in a single forward pass, avoiding the substantial overhead incurred by one-proof-per-token generation. We make this batched proof sound with a weight-dependent quantization scheme that is both input-independent and unconditionally complete. On GPT-2 with a 512-token transcript, zkAgent achieves a 1,047.4× prover speedup over the state of the art (zkGPT, USENIX Security '25), amortizing to 0.30\,s/token. On a real-world coding-assistant execution, zkAgent completes end-to-end proving in 93.18s with 1.63s verification, making verifiable agent execution practical.

items.title: Verifying Consensus Protocols from LLM-assisted TLA$^+$: A Case Study of Byzantine Reliable Broadcast
items.abstract: TLA+ (Temporal Logic of Actions) is a formal specification language well-suited for distributed systems. However, writing proper TLA+ scripts requires high domain expertise. When it comes to modeling Byzantine behaviors for Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus protocols, the simulation of malicious behavior is a fundamental challenge: overly simplified modeling misses critical vulnerabilities, and verbose modeling leads to state-space explosion. In this paper, we present TLAssist, a large language model (LLM)-assisted tool for semi-automated TLA+ generation tailored for Byzantine reliable broadcast (RBC) protocols. We provide a highly structured workflow and domain-specific data format to improve the quality of LLM prompts. Using six RBC protocols as case studies, we have some interesting findings. First, the specification generated by TLAssist outperforms many open-source TLA+ scripts we are aware of, including those written by domain experts. Second, TLAssist can assist domain experts in identifying deep design flaws. Notably, our case study on the (2, 3, 4)-Optimistic RBC (a CCS'25 distinguished paper) captures a subtle issue that causes the violation of the totality property. Finally, TLAssist is useful for non-experts. Namely, we show that by revising the protocols slightly, the generated error traces effectively show complex corner cases that can facilitate understanding of the design.

items.title: VeriPRAC: Verifiable Formal Contracts for Secure Per Row Activation Counting
items.abstract: Rowhammer remains a major security concern for modern DRAM, yet no deterministic solution exists in commercial devices. The latest JEDEC specification introduces Per Row Activation Counting (PRAC) to provide a principled framework for secure in-DRAM mitigation. Since the introduction of PRAC, a number of mitigations have been proposed based on PRAC. However, these proposals only provide ad hoc security analyses without necessarily considering the worst-case scenarios. In this work, we define PRAC contracts that provide formal bounds for a generic set of mechanisms in a PRAC mitigation. Our key insight is that these generic mechanisms introduce gaps in tracking accesses to DRAM, making it possible for an attacker to craft a variety of strategies that silently survive the mitigation actions performed by PRAC. Using these silent survival strategies, we then construct EchoTrail, a provably optimal attack structure against PRAC contracts. Leveraging EchoTrail, we then develop VeriPRAC, an automatic contract verification tool that checks a given PRAC-based mitigation against its intended PRAC contract. VeriPRAC finds that all state-of-the-art mitigations violate their intended contract, and in one case, an aggressor can reach up to 7.5k activations despite the intended bound of the contract being only 99.

items.title: VLM-DC: Vision--Language Model for Automotive Data Collection
items.abstract: The development of advanced driver-assistance systems (ADASs) and autonomous driving technologies depends on high-quality, representative driving data. Traditional collection methods either demand extensive manual filtering or rely on rigid thresholds that miss critical edge cases. To overcome these limitations and meet diverse operational and system requirements, this work introduces a two-module, vision–language model (VLM)-based framework for intelligent and targeted data collection. The first module employs a cloud–edge multiagent architecture, where a cloud-based large language model (LLM) coordinates sensor selection and an edge-deployed VLM evaluates scene relevance. This approach achieves 91.35% overall precision, reduces storage by 28.30%, and shows promising performance on geographically distinct out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. The second module implements a distributed VLM architecture with knowledge distillation (KD), deploying a lightweight vision encoder on vehicles and a language decoder in the cloud. A selective token transfer mechanism reduces model size by 71% and bandwidth use by 50% while maintaining 91.86% overall accuracy. Both modules outperform larger baselines while remaining computationally and communication efficient. Overall, this framework shifts automotive data collection from exhaustive recording to selective capture of valuable driving moments, accelerating ADAS development and validation.

items.title: Uncovering Hidden Attack Surfaces in Web Applications via Semantic-Aware Black-Box Scanning
items.abstract: Web application scanners are indispensable tools for black-box vulnerability discovery. However, modern web applications increasingly rely on dynamic client-side rendering, where many HTTP requests are generated only in response to specific, meaningful user interactions. These interaction-triggered requests and the vulnerabilities they may conceal create a hidden attack surface that traditional scanners struggle to explore, as they lack the semantic understanding needed to identify and execute purposeful action sequences. In this paper, we present SemScanner, a novel approach that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to achieve semantic-aware web scanning, effectively uncovering this hidden attack surface. SemScanner performs per-page semantic analysis to generate meaningful interaction tasks, which are then executed by LLM-driven agents. Through this process, it constructs a Web Application Semantic Graph (WASG) that models the application's attack surface enriched with semantic context. Building on this graph, SemScanner formulates targeted audit tasks and deploys specialized agents to perform context-adaptive testing, thereby exposing vulnerabilities that conventional approaches may miss. We evaluate SemScanner on 20 real-world web applications, comparing it against state-of-the-art scanners. SemScanner identifies 59 previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities, nearly three times the number discovered by the strongest baseline. All identified zero-day vulnerabilities have been responsibly disclosed, with CVE identifiers assigned.

items.title: Turning Everyday Earphones into a Full-Duplex Speech Eavesdropping Platform via Zero-permission IMU
items.abstract: Speech eavesdropping has become a significant security concern. While non-acoustic side channels (e.g., mmWave and RFID) offer eavesdropping pathways, they invariably rely on external hardware deployed in proximity to victims. This limits their stealth and practicality. Earphones, by contrast, pose a more insidious threat. Their embedded inertial measurement units (IMUs), accessible without user permissions, create a hardware-free stealthy side channel. In this paper, we propose a novel side-channel attack that achieves the first open-vocabulary, full-duplex speech eavesdropping on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) earphones. This attack uniquely accomplishes full-duplex recognition of both 'what you say' (user speech) and 'what you hear'(audio played through the earphones), even when overlapping (e.g., talking while listening to music or multi-person conversing). We resolve the severe mutual interference inherent to this underdetermined signal separation problem. Constrained by COTS earphones' fixed IMU sampling rates of merely 25~Hz, we propose a multi-axial data fusion strategy to extract speech features from this limited bandwidth. A dual-stream attention network, along with a phoneme-based pixel-reorganization strategy (to support open-vocabulary recognition) and large language model (LLM)-assisted refinement, is employed to accurately recognize sensitive speech. Extensive evaluations on COTS earphones demonstrate the attack's practicality and urgent threat to speech privacy.

items.title: Trustworthy LLM Unlearning and Beyond
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can retain personal, copyrighted, or harmful information that may later require removal. My dissertation studies trustworthy LLM unlearning as an integrated process of specifying the forgetting target, performing robust single and continual deletion while preserving capabilities, and verifying forgetting through representation diagnostics and recovery tests. My work develops dual-granularity target construction, utility-preserving deletion, and recovery-based verification for these stages. A complementary SoK organizes safety forgetting across benchmarks, algorithms, and evaluation, while identifying behavior probing, graceful forgetting, and model regularization as functional uses. Future work will formulate retraining-based verification criteria and extend the framework to agents whose state spans model weights, memory, retrieval, tools, and interaction histories.

items.title: Tricycle: Private Transformer Inference with Tricyclic Encodings
items.abstract: The growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) in privacy-sensitive settings demands inference mechanisms that preserve data confidentiality. Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a principled solution by enabling computation directly on encrypted data; however, existing solutions struggle to scale to full LLMs. We present Tricycle, a system for efficient private transformer inference. At its core, Tricycle introduces tricyclic encodings, a novel packing scheme that enables batch matrix multiplications with optimal multiplicative depth while naturally supporting multi-head attention. We demonstrate that Tricycle's matrix multiplications are particularly amenable for integration with other optimizations including Baby-Step Giant-Step optimizations, optimized block matrix multiplications, lazy relinearization, and complexification, which significantly improve performance. We further introduce statistical max estimation, a lightweight method for stabilizing softmax under HE. We implement Tricycle end-to-end on a GPU-accelerated CKKS pipeline and evaluate it on BERT models. For BERT-Base with 128 tokens, Tricycle achieves 100.5 seconds latency on a single GPU, yielding 6× and 3.4× speedups over prior state-of-the-art systems, Thor and Powerformer, respectively. These results demonstrate that careful design of packing, algorithms, and optimizations can significantly reduce the cost of private LLM inference, bringing practical deployment closer to reality.

items.title: The Illusion of Rust Safety: Detecting Modular Unsafe Functions with LLMs
items.abstract: Memory safety vulnerabilities account for approximately 70% of reported security bugs, prompting the adoption of Rust, a systems programming language designed to prevent such issues through compile-time checks. While Rust categorizes code into safe and unsafe regions, we identify a previously understudied class of vulnerabilities: modular unsafe functions (MUF) in Rust code. These functions appear safe to the compiler but are, in fact, unsafe within the whole module's APIs and can cause undefined behavior without using the unsafe keyword, leading to a misleading sense of safety and unsound issues in Rust. We present the first systematic study of mufs, defining five root cause categories from empirical analysis. We develop Coin, a detection system using fine-tuned large language models for vulnerability identification and proof-of-concept generation. Coin achieves 63.7% precision and 80.4% recall on labeled evaluation set, outperforming existing tools. On evaluation of 10,000 randomly sampled Rust crates, Coin identified 26 unknown mufs with 14 developer confirmations and 10 CVE assignments.

items.title: TWIST: Private Tenant-Dedicated LLM Serving via Joint Model-Token Transformation
items.abstract: Organizations increasingly host open-weight large language models (LLMs) on dedicated cloud instances to avoid the opaque data control imposed by closed-source APIs and the burden of costly local infrastructure. However, this deployment paradigm inadvertently exposes sensitive tenant prompts and outputs to service providers. Existing protection routes do not fit this setting well in practice: cryptographic inference incurs prohibitive overheads; Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) rely on specialized hardware that is difficult to deploy consistently across heterogeneous legacy accelerators; and traditional data-only obfuscation methods, such as token replacement, require substantial perturbation to achieve meaningful privacy, often causing severe utility degradation. To address this gap, we present TWIST, a practical system for private open-weight LLM serving on dedicated cloud instances. Rather than perturbing input tokens alone, TWIST applies a shared, structure-preserving transformation to both the model weights and input tokens. This coupled design extends protection beyond data-only obfuscation and addresses the traditional utility bottleneck. We analyze leakage to an honest-but-curious provider using Rényi-metric differential privacy (RmDP), and show a smaller privacy budget than a data-only baseline with the same online mechanism. Practically, we implement TWIST for modern dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, including attention, FFN, and MoE routing modules, without disrupting standard serving pipelines. Evaluations on the 671B-parameter DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus model show that TWIST reduces token recovery rate to under 5% against advanced inversion attacks, while incurring only 0.0% - 3.5% accuracy loss and <10% inference speed loss, offering a practical solution for private tenant-dedicated LLM serving.

items.title: SymSan: Mitigating Malware Embedding in Large Language Models via Parameter Space Symmetry
items.abstract: Despite the considerable advantages of open-source large language models (LLMs) in terms of interpretability and customizability, the full-access sharing paradigm inevitably exposes them to a severe security threat, i.e., malware embedding attacks (MEAs), where adversaries embed malware binaries (i.e., payloads) into model parameters for subsequent execution. While existing sanitization defenses have been explored to eliminate payloads within parameters, they exhibit limited generalization against emerging MEAs and lack theoretical guarantees for model utility preservation. In this paper, we propose SymSan, an effective LLM sanitization method grounded in parameter space symmetry theory. SymSan leverages rigorously designed permutation and scaling symmetries, systematically transforming parameter matrices across complementary component pairs, thereby eliminating embedded payloads while ensuring mathematical functional equivalence. Experiments across diverse LLMs against a wide spectrum of MEAs demonstrate that SymSan achieves at least 0.47 BER against all evaluated existing MEAs while maintaining equivalent model performance on both foundational and downstream tasks, significantly outperforming all baselines.

items.title: Securing Software in the Age of Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new capabilities for software security by interpreting source code and natural-language specifications, and generating plausible code. However, their probabilistic behavior, hallucinations, limited security knowledge, and inconsistent outputs make their direct use non-trivial. This dissertation investigates how LLMs can identify code requiring protection, discover and repair vulnerabilities in existing software, and improve the security of generated software code while accounting for reliability and deployment costs. The completed research provides results across three settings. LLM-CAL identifies cryptographic code for fine-grained TEE boundary establishment, reducing the Trusted Computing Base by 81.20%. RESTing-LLAMA uses semantic OpenAPI documentation to discover 11 vulnerabilities across real-world REST APIs with fewer requests and a lower false-positive rate than existing fuzzers. RAVEN combines agentic retrieval, repository-level dependency analysis, and iterative refinement to achieve an 83.13% repair success rate across 160 real-world CVE instances. The ongoing research examines the trustworthiness of LLM-based code generation through knowledge-poisoning attacks against RACG systems and an agentic Graph RAG framework for retrieving CWE-structured security knowledge. Together, these studies examine how LLMs can be adapted for securing existing and generated software.

items.title: POSTER: Realistic Enough for What? Metrion: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Cyber Environments
items.abstract: Cyber environments are increasingly used to evaluate offensive and defensive AI agents, but existing evaluations often describe environments by implemented features or broad claims of ''realism'' rather than by the realism properties required for a specific evaluation objective. To address this gap, we propose Metrion, a framework for assessing the realism of the cyber environment relative to an evaluation objective. Rather than assigning a single realism score, the framework derives realism dimensions from MITRE ATT&CK and D3FEND matrices, maps evaluation objectives to required environment properties, and reports unmet critical requirements for a given environment-objective pair. A worked example shows that the same environment can be suitable for credential-based privilege escalation but unsuitable for targeted data exfiltration. An interactive scorecard and a preliminary evaluation of published environments are available online. The poster seeks feedback on the granularity of the dimension set, the three-level requirement scale, and the use of ATT&CK and D3FEND as the basis for derivation.

items.title: POSTER: ROS2Pot: An Agentic Honeypot for Proactive Defense Against LLM Agents in ROS 2/DDS Systems
items.abstract: ROS 2 and its underlying Data Distribution Service (DDS) middleware and Real-Time Publish-Subscribe (RTPS) wire protocol have become a high-value attack surface for safety-critical robotic systems. Meanwhile, large language model (LLM) driven agents are reshaping the attacker profile from human penetration testers into autonomous entities capable of multi-step intrusion—yet these agents' own architectural weaknesses open paths for defensive counteraction. To date, no agentic honeypot has been built on ROS 2 to counter LLM-driven adversaries. We present ROS2Pot, whose contributions are threefold. (i) To our knowledge, it is the first publicly described interactive ROS 2 honeypot, built on rclpy atop Fast-DDS and combining rosbag replay with on-demand PyBullet physics simulation to deliver both high interaction and DDS-observable physical fidelity. (ii) To our knowledge it is also the first to cast LLM-driven agents as the explicit adversary class in ROS 2 robotic systems, mapping the systematized LLM-agent weaknesses of Ayzenshteyn et al. [1] onto concrete exploitation points in the ROS 2 attack surface. (iii) It introduces an agent-versus-agent paradigm in which the honeypot itself runs as an LLM agent and weaponizes two of these weaknesses into ROS 2-native deception primitives. Evaluation against five LLM-driven red-team agents spans three levels. At the protocol level, introspection responses are byte-identical to those of a real reference. At the physical level, the honeypot remains operationally indistinguishable from the reference under the injected control commands we replay. At the counteraction level, a two-stage trap confirms an LLM attacker through an invisible honeytoken and then elicits its operational objective by reverse prompt injection, with susceptibility varying sharply by model and objective and a measurable detect-but-not-extract funnel.

items.title: POSTER: LHPD: LLM-Based Heuristic Pre-Training for Malware Detection
items.abstract: Malware sandboxes produce rich behavioral reports, yet these reports are lengthy, deeply nested JSON documents that defy direct analysis. In this paper, we address how general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) can reconstruct coherent behavioral chains of malware from such reports, and propose LHPD, a detection framework that bridges the cognitive reasoning gap between generic LLMs and expert analysis. LHPD introduces Semantics-Driven Feature Reconstruction (SDFR) to reorganize raw JSON reports into four complementary semantic dimensions—signatures, PE metadata, the import address table, and time-ordered API sequences—reducing structural noise while preserving causal links between high-level alerts and low-level traces. A Heuristic-Based Fine-Tuning Strategy (HBFS) then progressively aligns models with curated security heuristics before refining them on the reconstructed corpus. On a CAPE-based dataset of 13,623 reports, the LHPD-tuned Qwen3-32B attains 94.87% accuracy, surpassing both dedicated detectors and generic LLMs, and remains robust under few-shot settings.

items.title: POSTER: Defending Against LLM-based Cyberattack Agents via Safeguard-Oriented Decoys
items.abstract: The emergence of autonomous agents that leverage foundation Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct cyberattacks requires new defensive approaches. This poster proposes safeguard-oriented decoys as a technique to activate LLM safeguards suppressed by attacker framing. Our preliminary results on 14 CTF challenges against 5 foundation LLMs demonstrate that safeguard-oriented decoys are effective at slowing down or even blocking attack agents.

items.title: POSTER: Assessing Open-Source Large Language Models for Leaked File Classification
items.abstract: Publicly accessible cloud object-storage buckets (e.g., Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage) pose a significant security risk to organizations by unintentionally exposing sensitive documents. Automated file classification is essential for detecting such leaks; however, accurate risk evaluation requires semantic understanding beyond keyword matching and metadata analysis. Although large language models (LLMs) can interpret document content and identify sensitive information, their adoption is often limited by the privacy risks of sending exposed data to third-party APIs. In this paper, we evaluate locally deployed open-source LLMs for automated severity classification of files found in public buckets, using model quantizations that balance accuracy and inference speed. Our experiments demonstrate that resource-efficient LLMs can support practical leak-detection workflows, enabling organizations to discover and remediate exposed sensitive information.

items.title: POSTER: A Context-Consistent Attack Exploiting the Inspection--Execution Gap in Code-Executing Agents
items.abstract: Code-executing agents often rely on inspection before execution, assuming that the artifacts inspected statically represent what will later be executed. We identify an inspection–execution gap: after static inspection, a runtime transformation produces the actual executable payload, which reaches a code-execution sink without being inspected. We instantiate this gap through a context-consistent attack embedded in a least-significant-bit (LSB) image-steganography project: a no-overwrite guard preserves an attacker-prepared stego image, from which an embedded executable payload is later extracted and passed to the sink. Using harmless canaries, we conduct 900 baseline trials in the same fixed agent scaffold, varying the large language model (LLM) backend across nine models (100 trials per model) and observe an attack success rate (ASR) of 87.3%. We also observe successful traces in which agents explicitly recognize the risk yet proceed, showing that attack success is not explained solely by inattention. We additionally test four prompts with progressively more explicit inspection guidance; their effects vary substantially across models. These findings motivate a post-extraction authorization checkpoint that binds inspection and authorization to the exact extracted payload immediately before execution. The code is available.

items.title: PORTA: Systematic Discovery of Vulnerabilities in Identity Brokers
items.abstract: Identity brokers such as Keycloak, Vault, and Dex translate authentication proofs from an upstream identity provider into sessions for downstream services. Due to their central role in authentication and trust mediation, a single vulnerability in a broker compromises every downstream service behind it. In fact, recent incidents have demonstrated that even widely adopted platforms are not immune to such issues, highlighting the critical need for systematic analysis. To build such an analysis, this work first defines invariants for broker operation. These invariants are not completely covered by existing authentication specifications, primarily because brokers are unique in their duality, i.e., acting simultaneously as a relying party and an identity provider. The invariants capture the properties that identity brokers must uphold throughout their workflows, as all 60 previous CVEs we consider violate at least one invariant. Within these workflows, we further define high-level action categories. Equipped with this information, our automated tool Porta leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate API invocation sequences corresponding to the high-level action categories, and oracle assertions aligned with the specified invariants. Porta identifies 33 previously unreported security vulnerabilities in seven popular open-source brokers. We study these novel vulnerabilities and trace them to eight recurring patterns. We responsibly disclosed all discovered vulnerabilities: 29 have been confirmed, 14 patched, and 19 assigned CVE numbers, with 10 CVEs rated as critical.

items.title: MetaMancer: Practical Tool Selection Attacks against LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on third-party tools, making tool selection a critical security boundary. By manipulating tool metadata, an attacker can steer an agent toward a malicious tool and thereby redirect downstream execution, even without controlling the user query or interacting with the victim system. Although prior attacks reveal the vulnerability of tool selection, they fail to fully capture the adversarial problem in realistic settings. Mounting a practical attack remains highly challenging, because the attacker should manipulate the complete tool metadata under a strict transfer-based black-box setting while preserving effectiveness, stealth, and robustness. To address this challenge, we formulate adversarial tool selection as a semantically constrained bilevel optimization problem, and propose MetaMancer, a multi-agent semantic optimization framework that estimates effectiveness and constraints in a surrogate ecosystem, and reconciles them through semantic projection and atomic joint updates. Experiments on ToolBench and MCPTools, spanning 20 tasks, 9,729 candidate tools, 8 target LLMs, and 6 representative defenses, demonstrate that MetaMancer achieves end-to-end attack success rates of 92.7% and 93.8% without defenses, and retains 91.2% and 92.2% after averaging over six defenses, exceeding state-of-the-art attacks by over 50 percentage points under defenses. These results indicate that the tool selection boundary of LLM agents remains under-protected. To mitigate this threat, we propose Core View Reconstruction (CVR), a lightweight defense that reconstructs tool metadata within the core capability boundary implied by required parameters. CVR reduces the end-to-end attack success rates of MetaMancer to 18.0% and 17.6%, while consistently suppressing other tool selection attacks.

items.title: MChammer: A Systematic Characterization of CPU-Level Rowhammer Countermeasures on DDR5 Systems
items.abstract: Rowhammer is a fault attack in computer hardware which allows attackers to flip bits in memory without the need to access them. Since its discovery by Kim et. al. (ISCA 2014) Rowhammer has been used to bypass the security of countless mechanisms. Recognizing the danger, DDR5-based systems now aim to mitigate Rowhammer via both CPU and DIMM level countermeasures. In this work, we systematically characterize the hardware countermeasures present on DDR5-based systems. We begin by presenting a physical-to-DRAM address reverse engineering tool with high accuracy and speed. We then reverse engineer the behavior of AMD and Intel platforms when executing Rowhammer workloads, showing that AMD platforms generate very different DRAM command streams during hammering compared to their Intel counterparts. Next, we also document the behavior of Targeted Row Refresh (TRR) on both CPU and DIMM level as well as analyze the processor's understanding of on-DIMM row remapping across Samsung, Hynix, and Micron DIMMs. Combining the above analyses, we present end-to-end Rowhammer flips on Samsung DIMMs on both AMD and Intel machines, with all countermeasures enabled. We then proceed to analyze the sudo binary on recent versions of Linux, which was previously hardened against opcode flipping attacks. Despite this, we show that Rowhammer on sudo is still possible, allowing unprivileged users to obtain root access on DDR5-based systems.

items.title: Learning Less While Asking More: How LLM-Based Assistance Shapes Vulnerability Learning
items.abstract: Large language model assistants have become a popular way to learn about software vulnerabilities, yet whether they effectively support this process remains unclear. We present a controlled within-subject study with 70 participants comparing LLM-based assistance with web search across five dimensions of vulnerability understanding. We find that LLM-based assistance is associated with smaller measured learning gains than web search, with the disadvantage concentrated in reasoning-oriented dimensions such as understanding causes, runtime behavior, and security consequences. Process analysis reveals that LLM sessions involve broader but faster-shifting queries, earlier movement toward solution-seeking, and reduced sustained engagement with explanatory content. Despite these smaller measured gains, participants consistently perceive LLM assistance as more helpful, clearer, and more efficient, yet report comparable workload to web search. These findings reveal a gap between perceived support and measured learning gains. Motivated by this gap, we design VulnScaffold, a scaffolded LLM-based learning system that restructures query formulation, response organization, and reflective practice. A preliminary evaluation suggests promising improvements in both learning outcomes and user experience, helping address the gap identified in LLM-based learning.

items.title: Large Language Models For Narrative-Driven Cyber Deception
items.abstract: Research consistently shows that cyber deception can slow down adversaries, degrade their performance, and reveal their intentions and long-term planning. Yet the gap between this research and the real world remains vast. A deception storyline encompasses decisions on which assets to deploy, where to place them, what each one communicates to an attacker, and how they collectively shape the attacker's understanding of the environment. However, whether deploying deception as a structured storyline produces better defensive outcomes than simply deploying deception ad hoc remains an open and largely unstudied question. Three unsolved problems keep this gap wide open: (i) there is little, if any, research comparing strategic to ad-hoc deception deployment, (ii) to this day, there is no publicly available automated system capable of designing and deploying complete, coordinated deception storylines, and (iii) no empirical study compares the defensive performance of automated storylines against those that human experts design. To address these gaps, the primary scientific contribution of this thesis proposal is to systematically study, understand, design, implement and evaluate the mechanics of effective AI-based cyber deception storylines. Specifically, we propose using LLM-based scaffolds to create cyber deception storylines. Our approach will use autonomous agents to determine the selection, placement, tactical purpose, personality of deception assets, and the overall narrative by analysing target network topologies and defence goals from the user. Every decision in creating a deception storyline will be explicitly grounded in well-known previous work on deception theory and best practices. We propose implementing this methodology within a framework that, in addition to automated storyline creation, actively orchestrates and manages the deployed decoys. A critical contribution to this thesis proposal is strong validation. To validate this approach, our evaluations follow a structured plan: (i) creation of a SoK for summarising and systematising existing knowledge on how to evaluate deception against human adversaries, (ii) assessing our framework against autonomous AI-based network attacking agents, (iii) assessing our framework against professional human adversaries, (iv) comparing our AI-based cyber deception storylines against human deception expert-designed storylines. Thus, we hope to develop a principled understanding of how AI-coordinated deception alters the behaviour of both AI and human adversaries.

items.title: Knock, Knock: Who's There? Towards Adversary-Aware Adaptive Cyber-Deception
items.abstract: Cyber-deception misleads attackers to protect systems, but it has traditionally assumed a fixed adversary, usually a human, occasionally a script. AI-driven agents are emerging as a new adversary class, and the absence of ground truth makes identifying the agent behind an interaction difficult. This dissertation investigates adversary-aware deception that infers an operational adversary profile and adapts accordingly. Preliminary results show that deception measurably affects attacker behaviour, that activity that does not resemble conventional automation can be isolated without ground truth, and that AI agents are both susceptible to deception and identifiable through stable behavioural fingerprints. The remaining work composes these into a system that infers an operational adversary profile and selects a deception strategy accordingly.

items.title: Janus: Characterizing Bidirectional Privacy and Security Risks in LLM-Integrated Android Apps
items.abstract: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into mobile applications has introduced a new class of privacy and security risks that existing analysis techniques are poorly equipped to address. Unlike conventional third-party service integrations, LLM integrations are bidirectional: sensitive user data flows into model endpoints as part of carefully constructed prompts, and model-generated text flows out into app logic, UI surfaces, notifications, and downstream APIs. Both directions introduce distinct risks, including data leakage, unsafe reuse of model outputs, and input-safety weaknesses, that have not been systematically studied at scale. We present Janus, a static analysis of end-to-end LLM interaction pipelines in Android apps. It recovers request construction semantics, identifies response-entry points and their downstream propagation, and employs a multi-agent reasoning layer to classify privacy- and security-relevant findings. We evaluate Janus on a curated micro-benchmark suite and use it to conduct the first systematic characterization of privacy and security risks in LLM-integrated Android apps. We find that such risks are prevalent in practice, with recurring categories such as client-side secret exposure (e.g., embedded API keys and system prompts), sensitive-data outsourcing to third-party LLM services without corresponding disclosure, secondary leakage of LLM responses to downstream components, and prompt/input-safety weaknesses such as prompt-injection-prone handling. We also present representative case studies that illustrate how these risks manifest in deployed apps and what concrete harm they may enable. In line with our ethical process, we responsibly disclosed critical findings to affected developers.

items.title: Jailbreaking via Activation Dilution: Neuron-Guided Adaptive Decomposition of Language Models
items.abstract: Aligned large language models (LLMs) often refuse harmful requests under direct prompting, motivating decomposition-based jailbreak attacks that split an unsafe task into multiple narrower sub-questions. Although such attacks can reduce refusal, existing methods typically rely on static or heuristic decomposition strategies and lack principled mechanisms for improving decomposition quality or selecting among decompositions of different granularities. In this work, we propose a unified decomposition-based jailbreak framework that combines reinforcement-learning-based policy improvement with neuron-guided adaptive selection. We first train a weak decomposer using online reward-based optimization, where generated sub-questions are evaluated by downstream refusal behavior and helpfulness. We then construct a neuron-based risk score based on internal activations of a strong model and use it at inference time to rank candidate decompositions and select the lowest-risk candidate for execution. The trained decomposer and reference-model scorer are reused across target models without target-specific training. Tested on multiple aligned strong models, the proposed pipeline consistently reduces refusal while maintaining helpfulness. Compared with representative automatic jailbreak baselines, it achieves stronger attack performance with substantially lower refusal exposure, which is particularly important in commercial API settings where repeated refusals may increase the risk of monitoring, throttling, or access restrictions. Our mechanistic analyses further suggest an activation dilution effect: when a harmful request is decomposed into separately executed sub-questions, safety-relevant signals are dispersed across queries, whereas recombining them into a single batched prompt partially restores risk. These results show that effective decomposition-based jailbreaks depend not only on whether a task is decomposed, but also on how the decomposition policy is learned and how decomposition granularity is controlled at inference time.

items.title: Intelligent visual perception beyond classification: a survey of deep learning and foundation models
items.abstract: Intelligent visual perception has advanced from traditional image classification to thorough comprehension of objects, scenes, relations, spatial context, and semantic information. This paper surveys the development of intelligent visual perception, particularly focusing on DL and foundation models. This section provides a comprehensive overview of visual recognition, detection, segmentation, and scene understanding, including key methods such as convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, attention mechanisms, encoder-decoder architectures, generative models, and Vision Transformers. The study also explores feature attribution, visual attention, visual reasoning, and multimodal vision-language models, which combine visual and text information for tasks such as visual question answering, captioning, and visual generation. This study examines recent foundation models incorporating vision-language architectures for their transferability, contextual understanding, and generalized perception capabilities. The study also discusses challenges related to computational efficiency, environmental variability, data requirements, robustness, explainability, and real-time deployment. Finally, it contrasts current developments to identify new approaches to scalable, interpretable, multimodal, and human-centric visual intelligence systems.
items.venue: Future Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence

items.title: High-Quality EEG-to-Image Reconstruction via Dual-Branch Feature Extraction and Cascaded Conditional Diffusion
items.abstract: Reconstructing visual stimuli from electroencephalography (EEG) signals holds significant value for uncovering the underlying mechanisms of the human visual system. However, due to the inherently low signal-to-noise ratio and limited spatiotemporal resolution of EEG, the current reconstruction methods face substantial challenges in achieving precise semantic alignment and high-fidelity image generation. Moreover, some prior EEG reconstruction approaches rely on additional large-scale EEG data for representation pretraining. To address these challenges, we propose MindScryer, a novel end-to-end framework for EEG-based image reconstruction. The proposed framework employs a dual-branch encoder. One branch incorporates a self-supervised transformer to extract temporal features, while the other utilizes a depthwise separable convolutional module to capture frequency-spatial representations. This architecture enhances the EEG signal representation across multiple dimensions. Next, an improved contrastive learning mechanism is introduced to align the EEG embeddings with CLIP embeddings derived from textual descriptions generated by a large language model. This approach highlights key visual semantics and mitigates cross-modal heterogeneity. Finally, a cascaded diffusion model integrates both fine-grained aligned EEG embeddings and coarse-grained categorical information to synthesize high-quality images with improved semantic consistency. Experimental results on the block-design visually-evoked (BDVE) dataset demonstrate that MindScryer significantly enhances the accuracy and visual clarity of EEG-based image reconstruction, while zero-shot evaluation on the external THINGS-EEG dataset confirms its strong cross-dataset generalizability and application potential. These capabilities further enable seamless integration of neural sensing into IoT-driven systems by providing high-level semantic visual representations. The source code associated with our work is available at: https://github.com/FLieWen/MindScryer.

items.title: Governing AI Agent with Capability and Delegation Chain
items.abstract: As LLM-based agents move from personal productivity assistants to enterprise workflow executors, security requirements shift from controlling model outputs to governing real-world decisions and tool invocations. Existing defenses improve robustness, but still struggle to enforce fine-grained, verifiable authority continuously across multi-hop delegation in autonomous workflows. We present CapAgent, an access-control and identity-delegation framework for AI agents that combines capability-constrained credentials with delegation-chain semantics. In CapAgent, authority is encoded as cryptographically protected, derivable credentials with explicit API/parameter constraints, lifecycle rules, and cross-hop provenance. CapAgent couples a protocol for issuance, derivation, verification, and auditing with a three-layer architecture, and we implement it as a layered SDK with CLI and MCP integration, together with a multi-agent governance prototype for intent compilation. Our evaluation includes symbolic verification, enforcement case studies of out-of-scope actions, public agent-security benchmarks (ASB and AgentDojo), and performance measurements of core operations. Results indicate that CapAgent achieves least-privilege multi-hop delegation with practical near-local overhead, supporting production-grade autonomous agent operations.

items.title: Global-View Reasoning with LLMs for Real-World Vulnerability Detection
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in code generation and other software engineering tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world security vulnerability detection still remains limited. A key observation is that while LLMs exhibit strong semantic understanding and security analysis capabilities on code snippets, these strengths are rarely extended to large-scale real-world programs. In this work, we propose SemScan, a novel vulnerability detection approach that harnesses LLMs' local reasoning capabilities to enable global security analysis. SemScan establishes an iterative loop of evidence collection and evidence-guided semantic synthesis. Our evaluation on a Python CVE vulnerability dataset and 200 popular real-world Python projects demonstrates that SemScan significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tools, uncovering 62 previously unknown serious vulnerabilities, including remote code execution and insecure deserialization flaws. To date, 22 of these vulnerabilities have been confirmed and assigned CVE identifiers.

items.title: GA-LLMSS: Text-Spatio–Temporal Graph-Guided and Cross-Modal Alignment-Enhanced Large Language Model Empowered Soft Sensor
items.abstract: Data-driven soft sensing has gained widespread application in modern industrial processes for real-time, low-cost estimation of key quality variables, but existing models are generally constrained by single-modal numerical inputs and limited representational generalization. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in time-series tasks due to their sequence-pattern generalization, textual reasoning, and cross-modal knowledge transfer abilities, yet their application in soft sensing remains limited.
