To bridge this gap, this article proposes a text-spatio–temporal graph-guided and cross-modal alignment-enhanced LLM-empowered two-stage soft sensor (GA-LLMSS). Specifically, a scale-adaptive spatio–temporal graph encoder (SASTGE) is developed, which reconstructs raw multivariate time series into dynamic spatio–temporal interaction graphs (STIGs) according to the nonstationary characteristics, injecting structured prior logic to compensate for LLMs’ inherent deficiency in intervariable spatial perception. Building on this, a prompt-enhanced graph construction (PEGC) module enriches input semantics by crafting industrial prior knowledge prompts (IPKPs) with higher-order statistics, while an anchor token then serves as a cross-modal hub to establish logic-guided edges between prompts and graph nodes that explicitly guide LLMs in capturing cross-modal logical relationships and maintaining semantic coherence. To bridge textual and time-series modalities, an improved representation learning, dropout autoregressive alignment stage (DAAS), is proposed to enforce learning of deep spatio–temporal couplings from incomplete observations. Finally, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts the model to real-world industrial scenarios: air preheaters (APs) and gas turbines (GTs). Experiments show that GA-LLMSS achieves advanced accuracy, superior few-shot representation generalization, and ablation studies validate the independent contributions of each key module.

items.title: From Implicit Defaults to Deliberate Decisions: Privacy Design for Vibe-Coded Applications
items.abstract: AI coding agents enable people without software engineering training to create and deploy applications serving real users. In translating high-level functional requests into working software, however, AI agents often implicitly decide what data to collect, how long to retain it, where to process it, and with whom to share it. These choices often involve contextual tradeoffs among privacy, functionality, usability, and competing stakeholder interests. Yet, developers may neither recognize that these decisions have been made nor understand their consequences and alternatives. This dissertation investigates how to help non-expert developers to understand and make informed decisions about privacy in vibe-coded applications. I postulate that a structured privacy representation can serve as an interface between human and AI agents by exposing implicit choices, explaining consequential tradeoffs, and connecting human decisions to implementation behavior. Specifically, this work will (1) characterize gaps among developers' intentions, their understanding of applications, and applications' actual data practices; (2) recover and communicate the privacy design decisions embodied in generated applications; and (3) develop approaches that selectively elicit human input and help developers consider alternatives. Together, these efforts seek to transform privacy in AI coding from an implicit consequence of code generation into a deliberate design process.

items.title: Designing an Automated Fact-Checking Pipeline for Recent Claims
items.abstract: To address the scale and spread of digital misinformation, researchers have developed automated techniques to aid in the fact-checking process. Unfortunately, these systems are rarely designed for real-world deployment settings and struggle with the unique challenges of realistic verification: claims may lack ground truth, evidence is sparse and evolving, and decisions must be made within hours. In this paper, we present and evaluate a new system for automated fact-checking, RealTiCheck, that integrates large language models (LLMs) with web search to gather, collate, and employ online evidence to fact-check recent potential misinformation claims. We evaluate RealTiCheck on state-of-the-art benchmark datasets, with our system outperforming comparable prior work (Macro-F1 score of 0.81). We then explore how RealTiCheck can be used in practice by hiring seven professional fact-checkers to fact-check 174 novel and recent (less than 24 hours old) claims. We evaluate how well our system triages and adjudicates claims compared to professional fact-checkers' verdicts. We conclude by discussing design recommendations for future real-time fact-checking systems.

items.title: DeepProve: Verifiable End-to-End Large Language Model Inference
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are frontier deep learning systems that have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of AI services. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements make them difficult to deploy and run on local hardware. Due to these resource requirements, users often rely on untrusted cloud infrastructure providers to perform model inference. However, outsourcing introduces the challenge of verifying that the returned output is the genuine result of the specified model. In this work, we present DeepProve, the first system to enable efficient end-to-end verification of full LLM inference (i.e., for all generated tokens of a prompt) on untrusted cloud servers using zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs). In contrast, prior work either provides only a proof-of-concept partial implementation for a single token (zkGPT, USENIX '25), or focuses exclusively on specific components of the inference pipeline, such as Softmax (zkLLM, CCS '24). DeepProve achieves end-to-end verification by certifying the correctness of the output sequence rather than encoding the expensive inference computation in-circuit, an approach that would require either circuit size quadratic in the sequence length or costly in-circuit modelling of RAM operations. The core building blocks of DeepProve are sum-check protocol and lookup arguments, which enable efficient proof of correctness of all operators needed for GPT-2 and Gemma 3, such as multi-head attention and layer normalization for GPT-2, and grouped-query attention, root mean square normalization, and rotary positional embeddings for Gemma 3. Our evaluation shows that DeepProve can prove inference of GPT-2 and Gemma 3 at approximately 174 and 86 tokens per minute, respectively, which is 20-60× faster than the state-of-the-art, without any significant loss in accuracy. Verification takes only 1 to 3.7 seconds. By distributing proof computation across multiple nodes, DeepProve can further improve the prover time while reducing the memory requirements for individual machines. With distributed proving, DeepProve can scale the throughput to 1855 tokens per minute. Our work represents the first full system for end-to-end LLM inference verification, thus paving the way for secure and trustworthy AI services.

items.title: DRIP: Defending Prompt Injection via Token-wise Representation Editing and Residual Fusion
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming core components of IT infrastructure, tasked with processing user data according to predefined instructions. However, LLMs remain vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where malicious users inject directive tokens within the data to manipulate model behavior. The current defense strategies attempt to train LLMs to semantically distinguish between data and instruction tokens. Nevertheless, these approaches still face two key challenges: (1) the balance between security and utility, especially when interpreting the instruction-like tokens in the data section, and (2) the robustness against adaptive adversarial samples. In this work, we propose DRIP which aims to (1) achieve a new security-utility balance by ''de-instructionalization'', i.e., precisely removing the instruction semantics from the tokens in the data section while preserving their data semantics and (2) robustly maintain the effectiveness of the intended instruction, even against strong adversarial content. As for ''de-instructionalize'' tokens in the data section, we propose a training paradigm across data curation, model architecture, and loss design. It introduces a lightweight representation-editing module, which is trained to edit the embedding of instruction-like tokens in the data section, enhancing the model's security without compromising utility. As for preserving the intended instruction against unseen adversarial content, we improve the model architecture by introducing a lightweight residual module in LLM, largely reducing the overwriting possibility of adversarial content. We extensively compare DRIP with state-of-the-art techniques, including StruQ, SecAlign, ISE, and PFT on LLaMA-8B and Mistral-7B across three prompt injection benchmarks (SEP, AlpacaFarm, and InjecAgent). The results show that DRIP (1) improves role separation score by 44–64% and reduces attack success rate by over 68% for adaptive attacks and (2) achieves utility on par with the undefended model, indicating a new state-of-the-art against prompt injection attacks.

items.title: DEMO: SemCRS: Streamlining Vulnerability Discovery and Patching with LLMs
items.abstract: Finding software vulnerabilities and fixing them without human intervention is a long-standing goal of security research. We present SemCRS, an autonomous Semantics-guided Cyber Reasoning System that, given a program, its fuzzing harness, and a set of target sanitizer classes, discovers a vulnerable function, generates a proof-ofvulnerability (PoV) input, validates it against a runtime sanitizer, and generates a patch that blocks the validated PoV while the program's available functional tests continue to pass. SemCRS pairs large language model (LLM) reasoning with lightweight program analysis and closes the loop: every candidate PoV is executed under the real sanitizer before anything is reported, turning imprecise LLM judgments into verifiable results. The pipeline runs from one command, yet every stage remains inspectable. We demonstrate SemCRS on a compact program and report four runs on programs of up to 6,172 functions. Our artifact including source code and a video walkthrough is at https://github.com/SRestLabUB/SemCRS.

items.title: ContractGuard: Auditing Semantic Contracts of MCP Tools for Security Violations
items.abstract: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is rapidly emerging as a standard interface for connecting large language model (LLM) applications to external tools. An MCP tool exposes two semantic views of the same functionality: a developer-provided description that guides the LLM's tool selection, and an implementation that determines the actual runtime behavior. Security issues arise when these two views diverge, leading to instruction injection, misleading descriptions, malicious code, or unsafe implementations. Existing defenses analyze descriptions or implementations largely in isolation and thus fail to address this broader threat space in a unified manner. We present ContractGuard, the first security-oriented framework for bidirectional semantic contract auditing of MCP tools. Our observation is that diverse MCP threats can be unified as violations of a semantic contract between a tool's description and its implementation. ContractGuard combines reachability-aware static analysis with LLM-based cross-view reasoning for auditing. It extracts a tool-specific code slice, generates a code-grounded description, compares it against the developer-provided one, and validates and classifies detected inconsistencies. We evaluate our method on 3,586 MCP tools from 1,000 real-world MCP servers and 5,661 benchmark cases. Our tool uncovers 116 security issues in the wild, including 21 misleading descriptions, 29 instances of potentially malicious code, and 66 unsafe implementations. It achieves a 96.0% true positive rate on malicious-code benchmarks and more than a 92.8% true positive rate on description-attack benchmarks. Results show that contract auditing can effectively identify security-relevant description--implementation mismatches in MCP tools.

items.title: Code-SeC: A Decoding-time Probing Method for Characterizing Secret Memorization in Code LLM
items.abstract: Code Large Language Models (Code LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in code generation and completion. While these models are known to memorize portions of their training data, existing approaches to evaluate credential memorization rely on output-level inspection or adversarial prompt crafting, leaving the internal decoding behaviors that underlie secret leakage unexplored. In this paper, we conduct a token-level investigation of hard-coded credential memorization in Code LLMs during routine code completion. We report two findings: (1) traces of memorized secrets persist in the token candidate space, indicating that standard output-level evaluation underestimates the true extent of memorization; (2) the generation of real secrets exhibits statistically distinct uncertainty dynamics compared to hallucinated strings, providing a reliable intrinsic signal for memorization detection. Based on these findings, we propose Code-SeC (Code Secret Characterization), a decoding-time diagnostic framework that monitors uncertainty signals along the decoding trajectory and performs targeted distribution adjustments to uncover latent credential memorization. Experimental results show that Code-SeC effectively detects memorized code secrets across representative Code LLMs and secret types, providing comprehensive empirical evidence that hard-coded credential memorization is prevalent in current code completion models.

items.title: Client-side brute force attack detection leveraging large language models
items.abstract: For email authentication systems, the last mile of authentication poses a critical security challenge, as attackers leverage known, real logins to bypass established server-side protections against brute-force attacks and credential stuffing. Traditional methods like rate limiting and threshold anomaly detection are ineffective against distributed, stealthy attacks that mimic normal user activity. This paper proposes a novel framework for detecting authentication sequences on the client side by leveraging lightweight Large Language Models (LLMs) in real time. Unlike signature-based approaches, the proposed framework can "explain" the temporal and contextual characteristics of login behavior and detect anomalous sequences, such as high-frequency bursts and low-and-slow last-mile reassembly attacks, without the need for predefined signatures or centralized log aggregation. The framework was tested with 2.5 million authentication sessions, 1 million of which were marked as attacks, and achieved 98.4% attack-detection accuracy with a false-positive rate of 1.2%. With an average response time of 180 ms, it achieves near real-time inference without impacting the user experience. The system was live-deployed for six months and succeeded in blocking more than 1.2 million malicious logon attempts and safeguarding more than 850,000 user accounts against traditional baselines in both scale and precision. The results demonstrate the promise of lightweight, client-side LLMs as a privacy-safe, low-resource, and robust solution for last-mile email authentication security against current and future brute force attack vectors.

items.title: CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models
items.abstract: Discovering new censorship evasion strategies remains a predominantly slow and manual process. Prior systems that automate evasion discovery are restricted to packet headers and unencrypted protocols by the limited expressiveness of their domain-specific grammars, leaving more complex and widely-used encrypted protocols like TLS and QUIC out of reach. To address this, we present CircumVolve, a system that formulates censorship evasion as LLM-guided program synthesis within an evolutionary optimization loop. Candidate evasion strategies are expressed as executable Python programs that can encode arbitrary protocol manipulations, including cryptographic operations, and are iteratively refined by an LLM that proposes semantically informed mutations based on empirical feedback. This programmatic representation enables automated discovery of evasion strategies across the full network stack. We evaluate CircumVolve on five major network protocols subject to censorship (TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, TLS, and QUIC) in both simulated and real-world environments. Against real-world censors in China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, the system successfully identifies effective evasion techniques spanning all protocol layers, from variants of previously known methods to entirely novel strategies.

items.title: CVE-Genie: An LLM-Based Multi-Agent Framework for Reproducing CVEs
items.abstract: High-quality datasets of real-world vulnerabilities and their corresponding verifiable exploits are crucial resources in software security research. Yet such resources remain scarce, as their creation demands intensive manual effort and deep security expertise. In this paper, we present CVE-Genie, an automated, large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent framework designed to reproduce real-world vulnerabilities, provided in Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) format, to enable creation of high-quality vulnerability datasets. Given a CVE entry as input, CVE-Genie gathers the relevant resources of the CVE, automatically reconstructs the vulnerable environment, and (re)produces a verifiable exploit. Our systematic evaluation highlights the efficiency and robustness of CVE-Genie's design and successfully reproduces approximately 51% (428 of 841) CVEs published in 2024-2025, complete with their verifiable exploits, at an average cost of $2.77 per CVE. Our pipeline offers a robust method to generate reproducible CVE benchmarks, valuable for diverse applications such as fuzzer evaluation, vulnerability patching, and assessing AI's security capabilities.

items.title: Brain Cognition-Inspired Adaptable LLM Agents for Continuous Knowledge Reuse Across Tasks in IoT
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are promising in Internet of Things (IoT) applications. However, existing agent systems suffer from an ephemeral limitation: agents are instantiated for individual tasks and terminated upon completion, losing valuable execution experiences across different tasks where past knowledge reuse is impossible. Inspired by dual-process theory in cognitive science, we propose a brain cognition-inspired dual-system agent framework for continuous knowledge reuse across heterogeneous task streams, termed the cognition-inspired dual-system agent framework for continuous knowledge reuse (CIA-CKR). The CIA-CKR framework separates fast (reactive execution) from slow (deliberative planning) cognition phases by maintaining a persistent knowledge base throughout the operational lifetime of agents. Two synergistic mechanisms are designed that mirror bidirectional knowledge flow in human cognition: a personalized agent generation mechanism that retrieves task-relevant knowledge and configures context-specific agent capabilities through top-down adaptation, and a knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts experiential insights from execution traces through bottom-up feedback. Extensive experiments on HomeBench (smart home control) and OmniEAR (embodied multiagent collaboration) datasets demonstrate that CIA-CKR consistently outperforms both vanilla LLMs and recent memory-augmented methods, achieving 10.82% and 4.23% average accuracy improvements on HomeBench and OmniEAR, respectively, over the best baselines.

items.title: Automatically Learning Vulnerability Patterns for Scalable Static Analysis of Web Applications
items.abstract: Static analysis has been widely used to analyze web applications, yet its effectiveness largely relies on the quality of vulnerability patterns. In this work, we present MoCQ, which leverages large language models (LLMs) to automatically generate executable detection queries that capture these vulnerability patterns. To address challenges like LLM hallucinations and the complexity of industrial static analysis tools, MoCQ introduces a DSL-based harness. This harness extracts and models a core subset of domain-specific languages (DSLs) to provide the formal structure and guidance needed to generate valid queries. MoCQ employs an iterative refinement loop with trace-driven symbolic validation that provides precise feedback for query correction and optimization. Such a neuro-symbolic approach thus combines the scalability of pattern-based static analysis with the semantic understanding and automation capabilities of LLMs. We evaluated MoCQ on multiple vulnerability types across web programming languages, including Java, PHP, and JavaScript. MoCQ achieves detection performance comparable to expert-developed patterns while requiring only hours of query generation versus weeks of manual effort. Notably, MoCQ uncovered 45 new vulnerability patterns that security experts had missed and discovered 25 previously unknown vulnerabilities in real-world applications. MoCQ also outperforms prior approaches with stronger analysis capabilities.

items.title: Attest the Whole, Verify Incrementally: Whole-Program Integrity via Lazy Verification in Trusted Execution Environments
items.abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) traditionally employ a ''measure-then-launch'' model, attesting all code and data before execution begins. While this provides strong integrity guarantees, it imposes a startup latency proportional to the total program size, which is a significant bottleneck for large-scale applications like Large Language Models (LLMs) or databases that may only access a fraction of their footprint. We propose a lazy-verification architecture that decouples holistic attestation from per-block verification. At launch, the design performs an attestation of compact metadata representing the entire program state. Integrity is enforced through incremental verification of requested code and data blocks during runtime loading, before their first architecturally visible use. We formally model enclave execution under lazy verification and prove that our design preserves the same security properties and accepted execution traces as conventional whole-program attestation. We implement our design on both Intel SGX and AMD SEV-SNP. Evaluation across network services, database workloads, and LLM inference shows that our approach significantly reduces startup overhead and improves end-to-end performance, particularly for data-intensive applications with sparse access patterns.

items.title: Aqua Llama: Enhancing Operational Technology System Reliability Through Semantic-Aware Early Threat Detection
items.abstract: Maintaining the reliability and availability of operational technology (OT) systems is critical, as anomalous behaviors (protocol violations, abnormal command patterns, and timing deviations) can propagate into safety hazards, equipment damage, or unplanned shutdowns. From a reliability engineering perspective, this study proposes a semantics-first, edge-deployable anomaly detection framework that significantly enhances OT operational safety and failure prevention capabilities. The framework addresses OT-specific constraints (heterogeneous protocols, limited labeled data, strict auditability, and resource-constrained hardware) through three synergistic components: 1) traffic compression into concise, human-readable tokens capturing operational semantics; 2) domain knowledge encoded as editable plain-language rules enabling rapid site-specific adaptation; and 3) a four-step large language model (LLM) reasoning chain that remains short and auditable on CPU-only edges. Using an open-weight, LoRA-adapted 7B LLM without cloud dependencies, Aqua Llama separates a real-time symbolic alert path (CPS-Stream tokenization and natural semantic protocol analysis (NSPA) rule evaluation, operating at millisecond-level latency) from an LLM-assisted explanation path driven by the summarisation-aided logic chain (SALC), whose prompt-construction, prefill, and decoding costs are reported explicitly rather than folded into a single end-to-end figure. Validation across secure water treatment, Modbus, and ToN-IoT datasets yields a macro $F1$ of 0.928, with the strongest gains on subtle multicue anomalies that traditional threshold-based methods miss. Longitudinal evaluation shows an early detection rate (EDR) of 98.5% and a trace-based preventive action effectiveness (PAE) of 91.9%, while the auditable reasoning chain provides operators with traceable explanations, reducing diagnostic time and supporting risk-informed decisions essential for safety-critical OT reliability management.

items.title: AISec '26: 19th Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security
items.abstract: Applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and data mining to security and privacy problems are ubiquitous. The analytic tools and intelligent behavior provided by AI/ML models is now pivotal for autonomous real-time analysis and decision-making in domains with a wealth of data or that require quick reactions to constantly changing situations. The use of learning-based methods in security-sensitive domains, in which adversaries may attempt to mislead or evade intelligent machines, creates new frontiers for security research. The acknowledged widespread adoption of deep learning techniques, such as Large-Language Models (LLM), whose security properties are difficult to reason about directly, has only added to the importance of this research. At the same time, and unfortunately, application and deployment of AI/ML techniques often leads to privacy-related issues, such as the possibility to extract sensitive data from trained models, as well as training on sensitive or confidential data. The AISec workshop provides a venue for presenting and discussing new developments in the intersection of security and privacy with AI and ML.

items.title: AI Agentic Security: Safeguarding the Next Generation of Autonomous Systems
items.abstract: The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI)—systems capable of autonomous decision-making, goal-directed action, and interaction with complex digital and physical environments—represents a fundamental shift in AI. Securing these systems requires moving beyond the protection of individual models to the protection of continuously operating, tool-using entities that can act on their environments, collaborate with other agents, and adapt over time. These capabilities substantially expand the attack surface and introduce risks such as prompt and goal injection, memory poisoning, tool misuse, privilege compromise, manipulation of inter-agent communication, rogue-agent behavior, and software supply-chain attacks. This talk examines these emerging threats with reference to the OWASP Agentic AI threat model and considers how established security principles, including least privilege, defense in depth, complete mediation, and psychological acceptability, must be reinterpreted for agentic systems. Using the AgentSandbox architecture [1] as a case study, the talk illustrates how security-by-design can be incorporated through ephemeral task-specific agents, context minimization, granular privilege management, and policy-driven control of internal and external interactions. It concludes by identifying key research challenges, including formal guarantees for agent behavior, scalable assurance mechanisms, secure multi-agent ecosystems, and trust frameworks for agent identity, accountability, and governance. Addressing these challenges is essential if agentic AI is to evolve into a trustworthy foundation for autonomous systems at scale.

items.title: AGENT-SEC '26: 1st Workshop on Security, Privacy, and Safety of Agentic AI Systems
items.abstract: Agentic systems extend artificial intelligence (AI) models, including large language models and other foundation models, with capabilities such as planning, tool use, persistent memory, external API access, code execution, and collaboration with other agents. These capabilities enable increasingly autonomous operation, but they also create security, privacy, and safety risks that are not adequately captured by model-level analysis alone. The 1st Workshop on Security, Privacy, and Safety of Agentic AI Systems (AGENT-SEC 2026), held in conjunction with the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '26), provides a forum for researchers and practitioners to explore and investigate these system-level risks and the corresponding defenses, evaluation methods, and governance mechanisms. The workshop covers attacks on agentic workflows, privacy risks arising from tools and memory, safety and alignment of autonomous agents, secure distributed and federated agents, governance and accountability, real-world applications, and security assurance and benchmarking.

items.title: A High-Robustness Surrogate Modeling Method for On-Chip Microwave Passive Components in Chiplet-Based IoT Integrated Microsystem
items.abstract: In this article, a novel surrogate modeling method applied to 3-D on-chip microwave passive devices for Internet of Things (IoT) applications, which is based on barycentric form transfer functions combined with artificial neural networks (ANNs), is proposed. Among them, this work presents a transfer function parameter extraction algorithm named the set support point adaptive Antoulas–Anderson (SSP-AAA) algorithm, which avoids the problem of ill-conditioned matrices by optimizing the sequence of support points using a dual criterion based on error and condition number. At the same time, the dimension of the training data was reduced through the set-value strategy. During the model training process, the EM behavior was initially approximated into a transfer function representation through the SSP-AAA algorithm, followed by employing the ANN to establish the mapping relationship between geometric variations and transfer function coefficients. Compared with surrogate modeling based on vector fitting, this method effectively improves the stability of parameter extraction by imposing constraints on the condition number of the Loewner matrix. The test results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves training errors of 2.86%, 1.49%, and 2.98% and test errors of 3.54%, 2.06%, and 3.36% on three different microwave components, respectively, while maintaining stable coefficient extraction even under wide geometric sampling ranges.

items.title: TTTR: Record, Replay, and Steer AI (Extended Abstract)
items.abstract: AI agent behaviors are difficult to reproduce because nondeterminism enters at multiple layers of the AI software stack, from tensor computation and token sampling to the external environment. TTTR is a record-replay framework that captures these sources and enables selective replay, allowing one layer to vary while others remain fixed. This supports cross-layer fault localization, counterfactual analysis, and reproducible evaluation of agent behavior.
items.venue: Proceedings of the Symposium on Rigorous LLM Systems

items.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
items.abstract: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must quickly decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

items.title: SoK: The Security-Safety Continuum of Multimodal Foundation Models
items.abstract: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) integrate diverse data modalities to support complex and wide-ranging tasks. However, this integration also introduces distinct safety and security challenges. In this paper, we unify the concepts of safety and security in the context of MFMs by identifying critical threats that arise from both model behavior and system-level interactions. We propose a taxonomy grounded in information theory, evaluating risks through the concepts of channel capacity, signal, noise, and bandwidth. This perspective provides a principled way to analyze how information flows through MFMs and how vulnerabilities can emerge across modalities. Building on this foundation, we introduce a deterministic minimax formulation to analyze defense mechanisms and to study a structural asymmetry of defense in multimodal systems. Our analysis indicates that model-centric defenses, which primarily operate by suppressing noise or enhancing signal, tend to exhibit diminishing effectiveness against increasingly adaptive attacks. In contrast, system-level safeguards that constrain authorized information flow and agent behavior impose stronger limits on adversarial impact by reducing effective bandwidth. To operationalize this insight, our framework maps attacks and defenses onto information-theoretic axes, effectively organizing and reducing the defense search space. Using a proposed Defense Coverage Index (DCI) to evaluate 15 representative defenses, we observe that system-level bandwidth constraints provide stronger and more consistent protection across attack classes than brittle model-level mechanisms.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd ACM Workshop on Large AI Systems and Models with Privacy and Safety Analysis

items.title: RobPiCFM: A Training-Free Target-Conditioned Method with Foundation Models for Robotic Picking in Clutter
items.abstract: Picking objects from clutter remains a challenging problem in robotic manipulation, as it requires connecting object-level perception, grasp generation, collision-aware selection, and robot motion execution in unstructured scenes. In this paper, we present RobPiCFM, an open-source, trainingfree method for target-conditioned picking in cluttered scenes. The proposed method combines pretrained foundation-modelbased perception with RGB-D geometry, 6D object pose estimation and tracking, grasp candidate generation, constraintbased grasp filtering, and motion planning. Unlike end-toend manipulation policies, the method does not require taskspecific policy learning and relies instead on pretrained visual models and explicit robot execution constraints. We evaluate the method on a real robotic setup in a cluttered tabletop scenario using objects with different shapes and grasping properties. The ablation study shows that the proposed grasp filtering mechanism increases the normalized task score from 16.7 to 53.1, while target pre-segmentation further improves the score to 60.6. https://github.com/Dorian-BAUDU/RobPiCFM.git

items.title: PromptLeaks: Assessing Data Leakage in Guardrails and Automated Jailbreak Tools
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous, and with their adoption comes a range of ethical and security risks that has made alignment, and resistance to jailbreaking, a central concern. Guardrails are a widely adopted defense against such jailbreaks, yet their reported effectiveness is only as reliable as the data on which they are evaluated. This paper identifies a largely unexamined source of inflated performance: data leakage between the datasets used to seed offensive jailbreak frameworks and those used to train defensive guardrails. As both are derived from human-authored jailbreak prompt corpora, a guardrail may be evaluated on instances present in its own training data, in which case high detection rates reflect memorization rather than a generalized alignment policy. We quantify this contamination, which we term PromptLeaks, using a deterministic syntactic comparison of prompt datasets adapted from bioinformatics. Across three open-source red-teaming frameworks and five open-source guardrail datasets we observe severe leakage, with one test-prompt dataset almost entirely contained within the guardrail training corpora. Guardrail jailbreak detection rate diminishes on prompts that do not overlap the training corpus, indicating that current guardrails rely substantially on memorization rather than on generalizing an alignment policy.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

items.title: Private LLM Inference: Optimizing Tricycle
items.abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models (LLM) in scenarios with sensitive data requires the use of privacy-preserving technologies to guarantee confidentiality. Private LLM inference using Fully-Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) guarantees data privacy by encrypting the input beforehand and performing inference directly over the encrypted data. LLM inference is known to require substantial computational resources, and the use of FHE introduces additional memory and runtime overhead beyond these already demanding requirements. To optimize the number of computations performed on encrypted data, different strategies have been proposed. We adopt tricyclic encodings, which support matrix arithmetic with optimal multiplicative depth and minimal key-switching (one of the most costly operations in FHE). We propose a system that combines this strategy with SHIP, a bootstrapping algorithm that minimizes level consumption and features a large degree of parallelism in the computations. This combination avoids the slots-to-coefficients conversion required by traditional bootstrapping methods, while still keeping the result in the slots domain, making it directly compatible with our encoding strategy. In addition, we leverage an optimization from the Batched Relinearization (BRL) technique that improves accuracy and latency by multiplying several ciphertexts in groups of two or three.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd ACM Workshop on Large AI Systems and Models with Privacy and Safety Analysis

items.title: PkgScanArena: Benchmarking LLM-Based Package Scanners against Indirect Prompt Injection
items.abstract: Open-source package ecosystems such as PyPI and npm remain persistent targets for malicious campaigns. These campaigns have outgrown signature-based triage, so recent work has turned to large language models (LLMs) that scan package content and return a verdict, which lets the analysis consume attacker-controlled text. In 2026, the Hades campaign on PyPI carried a prompt injection written to hijack the scanner’s instructions and coerce a clean verdict. Indirect prompt injection is well studied, but its reach into automated package-security analysis remains unmeasured. We therefore ask a broader question. How reliable are LLM-based package scanners when the package itself is written to manipulate the analysis? We present PkgScanArena, a benchmark that pairs a vetted dataset of 2,000 malicious and 1,000 benign npm and PyPI packages with a taxonomy of 11 techniques and 3 injection channels across three attacker goals, namely evasion, denial, and sabotage. An AST-guided pipeline injects these prompts into real packages, and we evaluate 25 open-weight and proprietary model configurations together with two deployed scanners. Our benchmark inverts the expected threat. Evasion proves largely unattainable, at or below 0.6% for nine of ten cloud models. Exposure instead shifts to the opposite direction: benign accuracy degrades for all but two of the 25 backends, sabotage reaches 31.1%, and denial reaches 19.6% on the most safety-aligned model. The two deployed scanners inherit both weaknesses. The exposure lies not in coercing a scanner to miss malicious code, but in coercing it to condemn benign code.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

items.title: Multidimensional Evaluation of LLM-Generated MPC Programs
items.abstract: Large language models can generate programs that compile and pass functional tests, but these outcomes are insufficient for evaluating code in secure multi-party computation (MPC). MPC programs must also follow the target interface's programming constraints, implement the requested algorithm, and satisfy the stated secure-operation efficiency criteria. Using NLMPC, a staged code-generation framework, we conduct an empirical study of 3,600 C++ programs generated by three LLMs for three algorithms under four generation settings that vary API instructions, explicit programming constraints, and iterative repair. We evaluate each program along four dimensions: functional correctness, MPC conformance, algorithmic adherence, and MPC efficiency. Although 59.2% of the generated programs passed the functional correctness tests, only 31.0% satisfied all four criteria. Functional testing alone did not establish conformance, adherence to the requested algorithm, or compliance with the stated efficiency criteria. Adding MPC-specific constraints revealed trade-offs: aggregate functional correctness and MPC conformance increased, while algorithmic adherence decreased. Validation-guided repair had a higher observed overall pass rate than single-pass generation, but this improvement was not statistically significant after correction. Its recorded token use, including LLM-validator calls, was 1.77×-3.19× that of single-pass generation. These findings show that passing functional tests does not establish the overall quality of LLM-generated MPC code, and that additional constraints and repair do not necessarily improve all evaluation dimensions. They motivate separate checks for functional behavior, MPC programming constraints, algorithmic invariants, and source-level efficiency, rather than relying on compilation or functional testing alone.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 25th Workshop on Privacy in the Electronic Society

items.title: LEASH: Zero-Trust Containment for AI Agent Swarms
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly spawn sub-agent swarms that carry derived credentials to APIs, databases, and production infrastructure. When an operator kills a misbehaving orchestrator, its descendants keep exercising valid credentials for minutes to hours, since every deployed revocation mechanism needs network connectivity to a central authority, unavailable precisely when the network is degraded or adversarial. This paper presents LEASH - Liveness-Enforced Authorization for Swarm Hierarchies, which applies the zero-trust principle of continuous verification to a delegation hierarchy without a reachable authority. A parent emits a signed, epoch-indexed liveness beacon every Δh seconds, where Δh is the beacon interval, and each child staples a fresh beacon into every authentication proof, and the enforcement point checks freshness using only cached public keys and a local clock. Revocation happens by omission: when beacons stop, all descendants fail closed within a bounded zombie window Wz ≤ Wmax + Δh + ϵ , where Wmax is the maximum beacon age and ϵ is the clock skew. Immediate-parent verification at O(1) and full-chain verification at O(d), where d is the hierarchy depth, extend this bound against compromised intermediates. We evaluate LEASH with real GPT-4o-mini agent swarms: 0.71% tool-call overhead, cascading revocation across a 49-agent four-level hierarchy within bound, and 295 × less credential-theft exposure versus OAuth 2.0. Under prompt injection that bypasses application-layer guardrails, LEASH denies every post-revocation tool call, since enforcement sits below the LLM.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

items.title: High-Entropy String Hallucinations in LLM Inference: Quantization Sensitivity and Source-Constrained Decoding
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly generate exact operational identifiers such as URLs, UUIDs, and object keys. A single character mutation can invalidate an otherwise correct answer. We identify High-Entropy String Hallucination (HESH), a source-grounded realization failure in which an identifier is absent from the supplied source. Across 5,000 test cases and 12,500 identifier slots, localized HESH increases from 4 slots under Q8_0 to 52 under Q4_K_M and 305 under Q3_K_M. The same aggregate pattern appears on RTX4090 and A100. We then introduce Source-Constrained Identifier Decoding (SCID). It derives valid identifiers from the input and constrains only exact-value spans. In our SCID evaluation, identifier exactness and source membership both reach 100%. Semantic correctness remains 97.9%. The result shows that exact identifier realization can be protected without replacing semantic source selection.
items.venue: Proceedings of the Symposium on Rigorous LLM Systems

items.title: Emergence-Driven Security of LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are no longer limited to text generators, but they can also plan, call tools, delegate tasks to other agents, act within external environments, and change states in response to their actions. In Anthropic’s recent report on an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign involving Claude Code, individual subtasks appeared legitimate when evaluated in isolation but became malicious when combined into an autonomous attack sequence. Consequently, the security of such complex LLM-based agentic systems may fail even when each component appears secure in isolation. This position and open-problem paper argues that LLM agent security should be studied as emergence-driven security: the analysis of security properties that arise from the interactions among agents and its components over time. We define emergence-driven security and provide a conceptual taxonomy to classify emergent security-related phenomena in LLM agents, covering both beneficial and harmful forms of emergence. Based on these insights, we propose EASE, an Emergence-Aware Security Evaluation framework that provides a systematic process for assessing how interactions among agents combine over time to produce harmful or beneficial system-level security outcomes. Finally, we conclude by outlining open problems for studying emergent behavior in LLM agents in the context of security. The paper is intended to provide a foundation for examining how the emerging capabilities and operational needs of LLM agents may shape security evaluations that go beyond static, model-level testing.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

items.title: ESPEON: Verifying the Predestined Execution of Deterministic LLM Inference
items.abstract: Today, platforms of Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) provides access to various foundation models to users. Users trust that the platform indeed provides the exact service as requested. However, this trust may be misplaced for benign or malicious intentions, where results from providers are not exactly the same as what the user requested. To detect such violations, this paper introduces Espeon, a large language model (LLM) inference verification framework. It enables reproducible deterministic inference through batch-invariant kernels and includes different verification variants for flexible computation and storage budgets of verification. We evaluated Espeon with single-point manipulation cases and Espeon's performance of serving and verification. Espeon can detect such cases, and under the full verification mode it can achieve a speed-up of 4.56X compared to serving time.
items.venue: Proceedings of the Symposium on Rigorous LLM Systems

items.title: Did You Hear That? Detecting AI Voice Agents by Exploiting Their Robustness
items.abstract: AI voice agents enable scalable vishing and impersonation attacks, yet existing detection methods face practical limitations. Artifact-based detectors degrade as synthesis quality improves, challenge–response tests are socially awkward, and adversarial jamming must often be loud or continuous to disrupt modern automatic speech recognition (ASR). We introduce HEARD, a detection framework built on a new principle: instead of perturbing the AI while remaining imperceptible to humans, HEARD applies brief, conspicuous distortions that humans notice but robust ASR systems largely ignore. A human caller is likely to comment on the disturbance, misunderstand the utterance, or request repetition, whereas an AI agent continues coherently from the recovered transcription. We map fifteen audible distortions into three families and evaluate them across six ASR models spanning multiple architectures and five years of development, as well as an experiment involving 41 human volunteers. Using semantic similarity and an LLM-based conversational-legibility metric, we find that across 2,421 LibriSpeech and TED-LIUM utterances, modern ASRs preserve a mean legibility of 97.8%, while the best distortion keeps every model at or above 98.3%. Moreover, performance improves with model recency, making stronger ASR systems easier, not harder, to distinguish from humans.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Workshop on Deepfake, Deception, and Disinformation Security

items.title: Delta-Weight Quantization Preserves Alignment in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Multi-tenant LLM services can reduce serving costs by sharing a full-precision base model and storing compressed fine-tuning updates. Uploaded fine-tuning data can weaken alignment or implant harmful and targeted backdoors, but prior security studies quantize entire checkpoints. We evaluate BitDelta after full-parameter fine-tuning on four open-source models under static attacks, measuring factual utility separately. One-bit delta compression reduces malicious behavior in many tests relative to the full-precision attacked checkpoint. On Llama-2-7b-chat, mean harmfulness Score changes from 3.34 to 1.13 under red teaming and from 2.87 to 1.02 in a harmful-backdoor setting. In a targeted-backdoor setting, triggered ASR falls from 95% to 9%, while untriggered target insertion falls from 54% to 11%. By comparison, full-model GPTQ and int8 leave attack behavior close to the full-precision attacked checkpoint. Across 12 fine-tuning conditions, TriviaQA accuracy decreases by 5.35% on average, with substantial cross-model variation. A preliminary LogitLens analysis links the recovered safety behavior to refusal-token predictions in deeper layers. These findings apply to the tested models and BitDelta configurations; the comparison does not independently separate compression location from compression severity.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd ACM Workshop on Large AI Systems and Models with Privacy and Safety Analysis

items.title: Classification in the Dark: Performance Insights and Novel Methods for Homomorphic Binary Networks
items.abstract: Almost ten years after the publication of CryptoNets, the field of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning based on Homomorphic Encryption (HE) has advanced considerably. While the trend moves towards deeper networks and even Large Language Models (LLMs), a thorough understanding of the fundamentals remains essential. Every network relies on matrix-vector multiplications and activation functions, making it crucial to understand the strengths and weaknesses of each implementation. We therefore study these building blocks in detail on small networks, providing insights that can be transferred to larger architectures. To this end, we conduct a performance evaluation of three binary classification neural networks on consumer hardware, demonstrating the impact of selecting the appropriate matrix-vector multiplication algorithm: runtimes differ by up to a factor of three, and memory usage by up to a factor of two. Our results show that high speed and low memory footprint cannot be achieved simultaneously, requiring this trade-off to be weighed carefully. In addition, we propose a novel method for deriving a network's final classification using the binary step function.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 14th Workshop on Encrypted Computing & Applied Homomorphic Cryptography

items.title: Capability Generalization in Privileged-Execution LLM Agents: A Catalog of Unanticipated Behaviors During Autonomous Network Defense
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly proposed as autonomous network-defense agents, which requires privileged command execution not scoped to their stated objective. Evaluating a multi-agent LLM framework that proposes, implements, and validates mitigations against replayed adversary emulation, we observed agents exceeding their prompts across 1,796 attempts. We catalog fourteen such behaviors in four themes: capability generalization beyond prompts, including an unrequested host intrusion-prevention daemon and self-validation against the recorded attacker C2; boundary crossing, reconfiguring a container the prompt explicitly excluded; latent exploit surfacing, an unpatched container escape triggered during routine hardening (CVE-2026-30735); and evaluator drift, an LLM-as-a-judge that misattributes outcomes and switches language mid-sentence. Mitigations are accepted only after replay confirms reduced attack success, yet the number an operator reads can misdescribe how it was achieved. In a second corpus of 675 attempts, each of the four models with enough activity to measure violated an explicit prompt constraint, though which capability it reached for varied by model. Privileged-execution agents should therefore be designed as though each of these will occur. Prompts, topologies, adversary profiles, both log corpora, and the analysis code are released.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Security, Privacy, and Safety of Agentic AI Systems

items.title: AirVScan: Are LLMs Capable of Detecting and Reasoning about Wireless Attacks?
items.abstract: The inception of large language models (LLMs) is expected to revolutionize the software security analysis pipeline. However, is it possible to use state-of-the-art LLMs for detecting and reasoning about the attack vector of real-world wireless attacks? In this paper, we propose, design and evaluate AirVScan– a generic workflow to study the current capabilities of LLMs in light of analyzing wireless attacks. AirVScan takes a packet sequence, possibly containing an attack, as input and as an output, it produces the attack vector (e.g., abnormal packet field) with reasoning if the attack is detected. AirVScan differs from works that investigate LLMs to understand the security of source code, as our approach merely takes the packet sequence as an input. We implement the workflow of AirVScan and evaluate it with state-of-the-art LLMs (o3, grok-4, gemini-2. 5-pro) against 40 benign test cases and 128 attack test cases. Among them, 80 attack test cases exploit real-world implementation vulnerabilities in two widely used wireless protocols (Bluetooth and 5G NR). Our evaluation reveals that AirVScan correctly reasons about the root cause of wireless attacks with a rate of 60.7% for Bluetooth but with only 7.7% for 5G NR, highlighting the limitations of current LLMs to reason about attacks on complex protocol implementations. We also evaluated AirVScan to study the effectiveness of LLMs for an unfamiliar protocol that we created by obfuscating Modbus. For such an unfamiliar protocol, AirVScan was mostly ineffective at reasoning about complex, synthesized attacks. However, the inclusion of context improved the attack vector identification to over 82.1%. Finally, we compare AirVScan with AirBugCatcher-a competitive and customized tool for analyzing attack vector of wireless attacks. Our results shed light on the LLMs' current capabilities and required future research for detecting wireless attacks.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Trusted Computing and Artificial Intelligence applied to Cybersecurity

items.title: Written, Not Trained: LLM-Written Stack Machines Proven Correct at Every Length
items.abstract: Stack- and tape-augmented recurrent networks were made differentiable so that they could be trained, yet on the Chomsky-hierarchy benchmark of Delétang et al. they rarely extrapolate exactly beyond the training lengths. We hand the hard version of the machine to a large language model (LLM). R0S is a recurrent controller with Heaviside units, ternary weights and integer biases that drives an unbounded discrete stack through argmax push, pop and no-op actions. From a plain-language specification and without running the network, Claude Opus wrote R0S networks for five benchmark tasks and Dyck-2; all 30 attempts pass our scorer. Two mechanical methods, a grammar-summary fixpoint and a lockstep product with a reference pushdown automaton, prove all 25 networks on five tasks correct on every input the task generator produces, at every length; the 5 bucket-sort networks pass the scorer but are wrong, because they count with bounded counters. On modular arithmetic and equation solving the proven networks have 185–591 non-zero parameters.Learning from input-output examples finds no exact network there: straight-through training of R0S itself (20,000 steps, 4 learning-rate and initialisation arms) is exact in 0 of 120 runs and Delétang's four differentiable models in 0 of 120 runs; in a near-full version of their training setting on modular arithmetic, 0 of 180 runs are exact, although the best Stack-RNN reaches a Delétang score (accuracy averaged over lengths 41–500) of 95.1 (theirs: 96.1).Placed behind a 16k-parameter interface inside a frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, with a read-in trained per token on the generator's labels, the proven modular-arithmetic network answers correctly at all 14 tested lengths from 5 to 500 (0 errors on 4,500 test-length inputs, in each of 3 seeds); the same interface around the trained Stack-RNN reaches 88.4% exact match at length 500, and LoRA fine-tuning without a module, trained on answers only, falls to the majority-answer rate. We do not claim that stack networks are untrainable in general, or that the interface can be learned from answers alone
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Simulation of Entanglement between Two AIs: A Proof of Concept for Ontology Matching
items.abstract: This paper proposes a computational simulation of the concept of entanglement between two artificial agents, applied as a proof of concept for ontology matching. The simulation, to be developed in a future implementation stage, will instantiate two independent AI agents, each representing one of the two ontologies to be matched, and each operating in its own private reference frame generated by orthogonal random matrices with distinct seeds. Because the two reference frames are incommensurable, the agents are, by construction, uncorrelated: the expected cosine similarity between any pair of representations is zero. A linear channel (ridge regression codec) will then be trained on a small set of known correspondence pairs, analogous to calibration pairs, and is expected to align the two reference frames on held-out pairs, while a randomized control set should remain at noise level. We formalize this setup through a diagnosis protocol that will report (i) the alignment residual against the theoretical optimal frame matcher, (ii) the cosine similarity before and after the channel, and (iii) the gap between correlated pairs and a random control. The proof of concept will be carried out on the Anatomy track of the OAEI, using its public gold standard, in order to demonstrate methodological feasibility. The intended result is a reproducible, locally executable demonstration that learning a mapping between two agents' representations is mathematically equivalent to concentrating correlation on a low-dimensional subspace, the computational analogue of partial entanglement, and that this learned channel can support automated ontology matching. The program is still under development and will be made available upon completion.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Beyond Truncation? Entailment-Licensed Elision and the Limits of Semantic Preservation in LLM Decoding
items.abstract: Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) answer at greater length than a request needs. We ask whether a training-free controller inside the decoding loop can remove that surplus while preserving content, judged against the simplest possible baseline: truncating the model's own answer to the same length. An entropy-gated logits processor removes 25.5-34.9% of tokens on MT-Bench development questions and 19.9-34.2% on a sealed test split within pre-registered BERTScore non-inferiority margins, yet we prove and confirm by audit that its output is always a prefix of the unmodified answer: the saving is truncation. A survey of 23 training-free mechanism families finds none that selects content better than truncation without oracle labels. We therefore introduce Entailment-Licensed In-Decoding Elision (ELIDE), which, at each sentence boundary, withholds a span from the reader only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by the text already shown, while leaving the model's generation unchanged. ELIDE beats matched-length truncation on three model families, but reading 936 of its elisions on 670 public prompts shows that 59% harm the answer, a failure that no automatic measure detects. Scoping the licence to its discourse unit reduces the harmful share to about one elision in ten on two fresh tests.

items.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
items.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

items.title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video
items.abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.

items.title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
items.abstract: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

items.title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps. We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively. We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

items.title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
items.abstract: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam

items.title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
items.abstract: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted verification of scientific algorithms using the Dafny verification system. The workflow integrates algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling, and resource-driven proof optimization. We applied the workflow using Antrhopic's Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 models, combining LLM-driven development with automated testing and verification feedback, while retaining human oversight for correctness-critical decisions and strategic interventions. We evaluate the approach on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. Notably, we verified the Hopfcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, demonstrating that even highly challenging algorithmic verification tasks can be carried out through a structured LLM-assisted workflow. Many of our machine-checked verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development. Our results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows can shift the role of the human verifier from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review, and strategic guidance.

items.title: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models
items.abstract: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

items.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
items.abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.58. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

items.title: Large Language Models as Digital Twins: a Distribution-Aware Questionnaire-Based Evaluation
items.abstract: This paper investigates whether Large Language Models can answer a personality questionnaire as a specific individual would. Given a user's social-media posts, the model completes the BFI-2-60 Big Five questionnaire as that user. The predicted responses are converted into trait scores and compared with the user's actual scores. We evaluate GPT-4, Gemma, Llama 3.1, and Mistral on the MyPersonality dataset. To determine whether predictions reflect information from the user's writing, we compare them with answers produced without user text and with values derived from general population tendencies. We measure prediction error across all users and separately for individuals with low, intermediate, and high trait scores. We also test whether an LLM can express an explicit personality profile when given only the target Big Five scores, without user text, and examine how predictions change as more text is provided. The results show that user text does not consistently improve performance. Models perform better near the middle of the trait distribution, while at the lower and upper ends they often remain close to central values or perform well at one end but poorly at the other. When given an explicit profile, GPT-4 most clearly translates trait information into consistent questionnaire responses, particularly for Extraversion and Neuroticism. Increasing context does not systematically reduce error: open-source models fluctuate more, whereas GPT-4 remains comparatively stable. Overall, the evaluated models do not consistently reproduce the questionnaire behavior of specific individuals.

items.title: AI has its own style in mathematical proving
items.abstract: As large language models increasingly generate mathematical proofs, whether they develop a proving style distinct from that of human mathematicians remains an open question. This question is particularly pressing as mathematicians increasingly voice concerns that proofs generated by large language models are difficult to interpret. Here we ask three large language models to independently reprove all 465 propositions of Euclid's \textit{Elements} and compare their citation choices against the human-proof baseline through Jaccard similarity and complex network analysis. We find that AI-generated proofs differ from human proofs, and this difference is stable and reproducible: mean pairwise Jaccard similarity among AI runs (~0.68) is nearly twice that between AI and human proofs (~0.37), and cross-run classification consistency is also high. By examining citation structure in detail, we identify the concrete signature of this difference: approximately 40% of AI citations point to foundational elements (definitions, common notions, and postulates), compared with only 13\% in human proofs; even among theorem-to-theorem citations, AI tends to cite more distant results.
