Roughly half of AI's extra citations trace to the upstream dependencies of the human proof. Together, these findings suggest that the AI proving style is a tendency to construct arguments on its own from foundational elements rather than directly citing later, more established results, which we term "building from the ground up". Our findings offer a new perspective on how AI systems organise and invoke mathematical knowledge, with implications for understanding the interpretability of AI-generated proofs.

items.title: A Joint LLM and Optimization Agent Solution for Drone Scheduling in Victim Search Missions
items.abstract: Victim search in wilderness areas is time-critical. Drones enable rapid area search, but scheduling them is challenging because victims may continue moving, detection results are uncertain, and effective decisions must combine structured mission information with unstructured contextual clues and domain knowledge. To address this, we propose an agent-aided drone scheduling system. The system employs an agent at the ground control station (GCS) to coordinate multiple drones over successive search cycles. In each cycle, the agent applies a scheduling policy that combines a large language model (LLM) for reasoning about where to search with an optimizer for determining how to dispatch the drones under energy constraints. Simulation results show that the proposed system consistently completes the victim-search mission, whereas none of the six non-LLM baselines does so and direct LLM scheduling is considerably less reliable. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/1643204431/llm-uav-victim-search.

items.title: HeMeR: Heterogeneous Memory Reconciliation for Embodied Agents via Structured KV Reuse
items.abstract: Embodied agents make decisions by combining information from heterogeneous memory modules, including declarative memory for explicit knowledge, procedural memory for learned routines, and working memory for current observations. During interaction, the memory contents required for decision making change with the agent's state, goal, and task progress, while many contents remain shared across consecutive decisions. However, existing memory modules are typically accessed through separate interfaces, so each updated memory context is often processed as a new input to the foundation model. This prevents selective key-value (KV) cache reuse for unchanged memory contents and forces full KV cache recomputation even when much of the memory context remains valid. We introduce HeMeR, an inference framework that performs KV reconciliation between dynamically updated memory contexts and reusable KV states. HeMeR tracks declarative, procedural, and working memory contents across action decisions, preserves KV states for unchanged contents, and reconciles only the KV states affected by memory-content updates. This enables efficient and stable inference as memory contents evolve during interaction. We evaluate HeMeR on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world robotic deployments requiring coordinated use of heterogeneous memory contents. In the real-world setting, HeMeR achieves 83.20% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.94 to 1.87 seconds compared with MemRL, while preserving compatible KV states as task progress updates the memory context.

items.title: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement
items.abstract: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment information to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering (\ace{}) harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. Our method, \acerl{}, evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks, \acerl{} achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit.

items.title: Beyond Compressing Everything: Contrastive Memory Learning for Selective Context Compression
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.

items.title: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.

items.title: Turning Multi-Agent Communication into Token-Level Credit with On Policy Self Distillation
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves problem solving in large language model multi-agent systems. Existing approaches overlook communication knowledge or compress it into scalar rewards, leaving coarse credit with little guidance on which decisions each agent should reinforce or revise. OPSD4MAS converts future communication into fine-grained token-level credit through On Policy Self Distillation (OPSD). An external model extracts facts and assesses their trajectory relations for coarse-grained filtering, followed by fine-grained leave-one-out filtering of target-token influence against agent-wise outcome advantages. The fact-conditioned policy supplies token-level credit, combined with GRPO through a linearly annealed joint objective. Our method improves mathematical pass@4 over GRPO by up to 20.00 percentage points. Ablations support complete filtering, while frozen-history injection diagnostics support fact utility. Together, these results support combining agent-level outcome guidance with communication-derived token-level credit. Code is available at https://github.com/Camel-Prince/OPSD4MAS.

items.title: When can an interpretability claim be trusted? Stability and certification of feature dimensionality, ridge leverage and the feature recovery rate
items.abstract: Interpretability tools increasingly support safety claims, such as that a sparse dictionary has recovered most of a model's features. Such claims rest on measurements with arbitrary thresholds, and small changes to the model weights, a different training seed or a different threshold can reverse them. We study two widely used measurements in toy models and synthetic dictionaries with known ground truth: the feature dimensionality of Elhage et al. and the feature recovery rate (FRR) with a cosine threshold. We characterize exactly where feature dimensionality is discontinuous and replace it with a regularized (ridge) version with sharp stability bounds: the ridge leverage score changes by at most $3\sqrt{3}/(8\sqrtλ)$ times the operator-norm change of the weights, and this constant cannot be improved; for the regularized dimensionality the stability constant grows like $ρ/4$ in the scale $ρ=R/\sqrtλ$, with explicit upper and lower bounds. We also prove certificates stating when a claim "feature $i$ is recovered" must survive a given change of the dictionary. The certificates held in every test and are informative for small perturbations, but certify no feature non-trivially across independently trained dictionaries; at the standard threshold, whether a feature counts as recovered changed with the training seed for 55 percent of features. Experiments use toy models only. The proofs, code and text were drafted by AI agents directed by the authors and checked by an independent blind AI reviewer and by numerical tests; the authors take full responsibility for the content.

items.title: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features
items.abstract: Existing large language models typically rely on massive fine-tuning datasets for safety alignment, which results in higher costs for safety alignment and often leads to the problem of over-refusal. We propose Less is Safer (LIS), a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment, constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. Specifically, we leverage Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) activations to efficiently select prompts that cover diverse and interpretable safety features. Then, we employ a multi-agent adversarial synthesis framework to generate harmless prompts that nevertheless elicit unnecessary refusals. LIS contains only 2.4K samples, yet outperforms much larger datasets, e.g., TRIDENT-Core (26K), TRIDENT-Edge (19K) and WildJailbreak (262K), in overall performance on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. Through ablation experiments, we demonstrate that neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone can achieve optimal results. We also used safety features from SAE, annotated by an LLM, for data filtering, but the results were inferior to those obtained using the pipeline proposed in this paper.

items.title: When Grammar Guides the Attack: Uncovering Control-Plane Vulnerabilities in LLMs with Structured Output
items.abstract: Content Warning: This paper may contain unsafe or harmful content generated by LLMs that may be offensive to readers. Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly serve as tooling platforms through structured output APIs, but the grammar-guided decoding that powers this feature opens a critical control-plane attack surface orthogonal to traditional data-plane vulnerabilities. We introduce Constrained Decoding Attack (CDA), a new jailbreak class that targets the LLM control plane. CDA is best characterized as a control-to-semantic pipeline: (1) schema-enforced logit masking injects a malicious prefix into the generation trajectory, and (2) the model itself completes the harmful intent. Unlike data-plane jailbreaks that rely on bypassing alignment with visible inputs, CDA acts on the decoding process itself, so internal safety alignment alone cannot stop it. We instantiate CDA with EnumAttack, which hides malicious content in enum fields, and the more evasive DictAttack, which decouples the payload across a benign prompt and a dictionary-based grammar. Across 13 proprietary/open-weight models and five standard benchmarks, DictAttack achieves 94.3--99.5% Attack Success Rate (ASR) on flagship models including gpt-5, gemini-2.5-pro, deepseek-r1, and gpt-oss-120b. While basic grammar auditing mitigates EnumAttack, DictAttack still sustains 75.8% ASR against SOTA jailbreak guardrails, exposing a "semantic gap" that demands cross-plane defenses bridging the data and control planes. Project page and code are available at https://ict-cda.github.io/.
items.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)

items.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
items.abstract: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.

items.title: Understanding and Preserving Safety in Fine-Tuned LLMs
items.abstract: Fine-tuning is an essential and pervasive functionality for applying large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks. However, it has the potential to substantially degrade safety alignment, e.g., by greatly increasing susceptibility to jailbreak attacks, even when the fine-tuning data is entirely harmless. Despite garnering growing attention in defense efforts during the fine-tuning stage, existing methods struggle with a persistent safety-utility dilemma: emphasizing safety compromises task performance, whereas prioritizing utility typically requires deep fine-tuning that inevitably leads to steep safety declination. In this work, we address this dilemma by shedding new light on the geometric interaction between safety- and utility-oriented gradients in safety-aligned LLMs. Through systematic empirical analysis, we uncover three key insights: (I) safety gradients lie in a low-rank subspace, while utility gradients span a broader high-dimensional space; (II) these subspaces are often negatively correlated, causing directional conflicts during fine-tuning; and (III) the dominant safety direction can be efficiently estimated from a single sample. Building upon these novel insights, we propose safety-preserving fine-tuning (SPF), a lightweight approach that explicitly removes gradient components conflicting with the low-rank safety subspace. Theoretically, we show that SPF guarantees utility convergence while bounding safety drift. Empirically, SPF consistently maintains downstream task performance and recovers nearly all pre-trained safety alignment, even under adversarial fine-tuning scenarios. Furthermore, SPF exhibits robust resistance to both deep fine-tuning and dynamic jailbreak attacks. Together, our findings provide new mechanistic understanding and practical guidance toward always-aligned LLM fine-tuning.
items.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)

items.title: Token Buncher : Shielding LLMs from Harmful Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning
items.abstract: As LLMs become more capable, harmful misuse through fine-tuning becomes increasingly risky. While prior work largely focuses on supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we show that reinforcement learning (RL) enables stronger safety alignment bypasses and more advanced harmful task assistance under matched compute budgets. To address this threat, we propose Token Buncher, the first defense designed specifically against RL-based harmful fine-tuning. This repository accompanies the Token Buncher paper and provides code to launch harmful-RL attacks, apply the defense, and evaluate safety and capability benchmarks.
items.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)

items.title: Time Flies When You Parallelise: Pareto-efficient Time Series Foundation Models with Linear Recurrences
items.abstract: Time series foundation models have demonstrated strong zero-shot forecasting performance, but computational efficiency remains a central architectural challenge. Temporal self-attention incurs quadratic cost in the number of temporal tokens, while nonlinear recurrent state transitions restrict parallel computation along the temporal dimension. We introduce ci-proto, a family of time series foundation models based on Mamba-3, whose linear state recurrences support chunk-wise parallel-in-time computation during training, and inference costs that scale linearly with sequence length. The architecture alternates recurrent temporal processing with cross-variate attention, supporting multivariate probabilistic forecasting with past-only and future-known covariates. Across fev-bench's 100 forecasting tasks, ci-proto XL sets a new state of the art among time series foundation models. The five ci-proto variants also make up the entire Pareto frontier for mean scaled quantile loss and mean absolute scaled error against both parameter count and median runtime.

items.title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint
items.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings support smaller local budgets for energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated setting.

items.title: StateAlign: Internalizing State-Aware Decision-Making for Reliable Multi-Turn Tool Agents via Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning has improved the tool-use capabilities of large language models. However, better task performance can coincide with increased tool hallucination. Reliable tool use requires decisions to follow the current task state: available information, tool capabilities, and task progress. Our analysis shows that agents sometimes execute when they should ask for information, retrieve it, or decline an infeasible request, even when reasoning identifies missing information. We introduce StateAlign, combining task-state construction with state-contrastive reinforcement learning. The data cover five task conditions and pair states with different action requirements. Outcome rewards guide task completion; token-level contrasts compare the same generated reasoning and actions under paired states to train outputs that fit the current state. Experiments across five base models from three families show improvements on BFCL v4 multi-turn, ToolSandbox, and When2Call. Ablations show that state construction improves performance and reliability under different reward designs. The complete method further reduces tool hallucination across three Qwen3 sizes. On Qwen3-8B, StateAlign improves BFCL v4 multi-turn accuracy from 45.5% to 55.2% and reduces no-tool hallucination on SimpleToolHalluBench from 62.2% under outcome-only training to 56.1%. Behavioral analyses show more consistent decisions, more complete multi-call execution, and stronger recovery after tool errors.

items.title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization
items.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), yet accurate FP4 quantization remains challenging. Practical formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 pair a 4-bit floating-point payload with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy highly sensitive to how each local distribution is scaled. Default maximum-absolute-value scaling preserves dynamic range, but can spend scarce FP4 levels on rarely occupied outlier regions and leave dense tensor values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize local element-wise reconstruction error, optimizing tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity. We propose SoScale, a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs. Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.

items.title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency
items.abstract: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.

items.title: SiC MOSFET switching-loss prediction under manufacturer shift: datasheet dataset, code and per-seed results
items.abstract: Curated dataset of switching energies from the official datasheets of 45 SiC MOSFETs from 6 manufacturers (283 records; 1200 V analysis cohort of 240 points from 15 devices and 5 manufacturers; 650 V-class and 1700 V records), complete Python code and results for: comparison of Ridge, Random Forest, Extra Trees, XGBoost and MLP under row-random, curve-grouped, device-held-out and manufacturer-held-out evaluation; zero-shot versus one-shot (power-law scaling law) prediction; split conformal prediction and SHAP; per-manufacturer generalization; an external check on published double-pulse-test energies of a 3.3 kV JBSFET (transcribed from V. Krishna, M.S. thesis, NC State University, 2021; not measured by the author); seed-level (10 seeds) and bootstrap results; result tables T01-T14 (CSV and Excel); Fig. 1-8. Reproduce: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt; python run_all.py. Verify: python src/verify_checksums.py. Self-audit: results/audit/audit_report.md.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models
items.abstract: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.

items.title: Self-Supervised Attention-Based Virtual Metrology for CMP MRR Prediction
items.abstract: Chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) is a critical semiconductor manufacturing process where material removal rate (MRR) is a key metric for process monitoring and advanced process control (APC). Virtual metrology enables MRR estimation from process time series signals, supporting run-to-run(R2R) control and process optimization while reducing reliance on physical metrology. Existing approaches typically rely on simplified linear assumptions or require handcrafted feature engineering. In this paper, we propose Global Regression Pretraining(GREP), a self-supervised, attention-based framework for CMP MRR prediction. GREP learns temporal representations from unlabeled sensor signals through global proxy-target regression, followed by supervised fine-tuning for MRR estimation. The framework is evaluated against a feature-engineered supervised baseline under three conditions: limited labeled data, sensor noise, and temporal process drift. Experiments on the PHM 2016 CMP dataset demonstrate competitive performance under limited labeled-data conditions, with improvements in selected cases and performance largely comparable to the baseline across different labeled-data fractions. Both models exhibit relatively small changes in prediction error with increasing noise, while GREP achieves a 17.0% RMSE reduction in the final temporal interval.

items.title: SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection
items.abstract: The easy access to Large Language Models (LLMs) has made AI-generated texts on the web increasingly ubiquitous, making AI-text detection a crucial task. Prompts greatly influence the generation process, but existing detectors focus solely on the generated texts --- supervised methods learn from labeled texts only, and zero-shot methods rely on the text's probability distributions --- ignoring the underlying generation process, which limits their robustness in open-world scenarios. We introduce SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection, a novel framework for detecting AI-generated text that transfers better across datasets. Specifically, we measure the prompt's influence and use it as a discriminative signal. We characterize the prompt's influence by introducing a Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) term that captures how much a prompt explains a text. Based on this quantity, SPADE trains one soft prompt per class to amplify the separation, and predicts the class whose prompt best explains the candidate text. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks against various detectors demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our method, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets.

items.title: SBA: A Practical Memory Performance Denial-of-Service Attack
items.abstract: Modern cloud platforms use memory bandwidth regulation to isolate co-located workloads, implicitly assuming that high aggregate bandwidth consumption implies high interference. We show that this assumption is fundamentally flawed. We present the Single-Bank Attack (SBA), a practical memory denial-of-service attack that induces extreme cross-core slowdowns---over three orders of magnitude on memory-intensive victims (e.g., LLM decode)---while consuming less than 1 GB/s of memory bandwidth. SBA exploits the gap between peak and worst-case DRAM throughput by concentrating memory write operations on a single bank, forcing persistent row conflicts and frequent write draining, thereby collapsing the memory service rate. Across Intel and AMD systems, including DDR5- and HBM2E-based platforms, SBA consistently causes orders-of-magnitude slowdowns under realistic multi-tenant settings, revealing a fundamental limitation of bandwidth-centric memory isolation. We further show that this localized contention propagates system-wide: single-bank congestion saturates memory controller queues and induces back-pressure into shared cache and coherence structures, ultimately throttling memory request injection across cores. Consequently, severe interference can arise even at low aggregate bandwidth, evading existing bandwidth-based QoS mechanisms such as Intel RDT MBA. To address this limitation, we propose IQ-MemGuard, a lightweight, software-based memory bandwidth regulator that detects sustained contention using microarchitectural signals and selectively throttles pathological request injection. Our implementation on an Intel platform effectively mitigates SBA, whereas Intel's hardware QoS mechanism fails completely.

items.title: SAGE-QA: Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Closed-Context Question Answering on SQuAD 2.0
items.abstract: Closed-context question answering (QA) requires a system to generate an answer strictly supported by a supplied passage, or to abstain when the passage lacks adequate evidence. SQuAD 2.0 is a widely used benchmark for this setting, scored by Exact Match (EM) i.e., character-level agreement with human reference spans after lexical normalization. For generative large language models (LLMs), however, an EM failure may reflect a valid paraphrase or an alternative passage-supported answer rather than a hallucination. The best prior leaderboard EM is approximately 91%, but evaluating generative models requires separating lexical divergence from factual error. We introduce SAGE-QA (Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Question Answering), a multi-tiered framework combining reference-based Semantic Equivalence Scoring (SES) and passage-based Re-Validation Scoring (RVS). On a fixed set of 10,000 SQuAD 2.0 validation examples, we compute EM and decision-matrix F1 from TP, TN, FP, and FN counts for zero-shot closed-weight frontier models and for open-weight models, untuned and fine-tuned. Zero-shot, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro reach 85.21 and 86.66 EM, outperforming untuned Llama 3 8B (56.88), gpt-oss-20b (66.28), and Llama 3.3 70B (71.39). Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adds 21.19 to 34.06 EM points, raising these models to 90.94, 87.47, and 94.24 EM, respectively. Auditing the frontier models with SAGE-QA and an external LLM judge yields dataset-wide SES scores of 92.81 for Claude Opus 4.6 and 91.67 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and hybrid RVS scores, which combine benchmark credit with passage-based judge assessments, of 97.96 and 98.02. Fine-tuned open-weight models perform best, with fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B surpassing the previous best known EM.

items.title: Review of Innovative MOSFET Architectures for Low Power and High Performance Applications
items.abstract: Semiconductor devices are pivotal technologies for almost all existing industrial sectors, as demonstrated by the recent chips shortages. The limits in scaling, performance and power consumption of electronic components, combined with the strong growth of ICT share in global electrical energy consumption, have put forward the need for alternative solutions. In this respect, innovative and disruptive device architectures have played a decisive role over the past 15 years and will continue to do so for future electronic circuits and systems. In this regard, FDSOI, multi-gate devices, nanowires, 2D devices, and 3D device architectures have shown promising electrical properties for many applications. This paper will review and compare innovative MOSFET architectures which are and will be needed for advanced electronic systems, like FDSOI, FinFET, Gate-All-Around, Nanosheets, Forksheet, CFET, and will address potential novel MOS Transistors with other disruptive architectures recently proposed for future high performance and/or low power ICs, such as the GAIA (Gate-All-Inside-and-Around) MOSFET.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning to Rank Using Coarse-grained Rewards
items.abstract: Learning to rank (LTR) plays a crucial role in various Information Retrieval (IR) tasks. Although supervised LTR methods based on fine-grained relevance labels (e.g., document-level annotations) have achieved significant success, their reliance on costly and potentially biased annotations limits scalability and alignment with realistic goals. In contrast, coarse-grained feedback signals, such as duration time and session-level engagement, are more accessible and affordable. Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a promising framework to directly optimize these objectives using reward signals, but most existing Reinforcement Learning to Rank (RLTR) approaches suffer from high variance and low sample efficiency. Motivated by recent advances in large language models (LLMs), we re-examine the problem of RLTR with coarse-grained rewards and propose new RLTR methods based on widely used RL algorithms for LLMs. We systematically compare supervised learning and RL-based methods across various model architectures and coarse-grained reward functions on large-scale LTR benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that advanced RL methods can directly learn from coarse-grained rewards and outperform strong supervised learning baselines even with fine-grained labels. This shows the great potential of RLTR for metric-agnostic ranking optimization. We release our code at: https://github.com/StibiumT16/RLTR .

items.title: Realisation of a Compact and Efficient Charge-Controlled Memristor Emulator for Neuromorphic Applications
items.abstract: The solid-state memristor developed by HP Labs confirmed the existence of the fourth fundamental circuit element and exhibited a non-linear resistance that depends on charge. However, its practical use in circuit-level applications is limited due to fabrication complexity, device variability and restricted accessibility. These limitations have spurred the development of compact, efficient memristor emulator circuits. In the present work, a novel charge-controlled memristor emulator employing two Operational Transconductance Amplifiers (OTAs), a single Voltage Differencing Transconductance Amplifier (VDTA), one grounded resistor and one capacitor is proposed. The architecture directly realises the charge-state variable via an OTA and a capacitor, yielding explicit charge-dependent memristance without requiring analogue multipliers or complex nonlinear blocks. The performance of the proposed emulator is validated through PSpice simulations in 0.18 μm CMOS technology, showing reliable operation up to 120 kHz with low power consumption. The simulation results verify the essential memristive characteristics, including pinched hysteresis loops (PHL) at the origin, frequency-dependent hysteresis reduction, non-volatility and electronically controllable resistance states. This is confirmed through both simulation and hardware implementation using the commercially available IC LM13700. The application of the proposed emulator is further demonstrated through its implementation in neuromorphic circuits, including associative learning and adaptive learning circuits.
items.venue: Journal of Circuits Systems and Computers

items.title: ReA-Bench: Benchmarking Responsible Agent Auditing
items.abstract: As agents perform tasks autonomously in local and cloud environments, auditing their execution trajectories can help service providers identify risks and improve agent harnesses and foundation models. Our analysis of production and red-team trajectories shows that some risks are repeatedly missed across auditing configurations. Overall recall obscures which risks are missed and whether higher recall comes with more false positives on legitimate behavior. Existing benchmarks offer limited insight into these failures. Generated trajectories can contain inconsistent tool calls and responses, conspicuous risky actions, or repetitive attack patterns. Grouping results by risk type also makes it difficult to tell whether auditors overlooked evidence, accepted an unsupported conclusion, or lacked information needed to make a judgment. We introduce ReA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for auditing responsible agent behavior. It organizes auditing challenges into six tiers: internal safety knowledge, contradictions within trajectories, evidence retrieval in long contexts, verification of sources and reasoning, indirect steering, and missing information. It includes challenging benign cases in which actions resemble risky ones but are consistent with the task and its authorization. It also provides paired trajectory versions to test whether auditors detect the same risks more reliably when the trajectory is shortened or missing information is supplied. Most samples are drawn from real production trajectories, with scenarios manually selected and adapted to preserve realistic tasks and risks that could plausibly arise during execution.

items.title: Quantum field lithography architecture specification EqX Architecture PoC Validation Report Update v.4
items.abstract: Quantum-Field Chip Lithography Architecture and the EqX Field-Native Core Solver: A Maskless, Zero-Thermal Paradigm for Atomic-Scale Semiconductor Manufacturing Abstract: Modern semiconductor manufacturing is rapidly approaching the physical limits of Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, constrained by multi-layer optical complexities, prohibitive photomask costs, and thermal-induced structural distortions. This research and architecture introduce a transformative paradigm: the Quantum-Field Chip Lithography Machine powered by the EqX Field-Native Core Solver. Transitioning from conventional optical projection to a real-time Virtual Electromagnetic Stencil and Topological Soliton Beam induction, the system achieves direct Atomic Lattice Deposition on silicon wafers. This drives a Zero-Thermal Etching process with zero material waste, fully supporting the fabrication of hundreds of 3D Stacked Microchip layers. Empirical Proof-of-Concept (PoC) validation across four rigorous engineering domains demonstrates that the EqX core solver unyieldingly maintains an absolute field stability index of 1.000, even when subjected to severe stochastic impulse noise (10^44) and adversarial NaN/Inf data corruption. It executes 100,000 continuous operational cycles at an average latency of just 1.109 microseconds per cycle, with zero cumulative latency drift or Zero-Thermal Overhead. Furthermore, it operates seamlessly across 8 parallel cores with Zero-Interference and achieves full RTL-Readiness for physical hardware synthesis, exhibiting a numerical precision delta of exactly zero (0.000000e+00) between FP64 and FP32 resolutions. Coupled with a defensive intellectual property isolation strategy (Abstracted Controller & Encapsulated Solver), this architecture is primed for immediate Soft IP licensing to elevate the semiconductor industry into its next era.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

items.title: Programmable Flexoelectric Engineering of Monolayer β-Te for Polarization-Sensitive Near-Infrared Photodetection
items.abstract: Abstract Function-defined flexoelectric bending provides an effective route to regulate the electronic and photoelectric properties of two-dimensional anisotropic semiconductors. Here, we propose a programmable flexoelectric engineering strategy for monolayer β-Te and investigate its near-infrared polarization-sensitive photoresponse using first-principles calculations combined with quantum transport simulations. Three representative bending profiles, denoted as Gau, Para, and Sin, are introduced to mimic localized indentation, global bending, and smooth wrinkle-like deformation, respectively. The results show that β-Te possesses a narrow band gap, strong in-plane anisotropy, and low stiffness, making it suitable for flexoelectric modulation. Function-defined flexoelectric bending effectively narrows the band gap, reconstructs the band-edge electronic states, and enhances bias-window transmission, especially along the zigzag direction. More importantly, the flexoelectrically engineered β-Te devices exhibit significantly enhanced near-infrared polarization-sensitive photocurrent and improved polarization selectivity, with a maximum photoresponse of approximately 35 a02/photon. This work demonstrates that programmable flexoelectric engineering is an efficient strategy for designing flexible, tunable, and high-performance near-infrared polarization-sensitive photodetectors.
items.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters

items.title: Printable Monolayer of Binary Polymer-Co-Grafted Au Nanoparticles for Nano-Floating-Gate Transistor Memory
items.abstract: Abstract Nano-floating-gate organic field-effect transistor (NFGOFET) memories are promising candidates for flexible, low-cost, and solution-processable nonvolatile memory devices. Their performance relies critically on the construction of a uniform nano-floating-gate/tunneling-dielectric (NFG/TD) layer, in which discrete nanoparticles serve as charge-storage sites and the surrounding polymer matrix functions as the tunneling dielectric. However, the solution processing of the upper organic semiconductor layer often causes solvent-induced erosion of polymer tunneling layers, disrupting the nanoparticle distribution and degrading charge transport and storage. Here, we report a solvent-resistant NFG/TD layer based on binary polymer-co-modified gold nanoparticles and in situ SiO2 interfacial engineering. Gold nanoparticles co-grafted with polystyrene and poly(4-vinylpyridine) form a printable monolayer in which polystyrene serves as the tunneling dielectric and poly(4-vinylpyridine) provides anchoring sites for TEOS hydrolysis. The SiO2 layer preserves the nanoparticle monolayer during active-layer printing and provides a stable inorganic tunneling barrier and a modifiable interface for improving semiconductor crystallization. This work establishes a general and scalable interfacial regulation strategy for the solution-process of printable multi-layered organic thin-film devices.

items.title: Poor Identifier Names in Introductory Programming: A Taxonomy and LLM Evaluation
items.abstract: Identifier naming is a fundamental aspect of code quality and a recurring challenge for novice programmers and this paper addresses how to provide scalable feedback on it. To this end, we develop a fine-grained taxonomy of naming issues and compile a dataset of 337 manually labeled identifiers drawn from novice code. Using this dataset, we investigate how reliably large language models (LLMs) can detect poor identifiers in an introductory programming context, and we compare their labels with human annotations. Our evaluation shows that LLM–human agreement is comparable to agreement between human raters. We argue that human agreement provides a more realistic benchmark than exact label matching - since humans do not always agree, we cannot expect an LLM to always agree with a human annotator. Our findings demonstrate that LLMs can feasibly provide naming feedback to novices, and furthermore, our study informs refinement the proposed taxonomy and highlights opportunities to integrate naming-focused feedback and discussion into programming instruction.

items.title: PiMRef: Deducing Ever-evolving Spear-phishing Emails with Knowledge Base Invariants
items.abstract: Phishing email is a critical step in the cybercrime kill chain due to the high reachability of victims' email accounts and the low cost of launching phishing campaigns. This ever-evolving nature of phishing emails makes traditional rule-based and feature-engineering-based phishing email detectors fight an uphill battle in the cat-and-mouse game of defense and attack. In this work, we show that, large language models (LLMs) can be effectively exploited to generate profile-grounded spear-phishing, compromising major paradigms of phishing email detectors. To defend against such LLM-based spear-phishing attacks, we propose PiMRef, the first reference-based solution to detect ever-evolving phishing emails using knowledge-based invariants, targeting the identity-impersonation attacks that characterize spear-phishing. Our rationale lies in the fact that convincing phishing emails often include ``disprovable claims'', which contradict certain real-world facts. Technically, given an email, PiMRef (i) discovers the claimed identity of the sender, (ii) verifies the sender's email domain against a dynamically expandable knowledge base, and (iii) infers call-to-action instructions that encourage next-step engagement. Compared to existing baselines such as D-Fence, HelpHed, and ChatSpamDetector, PimRef reduces the false-positive rate to 0.81\% while maintaining a recall of 90.7\%-93.1\% on conventional phishing benchmarks such as Nazario and PhishPot. On SpearMail, our newly constructed benchmark of 14,672 LLM-generated spear-phishing emails targeting 681 public profiles, PimRef reaches a recall of 86.4\% without incurring additional false positives. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/code-philia/PhishEmail.
items.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)

items.title: PBFuzz: Agentic Directed Fuzzing for PoV Generation
items.abstract: PBFuzz: Agentic Directed Fuzzing for PoV Generation Artifact for the CCS 2026 paper. PBFuzz is a directed fuzzer that uses an LLM agent to generate property-based test inputs targeting specific bug locations. Given a bug ID and static call-graph analysis, the agent iteratively synthesizes Python input generators, executes the target under Magma canary instrumentation, and uses GDB/LLDB feedback to guide generation toward triggering the bug. This artifact contains the PBFuzz source code, Docker build scripts, and pre-built static analysis results for 9 Magma bugs (LUA001, PDF002, PHP014, PNG006, SND001, SQL012, SSL002, TIF006, XML002). Magma benchmark cloned from GitHub as part of setup.This research artifact is also actively maintained at: https://github.com/sgzeng/pbfuzz.gitPaper preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04611
items.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)

items.title: Operation Identity Evidence Archive: 8 Synthetic Cases
items.abstract: Operation Identity Evidence Archive is an original offline educational software package for reviewing a saved operation identity after an ambiguous result. It keeps the request, assumed dispatch and unresolved or assumed result evidence separate. Every output retains retry_authorized: false. Contents and reproduction Version 1.0.0 contains a Python standard-library checker, an explicit eleven-field contract, a JSON schema, eight synthetic fixtures and eight retained expected reports. The archive also includes a local test suite, a reproduction command, source references and file checksums. No dependency installation is required. Run python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v, then python3 reproduce.py from the extracted package directory. The second command compares all eight generated reports with retained bytes. Run python3 evidence.py fixtures/01-unresolved.json to inspect a single report. Invalid input exits 2 without a success-shaped result. Method and verification boundary The checker compares a saved fingerprint with a specified compact, sorted-key Python JSON representation of the synthetic request. It collects all evidence gaps and applies ordered review gates for missing identity, absent pre-dispatch evidence, unresolved results and missing result references. An unestablished dispatch never becomes proof that an operation did not occur. Local verification covers the authored behavior and all 72 combinations of the specified dispatch, result, reference, pre-dispatch-record and reviewer states. The eight fixtures demonstrate individual gates and combined gaps. This is verification of a local educational model, not an external API, provider, client system or recovery process. No network operation or retry was performed. A matching request fingerprint does not authenticate a record or guarantee deduplication across concurrent requests. A result reference in a fixture is an invented premise, not a completed provider lookup. Even a recorded-result review state grants no permission to repeat an effect. The exact serialization profile and assumptions are documented in CONTRACT.md. Provenance, rights and context Prepared by Dmytro Nasyrov, affiliated with Pharos Production. AI assisted preparation, implementation and root technical review. No independent human review or peer review is claimed. All operation IDs, requests and result references are synthetic. The background reference is the Amazon Builders' Library discussion of idempotent APIs. It explains the importance of request identity when a response is missing. The archive's schema and gate ordering are authored choices, not an AWS-prescribed standard. The affiliated engineering context is Pharos Production AI agent development. The public service description is not evidence of client deployment or performance for this artifact. The original code, documentation and synthetic fixtures are licensed under MIT. The official company logo is excluded and remains its owner's property. External source pages are referenced, not redistributed. Python 3.10 or later is required; execution was checked with Python 3.14.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: One Leak Away: How Pretrained Model Exposure Amplifies Jailbreak Risks in Finetuned LLMs
items.abstract: Finetuning pretrained large language models (LLMs) has become the standard paradigm for developing downstream applications. However, its security implications remain unclear, particularly regarding whether finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained sources. We investigate this question in a realistic pretrain-to-finetune threat model, where an attacker has full access to a released pretrained LLM but no access to its proprietary finetuned derivatives. Empirical analysis shows that adversarial prompts optimized on the pretrained model transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, revealing inherited vulnerabilities from pretrained to finetuned LLMs. To further examine this inheritance, we conduct representation-level probing, which shows that transferable prompts are linearly separable within the pretrained hidden states, suggesting that transferability-relevant structure is already encoded in pretrained representations. Building on this insight, we propose the Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack, which steers optimization toward transferability-relevant directions. Experiments across multiple LLM families and diverse finetuned tasks confirm PGP's strong transfer success, underscoring the security risks inherent in the pretrain-to-finetune paradigm. Finally, we demonstrate that the same representation-level insights also enable a lightweight defense that mitigates pretrain-to-finetune jailbreak transfer while preserving downstream utility.
items.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)

items.title: ORCHID-SAGE: Fully Reproducible CALPHAD Assessment from Evidence to Phase Diagram
items.abstract: Knowledge of phase stability is the first requirement for materials design, and predicting the conditions under which new materials can be synthesized has become a key capability of self-driving laboratories (SDLs). For inorganic materials, notably alloys, these predictions come from thermodynamic databases built with the CALPHAD method. Building a database, however, requires expert judgment at many steps, and because these decisions are rarely recorded, others can use a database but cannot regenerate or update it. Machines can already collect the data, build a first model with machine-learned interatomic potentials and refine it against experiments. The assessment itself, the sequence of judgments that turns these parts into a reliable database, is still carried out by human experts. We argue that it can be automated reproducibly only if the expert knowledge behind an assessment is encoded in formal protocols, so that an assessment delivers a record of its construction and not only its parameters. We introduce ORCHID-SAGE, a standard that organizes this record into reproducible and automatable protocols. In this first attempt, applied to Cr-Ni, the database was regenerated from its record by a script on a second machine, by an AI agent working only through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and by a refit from public sources only, with the same predictions. Recorded in this way, a database need no longer be fixed at publication but can be updated by AI agents as SDLs and other sources provide new evidence, while the judgment remains with people and on the record.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements to Hyperparameter Translation for Quantum Software via LLMs
items.abstract: Quantum software engineering (QSE) lacks validated approaches for translating natural-language non-functional requirements (NFRs) into execution parameters such as shots and transpiler optimization levels. Existing methods emphasize semantic similarity rather than execution outcomes. We evaluate seven large language models (LLMs) against a deterministic heuristic baseline using 540 synthetic and 18 real-world user stories. We assess semantic accuracy and execution outcomes, including time, cost, top-state probability, and two-qubit gate exposure, through Qiskit/Aer simulations. All LLMs significantly outperformed the heuristic in semantic accuracy, achieving 55.6 to 83.3 percent on real-world stories compared to 16.7 percent for the heuristic. However, no LLM demonstrated statistically significant superiority over others on the real-world dataset. Speed- and cost-oriented configurations reduced execution time and cost, but fidelity improvements were not supported. Some failures resulted from provider safety refusals rather than translation errors. Our findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as middleware for NFR-to-configuration translation in QSE, while emphasizing execution-based validation, human oversight, and careful interpretation of model differences.

items.title: Nb2O5 Interlayer Engineering for Switchable Polarization and Tunneling Electroresistance in HZO-Based Ferroelectric Tunnel Junctions
items.abstract: Abstract Hf1–xZrxO2 (HZO)-based ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs) enable polarization-controlled resistance switching at nanometer-scale thicknesses, offering potential for nonvolatile memory and multilevel conductance operation. In metal–ferroelectric–insulator–ferroelectric–metal (MFIFM) structures, highly insulating interlayers such as Al2O3 can suppress leakage at the expense of switchable polarization and low-resistance-state (LRS) transport. Here, Nb2O5 is explored as an alternative interlayer with a relatively low electron-transport barrier, and Al2O3- and Nb2O5-inserted MFIFM FTJs with identical HZO layer thicknesses and total dielectric-stack thicknesses are directly compared. Replacing Al2O3 with Nb2O5 increases the positive-up–negative-down (PUND)-derived 2Pr from 17.2 to 27.4 μC/cm2, accompanied by a higher fitted orthorhombic-phase contribution and a higher out-of-plane texture index. The Nb2O5-inserted device also exhibits a higher tunneling electroresistance (TER) ratio than its Al2O3-inserted counterpart (60 vs 36 at a read voltage of 1.2 V), accompanied by a larger relative increase in LRS current than in high-resistance-state (HRS) current. The Nb2O5-inserted device further exhibits a higher breakdown voltage than the Al2O3-inserted counterpart, maintains distinguishable polarization states up to approximately 107 switching cycles, and demonstrates repeatable overall multilevel conductance-update behavior over 20 consecutive cycles, despite variations in individual intermediate conductance levels. These results establish interlayer selection as an effective strategy for modulating switchable polarization, resistance-state transport, and electrical reliability in HZO-based MFIFM FTJs.

items.title: NVBleed: Covert and Side-Channel Attacks on NVIDIA Multi-GPU Interconnect
items.abstract: Multi-GPU systems are becoming increasingly important in highperformance computing (HPC) and cloud infrastructure, providing acceleration for data-intensive applications, including machine learning workloads. These systems consist of multiple GPUs interconnected through high-speed networking links such as NVIDIA's NVLink. In this work, we explore whether the interconnect on such systems can offer a novel source of leakage, enabling new forms of covert and side-channel attacks. Specifically, we reverse engineer the operations of NVlink and identify two primary sources of leakage: timing variations due to contention and accessible performance counters that disclose communication patterns. The leakage is visible remotely and even across VM instances in the cloud, enabling potentially dangerous attacks. Building on these observations, we develop two types of covert-channel attacks across two GPUs, achieving a bandwidth of over 70 Kbps with an error rate of 4.78% for the contention channel. We develop two end-to-end crossGPU side-channel attacks: application fingerprinting (including 18 high-performance computing and deep learning applications) and 3D graphics character identification within Blender, a multi-GPU rendering application. These attacks are highly effective, achieving F1 scores of up to 97.78% and 91.56%, respectively. We also discover that leakage surprisingly occurs across Virtual Machines on the Google Cloud Platform (GCP) and demonstrate a side-channel attack on Blender, achieving F1 scores exceeding 88%. We also explore potential defenses such as managing access to counters and reducing the resolution of the clock to mitigate the two sources of leakage.
items.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)

items.title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
items.abstract: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.

items.title: MuSeToM: Multi-Sensory Evaluation of Belief Revision with Textual Cues Across Six Senses
items.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer mental states in others, is pivotal for human social cognition. Existing evaluations of ToM in large language models (LLMs) mainly focus on static belief attribution and false-belief reasoning, leaving a critical aspect of social reasoning underexplored: can LLMs decide whether perceptual evidence is sufficient to justify another person's belief revision? To address this gap, we present MuSeToM, a human-validated, text-based benchmark for evaluating epistemic belief revision in ToM reasoning. MuSeToM contains 2,415 instances adapted from BigToM and OpenToM, with textual cues spanning six sensory categories, and tests whether models can determine when a protagonist should revise a belief and infer the resulting updated belief state. Using MuSeToM, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs under direct and chain-of-thought prompting, revealing a pronounced dissonance: while models often detect that a belief may change, they struggle to identify the updated belief and frequently over-update on perceptually salient but epistemically insufficient cues.

items.title: MirrorGuard: Toward Secure Computer-Use Agents via Simulation-to-Real Reasoning Correction
items.abstract: Large foundation models are integrated into Computer Use Agents (CUAs), enabling autonomous interaction with operating systems through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) to perform complex tasks. This autonomy introduces serious security risks: malicious instructions or visual prompt injections can trigger unsafe reasoning and cause harmful system-level actions. Existing defenses, such as detection-based blocking, prevent damage but often abort tasks prematurely, reducing agent utility. In this paper, we present MirrorGuard, a plug-and-play defense framework that uses simulation-based training to improve CUA security in the real world. To reduce the cost of large-scale training in operating systems, we propose a novel neural-symbolic simulation pipeline, which generates realistic, high-risk GUI interaction trajectories entirely in a text-based simulated environment, which captures unsafe reasoning patterns and potential system hazards without executing real operations. In the simulation environment, MirrorGuard learns to intercept and rectify insecure reasoning chains of CUAs before they produce and execute unsafe actions. In real-world testing, extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and CUA architectures show that MirrorGuard significantly mitigates security risks. For instance, on the ByteDance UI-TARS system, it reduces the unsafe rate from 66.5% to 13.0% while maintaining a marginal false refusal rate (FRR). In contrast, the state-of-the-art GuardAgent only achieves a reduction to 53.9% and suffers from a 15.4% higher FRR. Our work proves that simulation-derived defenses can provide robust, real-world protection while maintaining the fundamental utility of the agent. Our code and model are publicly available at https://bmz-q-q.github.io/MirrorGuard/.
items.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)

items.title: Mind the Accuracy-Approval Gap: How Users Evaluate Sycophantic AI in Everyday Tasks
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, a tendency to agree with users, flatter or affirm them, and preserve their face, even when independent judgment or critical feedback would be more useful. Prior work has largely evaluated sycophancy through benchmark evaluations, but less is known about how users perceive and respond to sycophantic AI in everyday tasks. We combine benchmark evaluations with two large-scale user studies. We study four personas defined through system prompts: objective (instructed to prioritize accuracy over agreement), soft-sycophantic, hard-sycophantic, and baseline (no persona-specific system prompt). Benchmarks show that even baseline exhibits substantial sycophancy, agreeing with users'stated views 71.7% of the time on NLP Survey, compared with 54.8% for objective and 89.5% for hard-sycophantic. Under conversational pressure on TruthfulQA, accuracy ranged from 81.9% for objective to 59.6% for baseline and 8.7% for hard-sycophantic. Participants were assigned to one of the four personas, and either discussed contested policy topics or collaborated with AI on email writing. Despite its higher accuracy under pressure, objective AI was rated significantly less respectful and satisfying than the other personas, and less trustworthy than baseline. Baseline and sycophantic personas did not differ significantly. Persona did not significantly affect how often participants changed their opinions, although participants who discussed with objective AI had greater odds of reduced confidence. Objective AI prompted greater writing expansion than soft-sycophantic AI, but final writing quality did not differ significantly across personas. These findings highlight a tension between accuracy and user approval: personas with substantially lower accuracy under conversational pressure received more favorable ratings for respect and satisfaction than objective AI.

items.title: Meta-predictive ensembles of LLM pipelines for automated named entity recognition in aerospace software requirements
items.abstract: In safety-critical aerospace systems, errors in requirements engineering can lead to significant operational risks, which makes accurate information extraction essential. Named Entity Recognition (NER) plays a crucial role in this process by supporting tasks such as requirements classification and automated test case generation. Despite the emergence of diverse language model–based predictive pipelines across multiple domains for NER, the aerospace software development field has so far witnessed only limited exploration of the capabilities of foundational large language models (LLMs). This study investigates the effectiveness of foundational LLMs, recurrent architecture–enhanced LLMs, and generative models under domain-specific constraints. However, single-model approaches struggle with stability, domain shifts, and difficulty in capturing long-context dependencies, which motivates the need for more robust solutions. To address this, the study proposes a novel meta-predictive pipeline that integrates heterogeneous models for improved robustness. To develop a robust and precise meta predictor, it benchmarks the performance of 15 foundational LLMs, 30 recurrently enhanced LLMs, and 4 generative language models, including DeepSeek, ChatGPT, LLaMA, and Gemini. Finally, 12 distinct meta-predictors were developed based on foundational LLMs and recurrent architectures. The best performing meta predictor on the public AeroBERT-NER benchmark dataset achieved 94.73%, 93.59%, and 94.17% precision, recall, and F1-score, respectively. The key findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach to improve reliability and scalability in aerospace requirements engineering workflows.
items.venue: International Conference on Automated Software Engineering

items.title: MIRAGE: Misleading Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Black-box and Query-agnostic Poisoning Attacks
items.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enhance LLMs with external knowledge but introduce a critical attack surface: corpus poisoning. While recent studies have demonstrated the potential of such attacks, they typically rely on impractical assumptions, such as white-box access or known user queries, thereby underestimating the difficulty of real-world exploitation. In this paper, we bridge this gap by proposing MIRAGE, a novel multi-stage poisoning pipeline designed for strict black-box and query-agnostic environments. Operating on surrogate model feedback, MIRAGE functions as an automated optimization framework that integrates three key mechanisms: it utilizes persona-driven query synthesis to approximate latent user search distributions, employs semantic anchoring to imperceptibly embed these intents for high retrieval visibility, and leverages an adversarial variant of Test-Time Preference Optimization (TPO) to maximize persuasion. To rigorously evaluate this threat, we construct a new benchmark derived from three long-form, domain-specific datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MIRAGE significantly outperforms existing baselines in both attack efficacy and stealthiness, exhibiting remarkable transferability across diverse retriever-LLM configurations and highlighting the urgent need for robust defense strategies.
items.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)

items.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
items.abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

items.title: Label-Efficient Document-Grounded Factuality Detection via Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent claims that are unsupported by a given source document, motivating accurate and efficient document-grounded factuality detection. Existing LLM-based evaluators often require repeated inference and incur high computational cost, whereas compact factuality detectors are efficient at inference time but commonly rely on large labeled or synthetically generated corpora. We propose CPIL (Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning), a two-stage Siamese framework that converts a small labeled set into relational supervision without acquiring additional factuality labels. CPIL constructs positive pairs from distinct label-preserving paraphrastic views of the same document-claim instance and negative pairs from opposite-label examples associated with the same source document. It further introduces quantile-aware semi-hard negative mining, which derives a boundary from the positive-pair similarity distribution and balances informative negatives with broader coverage. In the two-stage training procedure, Stage 1 learns an encoder from these task-aware pairs, and Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the encoder and a linear classification head for binary factuality prediction. At inference time, CPIL requires no paraphrase generation, pair construction, or Siamese comparison and uses only one encoder-classifier forward pass. On the 11-task LLM-AggreFact benchmark, CPIL-2% and CPIL-3% achieve macro-F1 scores of 81.04 and 81.60 while using only 2-3% of the FactCG-released labeled pool. Both settings outperform all compared compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references. Ablations and sensitivity analyses support the contributions of task-aware pair construction, dynamic negative mining, and multi-pivot paraphrasing.

items.title: Kosmo-GFM: A Production-Ready Geometry Foundation Model
items.abstract: We present Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that integrates a geometry foundation model (GFM), a pose optimization engine (PoseEngine), and reconstruction-derived supervision from KosmoWorld. GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's geometric predictions. On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees among the compared methods. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across the five evaluated datasets. Across 34 scenes completed by all compared reconstruction systems, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours, approximately 20% of GLUEMAP's 69.67 hours. PoseEngine Flash provides a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with a measured mixed-precision runtime of 2.62 hours, approximately 4% of GLUEMAP's runtime. Separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends with increased data, model computation, and training budgets. These results support the use of learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline.

items.title: Identification automatique de domaines de connaissances dans un dictionnaire universel du XVIIIe s.
items.abstract: On se propose de présenter les résultats d’une recherche visant à l’identification et à la classification automatique de domaines de connaissances dans un dictionnaire universel du XVIIIe siècle.L’œuvre support des analyses est l’édition de 1743 du Dictionnaire Universel François & Latin (désormais, DUFLT) dit de Trévoux. Environ 20 % des articles héberge un ou plusieurs paragraphes associés à une marque de domaine (Pétrequin 2009, Turcan 2024) qui stipule de quelle science (astronomie ...), art (poësie ... forge...) ou métier (charron ...) relève le contenu. On est loin de la systématicité de l’Encyclopédie de Diderot et d’Alembert (1751-1772) où 83% environ des articles est pourvu d’une marque de domaine (données tirées de l’ARTFL et de l’ENCCRE). Notre objectif est de parvenir à une classification complète de l’ensemble des paragraphes du dictionnaire en leur affectant un ou plusieurs domaines de connaissance.
