items.title: PENSA: A Spatial Accelerator for BitNet b1.58 Inference on an HBM-equipped AMD Alveo FPGA
items.abstract: Ternary large language models (tLLMs) replace general multiplication in dominant linear layers with sign-controlled accumulation, shifting hardware bottlenecks toward packed-weight delivery, reduction, and operator occupancy. PENSA is an end-to-end FPGA accelerator for the BitNet b1.58 2B4T model on an AMD Alveo U50. Two row-partitioned ternary matrix engines consume packed TQ1_0 weights from eight independent high-bandwidth memory (HBM) pseudo-channels, each processing 1,280 ternary weights per cycle through sign selection and integer reduction. The sequencer, attention, and vocabulary-projection units remain resident on the FPGA, while two-stream interleaved scheduling overlaps sequences across the persistent pipeline to form the Penta-Unit. At 104.1~MHz, PENSA achieves 58.09 tok/s at context 128 and 24.60 tok/s at context 2048, corresponding to 2.14-3.14$\times$ the throughput of a same-model Xeon E-2356G baseline. The resulting system demonstrates end-to-end FPGA execution of 2B-scale BitNet topology without modifying its model structure.

items.title: Lightweight Neural Fault Diagnosis of Analog Electronic Circuits: The Value of a Second Measurement Node and the Limits of Transfer under Severity and Operating-Condition Shift
items.abstract: A classifier can identify large component deviations in a simulated analog circuit and still fail when the deviation becomes smaller or the measurement conditions change. This study evaluates a compact neural diagnostic method with that distinction made explicit, and reports the negative results as carefully as the positive ones. Complex transfer estimates at eight excitation frequencies are normalized by the nominal circuit response and supplied to a multilayer perceptron with 32 and 16 hidden units. Two observation nodes are used, and an output-only variant isolates the value of the additional measurement. The numerical benchmark covers a Sallen–Key low-pass filter and a cascade of two active first-order filters. Circuit realizations are generated independently for training, validation, calibration and six test domains, and the test domains enter none of the model-selection decisions. Across five training seeds, the two-node network reaches 100.00 % matched-domain accuracy on both circuits and 98.25 % and 99.96 % accuracy at a waveform signal-to-noise ratio of 20 dB. Accuracy falls to 79.85 % and 83.56 % for unseen 12–24 % component deviations, and to 56.77 % and 76.41 % under combined stress. A support vector machine performs better under combined stress, by 4.41 and 4.33 percentage points, whereas the neural model improves on the output-only network by 7.84 and 11.49 points. The network has 1,737 trainable parameters. A local sensitivity analysis explains both the benefit and the limit of the second observation node, and an exact parameter-scaling invariance of the Sallen–Key topology is shown to bound what any classifier can recover from these measurements. Confidence analysis shows that nominal-domain temperature scaling does not ensure reliability after a severity shift: expected calibration error increases after calibration in every shifted domain, and a fixed rejection threshold accepts fewer than 10 % of mild-fault cases. The results support a small diagnostic model inside a specified operating envelope, identify the measurements and experiments required before deployment, and should not be read as a claim of robustness outside that envelope.
items.venue: International Journal of Computers and Informatics

items.title: LV-RM 3 : Logic Synthesis and Verification of Computing-in-Memory Systems Using 3-Input Resistive Majority Gates
items.abstract: Resistive random-access memory (ReRAM) is a promising non-volatile technology that enables both data storage and in-memory Boolean computation, with 3-input resistive majority (RM \({}_{3}\) ) logic as a native computational primitive. Efficiently synthesizing, mapping, and verifying RM \({}_{3}\) -based logic under device constraints remains a critical challenge for ReRAM-based computing-in-memory (CiM) architectures. This paper presents an end-to-end framework for logic synthesis, mapping, and verification tailored to RM \({}_{3}\) -based ReRAM systems. The proposed approach employs an RM \({}_{3}\) -based logic representation and integrates exact synthesis, algebraic rewriting, and inversion-aware optimization to reduce logic complexity and hardware cost. A dynamic mapping and instruction-generation strategy is further developed to optimize execution efficiency and resource utilization on crossbar arrays. To ensure correctness, a dedicated intermediate representation, ReRAM micro-operation intermediate representation (ReMOIR), is introduced to model stateful execution and enable SAT-based equivalence checking between logic specifications and generated micro-operation sequences. Experimental results on the EPFL benchmark suite demonstrate that the proposed method reduces logic network size and depth by 14% and 17.7%, respectively, compared to majority-inverter graph (MIG)-based approaches. In addition, it outperforms the SIMPLER MAGIC architecture, reducing execution cycles by 10.16% and ReRAM usage by 41.11%. The proposed framework is implemented in the open-source logic synthesis tool ALSO .
items.venue: ACM Journal on Emerging Technologies in Computing Systems

items.title: IOCaps: de/centralized capabilities for I/O protection
items.abstract: Modern computing systems interact with a minefield of potentially buggy or malicious peripherals such as block storage, network devices, fixed-function video decoders and NPUs, and fully programmable GPUs and FPGAs. These peripherals must be allowed to perform direct memory access (DMA) on host memory, for high-speed bulk memory transfer, but must not be allowed to access memory not meant for them. IOMMUs can thwart DMA attacks via address translation but are limited in spatial security, temporal security, and performance. IOMMUs by definition are limited to page-granularity protection. IOMMUs have to perform slow walks over page tables (stored in slow DRAM) on the critical path, limiting throughput and increasing latency. IOTLBs can cache page table walks but I/O tends to have low locality, constantly accessing new pages and unmapping old ones, making caching ineffective. Invalidating IOTLB entries is so slow that Linux defers invalidation, leading drivers to accidentally access and reuse memory while it may still be exposed, to avoid an otherwise debilitating performance hit. This thesis proposes IOCaps: a capability-based system inspired by CHERI that replaces slow page table walks with fast cryptographic validation, allows peer-to-peer capability delegation and reduction, and improves protection granularity and invalidation latency. Instead of defining access control policies with a cache backed by DRAM page tables, IOCaps are access tokens that are stored by the peripherals, attached to each access, and validated by the host against a set of keys stored in fast SRAM. A Macaroon-inspired Message Authentication Code (MAC)-chaining system allows IOCaps to be reduced and passed between peripherals, facilitating CHERI-like compartmentalization, while remaining secure. IOCaps, like CHERI capabilities, encode the bounds of accessible regions at sub-page precision, avoiding accidental exposure of sensitive data near exposed regions. While IOCaps do not enable translation they can still be layered on top of IOMMU translation if needed, for example, for virtualization. Using separate systems for protection and translation should allow translation to be made less granular, using high-locality hugepages to be more IOMMU-friendly, without sacrificing protection granularity—the best of both worlds. After justifying and describing the basic system, this thesis investigates spatial security, temporal security, and performance to show IOCaps are a viable alternative to IOMMU protection. Spatial Security. IOCaps must be compact to avoid bottlenecking DMA throughput, but must still represent a 64-bit address region with high precision and multiple reductions, which I show is viable through a new approach to compression. Temporal Security. Because protection is no longer backed by a persistent page table, IOCap lifetimes are entirely dependent on that of the keys used to validate them, requiring more keys per peripheral than prior art in the same vein. I investigate different MAC functions, fundamental limits on the number of keys per system, and allocation methods that allow IOCaps to scale to underprovisioned systems without loss of security. Performance. I implement an IOCap protection system in practice using QEMU-based emulation and real FPGA hardware, integrate it with existing CheriBSD VirtIO drivers, and demonstrate that the impact on bulk DMA throughput is minimal.

items.title: HETEROGENEOUS MEMORY ARCHITECTURES FOR HEALTHCARE COMPUTING: A CRITICAL REVIEW OF DESIGN TRADEOFFS AND WORKLOAD AWARE DATA PLACEMENT
items.abstract: Healthcare devices and services handle very different kinds of data. Wearable sensors collect signals continuously, imaging systems process large arrays, and clinical databases must keep records safe after a failure. These tasks need different combinations of memory speed, bandwidth, capacity, persistence, energy use, and reliability. This narrative review examines how conventional and emerging memories can meet these needs. It covers SRAM, DRAM, LPDDR, high-bandwidth memory, NAND flash storage, MRAM, resistive RAM, phase-change memory, and ferroelectric memories. The discussion separates device properties from the performance of controllers, software, and complete applications. It also distinguishes healthcare results already reported in the literature from uses that still need testing. Four studies published in 2026 provide examples from medical imaging and ECG processing. Their measured, projected, and estimated results are kept separate. The review then describes a conceptual method for placing data across memory tiers. It first checks whether a configuration meets capacity, timing, bandwidth, persistence, energy, endurance, and security requirements. Configurations that pass these checks can then be compared using workload priorities. The method has not been implemented or experimentally evaluated. The review identifies further work needed on workload description, recovery after failure, memory endurance, and the cost of moving data. It also sets out the information needed for reproducible evaluation. Using several memory technologies together may help healthcare systems, but the benefit depends on the application and platform. Nominal device speed alone is not enough to justify a design choice.

items.title: Gate Dielectric Engineering and Performance Optimization of Monolayer MoS2 Field-Effect Transistors
items.abstract: 随着硅基电子器件特征尺寸持续缩小，短沟道效应和热耗散瓶颈问题日益严峻。二硫化钼（ molybdenum disulfide,MoS2）作为典型的二维过渡金属硫族化合物（ transition-metal dichalcogenides,TMDCs），因其原子级厚度、直接带隙以及优异电学特性，在下一代低功耗场效应晶体管中展现出巨大潜力。但其原子级沟道使载流子易受界面散射与介电环境影响，仍严重制约器件输运性能。本文通过构建MoS2背栅场效应晶体管模型，系统对比了二氧化硅（ SiO2）、氧化铝（ Al2O3）、二氧化铪（ HfO2）三种栅介质对器件电学性能的影响，并进一步对HfO2栅介质进行厚度优化。结果表明，HfO2高介电常数栅介质通过强介电屏蔽有效抑制库仑杂质散射，在10 nm厚度处实现最优性能：跨导达666 μS，开关比~1013、亚阈值摆幅~70 mV/dec，但受远程界面声子散射影响，其载流子迁移率降至137cm2/(V·s)。本研究阐明了MoS2场效应晶体管栅介质选择与厚度设计对MoS2晶体管电学输运特性的竞争机制，为二维半导体晶体管的栅介质工程研究提供了重要的理论参考。

items.title: Fully Integrated Deep-Ocean Flexible Temperature–Depth Sensor with Neural Network Compensation
items.abstract: Earth’s deep ocean shapes global heat transport, carbon cycling and abyssal circulation, yet large regions remain undersampled. While conventional instruments provide precise single point measurements, their rigidity and weight limit deployment on emerging platforms that could extend observational reach. Here, we introduce the fully integrated, flexible temperature–depth sensor deployable on curved and mobile surfaces for deep-sea measurements. The compact, lightweight, stress-adaptive low-power electronics (average quiescent current: 24.63 µA) unit operates as a co-designed cyber–physical platform, where the porous laser-induced graphene–polydimethylsiloxane composite sensing element achieves a broad measurement range over 0–10 MPa hydrostatic pressure, while temperature–pressure compensation through a dual-hidden-layer neural network combined with polynomial fitting yields a depth error of ≤±0.91% full scale and temperature accuracy of ≤±0.29 °C. Deep-sea trials to 4812.2 m show structural integrity under ~50 MPa hydrostatic pressure, demonstrating durability in extreme environments and enabling sensing on platforms inaccessible to conventional instruments. Marine pressure monitoring helps reveal ocean dynamics and assess human impacts. This work reports a self-contained low-power flexible marine temperature depth (FMTD) sensor featuring wide range, high precision and restrained temperature drift.

items.title: Beyond Host-Side Control: HBM Controller Partitioning Across Host and HBM Base Dies
items.abstract: Recent generations of high bandwidth memory (HBM), such as HBM4, allow the base die of the memory stack to be manufactured using a logic process that can accommodate more complex controller functions next to the DRAM. We present the first systematic quantitative study of function-level controller placement between the host and the HBM4 base die on a silicon interposer. We divide the controller into its main functions and evaluate four placements, from a complete host controller to a complete base die controller, with intermediate placements that move maintenance or scheduling to the base die. We extend Ramulator 2 with HBM4 timing and maintenance, model a die-to-die (D2D) link with timing checks at the DRAM interface, and compose area, energy, and temperature from synthesized controller blocks, modeled storage, and interface data. A provisioned D2D link preserves per-stack bandwidth and adds about twice its one-way delay to unloaded latency. Maintenance moves to the base die with no bandwidth cost and frees host command slots, and the freed share grows with stack height. Replacing the wide interface with a D2D link saves 61% of host shoreline and 16.85 mm2 of host area per stack. The D2D link dominates the added base die area and power, and the base die runs cooler under streaming with link energy below 0.4 pJ/bit. Shared control delivers up to 1.72x the throughput of static partitioning between two requestors.

items.title: Back-end-of-line-integrated carbon nanotube modules for acceleration of silicon logic and clock networks
items.abstract: Abstract Geometric transistor scaling no longer delivers proportional timing gains in advanced silicon logic integrated circuits (ICs), where operating frequency is increasingly bounded by high-capacitance, fanout-limited logic paths and clock networks. The emerging τ-scaling perspective reframes this limitation as a time-constant problem across the driver-interconnect-load system. Here we report τDrive, a monolithic three-dimensional (M3D) carbon-nanotube (CNT) active timing overlay that selectively compresses the dominant τ of silicon logic and clock paths. Unlike topology-folding approaches that primarily shorten interconnects, τDrive preserves the underlying silicon complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) fabric and inserts back-end-of-line (BEOL) integrated CNT timing cells only at load-critical driver stages. A 180-nm Si/500-nm CNT experimental platform verifies low-temperature CNT-on-Si integration, and will enable CNT-assisted Si ring oscillators to achieve a 294% output-swing improvement and 30% effective-current enhancement with a fanout (FO) of 5. In simulations of a 3-nm Si central processing unit (CPU) using calibrated 10-nm CNT CMOS standard cells, selective CNT insertion reduces FO = 39 local delay and transition by 87.5% and 89.5%, respectively, and a single-cell replacement improves the full-CPU logic-path maximum frequency (Fmax) by 2.3%, while selective clock-tree enhancement raises the frequency bound from 2.85 to 2.93 GHz with only a 0.01 mW increase in clock-tree synthesis (CTS) power. These results establish CNT-on-Si M3D as a low-intrusion, vertically accessible drive resource for post-geometric τ compression, as well as a novel logic-folding approach.

items.title: BEOL-compatible monolithic integration of property-tunable complex oxide single crystals on Si for advancing the more-than-Moore paradigm
items.abstract: Complex oxide single-crystal thin films offer diverse functionalities essential for advancing the More-than-Moore paradigm in semiconductor technology. However, their direct integration with Si-based complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) circuits remains challenging due to thermal budget constraints and the difficulty of applying oxide-engineering techniques—such as strain, interface, and domain engineering—for tailoring properties on silicon. In this work, we demonstrate room-temperature monolithic integration of complex oxides onto silicon by combining epitaxial lift-off and surface-activated metal bonding, effectively overcoming thermal limitations. This method allows the application of oxide-engineering methodologies on silicon substrates, as demonstrated using ferromagnetic SrRuO 3 and ferroelectric Pb(Mg,Nb)O 3 -Pb(Zr,Ti)O 3 . Moreover, we highlight its practical potential through the fabrication of flexible ferroelectric heterostructures and electrically-controllable energy storage devices with a one-transistor, one-capacitor structure. This integration strategy facilitates the incorporation of emergent oxide functionalities into CMOS via back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes, bridging complex oxide science with silicon technology for advancing the More-than-Moore paradigm.

items.title: Advanced semiconductor materials for future electronic systems: from conventional to quantum devices
items.abstract: Modern electronics have advanced through the continuous improvement of semiconductor technology. However, the fundamental limitations of conventional silicon, including scaling constraints, short-channel effects, and quantum phenomena, necessitate advanced semiconductor materials and next-generation device architectures. This review discusses the development of semiconductor materials from conventional elemental and compound semiconductors to wide-band-gap, two-dimensional (2D), organic, and quantum semiconductors for future electronic systems. It covers semiconductor physics, band structure engineering, material characterization, device performance metrics, and recent advances in crystal growth, epitaxial growth, film deposition, nanofabrication, and doping techniques. This review also examines emerging semiconductor devices, including FinFETs, gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, neuromorphic and memristive devices, spintronics, and quantum semiconductor devices. Atomically thin 2D semiconductors offer remarkable electrostatic control for future miniaturization, while wide-band-gap semiconductors provide higher breakdown field strength and stability than silicon. Furthermore, the review evaluates defect engineering, interface reliability, quantum–material quality, heterogeneous integration, and fabrication compatibility, particularly the BEOL thermal budget below 400 °C, which is critical for integrating new semiconductor channels with silicon logic. Consequently, low-temperature deposition processes such as atomic layer deposition (ALD), plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD), and selective CVD/MOCVD methods provide beneficial routes for heterogeneous integration.

items.title: The World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA): Hardware-Algorithm Co-Design for Embedded AI in Robotics
items.abstract: Embedded AI is moving from perception to prediction. Robots now use world models$\unicode{x2014}$learned simulators that predict the outcome of candidate actions in a compressed latent space before any is executed. Every predicted step must be computed on board within a tight power and thermal budget, yet the energy these steps fundamentally require, and how far real hardware sits from it, have not been characterized. We derive lower bounds on the arithmetic operations and the CMOS dynamic energy of a latent state transition from information theory and Boolean circuit complexity. Profiling a DreamerV3-style Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) shows that every rollout operation is memory-bandwidth bound and that a GPU consumes at least $5.9\times10^{10}$ times the CMOS energy floor. Transient 3D thermal simulations show that this inefficiency is also a thermal one, since sustained back-to-back planning heats a millimeter-scale silicon tile to 556 K even behind an ideal copper heat spreader. Guided by this chain from bound to bottleneck, we propose the World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA), a chip architecture for embedded world model planning that combines near-memory computation, real-time entropy estimation, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads. With a design target of 40x lower power, the same tile stays near ambient at 306 K in simulation, pointing toward practical planning on thermally constrained robots.

items.title: ЕКСПЕРИМЕНТАЛЬНЕ ТЕСТУВАННЯ ПЕРЕТВОРЮВАЧА ЧАСТОТИ НА ОСНОВІ GAN ТРАНЗИСТОРІВ ДЛЯ ЕЛЕКТРОПРИВОДІВ ЗМІННОГО СТРУМУ З ПІДВИЩЕНОЮ ЧАСТОТОЮ ШИРОТНО-ІМПУЛЬСНОЇ МОДУЛЯЦІЇ
items.abstract: The experimental results of testing a GaN HEMT based high frequency inverter for controlled electric drives applications are presented. The dead-time insertion impact on the quality of stator reference voltage tracking is also highlighted within this paper. The most used algorithm of dead-time compensation is presended. In that algorithm the polarity of compensation voltage is defined by stator’s currents directions and ithe magnitude of that voltage is defined by dead-time interval duration. It is shown that even without dead-time compensation GaN HEMT based inverter demonstrates better performance that IGBT based inverter in term of stator reference voltage tracking. The ability of GaN HEMT based inverter to operate with PWM carrier frequency up to 60 kHz with dead-time of 50 ns was experimentally proven. Corresponding phase-current waveforms and phase portraits are presented. References 10, Figures 10.

items.title: Wavon Field-Based Generalized In-Memory Computing Chip Architecture
items.abstract: What if a chip could be wired by field instead of lithography? The Wavon architecture answers with a single structural proposition: computation need not be carried by wired electrons at all. It replaces fixed interconnect with a blank topological lattice, in which 20-80 GHz millimetre-band electromagnetic evanescent waves act as the signal carrier, and solid-state magnetic skyrmions hold the state of the machine. Nothing in the substrate is hardwired. PDMM software instructions rewrite the steady-state MTJ magnetoresistance, configuring waveguide routing and model weights online, while the physical eigenstructure of the field does the arithmetic: discrete topological boundaries compress the O(n²) cost of conventional matrix multiply-accumulate into a constant O(1) latency intrinsic to MEPS wavefront evolution. The chip leaves the fab as a uniform blank lattice on a 28 nm ultra-near-field substrate, built by a three-layer ultraviolet nanoimprint co-integration process. Vernier Moiré fringes formed by lattice arrays and passive metallic meshes deliver physical self-alignment between layers, removing the multilayer precision overlay lithography and heavy ion doping that conventional silicon requires, and removing any dependence on high-numerical-aperture front-end lithography across the full operational cycle. Interleaved coplanar MTJ and skyrmion arrangements form a globally vacuum-sealed microcavity tunnelling waveguide system that fixes the local guided-mode refractive index at unity with dn/dT = 0. Rare-earth-free, heavy-metal-free RE-TM heterostructures anchor the skyrmions with zero drift at room temperature. Two modes share one hardware origin: binary wavefront carry arithmetic for absolute-precision digital inference, and continuous field-state evolution for energy-level excitation of topological states. The full fabrication process adapts to mature mass-production semiconductor lines without specialised new equipment. in-memory computing, compute-in-memory, memory wall, power wall, quantum wall, von Neumann bottleneck, memristor, CBRAM, PCM, MRAM, silicon photonics, metasurface, VCMA, MTJ, skyrmion, magnetic skyrmion, evanescent wave, lithography, nanoimprint lithography, CPU, GPU, TPU, photonic computing, topological photonics, 3D integration, 28 nm, post-Moore, AI accelerator, neuromorphic computing, non-volatile memory, synaptic plasticity, write endurance
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Understanding the Surface and Interfacial Structure of N -Heterocyclic Carbenes on Ruthenium Substrates: An X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopic Approach
items.abstract: Abstract N-Heterocyclic carbenes (NHCs) are exceptional σ-donors and bind strongly to a wide variety of transition metals. Their unique binding properties have expanded the potential applications of NHCs to area-selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD) for microelectronics fabrication. This new application area requires a deeper understanding of the NHC-to-metal interaction beyond the scale of small molecule NHC–metal complexes. Various surface characterization techniques have been applied to study the NHC-deposited metal surfaces, but to date, most studies have been limited to NHCs deposited on single crystals. Ru is an appealing material in the semiconductor industry because of its moderate resistivity and low electromigration rate. There remains a lack of understanding regarding the surface chemistry of NHCs on Ru metal, with the knowledge gained from NHCs on single crystals not necessarily transferable to NHCs on the polycrystalline substrates encountered in microelectronic devices. To bridge this gap, we report herein an in-depth X-ray photoelectron spectroscopic investigation into the interactions between NHCs and polycrystalline Ru surfaces. Two NHC derivatives with different wingtip and backbone groups were employed. Using different incident energies providing varied penetration depths, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopic measurements were conducted to provide insight into how changes in the NHC structure impact the surface coverage density, molecule-to-metal charge transfer, and the ability to protect Ru surfaces.
items.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters

items.title: Toward autonomous decision support in semiconductor manufacturing: a review of planning, scheduling, dispatching, and execution control
items.abstract: Abstract Semiconductor manufacturing is a high-stakes cyber-physical production domain in which planning targets, scheduling feasibility, dispatching actions, process-control feedback, and human oversight must remain continuously aligned. This paper presents a structured state-of-the-art review of semiconductor smart manufacturing from the perspective of autonomous intelligent systems (AIS). The review does not treat planning, scheduling, dispatching, real-time dispatching (RTD), advanced process control (APC), manufacturing execution systems (MES), advanced planning and scheduling (APS), and enterprise resource planning (ERP) as separate production-management topics. Instead, it synthesizes them as bounded components of a human-supervised closed-loop decision architecture. The central artifact is an AIS reference model that maps fab layers to state inputs, decision-support functions, human authority, and audit or safeguard mechanisms. The review also develops a deployment-maturity matrix for classical optimization, simulation, rule-based dispatching, predictive learning, reinforcement learning, digital twins, LLM-enabled orchestration, and industrial software infrastructure. The synthesis shows that classical methods remain central because they provide interpretable constraints and executable interfaces. Learning-based and large-language-model-enabled methods can strengthen state estimation, policy adaptation, semantic mediation, and human-system interaction, but only under validated simulation or offline evaluation, bounded authority, safe fallback, access control, and auditable records. Semiconductor fabs should therefore not be described as fully autonomous systems. A more defensible AIS framing is trustworthy, human-supervised autonomous decision support: systems that sense changing fab states, evaluate alternatives, recommend or execute approved actions, and feed outcomes back into planning, scheduling, dispatching, and process-control decisions.

items.title: Topology as a Design Variable: Joint Architecture-Sizing Optimization for SRAM
items.abstract: SRAM's power-performance-area-stability trade-off depends on bitcell topology, a discrete architectural choice that interacts non-separably with continuous transistor sizing. However, no open-source SRAM tool treats topology as an optimizable variable. OpenRAM generates SRAM layouts but performs no optimization, while OpenYield supports high-fidelity evaluation but restricts optimization to scalar sizing of a fixed 6T cell. OpenYieldV2 closes this gap through three integrated contributions. First, a fully parameterized compiler generates complete 6T and 10T SRAM macros with peripheral circuits and replica-bitline self-timing, enabling topology comparison under identical simulation conditions. Second, a few-shot TabPFN surrogate learns topology-dependent PPA responses with limited full-macro SPICE samples. Third, a coarse-to-refined multi-objective optimizer combines global exploration of discrete architectural choices with local refinement of continuous transistor sizes. Experiments across varying design conditions reveal a topology decision boundary that shifts with operating constraints rather than following a fixed design rule. Jointly optimizing across this boundary improves hypervolume by up to 17.3\% over the strongest single-topology baseline. OpenYieldV2 is open-source to support reproducible SRAM design research.

items.title: TinyML on the Edge: Optimizing Neural Networks for Low-Power Microcontrollers
items.abstract: To enable autonomous sensing at the extreme edge, machine learning models must escape the cloud. TinyML brings deep learning capabilities directly to resource-constrained hardware such as microcontrollers. Traditional Internet of Things (IoT) frameworks rely on sending massive raw sensor payloads to cloud environments, introducing severe latency, bandwidth congestion, and privacy vulnerabilities. This paper presents a cohesive design flow for optimizing deep neural networks (DNNs) using post-training quantization and structured weight pruning. We demonstrate a highly optimized implementation of a Keyword Spotting (KWS) model deployed on a resource-constrained ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller. The proposed optimization pipeline yields an 86\% reduction in Flash memory footprint and a 6.3$\times$ reduction in inference latency, while dropping overall system active power draw down to 11.2~mW. Our results confirm that complex pattern matching can run locally and autonomously on standard low-cost embedded chips.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Threshold voltage engineering via diode-embedded p-GaN gate HEMTs
items.abstract: Abstract In this work, enhancement-mode (E-mode) p-GaN/AlGaN/GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) with monolithically embedded gate diodes are investigated to explore the use of embedded diode width as a design parameter for threshold-voltage engineering. The embedded diode geometry modulates the electrostatic potential within the gate stack, thereby tuning the threshold voltage. A wide threshold-voltage tuning range of 1.45–3.3 V was achieved, where 1.45 V corresponds to the reference device without an embedded diode and 3.3 V corresponds to the device with a diode-to-HEMT channel ratio of 0.1. In addition, the diode-embedded structure exhibits improved forward gate breakdown voltage while maintaining comparable on-resistance and off-state breakdown voltage. Pulsed bias measurements reveal that smaller diode widths effectively suppress negative threshold-voltage shifts, indicating enhanced dynamic gate stability. These results demonstrate that monolithically embedded gate diodes provide an effective and scalable approach for threshold-voltage engineering and reliability enhancement in E-mode GaN HEMTs for power-switching applications.

items.title: Robust & Scalable Website Fingerprinting via Minimal DRAM Traffic
items.abstract: Website fingerprinting attacks infer websites visited by users and threaten their privacy. These attacks are classified as on-path, which monitor network traffic, and co-located, which exploit shared system resources. Existing co-located attacks, such as sweep-counting and loop-counting, achieve over 90% accuracy but suffer significant performance degradation on many-core systems. Loop-counting accuracy drops from 93% on 8 cores to 50% on 24 cores, while sweep-counting accuracy decreases from 84% to 45% across multiple Core Complex Dies (CCDs). To address these limitations, we propose memory-chasing, a scalable website fingerprinting attack that exploits DRAM traffic interference through pointer-chasing traversals with minimal interference. By counting DRAM accesses over fixed intervals, the attack generates distinctive traces for website classification. Evaluated on the top 50 websites, memory-chasing achieves 96% accuracy on a 24-core system, 86% across multiple CCDs, 80% across multiple sockets, and 97% in an open-world setting. Extensive evaluation across hardware configurations, browsers, operating systems, isolation mechanisms, system noise, and countermeasures demonstrates its robustness and scalability.

items.title: Resolving hidden interface-trap capture times through stochastic current transients in multitrap nanoscale transistors
items.abstract: Charge trapping at semiconductor–dielectric interfaces governs threshold-voltage instability, low-frequency noise, and stochastic variability in nanoscale transistors. In the intermediate multitrap regime, the drain-current transient is neither a defect-resolved signal from a single trap nor a fully averaged ensemble response, making the underlying trap kinetics difficult to infer directly. Here, a framework combining pulsed current–voltage measurement and self-consistent stochastic modeling is introduced for extracting statistical capture-time descriptors of interface-trap ensembles from sensing-phase drain-current transients. The approach analyzes repeated subthreshold transients using both the mean current and its cycle-to-cycle fluctuation, while explicitly incorporating trap-to-trap dispersion, sensing-bias-dependent capture kinetics, and electrostatic feedback induced by progressive trap filling. Simultaneous fitting across multiple sensing biases identifies a common model-constrained parameter pair within an assumed log-normal parameterization of the capture-time-constant distribution. Within the assumed model, this analysis distinguishes intrinsic trap-to-trap kinetic disorder from measurement-induced electrostatic renormalization, revealing that the measured transient is not a direct image of the intrinsic time-constant spectrum but a dynamically reshaped response governed by finite-ensemble stochasticity and channel electrostatics. The framework provides a physics-based route for extracting hidden multitrap kinetic descriptors from stochastic electronic transients in nanoscale devices.

items.title: Resilience of Sub-10 nm MoSi2N4 and WSi2N4 TFETs Against Surface Roughness: Device and Digital Applications
items.abstract: Abstract Monolayers of the \((\mathrm{MA}_2\mathrm{Z}_4)\) family, particularly \((\mathrm{MoSi}_2\mathrm{N}_4)\) and \((\mathrm{WSi}_2\mathrm{N}_4)\), are promising channel materials for steep-slope tunnel field-effect transistors (TFETs) in beyond-CMOS electronics. However, interface imperfections introduce critical device variability. Here, we investigate the impact of substrate surface roughness on sub-10 nm \((\mathrm{MoSi}_2\mathrm{N}_4)\) and \((\mathrm{WSi}_2\mathrm{N}_4)\) TFETs using a tight-binding model within the non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism. The surface corrugation induces localized midgap states, triggering parasitic trap-assisted tunneling that elevates the OFF-current and degrades the sub-threshold swing. Although both 2D channels show strong resilience up to an RMS roughness of \((\delta h \approx 150)\)pm-maintaining intrinsic delays as fast as \((\tau \approx 0.20\text{--}0.25)\) ps at \((L_\mathrm{ch} = 3)\) nm-higher roughness severely suppresses the ON-current and compresses the ON-OFF current ratio by four orders of magnitude. Monolayer \((\mathrm{WSi}_2\mathrm{N}_4)\) consistently demonstrates superior electrostatic robustness compared to \((\mathrm{MoSi}_2\mathrm{N}_4)\). Furthermore, inverter simulations reveal degraded transition slope with surface roughness. These results emphasize the need for atomically smooth substrates or planarization techniques to preserve steep-slope switching in scaled 2D nanoelectronics.

items.title: Physics-Based Gate Stack Optimisation of p-GaN/AlGaN/GaN HEMTs for Balanced Threshold Voltage and On-Resistance
items.abstract: Abstract In this article, the gate-stack design space of p-GaN/AlGaN/GaN HEMTs (high electron mobility transistors) is explored to achieve a balanced threshold voltage (V T ) and on-resistance (R on ). Physics-based analytical models for V T and R on are validated against experimental data and subsequently employed for a 10,000-point design-space exploration encompassing variations in p-GaN doping concentration, Schottky built-in potential, AlGaN thickness, and Al mole fraction. While a high V T is essential for robust enhancement-mode operation and adequate gate-noise immunity, a low R on is required to minimize conduction losses. The study reveals the inherent trade-off between V T and R on , and identifies an optimum gate-stack design region that balances these competing requirements. Based on the explored design space, practical design guidelines are established to maintain V T within the range of 1.7–2.2 V while achieving the lowest possible R on under process-induced variations of gate-stack parameters.

items.title: Phase-geometric classification of memristor hysteresis loops via self-crossings
items.abstract: Memristive devices have revolutionized non-volatile memory and neuromorphic computing, yet the geometry of their hysteresis loops -- in particular, the occurrence and robustness of multiple self-crossings -- remains poorly understood. Here we introduce a topological and algebraic framework that treats the number of transverse self-intersections of a memristor hysteresis loop as a robust integer-valued invariant. Drawing on differential topology, singularity theory, and cusp catastrophe, we employ discriminants and resultants to stratify the six-dimensional parameter space. This approach partitions the parameter space into structurally stable regions separated by explicitly computable catastrophe surfaces. We demonstrate that the crossing number remains strictly invariant under continuous deformations and changes only at self-tangencies or cusp singularities, thereby providing a complete classification of all multi-lobed hysteresis behaviors. These insights bridge device physics with modern singularity theory and suggest a clear roadmap for exploiting higher-order memory effects in next-generation electronics and brain-inspired hardware.

items.title: Next-Generation Interconnect Design
items.abstract: Continuous scaling of the complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) technology has exacerbated the power-delay bottlenecks in global on-chip interconnects, posing critical challenges in achieving energy-efficient and high-speed data transmission. This chapter explores a spectrum of innovative solutions to mitigate these issues, including low-swing signaling schemes, magneto-electric (ME) effect-based receivers, and spin-torque (ST) sensor-driven interconnect frameworks. Specifically, it analyzes techniques like multi- V dd and multi- V th voltage scaling, current-mode signaling, and the advanced modified Junction (MJ) driver to achieve low dynamic and static power consumption. Furthermore, it introduces a capacitively driven interconnect architecture utilizing ME-MTJ devices for efficient signal restoration without analog amplification, and a pipelined repeater framework employing ST buffers with domain wall (DW) motion for delay optimization. Simulation results demonstrate significant improvements in energy efficiency and signal integrity. These hybrid architectures provide promising pathways for scalable and low-power on-chip systems. Future developments will hinge on advancements in materials, device modeling, and integration strategies for deployment in emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators and neuromorphic processors.

items.title: Neuromorphic Computing and Neuromorphic Hardware for AutoML in Zero-touch Networks: Applications and Challenges
items.abstract: Owing to the fact that future communication systems are increasing in size and complexity, Zero Touch Networks (ZTN) is going toward pervasive networks that self-configure, self-optimize, and even self-heal with minimal human action. AutoML plays a crucial role in ZTN for adaptive model selection, hyperparameter tuning and real-time decision-making under dynamic network conditions. However, the latency and energy consumption of traditional cloud-based AutoML systems at edge devices are usually not acceptable. Recently, neuromorphic computing and hardware which are based on the human brain structure and function has become a promising alternative for large scale VLSI implementation because it possesses event driven processing, extremely large scale parallelism, ultra-low power consumption. We study in this paper the integration of neuromorphic computing paradigms for ZTN in AutoML. We explore how Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) and neuromorphic accelerators can enable real-time learning, adaptive control and anomaly detection in ZTNs. Core use cases such as self-heal network, 240 intelligent traffic optimization, predictive maintenance and edge driven autonomous orchestration are also considered. Moreover, it also reports some critical technical challenges where there are no suitable training platforms for the given specific SNN-based AutoML, and hardware–software co-design restrictions which can compromise meeting a particular network demand as well as syntonic with original network infrastructure & standard benchmark availability. Possible research directions, such as hybrid neuromorphic–conventional schemes and online learning methods, are highlighted. The study shows the potential that neuromorphic accelerator-aided AutoML can provide in helping achieve ZTNs more energy-efficient, scalable and fully autonomously operable and demonstrates the necessity of inter-disciplinary collaboration to circumvent current limitations.

items.title: Memory Window Improvement in Ferroelectric Thin-Film Transistors with HfZrO2/AlN Bilayers Grown by Atomic Layer Deposition
items.abstract: Abstract This study demonstrates proximity-induced ferroelectric switching in a stacked ferroelectric film composed of fluorite-structured HfZrO2 (HZO) and wurtzite-structured AlN, which are grown by thermal atomic layer deposition (ALD) and plasma-enhanced ALD (PEALD), respectively. The stacked film shows remanent polarization close to that of HZO but with a much higher coercive field, desirable for enhancing the memory window of ferroelectric thin-film transistors (FeTFTs) for storage applications. The FeTFT with a 5 nm-thick amorphous In–Ga–Zn–O (a-IGZO) channel layer, also grown by ALD, shows a memory window of ∼6.1 V, and data retention over 10 years. It also shows stable endurance cycles of ∼104. These enhancements over the single-layer HZO or stacked HZO/Al2O3 films, which show a minimal memory window of ∼0.3 V and ∼−0.3 V, respectively, are ascribed to the proximity ferroelectric effects between the soft ferroelectric HZO and hard ferroelectric AlN. These results, together with the conformal deposition of the HZO/AlN stack in high-aspect-ratio structures, demonstrate the feasibility of extending the ALD/PEALD-based Prox-FE materials platform toward three-dimensional (3D) process integration.

items.title: Intrinsically Self‐Assembled SrFeO x Topotactic Phase Transition Memristor
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Topotactic phase‐transition (TPT) oxide memristors contain ordered 1D oxygen‐vacancy channels (OVCs) that enable anisotropic oxygen‐ion migration and reversible brownmillerite/perovskite transition, offering a materials platform for neuromorphic computing. However, the lack of spatially predefined oxygen‐ion migration sites in conventional TPT films promotes stochastic perovskite SrFeO 3 conductive filament (CF) growth, compromising the response stability and state distinguishability required for reliable temporal signal processing. Here, a single‐component self‐assembled SrFeO x memristor with alternating vertical and horizontal superlattice‐like OVC regions is reported. Structural characterization, density functional theory calculations, and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations indicate that this intrinsic self‐assembled architecture directs oxygen‐ion migration through vertical channels while horizontal regions restrict stray out‐of‐plane transport, promoting localized CF growth. The device combines forming‐free bipolar switching, an ON/OFF ratio of ∼4.4 × 10 3 , low cycle‐to‐cycle (C2C) variation with CV(V SET )/CV(V RESET ) of 3.2%/0.6%, 16‐state retention over 10 4 s, and endurance up to 10 7 pulse cycles. Reproducible device‐to‐device (D2D) switching is obtained across 32 cells, with D2D CV(V SET )/CV(V RESET ) values of 10.1%/5.9%. Finally, the device's short‐term memory transforms temporal inputs into distinguishable states that a fixed linear readout decodes with 84.59% accuracy on a temporal classification task. This work highlights intrinsic OVC‐orientation engineering as a materials‐level strategy toward reliable single‐component TPT memristors.

items.title: Integration of AI/ML Techniques in VLSI Design
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are among the emerging technologies that will impact a wide range of electronics design and manufacturing. This chapter deals with the essentials in terms of novel devices, circuits, and architectures (system-on chip (SoC) and network-on-chip (NoC)). Here, we elucidate the AI-ML design techniques for optimizing digital and analog integrated circuits (ICs). This chapter also details the various stages of AI-ML-based design ICs with case studies.

items.title: Hybrid CMOS–MJT Circuits for High-Performance CIM Architecture
items.abstract: The rising ubiquitous demand for artificial intelligence (AI), deep learning, Internet of Things (IoT), big data applications, etc., has been backed at both the software and hardware levels. At the software level, algorithms such as Monte Carlo tree search, convolutional neural networks, ResNet, and EfficientNet are being used; meanwhile, at the hardware level, high-performance, energy-efficient graphics processing units (GPUs) such as GeForce RTX 50 series support the implementation of these applications. The achievement at the hardware level is underpinned by the relentless advancement in fabrication technologies such as progressive downscaling of complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) technology and the introduction of advanced transistor architectures such as Fin field-effect transistors (FinFETs) [ 1 , 2 ] and carbon nanotube field-effect transistors (CNTFETs) [ 3 , 4 ], which offer improved power efficiency with high performance in modern integrated circuits (ICs). A notable example is Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which, in 2025, successfully fabricated approximately 92 billion FinFETs for NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU using the 5-nm process technology. Despite these achievements, continued downscaling faces formidable challenges as transistor dimensions approach a few atomic layers. At such scales, quantum mechanical effects—especially quantum tunneling—become prominent, leading to increased leakage currents and elevated standby power dissipation [ 5–8 ]. This is particularly critical in volatile memory systems, where continuous power is required to retain stored information. Concurrently, the rise in operating frequencies contributes to higher dynamic power dissipation and escalates heat generation to levels nearing thermal design limits. Furthermore, as CMOS technology scales down, global interconnects become disproportionately longer relative to transistor dimensions. This results in additional dynamic power consumption and signal propagation delays [ 9 ], thereby compounding the overall power challenges in volatile memory systems. Let’s take an example of memory hierarchy as shown in Figure 10.1 . The on-chip cache levels, such as L1 and L2, primarily utilize static random-access memory (SRAM). Although SRAM offers high-speed performance, it suffers from significant standby power consumption due to subthreshold leakage currents. On the other hand, L3 and L4 cache levels, often implemented using dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), are constrained by the volatility of stored charge and require frequent refresh operations, leading to increased power demand.

items.title: High-Reliability Ultrascaled IGZO FETs for Multibit 2T0C DRAM toward Monolithic 3D Integration of an AI Accelerator
items.abstract: Abstract The continued scaling of silicon-based dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) slows down due to increased process complexity and reduced storage capacitance. Oxide semiconductors (OS), represented by InGaZnOx (IGZO), offer an attractive alternative owing to their ultralow leakage and low thermal budget, making them promising candidates for next-generation DRAM as well as monolithic three-dimensional (M3D) architectures. However, realizing IGZO devices with well-balanced overall performance, including high performance and high reliability under ultrascaled dimensions, remains challenging. Here, we report ultrascaled IGZO field-effect transistors (FETs) fabricated using an optimized O2 plasma-enhanced atomic-layer deposition (PE-ALD) process. The IGZO FETs deliver state-of-the-art performance, including an on-state current (Ion) of 785 μA/μm at a drain voltage of 0.5 V and a transconductance (gm) of 620 μS/μm at a drain voltage of 1.0 V alongside a contact resistance (Rc) of 164.5 Ω·μm with positive threshold voltage (Vth). Reliability degradation is effectively suppressed, with bias-temperature instability (BTI) down to 8 mV even at extremely scaled contact length (Lc) of 50 nm. Leveraging these optimized devices, we further demonstrated a scaled two-transistor-zero-capacitor (2T0C) DRAM capable of up to 6-bit per cell, long data retention over 4000 s, and write time down to 10 ns. We proposed an M3D-DRAM architecture with vertically stacked multilayer embedded memory for artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators, achieving 77× faster weight loading and 9.6× lower energy consumption compared with mature high-bandwidth memory (HBM) counterpart, while maintaining graphics processing units (GPU)-equivalent inference accuracy of 92.25%. This work demonstrates an effective approach for the co-optimization of performance and reliability in ultrascaled IGZO FETs, providing critical foundation for next-generation DRAM and M3D applications.

items.title: High-Performance Dual-Source Vertical TFET Design Using Gate Work Function Engineering and Fully Depleted SOI Substrate
items.abstract: In order to overcome short-channel effects and enhance input characteristics, such as obtaining a steeper subthreshold slope, lower threshold voltage, and a higher Ion/Ioff ratio, devices like tunnel field-effect transistors (TFETs) are being considered as alternatives to traditional metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) field effect transistors (MOSFETs). The band-to-band tunneling (BTBT) mechanism, which is in charge of the drain-to-source current, is the foundation of the TFET’s operation. This work proposes and uses technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulations to study an optimally designed dual-source vertical tunnel field-effect transistor (VTFET). The VTFET structure increases the device’s scalability by arranging the source, channel, and drain vertically. The switching mechanism of TFETs, which depends on quantum tunneling through a potential barrier instead of thermionic emission over the barrier as seen in conventional MOSFETs, is one of their main advantages. The creation of a two-dimensional model for a single-drain, dual-source n-type VTFET is the main contribution of this work. The device’s performance is greatly enhanced by the addition of an ultra-thin channel between the drain and gate regions; numerical simulations show an average subthreshold slope of 3.36 mV/decade and a minimum threshold voltage (VT) of 0.135 V. The 2D Synopsys TCAD tool has been used to analyze the effects of changes in channel thickness, source height, drain doping, source doping, temperature, and gate work function. High ON current and low OFF current have been recorded as https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> 1.48 × 10 − 4 A / m and https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> 6.74 × 10 − 13 A / m , respectively, with ION/IOFF current ratio in the order of https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> 10 8 − 10 9 .

items.title: High landing energy SEM dimensional metrology for High NA EUVL
items.abstract: BackgroundRecently, High Numerical Aperture Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography (High-NA EUVL) started delivering its first wafers, showing its potential by printing 18 and 16 nm pitch line/space. However, as feature sizes drop below 10 nm, questions are raised on the ability of the current metrology procedures and tools to properly characterize such small targets. In particular, it is critical to assess the impact of limited spatial resolution and identify possible ways forward.AimA high-resolution, low damage strategy based on high-landing energy (LE) is proposed.ApproachHigh-LE setting (15 keV) and standard low LE (500 eV) best-known methods are compared using both rigorous simulation and experiments. The comparison is performed for metal oxide resist (MOR) as well as for chemical amplified resist, after development inspection (ADI), and after etch inspection (AEI).ResultsOur results indicated that the 15 keV setting provides 3× better resolution and less ADI damage as compared with the 500 eV setting. AEI damages, throughput, and precision are comparable.ConclusionsUsing high LE provides the needed resolution for High-NA EUVL, with similar or better impact on damages compared with low LE.
items.venue: Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning Materials and Metrology

items.title: HfOx Seed-Layer Functionalization of MoS2 for Top-Gated HZO FeFETs
items.abstract: Two-dimensional MoS2 is a promising channel material for beyond-silicon memory devices, but its chemically inert van der Waals surface makes the direct atomic layer deposition (ALD) of continuous high-k and ferroelectric gate stacks highly challenging in technologically relevant top-gate architectures. Here, we demonstrate an ultrathin sputtered HfOx seed layer as a scalable surface-functionalization strategy enabling conventional H2O-based ALD of ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) on near-monolayer MOCVD-grown MoS2. The HfOx seed layer strongly improves HZO uniformity, while Raman spectroscopy and XPS indicate no significant structural degradation and only limited oxidation of the ultrathin MoS2 channel. Using this seed-assisted integration scheme, we realize top-gate MoS2 FeFETs with low gate leakage currents, efficient channel modulation, and nonvolatile memory operation. These results establish sputtered HfOx seed-layer functionalization as an effective route for scalable integration of ferroelectric HZO with two-dimensional MoS2 channels in top-gate memory devices.

items.title: GUS - Static Skyrmion Array Electromagnetic Evanescent Wave General Unified Storage Architecture
items.abstract: What if a high-capacity, massively parallel non‑volatile storage substrate built upon static skyrmion lattices could feed enormous weight snapshots and continuous training checkpoints for large‑scale AI systems, without the bandwidth and latency bottlenecks that plague conventional storage hierarchies? The GUS architecture is a standalone pure storage framework engineered to serve as the dedicated persistent memory tier for the Wavon field‑based generalized in‑memory computing stack. It delivers stable topological long‑term archiving and near‑field ultra‑fast register resources tailored for post‑silicon AI hardware, where all interlayer signal coupling relies on 20–80 GHz microwave evanescent eigenstates shaped by static magnetic skyrmion boundary conditions. The system adopts three‑dimensional stacked nanostructures bounded strictly by subwavelength near‑field geometry. The lattice spacing 𝐷, effective action radius 𝑅 of the static skyrmion electromagnetic evanescent mode, and vertical interlayer near‑field gap ℎ satisfy ℎ ≤ 𝑅 < 𝐷/2 and ℎ ≤ 𝐷/3. MEPS, the Microwave Evanescent Pattern of Skyrmion, represents the coupled eigenstate ensemble formed by the magnetic topological lattice and its full induced evanescent field spectrum, distinguishable from isolated magnetic skyrmions, optical skyrmions and exciton skyrmions. A top‑layer nanogrid differential GWD wavefield detector enables contactless, non‑destructive, globally parallel near‑field sampling and electrical readout, capable of streaming immense volumes of model parameters simultaneously. Write, retention and read pathways are fully decoupled at the physical layer. The fabrication pipeline is compatible with the 28 nm ultraviolet nanoimprint co‑integration and vacuum microcavity stacking process shared with Wavon. GUS is purpose‑built to host giant transformer weight banks, iterative training checkpoints and fixed topological axiom parameters. It segregates low‑speed topological rewrite events from high‑speed field computation, removing the classic storage wall and forming a matched two‑component hardware ecosystem designed for sustained, large‑capacity field‑state generalized in‑memory computing. storage wall, memory wall, power wall, RC delay, data movement bottleneck, flash, solid state drive, HBM, DDR, non-volatile memory, storage latency, write endurance, lithography, nanoimprint lithography, 3D stacked memory, magnetic skyrmion, topological storage, post-Moore, AI training
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Efficient Spiking Neural Networks with Autapse-Enhanced Temporal Coding?
items.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have emerged as a promising energy-efficient paradigm for multimedia processing. Within SNNs, temporal coding conveys information through spike firing time, leading to sparser spike activity than in rate coding SNNs. While this sparsity improves computational efficiency, it also limits the representational capacity of temporal coding SNNs. In this work, we propose the Last-Spike-Modulated Spike Response Model (LSM-SRM), a self-connected spiking neuron for temporal coding SNNs that integrates neuron's last spike firing time inspired by autapse in biology. This model adaptively modulates excitability and improves the utilization of historical information, consequently enhancing neuronal dynamics and network's representation. To address the history-dependent optimization challenge posed by autapse, we introduce a counting spike-timing-dependent plasticity rule as an event-driven backward approximation by decomposing post-synaptic current into the spike count term and average temporal decay factor. Extensive experiments on both static and neuromorphic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method. For example, on CIFAR100 and DVSGesture datasets, our method increases sparse spike activity by 1.27% and 2.48% while improving performance by 2.06% and 1.04%, respectively. Additionally, we are the first to report the performance of directly trained temporal coding SNNs on larger-scale Tiny ImageNet dataset, highlighting the potential of efficient temporal coding SNNs.
items.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

items.title: EXPERIMENTAL TESTING OF HIGH-FREQUENCY GAN HEMT BASED INVERTER FOR CONTROLLED ELECTRIC DRIVES APPLICATIONS
items.abstract: The experimental results of testing a GaN HEMT based high frequency inverter for controlled electric drives applications are presented. The dead-time insertion impact on the quality of stator reference voltage tracking is also highlighted within this paper. The most used algorithm of dead-time compensation is presended. In that algorithm the polarity of compensation voltage is defined by stator’s currents directions and ithe magnitude of that voltage is defined by dead-time interval duration. It is shown that even without dead-time compensation GaN HEMT based inverter demonstrates better performance that IGBT based inverter in term of stator reference voltage tracking. The ability of GaN HEMT based inverter to operate with PWM carrier frequency up to 60 kHz with dead-time of 50 ns was experimentally proven. Corresponding phase-current waveforms and phase portraits are presented. References 10, Figures 10.

items.title: EUV reticle defect disposition in fab using comprehensive wafer SEM analysis
items.abstract: Reticle defect disposition in wafer fab remains a critical challenge for extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUVL). Conventional approaches in the mask-shop rely on aerial image measurement system (AIMSTM) or mask SEM-based aerial image simulations (S2A). In this work, we present an alternative wafer-level, SEM image-based approach that enables dispositioning questionable defects directly within wafer fab manufacturing environments. Mask defects are evaluated through direct wafer printing and subsequent automated analysis using the KLA’s Wafer SEM Analysis (WSA) software to detect and confirm criticality of the defect originating from the mask. WSA leverages multiple SEM views of wafer patterns and performs critical dimension (CD) error and edge placement error (EPE) measurements to reliably identify, characterize, and confirm printed defects attributable to reticle imperfections. This analysis establishes a wafer‑level ground truth, reducing operator‑dependent judgment when distinguishing nuisance from real wafer print signatures. This methodology is developed and calibrated using data collected from EUV programmed defect masks (PDM), and then validated from wafer product data, demonstrating that WSA can consistently capture both critical and marginal printable defects across multiple test views while effectively separating non‑printing nuisance defects. WSA results are then exported to KLA’s KlearViewTM data management system where these are correlated with mask inspection and Reticle Analyzer™ data. This integration enables side-by-side comparison of mask-level inspection data and wafer-level print evidence within a single platform, providing robust benchmark for defect source analysis (DSA) in production. The workflow offers a systematic, consistent, and cost-effective solution for EUV mask defect qualification in high-volume manufacturing environments.

items.title: Design of Compact Energy-Efficient Ternary SRAM Cells
items.abstract: This chapter presents the design and evaluation of compact, energy-efficient ternary static random-access memory (SRAM) cells using carbon nanotube field-effect transistors (CNFETs), focusing on their application in modern Internet of Things (IoT) and embedded systems. Ternary logic offers a promising alternative to traditional binary logic by reducing circuit complexity and power consumption. Four different ternary SRAM architectures (TSRAM0–TSRAM4) are explored, with emphasis on read-disturb-free operation, delay reduction, and improved power-delay product (PDP). The designs are implemented and simulated using the Stanford 32nm CNFET model in the High Performance Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (HSPICE) environment. Analytical models are presented to evaluate power and current characteristics. Among all the designs, TSRAM4 demonstrates superior performance in terms of reduced delay, low PDP, and better thermal stability. Static and dynamic noise margins, as well as device-level parameters like carbon nanotube (CNT) count and channel length, are analyzed to confirm the robustness of the proposed architectures. The results suggest that CNFET-based ternary SRAMs, particularly TSRAM4, are strong candidates for future low-power, high-performance memory solutions in nanoscale very large-scale integration (VLSI) systems.

items.title: Design Optimization of Advanced FPGA Architectures Using Timing Closure Techniques
items.abstract: Field-programmable gate array (FPGA) designs with control signals have utilized maximum resources, which results in higher power and lower achievable clock frequency. Reset is one of the most common control signals in any digital design, having a direct impact on design parameters like maximum clock frequency, area, and power. The main significance of reset usage in FPGA design is that it makes an impact on area, routing, and timing closure. For achieving better timing optimization, the design should be converted from asynchronous resets to synchronous resets. In this chapter, we propose FPGA implementation of a 16-bit multiplier using the pipeline register concept using different approaches:the first approach is implemented using the asynchronous reset and synchronous reset concept; then next-generation approaches are implemented with synchronous reset with global buffer (GBUF), synchronous reset with the selection of power optimization option in a mixed mode clock manager (MMCM) IP, and synchronous reset with the selection of Jitter optimization option in MMCM IP. These designs are implemented and analyzed using Xilinx Vivado Design Suite software. The proposed designs are analyzed in terms of data required time, data arrival time, slack, total delay, high fanout, total power, and clock uncertainty with anoperating clock frequency of 100MHz and clock period 10ns. It is observed that the design with synchronous reset gives more positive slack compared to the design with asynchronous reset. Positive slack is further optimized using synchronous reset with GBUF design. The total delay of synchronous reset with GBUF design is less than that of synchronous reset without GBUF design. The total power consumption of synchronous reset with MMCM design is lesser than that of synchronous reset without MMCM design.

items.title: Deep learning-augmented ADC: a hybrid approach to automatic defect classification for EUV masks inspected with DUV optics
items.abstract: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography is central to advanced semiconductor manufacturing, but the high cost of actinic inspection necessitates the continued use of deep ultraviolet (DUV) optics. However, the resolution gap between DUV imaging and EUV feature sizes introduces significant challenges. DUV optics struggle to resolve sub-resolution fine patterns, making it difficult to distinguish signals caused by factors such as alignment errors or slight focus deviations from actual defect signals. These optical limitations generate an overwhelming number of false defects, resulting in excessive post inspection review effort and creating a critical manual review bottleneck. To address this, we present a novel deep learning–augmented hybrid Automatic Defect Classification (ADC) framework within the Calibre® DefectClassify tool, augmenting a production-proven rule-based solution with deep learning models. The deterministic rule-based engine enforces strict guardrails for high-contrast, high-severity “killer defects”. Meanwhile, the machine learning models resolve high-dimensional, low signal-to-noise ambiguities unique to DUV-based EUV inspections. These ambiguities include dummy pattern noise, focus variation, and contrast-induced artifacts. Validation on high-volume unseen dataset demonstrates this hybrid ADC framework achieves > 90% False-to-False (F2F) accuracy, substantially reducing manual review workload. Crucially, it maintains a zero killer-defect miss rate with 100% Real-to-Real (R2R) accuracy, providing a highly reliable and scalable inspection strategy for high-volume EUV mask manufacturing.

items.title: Comments on a 2026 stochastic subgradient method for VLSI placement: Exact formula checks and questions about the stochastic convergence argument
items.abstract: This independent technical note examines Yue, Dai and Yu, “An efficient stochastic subgradient method for the global placement problem in very large-scale integration circuits,” Journal of Global Optimization 95 (2026), 863–892, DOI: 10.1007/s10898-026-01619-4. It corrects a displayed ReLU identity, identifies an undefined component-wise quotient under a literal reading of the adaptive-penalty rules, and discusses discrepancies between the printed algorithm and analyzed recurrence. It examines filtration and conditional-expectation issues and provides a two-cell example refuting a covariance-sign inference in the convergence proof. This is not a counterexample to the main convergence theorem, and it does not establish that the numerical experiments are invalid. This deposit preserves the original note dated 3 November 2026 and its accompanying LaTeX source and exact-arithmetic Python script, initially prepared for private scholarly correspondence and now made public. References to private circulation in the PDF describe its original context. No private correspondence is included. This is an independent technical note, not a journal-issued corrigendum or an endorsement by the original authors. AI assistance and responsibility: An OpenAI language model was used for English improvement and numerical checks, and assisted with drafting and mathematical analysis, including development of counterexamples and draft arguments. The author bears full responsibility for the construction and verification of counterexamples, lemmas and propositions, all proofs and conclusions, and the final wording and mathematical correctness of the manuscript.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Circuit Theory-Informed AI for Condition Monitoring in Power Electronics
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence for power electronics is evolving toward a deeper comprehension of system intrinsic behaviors and dynamics. As a novel integration of neural computation and electric circuits, spike-based neuromorphic computing offers promising potential in high energy efficiency and adaptability for data-driven applications. Building on the latency-coding principles, this article proposes a framework for data-light condition monitoring that relies solely on three-phase AC current measurements. The AC current signals are encoded as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which are inherently compatible with spiking neural networks that can effectively facilitate the estimation of device parameters. Case studies are presented to validate the performances, while constraints and further optimizations are also evaluated and discussed, and future extensions of the methodology are provided.

items.title: BPB-GNN: Resource-Efficient Distributed GNN Training via Boundary-Aware Prefetching and Cost-Balanced Batch Construction
items.abstract: Distributed graph neural network (GNN) training is essential for large-scale graph learning, but existing mini-batch frameworks still suffer from substantial inter-partition communication overhead and indirect, coarse-grained GPU memory control. In distributed mini-batch training, remote sampled neighbors cause frequent feature fetching, while fixed seed-node batch sizes cannot accurately reflect the computation graph expansion induced by multi-layer sampling. This paper presents BPB-GNN, a resource-efficient distributed GNN training system that jointly optimizes inter-partition feature access, hierarchical storage management, and mini-batch construction. First, BPB-GNN introduces a training-centric boundary-aware prefetching strategy to localize high-value remote neighbor features associated with boundary nodes in training-node receptive fields. Second, it uses a DRAM/NVMe SSD hierarchy with priority-aware placement and dynamic migration to manage prefetched features under limited DRAM capacity. Finally, it constructs seed-node batches according to estimated sampling-induced load costs rather than equal seed-node counts, thereby balancing batch-level workloads and reducing peak GPU memory usage and its inter-batch fluctuation. These resource-efficient mechanisms may also improve the efficiency of large-scale GNN computation in computing power networks and JointCloud environments. Experiments on real-world graph datasets show that BPB-GNN achieves up to 5× speedup over the baselines while reducing peak GPU memory usage by up to 36%.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

items.title: Asymmetric Triple-Channel Schottky Barrier FinFET Biosensor for Cardiac Biomarker Detection
items.abstract: Abstract We have designed and simulated a new form of Schottky barrier FinFET, known as an SB-FinFET, that is designed to detect cardiac biomarker proteins without labels. The SB-FinFET uses an asymmetric, triple-channel stacked architecture, with the three channels positioned vertically on top of each other. The SB-FinFET consists of three channels made of silicon carbide (SiC), with nickel silicide (NiSi) Schottky contacts and hafnium oxide (HfO 2 ) insulating material as the gate dielectric to reduce the amount of intrinsic leakage current and improve the efficiency with which electrostatic coupling occurs. The architecture allows for the decoupling of current driving ability from sensing ability because of the difference in doping levels of the channels: the two outer channels have a doping density of 1 x 10 17 cm − 3 and are 4 nm deep, while the central channel has a doping density of 1 x 10 10 cm − 3 and is 1 nm thick. The two outer channels provide a suitable amount of current drive and gain, while the central channel serves as a high-sensitivity transducer that converts the biomarker/protein interaction into an electrical signal. The 3D TCAD simulation results exhibit an I ON /I OFF ratio of approximately 1 x 10 8 with low subthreshold swing for target biomolecules that have dielectric constants within the range of k = 1.5–3.5 (e.g., uricase, streptavidin, and troponin). The performance was further characterized through an analysis of linearity with transconductance (g m ) and through third-order nonlinearity metrics (VIP 3 and IIP 3 ). The SB-FinFET has been compared against other types of devices, including Negative Capacitance FET (NC-FET) and Tunnel FETs (TFETs), for sensitivity and complexities associated with fabrication. The results from these comparisons show that SB-FinFET's performance is similar to the two other device structures previously mentioned, while having a lower complexity and cost to fabricate them. The SB-FinFET is therefore an excellent experimental platform for developing new cardiac diagnostics devices that would allow for rapid diagnosis at or near the site of patient care.

items.title: ATLAS: Adaptive Task-Aware Federated Learning with Heterogeneous LoRA and Split Learning for Edge LLMs
items.abstract: Federated learning (FL) can adapt large language models (LLMs) without centralizing private data, but deployment on heterogeneous edge clients is constrained by task diversity, device variability, and communication cost. Standard task-agnostic aggregation and uniform-rank low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often cause negative transfer and poor resource matching. This paper presents ATLAS, a task-aware framework for parameter-efficient federated fine-tuning of transformer LLMs on heterogeneous clients. ATLAS combines representation-based task discovery, budget-aware heterogeneous LoRA allocation, state-consistent split federated learning, and LoRA-only graph regularization, together with INT8 LoRA communication and FP32 server-side computation. On a heterogeneous GLUE federation with three tasks, nine clients, and three backbones, ATLAS improves the macroaverage task score over standard FedAvg by 16.18 points on DistilBERT, 24.83 points on GPT-2, and 6.86 points on Qwen-2.5-0.5B, while reducing LoRA synchronization traffic and eliminating low-resource-client failures.
items.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

items.title: AI Surge Accelerates the Transition to Liquid Cooling: Rethinking Energy and Water Use in Data Center Cooling
items.abstract: Abstract The power density of AI workloads is rapidly driving shifts to liquid cooling. This study rethinks and assesses the global impact on energy and water demand of this cooling transformation. Results suggest that liquid cooling can reduce cooling energy use by 25-56% relative to air cooling, offering substantial energy savings for GW-scale AI data centers. Best-practice PUE values could be as low as 1.07-1.08 for today’s systems and 1.03-1.04 for emerging designs and WUE values from 0.38 to 2.63 L kWh⁻¹, depending on temperature conditions. We identify global free-cooling rack inlet temperature thresholds of 33 °C for evaporative systems and 49 °C for dry systems, demonstrating the practicality of 100% free cooling in many locations. The model finds that minimum PUEs do not necessarily coincide with minimum total energy use. Results quantify the large sustainability potential of liquid cooling and provide actionable targets for data center design and policies.

items.title: A full-hardware edge detection system based on a highly robust dual random number generator
items.abstract: Conventional edge computing hardware at autonomous driving terminals is limited by chip area and power efficiency for complex image data. Recently, researchers have used memristors to construct dedicated hardware systems, achieving advancements in multiple image processing fields such as pattern recognition and edge detection. However, a full-hardware image processing system with anti-interference, low power, and high real-time performance remains challenging. Here, we fabricated a volatile Ag/AlO x /n-Si memristor with exceptional stability and low power. High-resolution electron microscopy visualized Ag conductive filament formation. Integrating two memristors with a logic circuit, we designed a low-power edge detection unit using dual random number hardware computation. Its energy consumption is 92.3% lower than traditional logic circuits, with strong anti-interference. To validate practical use, we constructed a 32-channel parallel full-hardware system with 64 devices, achieving 31.25 frames per second and excellent edge detection.
