The system exhibits excellent scalability, stability, and anti-interference, offering great potential for edge vision hardware in autonomous driving, safety monitoring, and surgical assistance.

items.title: A Novel Technique for Low Power in Adiabatic Logic Based on FinFET
items.abstract: An efficient answer to the growing need for portable, low-power gadgets is adiabatic logic gates. This chapter presents several adiabatic logic designs, including differential cascode pre-resolved adiabatic logic (DCPAL), positive feedback adiabatic logic (PFAL), and 2N-2N2P logic circuits. The purpose of the study is to lower the power for fundamental gates such BUFFER, NAND, NOR, and XOR based on several adiabatic logic types and the suggested logic circuit in order to compare their efficiency in terms of average power consumption and latency at different frequencies. By providing the correct stacking, the NMOS transistor prevents the charge from being discharged toward GND. The effectiveness of the suggested logic circuit is evaluated by comparing its average power consumption and latency at various frequencies with the traditional PFAL logic circuit. Additionally, the suggested circuit and other adiabatic logic types are compared based on their power consumption at various frequencies. Complete simulations are performed at various frequencies using the HSPICE tool at 16 nm and 32 nm technology. Finally, graphs are used to illustrate the average power dissipation characteristics and compare the proposed PFAL-based logic family with the adiabatic logic family.

items.title: A Neural Physics Solver for Richards Equation
items.abstract: A new approach to discretise and solve Richards equation based on the finite element method (FEM) is presented. The novelty of the approach, called the Neural Physics method, is that it expresses the discretisation as a convolution neural network (CNN) whose weights are predetermined by the integrals of the basis functions in the FEM. The Neural Physics method is physically consistent as it represents a discretisation of the governing equation and can run on CPUs, GPUs and the latest AI accelerators, resulting in an increase in computational speed. The Neural Physics method is demonstrated for two different discretisations of Richards equation, including a multigrid method that is realised through a U-Net architecture. The accuracy and speed of these methods is tested on a problem with a known analytical solution and compared to a standard FEM, and shows that the Neural Physics method is almost an order of magnitude faster than a comparable FEM. Finally, the Neural Physics method is applied to a real-world test case with integrated experimental data and simulates the infiltration of water through a rain garden. This new approach therefore provides a route to efficiently and accurately solve Richards equation for a wide array of hydrological applications.

items.title: A Comprehensive Analysis FinFET, FeFET, CNTFET, Nanowire FET and Nanosheet FET for Low Power Applications
items.abstract: Abstract This research undertakes a comparative examination of semiconductor devices operating at the nanoscale, exploring their viability as substitutes for conventional Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistors (MOSFETs) within Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) architectures. Such nanoscale devices exhibit superior operational speed, reduced physical dimensions, and diminished energy consumption, thereby mitigating the inherent challenges encountered with traditional MOSFETs as their feature sizes are progressively reduced. In order to perpetuate the advancement of semiconductor technology as predicted by Moore's Law and to satisfy escalating performance benchmarks, it is imperative that nanoscale devices overcome short-channel effects while maintaining interoperability with Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) fabrication processes. The objective of this investigation is to furnish device engineers with a framework for selecting appropriate MOSFET alternatives that conform to contemporary standards of efficacy, scalability, and manufacturing feasibility, thereby contributing to the progress of low-power, high-performance semiconductor innovations.

items.title: ZYFA: Speed and Accuracy of FP8 FlashAttention on AMD CDNA4
items.abstract: Attention is a core building block of frontier models and often dominates compute-bound prefill at long context. FP8 matrix instructions offer twice the peak throughput of BF16, but they accelerate only matrix multiplication, and the softmax between the two matrix multiplications of attention runs on vector units that FP8 does not accelerate. On the AMD Instinct MI355X, the vendor's AITER kernels reach 39% of peak FP8 matrix throughput at 32K tokens, compared with 49% in BF16. Attention is also more numerically sensitive to quantization than feed-forward layers, and unlike NVIDIA's Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, the MI355X does not track the completion of matrix instructions in hardware, so overlapping the softmax with the matrix multiplications depends on instruction order. We present ZYFA, prefill kernels for the MI355X built on three techniques: (1) computing each FP8 probability directly from its score with a multiply-add and an integer conversion instead of an exponential; (2) a ping-pong schedule in which one group of threads computes its softmax while another executes its matrix multiplications; and (3) scaling each block of probabilities up by a power of two before rounding, and normalizing by the sum of the rounded probabilities. On attention inputs captured from three models and timed at sustained clock speeds, ZYFA achieves 1.16-1.76x the throughput of AITER. On the Gaussian inputs of kernel benchmarks at 32K tokens, it achieves 1.26-1.37x at head dimension 128 and 1.99x for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention. The sustained clock of the MI355X depends on operand values, so throughput on random inputs does not reliably predict throughput on real model activations. At head dimension 128, ZYFA's numerical error is within a few percent of that of Composable Kernel and Triton and 62-78% lower than that of AITER's. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zyphra/zyfa.

items.title: X-Ray Computed Tomography and Laminography Measurements of a 3D-Stacked IC
items.abstract: Advanced semiconductor packages manufactured using heterogeneous integration techniques challenge many conventional non-destructive testing processes. A three-dimensional (3D) structure of stacked integrated circuits (ICs), for example, complicates many existing non-destructive testing techniques. X-ray-based imaging methods, on the other hand, can fully penetrate the part and are ideal for visualizing the complex 3D heterogeneity. In this research, two related X-ray-based 3D imaging techniques, X-ray computed tomography (XCT) and X-ray computed laminography (XCL), are used to measure over-molded modules on a laminate substrate that includes stacked flip-chip Gallium Nitride on Silicon Carbide (GaN-on-SiC) dies. Differences between XCT instruments, XCT instruments versus an XCL instrument, and acquisition parameter settings on 3D reconstructions of the sample are explored. Reference measurement results are compared for image quality, acquisition time, and imaging artifacts. We discuss the current capabilities, limitations, and a potential outlook/roadmap for improving throughput for these types of instruments.

items.title: Variation-Resilient Low-Cost PUF with Trust-Based Authentication Implemented in 16 nm FinFET for IoT Security
items.abstract: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) generate unique chip identifiers from manufacturing variations, but transmissions over public networks can be exploited through eavesdropping. To improve variation resilience, the proposed SRPFD-PUF employs bit self-test (BST) for stable-CRP selection, while response-bit tolerance is considered in an illustrative authentication flow. By minimizing additional circuit overhead, strong baseline PUF metrics are maintained at low hardware cost, supporting integration in Internet of Things (IoT) devices. An illustrative PUF-based authentication flow is presented to demonstrate a potential IoT application; end-to-end protocol implementation and security validation remain outside the scope of this study. The three-condition BST screen yields a minimum simulated logarithmic reliability score of 98.93% under the evaluated PVT conditions within 0.675–1.05 V and −40–150 °C. With the circuit architecture and LFSR configuration disclosed, the evaluated machine-learning attacks yield prediction accuracies of 47.68–52.46%, indicating resistance to the tested modeling methods. The TSMC 16 nm FinFET physical design occupies 0.0117 mm2, while post-layout simulation estimates 0.3089 mW at 100 MHz; no fabricated-silicon measurements are reported.

items.title: Using Superelement Model in Active Thermal Cycle with Temperature Dependent Properties
items.abstract: Superelement (SE) is a modeling technique where the assembled stiffness matrix of a fully meshed model is reduced to a smaller subset of master degrees of freedom (DOFs) while condensing out internal DOFs with methods like Guyan reduction. The reduced stiffness matrix and its remaining master DOFs act as one SE in subsequent analysis to represent the stiffness behavior of the original meshed model. SE can be used to obfuscate critical intellectual property (IP) in the chip package design including internal geometry and part material properties, creating an obfuscated version of the chip that can be shared and used in board-level reliability simulations. However, traditional SE implementation based on Guyan reduction leads to a constant SE reduced stiffness matrix, therefore, it is not able to account for temperature-dependent material properties which have significant effects during thermal cycling. Previous research explored superimposing multiple SEs, each evaluated at a different (albeit uniform) temperature to capture temperature-dependent material properties in passive thermal cycling. This presentation expands on this concept and explores an extension to active thermal cycling where the temperature distribution within the chip package is not uniform. Using a generic example model, we demonstrated convergence to the full solid element behavior. A sensitivity study is performed to demonstrate robustness of the proposed method with respect to material property variations.

items.title: Two-dimensional transistors for capacitorless dynamic random access memory
items.abstract: The continued advancement of data-intensive technologies such as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and high-definition multimedia is placing unprecedented demands on storage systems, requiring innovations in device architecture and materials. Conventional dynamic random access memory (DRAM), based on the one-transistor-one-capacitor (1T1C) cell, is increasingly constrained by scaling challenges, including reduced storage capacitance, increased leakage currents, and complex fabrication requirements. To address these limitations, this thesis explores the development of capacitorless two-transistor-zero-capacitor (2T0C) DRAM architectures integrated with two-dimensional (2D) materials, aiming to achieve high-density, energy-efficient, and scalable memory solutions. The first part introduces a novel van der Waals (vdW) integration method for incorporating high-quality Al2O3 dielectrics onto 2D MoS₂ to fabricate damage-free MoS₂ transistors, overcoming the challenges posed by the lack of surface dangling bonds in 2D materials. By employing monolayer h-BN as a buffer, aluminum is deposited and oxidized to form aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃), which is then transferred onto the MoS₂ channel, preserving pristine interfaces and intrinsic device properties. The resulting MoS₂ transistors exhibit high ON/OFF ratios, low leakage currents, sharp subthreshold swings, and minimal interface trap densities. The fabricated 2T0C DRAM cells demonstrate fast write speeds and long retention times, highlighting the promise of this approach for next-generation memory applications. The second part of this thesis presents the design, fabrication, and characterization of a vertically stacked 2T0C DRAM cell employing CaNb₂O₆ (CNO) as the gate dielectric and MoS₂ as the channel material. Utilizing a substrate-assisted molten salt growth strategy, high-quality CNO nanoflakes with excellent dielectric properties were synthesized and integrated with exfoliated MoS₂ to form back-gate field-effect transistors. The vertical stacking of two such transistors, separated by a low-κ h-BN interlayer, enabled the realization of a monolithic three-dimensional (3D) 2T0C DRAM architecture exhibiting robust data retention exceeding 2000 seconds, multilevel storage capability, and excellent endurance. Comparative analysis demonstrates the promising scalability and operational stability of this 2D-material-based approach relative to state-of-the-art DRAM technologies. Overall, the research presented in this thesis establishes new paradigms for DRAM technology by leveraging the unique properties of 2D materials and innovative device architectures. The strategies demonstrated offer significant potential for the realization of high-density, energy-efficient, and scalable memory systems. These advancements hold significant promise for the evolution of memory technology, opening new possibilities for future technological progress in data storage and processing.
items.venue: PolyU Institutional Research Archive (Hong Kong Polytechnic University)

items.title: TCAD-Assisted Deep-Learning Surrogate Modeling of a Dielectric-Modulated FinFET Biosensor for HER2-Equivalent Dielectric-State Sensing
items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a TCAD-assisted deep-learning surrogate framework for a dielectric-modulated FinFET biosensor under a HER2-equivalent effective dielectric-state sensing condition. The first part establishes the device modeling of a three-dimensional silicon FinFET with an analyte-accessible nanocavity, where the nanocavity permittivity modulates the gate-to-channel electrostatic coupling and produces measurable changes in the drain-current transfer characteristics. The second part develops a multilayer-perceptron (MLP) surrogate model using logarithmic current and dielectric representations to reconstruct TCAD dielectric anchor states and predict the held-out HER2-equivalent k = 8 dielectric state. The framework is further extended to cavity-length and cavity-thickness screening , transconductance prediction, I ON /I OFF extraction, sensing-metric analysis, and computational-cost evaluation. For the surrogate-predicted k = 8 case, the extracted sensing parameters indicate an I ON /I OFF ratio of 1.72 × 10 9 , a threshold-voltage sensitivity of 0.26912, and a sensitivity of approximately 6300. Unlike direct clinical detection studies, the present work is restricted to device-level dielectric-to-electrical response prediction. It does not model HER2-antibody binding, concentration-dependent biomolecule loading, biological sample variability, or fabricated-device validation. Overall, the results show that the proposed surrogate can reproduce TCAD transfer characteristics, perform bounded interpolation at the HER2-equivalent dielectric state, and rapidly screen FinFET dielectric-geometry trends for biosensor design exploration.

items.title: TACT-KV: Tri-Axis Cosine Transform for Compressing Volumetric KV Caches in Medical VLMs
items.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) applied to 3D medical scans face a structural memory wall. A single CT or MRI volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, and the resulting key-value (KV) cache scales linearly with both batch and context. Existing KV compression methods operate on the cache's feature or token statistics, or apply 1D and 2D transforms, leaving the three-axis spatial structure in the cache unexploited. We propose TACT-KV (Tri-Axis Cosine Transform), a calibration-free KV compression method that exploits strong spatial correlations in visual KV states along all three anatomical axes of 3D scans. This correlation concentrates the KV cache energy under a frequency-domain transform. TACT-KV applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins via reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. We derive a close-form relation: the distortion reduction from adaptive bit allocation is dominated by the spectral concentration of the transformed cache. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs in our main comparison. The same advantage reproduces on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks, indicating that the benefit of exploiting three-axis structure generalizes beyond medical imaging. At equal high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TACT-KV scales the decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to $8\times$.

items.title: Synaptic Multi-Weight Wafer-Scale Domain Wall Magnetic Tunnel Junctions Driven by Spin Orbit Torque
items.abstract: Spintronic synaptic devices based on magnetic random access memory (MRAM) are a rapidly evolving class within the analog neuromorphic architecture. However, obtaining the multi-weight or analog behavior desired for improved neural network inference accuracy in scaled MRAM remains a challenge. In this study, we demonstrate and tune up to eight distinct resistance levels in 300 mm wafer-scale magnetic tunnel junction artificial synapses driven by spin orbit torque. By varying the applied in-plane field, multi-weight resistance states emerge through domain wall nucleation and pinning. These multi-weight states appear stochastically and can be addressed with an iterative programming algorithm to program a specific resistance. Electromagnetic simulations indicate the multiple states are due to domain wall nucleation mediated by in-plane field and applied voltage. Implementation of the measured multi-weight devices in a neural network yields a 96.1% inference accuracy using the MNIST dataset if all devices provide the same number of multi-weight states. When experimental device-to-device variation is included, the accuracy is 48.6%. Overall, this work demonstrates a route towards multi-weight artificial synapse MRAM, establishing a path towards scalable neuromorphic systems based on spintronics.

items.title: Synapse‐Integrated Physical Unclonable Functions for Trusted Inference in Neuromorphic Computing
items.abstract: Secure neuromorphic computing requires compact hardware primitives that can authenticate devices and protect synaptic states without relying on stored keys or large physical arrays. Here, we propose a noise‐spectroscopy physical unclonable function (NS PUF) based on a compact floating‐body (FB) transistor with a charge‐trap layer (CTL). In this platform, the low‐frequency noise power spectral density serves as a frequency‐domain fingerprint of stochastic FB dynamics, while the CTL provides programmable device states for reconfigurable synaptic security. Device geometry diversifies the spectral response landscape, enabling multiple device‐specific responses to be generated from the same compact physical array. The spectral responses are converted into bitmap challenge‐response pairs and optimized to suppress redundant readouts and improve response diversity. The NS PUF‐derived keys can be used to lock or reconfigure synaptic weight‐mapping rules based on bipartite‐sort coding, linking intrinsic device entropy with trusted inference in secure neuromorphic operation. By assigning new security roles to two technologies already compatible with modern microelectronics, FB dynamics and CTL programmability, this work establishes a scalable hardware foundation for secure neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Substrate-Dependent Cryogenic and UV Performance of AlGaN/AlN/GaN HEMTs and Photodetectors
items.abstract: Abstract AlGaN/AlN/GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) and metal–semiconductor–metal photodetectors (MSM-PDs) were integrated on Al2O3 and 4H-SiC substrates to quantify the impact of substrate selection on cryogenic electrical stability and ultraviolet (UV) optoelectronic performance. The HEMT/SiC structure exhibited a higher peak transconductance (gm) of 1.56 mS/2.34 mS at 300 K/130 K compared to the HEMT/Al2O3 structure (1.27 mS/1.83 mS). At 300 K, the gate-source voltage corresponding to peak gm was −0.3 V for the HEMT/SiC compared to −2.1 V for the HEMT/Al2O3, indicating different strain-induced polarization effects. For integrated sensing, the peak relative spectral response wavelengths were observed at 300 nm (on Al2O3) and 370 nm (on SiC). High-resolution characterization confirms that improved crystal quality and carrier transport in SiC-based heterostructures result from reduced lattice mismatch at the GaN/SiC interface. These findings establish the AlGaN/AlN/GaN-on-SiC platform as a compelling architecture for high-efficiency, switching GaN electronics and integrated cryogenic optoelectronic applications.

items.title: Substrate Yield Enhancement Enabled by Advanced Packaging Metrology System
items.abstract: Detecting dimensional errors in substrate fabrication induced by the manufacturing process is a challenge for high-density substrates. Such detection is especially important in advanced substrates that incorporate high-speed impedance-controlled circuits where a small change in linewidth and spacing can impact circuit performance. A 100% metrology inspection system has been developed that can detect these dimensional errors and provide the data needed to correct these errors. The Beltronics system can perform up to 10-billion line width, line space and pad diameter measurements on a 510mm x 515mm substrate in 5 minutes, to an accuracy of 0.15 microns. This new system provides real-time feedback to enable continuous inline process control to monitor the sizes of all features on the substrate during the fabrication process. The system compares the dimensions of features on the substrate to dimensions from the original CAD data to detect and classify defects. This paper presents an overview of this new technology and explains how it can be used to detect machine dependent distortions, such as non-linearities in the lithography lens or direct write exposure system, and design dependent distortions resulting from etch rates varying as a function of feature size, shape, and metal density in the neighborhood of each feature.

items.title: Solution‐Processed HZO–IGZO Thin Film Transistors for Multiclass Classification Tasks
items.abstract: In recent years, thin film transistors (TFTs) based on HfZrO (HZO) have made significant progress in the fields of memory and neuromorphic computing. However, the fabrication of conventional HZO TFTs usually relies on sophisticated techniques such as atomic layer deposition and rapid thermal annealing. Although these techniques improve device performance, they may increase cost and process complexity. To address this issue, this work proposes a low‐cost and simple solution‐based strategy for fabricating HZO TFTs. The fabricated devices exhibit typical counterclockwise hysteresis, successfully emulating various synaptic plasticity behaviors, as well as achieving stable multilevel conductance states under consecutive pulse stimulation. A three‐layer fully connected neural network constructed using the experimentally measured discrete conductance states of the devices achieves a recognition accuracy of 95% on the MNIST handwritten digit recognition task after 50 training epochs. Furthermore, the weight‐replacement model is extended to a ResNet‐18 deep convolutional neural network, attaining an accuracy of 87% on a 102‐class flower image classification task. The proposed solution‐based process, which requires no complex vacuum equipment, is simple and low‐cost, providing a feasible technological pathway for the development of low‐cost neuromorphic computing and image enhancement applications based on HZO TFTs.

items.title: Scaling Up Analog CIM: A Simulation Framework for Topology-Aware Mapping
items.abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) enables energy-efficient AI inference by performing in-situ matrix multiplication. The growing demand for deploying larger models motivates chiplet integration to expand CIM capacity. However, simulation abstractions based on local operator costs and aggregate communication metrics obscure the impact of weight-mapping topology when CIM system scales up. We develop a phase analysis that quantifies how strongly mapping topology affects system performance across hardware configurations and how mapping optimization translates into latency gains. To evaluate and exploit this design space, we present Isobar, a simulation platform integrating CIM decompositions, heterogeneous execution, and resource modeling. Validated against silicon measurements and cycle-accurate simulation, Isobar provides reliable cost estimates that enable effective mapping search across model and hardware configurations. For Gemma-7B prefill, Isobar-guided mapping reduces communication time by 23.3% and end-to-end latency by 18.6% relative to the strongest baseline. Isobar's system-level modeling show that analog CIM retains energy-efficiency potential relative to GPU when scaled to thousands of dies, and identify topology-aware mapping as a key design dimension for efficient execution.

items.title: Scalable laser cleaning on versatile CNT pellicles
items.abstract: As the demand for high resolution patterning in semiconductor manufacturing continues to grow, the adoption of EUV lithography has been expanding. In such EUV processes, CNT pellicle, which offer high EUV transmittance, thermal stability, and excellent mechanical properties have attracted considerable attention as a promising candidate to replace conventional pellicle materials. However, CNT pellicles can be exposed to particle contamination during both fabrication process and EUV lithography, which can induce pattern defects during subsequent exposure process. Therefore, the development of an effective particle removal technique is essential. In our previous study, we demonstrated that laser irradiation can effectively remove particles without causing damage to the irradiated region of the CNT pellicle. In this study, CNT pellicles were fabricated at a lab scale using a wet process, which allows free control of the CNT composition and membrane thickness. The resulting variations in pellicle structure were used to evaluate the applicability of the laser cleaning method. Additionally, a photodetector was employed to capture the moment of particle removal in real time during laser irradiation. Furthermore, particle removal was achieved not only by laser irradiation at a single spot but also via line scanning, demonstrating strong potential for application to practical pellicle cleaning processes.

items.title: Scalable infrastructure for strontium optical clocks with integrated photonics
items.abstract: Optical atomic clocks provide exceptionally accurate and precise signals for timekeeping and precision measurements, but they require high-power, free-space laser configurations that limit scalability. We introduce and explore a scalable infrastructure for strontium (Sr) optical-lattice clocks that incorporates co-design of atomic-beam slowing and a magneto-optical trap (MOT) from an effusion source, generation of complex, three-dimensional free-space laser configurations with a photonic integrated circuit (PIC) and metasurface (MS) optics, and laser stabilization to a frequency-comb supercontinuum generated with integrated nonlinear photonics. With these elements, we realize MOTs of all stable strontium isotopes ($^{84}$Sr, $^{86}$Sr, $^{87}$Sr, $^{88}$Sr) with populations commensurate with natural abundances, demonstrating precise beam control and robustness. Access to laser-cooled alkaline-earth atoms with scalable integrated photonics enables system engineering for optical clocks, quantum sensing, and quantum information, and our experiments demonstrate extensible technologies that advance toward a Sr optical clock largely free of bulk optics.

items.title: SEU Hardened Multi-Context Spintronic FPGA
items.abstract: Due to susceptibility to radiation-induced soft errors and resource constraints implementing large and complex designs on field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) in harsh environments is challenging. Therefore, to mitigate these issues, this paper proposes an innovative approach through the introduction of a single event upset (SEU)-hardened spintronic FPGA architecture that incorporates multi-context capabilities. Leveraging the non-volatile properties of magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ), the proposed design can store two/four distinct configurations internally, eliminating the dependence on external non-volatile memory which significantly boosts the system performance. Additionally, through post-layout simulation, we demonstrate our design immunity to SEU, which enhances its reliability and operational stability in environments susceptible to radiation-induced soft errors. The efficiency of the proposed design was also evaluated using the ROSSETA benchmark, which serves as a representative model for real-world FPGA applications.

items.title: Retaining Hole Conduction Using a Germanium Seed Layer for High- k HfO2 ALD on Salt-Assisted APCVD Tungsten Diselenide
items.abstract: Abstract Tungsten diselenide (WSe2) is the leading p-type channel candidate for two-dimensional complementary field effect transistors (CFETs). However, depositing high-k gate dielectric on its inert basal plane has still been a challenge. Modified atomic layer deposition (ALD) chemistries to avoid unintentional doping, plasma surface treatments, and interfacial seed layers are among a few promising methods for high-k integration. Extensive studies have been done on molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) to identify possible routes to high-performance NFET. This study presents a possible route to integrating high-k HfO2 on salt-assisted atmospheric pressure chemical vapor deposition (SA-CVD)-grown WSe2 on Si/SiO2 wafers. We compare evaporated Hf, Ti, and Ge seed layers, oxidized in ambient, prior to high-k ALD on SA-CVD WSe2. Because salt-assisted growths bind defect density to local precursor flux, plasma-based surface treatments can damage or modify the underlying channel material, making seed layers a favorable option over plasma processes. ALD without any seed layer suppresses the hole branch of both exfoliated and CVD WSe2 transistors, where peak drive currents were lowered by roughly six orders of magnitude. Seedless HfO2 ALD, Hf and Ti seeds eliminate hole conduction below 0.5 nA/μm. Germanium is the only one of the three seeds that we study that preserves the hole branch, at least at the level of an unseeded reference device at equal gate overdrive, and shows a +40 V threshold voltage shift, making the device hole dominant. Therefore, Ge is a promising seed for retaining hole conduction in WSe2 PFETs, and the seed-ALD high-k HfO2 is a possible dielectric stack for top-gated PFETs.

items.title: Proving That a GPU, NPU, DPU or Other Device Consumed the Intended Command, Used Current Memory Translations and Produced Only the Declared Effect
items.abstract: AI workloads reach hardware through runtimes, drivers, command queues, firmware and IOMMU/SMMU translations before a GPU, NPU, DPU or other device produces an effect. Permission to compute, driver acceptance, a descriptor that was inspected a moment ago and the host’s current page tables do not prove what the device actually did. A descriptor can change after it was checked; a stale IOTLB entry can direct DMA to the wrong page; a reset or firmware update can reuse a queue slot for another tenant; a replayed command can be consumed twice; and a SmartNIC or peer-to-peer path can produce a network or storage effect that no one authorized. This disclosure describes a vendor-neutral, non-actuating method for reconstructing silicon-level consistency from evidence. Each hardware command is bound to an original operation, principal and permitted class. The descriptor the device actually consumes is compared by digest with the approved one. Queue, mapping, firmware and device-incarnation generations must be current; DMA bounds and permissions must hold; translation invalidation must be acknowledged; admission must cover every effect path and be replay-safe; and device completion and the observed effect must correspond to the original operation. Results are combined in three-valued logic: a proven contradiction yields CONTRADICTED even when other evidence is missing, full support yields SUPPORTED, and gaps yield UNRESOLVED — in particular, missing effect telemetry is never treated as proof that no effect occurred. The document provides a 60-stage, six-phase silicon workflow and a separate 60-stage integratedembodiment, each with flowcharts, 72 technical invariants, twelve hardware variations (GPU, DPU/SmartNIC, CPU trusted domains, chiplets, firmware, peripherals), 48 formal relations, 60 engineering checkpoints, a comparison with existing mechanisms (IOMMU/SMMU and ATS invalidation, PCIe IDE and TDISP, confidential-computing device assignment, SR-IOV and function-level reset, doorbell and queue protections, device attestation with SPDM, GPU command validation and DPU offload) and anon-actuating reference evaluator in Python, JavaScript and Go with 90 shared synthetic vectors, all passing. It is not hardware-validated or certified; the laboratory is synthetic, self-authored and not peer reviewed. The author is open to acquihire or strategic collaboration. Keywords: AI safety; hardware security; GPU; NPU; DPU; SmartNIC; command descriptors; DMA; IOMMU; SMMU; IOTLB invalidation; ATS; TOCTOU; device reset; function-level reset; device incarnation; firmware update; replay prevention; PCIe IDE; TDISP; SPDM attestation; confidential computing; three-valued logic
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Prediction of Deep Neural Network for TCAD Analysis of Degradation Induced by Near-Interface Displacement Defects in 4H-SiC MOSFETs
items.abstract: Silicon carbide (SiC) devices used in space and nuclear environments are exposed to radiation that creates displacement defects (DDs), but the effect of DDs near the gate oxide/SiC interface has not been analyzed systematically. Using technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulation, this study analyzes how near-interface DDs in a 4H-SiC metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) affect the threshold voltage (Vth), transconductance (gm), and on-current (Ion), and builds deep neural network (DNN) models that predict these effects. The DDs were modeled as acceptor-like traps with varied energy levels, concentration, depth, lateral position, and distribution width. The degradation was largest at the channel entrance and the edge of the junction field-effect transistor (JFET) region. The center depth mattered little while the trap region reached the interface, whereas a small gap between the trap region and the interface strongly reduced the degradation. Shallow-level traps reduced Ion without shifting Vth, whereas only deep-level traps caused an actual Vth shift. The DNNs accurately predicted the degradation for new TCAD conditions in which the trap parameters simultaneously took values not used in training and outperformed grid interpolation and other regression models. The trained DNNs thus rapidly predict the degradation at the simulated lateral positions for radiation reliability assessment.

items.title: Polarized twin walls in a halide perovskite
items.abstract: Halide perovskites have emerged as promising materials for next-generation photovoltaics, laser sources, and X-ray detectors. There is intense debate as to whether some photoactive halide perovskites exhibit ferroelectric behavior and whether it might be possible to utilize the bulk photovoltaic effect to enhance the performance of halide perovskite solar cells. Here, using low-dose scanning transmission electron microscopy, we identify ferroelastic twin walls in vapor-deposited CsPbI 3 thin films, parallel to {110} and {112}. Remarkably, despite CsPbI 3 being centrosymmetric and nonpolar, we observe directly that Pb atoms shift at {110} twin walls driving a local ferroelectric-like polarization. These polar twin walls form an intrinsic array of nanoscale interfaces, spaced ~30 to 50 nm apart, embedded within the nonpolar perovskite lattice. In contrast, {112} twin walls do not show a polar displacement of Pb but strongly suppress octahedral tilt and off-center Cs atom displacements, revealing a different untapped structural degree of freedom. These findings reveal previously hidden nanoscale polarization in halide perovskite semiconductors, opening opportunities for enhanced conductivity and photovoltaic behavior through domain wall engineering.
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Physics-aware Jacobian calibration for bridging the simulation-to-real gap in LDMOS modeling
items.abstract: Abstract The simulation-to-real gap between idealized TCAD simulations and experimental data from fabricated devices limits the accuracy of data-driven modeling for semiconductor devices. This work proposes a Physics Aware Jacobian Calibration (PAJC) framework to improve neural network (NN) surrogate modeling of LDMOS devices under sparse experimental supervision. A Physics Prior Model (PPM) trained on large scale TCAD simulations provides first order response sensitivities through its Jacobian matrix, enabling corrections from a small set of experimental anchor samples to propagate across the design space. Using the corrected simulation data together with experimental samples, a Calibrated Proxy Model (CPM) is constructed for device performance prediction. Experimental results on LDMOS devices show that the CPM achieves an average Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 2.28% on an unseen experimental test set while preserving physically consistent trends between design parameters and device performance. The proposed framework provides a scalable approach for physics informed AI assisted semiconductor modeling under realistic process variations.
items.venue: Journal of Physics D Applied Physics

items.title: Physical mechanisms and fundamental limits of high-NA EUV lithography: A multi-physics simulation framework at the 8 nm half-pitch node.
items.abstract: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography at NA = 0.55 and λ = 13.5 nm shifts optical patterning into a domain where three mutually coupled physical effects must be handled on equal footing: (i) vector electromagnetic diffraction, in which the marginal-rayinclination θmax = 33.4◦ excites the longitudinal field component Ez and reduces TM-polarisation contrast by 0.76% at NA = 0.55 under dipole illumination—well below the theoretical worst-case unpolarised Richards–Wolf bound ∆C/C ≈ −NA2/4 = −7.6%, which is projected to reach −12.3% at NA = 0.70; (ii) quantum photon shot noise, in which only a few EUV photons (Eγ = 91.8 eV) are deposited per pixel at working doses, imposing a physical floor on line-width roughness (LWR) that resist chemistry alone cannot remove; and (iii) thin-film standing waves whose period Λ = λ/(2nr ) = 6.92 nm inside the resist film is roughly an order of magnitude shorter than the deep-UV equivalent, requiring sub-nanometre control of post-exposure-bake (PEB) diffusion lengths. A coupled GPU-accelerated simulation platform is presented that combines recursive transfer-matrix multilayer reflectivity, a partially coherent vector aerial-image engine, a four-stage resist pipeline, and Monte Carlo stochastic sampling (N = 1000 trials for CD-error statistics, N = 200 for line-width-roughness statistics, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and an independent-seed robustness check). At the 8 nm half-pitch node the framework yields NILS = 2.152 for vertical lines and NILS = 1.810 for horizontal lines, a 17.3% H–V asymmetry accounted for by the closed-form anamorphic ratio NILSH /NILSV = (My /Mx)−1/4 = 0.841. Monte Carlo analysis gives LWR 3σ = 2.10 nm for MOR SnOx versus 6.93 nm and 4.77 nm for conventional and high-NA CAR resists at their respective nominal doses. A Shannon-entropy analysis of the stochastic edge-gradient field gives H ≈ 15.78 bits; because this quantity retains a measurable grid-size dependence under a binning-invariance test, it is reported as an information-theoretic descriptor of edge disorder rather than as a strict thermodynamic bound. All quantitative results are simulation outputs benchmarked against published High-NA EUV data.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Novel Interconnect Materials for Advanced Packaging Assembly Processes
items.abstract: As advanced packaging continues to drive towards heterogeneous integration, new materials need to be developed to address the many challenges faced in the assembly process. Development of novel materials for the various assembly processes is crucial to ensuring high yield for the assembly process for reliable SiP applications, and high density, fine pitch interconnects. As ultra-fine pitch flip-chips become prevalent in advanced packaging, with reduced standoff of flip-chips and other IC packages, cleaning becomes ever more challenging, especially as the chip and package sizes increase. The shift towards using semiconductor grade ultra-low residue no-clean flip-chip fluxes, which eliminates the cleaning process, is therefore one of the solutions for overcoming these challenges. The flux residue left behind after the soldering process is minimal and is compatible with the underfill or molding materials used in the subsequent processes. Further, adhesive agents, which leave near zero residue, have also been developed to enable fluxless soldering for wafer/die bonding. Another challenge is the warpage induced open joints defects as the chips are becoming thinner and larger, and thermo-compression bonding (TCB), and laser-assisted bonding (LAB) are being explored as alternatives for the typical mass reflow process, to improve process yield with robust flux materials. With more semiconductor chips and smaller components packed into a smaller footprint, the deposition of solder paste for high density SiP applications has become very challenging. For fine feature solder paste applications, the quality of fine solder alloy powder, flux formulations, and solder paste rheology, are crucial to achieve consistent solder paste deposition and good soldering performance. Particularly, for solder paste applications down to 100um or less, fine solder alloy powder, robust flux formulations, and solder paste rheology have been developed to achieve consistent solder paste deposition and good soldering performance. Due to some packaging design where printing of solder paste may not be possible, dispensing or jetting can also be used as an alternative. This presentation will cover innovative materials for advanced packaging and heterogeneous integration, including novel ultra-low residue flux formulations for flip chip attach that is compatible with underfill and molding compound, adhesive agent for fluxless soldering, and solder paste for ultra-fine pitch printing. These novel materials are critical enablers for high density packaging applications. Use cases for high density SiP modules, TCB and LAB, for advanced packaging and 2.5D modules, will be discussed as well.

items.title: Neural Architecture Search of Time-to-First-Spike-Coded Spiking Neural Networks for Efficient Eye-based Emotion Recognition
items.abstract: Eye-based emotion recognition enables eyewear devices to perceive users' emotional states and support emotion-aware interaction. However, deploying such functionality on their resource-limited embedded hardware remains challenging. Time-to-first-spike (TTFS)-coded spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a promising solution due to their extremely sparse and energy-efficient computation, where each neuron emits at most one binary spike. While prior works have primarily focused on improving TTFS SNN training algorithms, the role of network architecture has been largely overlooked. This is particularly critical, as spike timing in TTFS SNNs is tightly coupled with architectural design, and eye-based emotion recognition requires compact yet highly efficient networks. In this paper, we propose TNAS-ER, the first neural architecture search (NAS) framework tailored to TTFS SNNs for eye-based emotion recognition. TNAS-ER presents a novel ANN-assisted search strategy that leverages a ReLU-based ANN counterpart to guide architecture optimization and stabilize training of the TTFS SNN. TNAS-ER employs an evolutionary algorithm, with weighted and unweighted average recall jointly defined as fitness objectives for emotion recognition. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TNAS-ER achieves high recognition performance with significantly improved efficiency. Furthermore, we evaluate TNAS-ER on neuromorphic hardware, confirming its superior energy efficiency and strong potential for real-world applications.
items.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

items.title: Mid-IR diffraction gratings fabricated via nanoimprint lithography for chirped pulse amplification
items.abstract: Abstract Lasers emitting in the 2 μm spectral region have attracted considerable attention in recent years owing to their wide-ranging applications in science and industry, including the detection of atmospheric constituents like H 2 O, surgical procedures in medicine, and LIDAR technologies. In industry, they can be utilized in high-precision machining and materials engineering. For these latter purposes, a high-power laser is needed. This can be achieved by amplifying the laser pulse, typically using chirped pulse amplification (CPA). The crucial component of CPA, used for the compression and stretching steps, is the grating waveguide structure (GWS). In the present paper, we explore the fabrication of GWSs via nanoimprint lithography (NIL) for operation at a central wavelength of 2050 nm. The GWSs were integrated into the topmost hafnium oxide (HfO₂) layer of a multilayer HfO₂/SiO₂ dielectric mirror. The fabrication process comprised master wafer production via laser interference lithography, stamp fabrication, NIL patterning, and reactive-ion etching. The desired etch depth in HfO 2 was a key challenge, which was addressed by implementing a chromium hard mask and a Taguchi experimental design. Scanning electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy revealed slight deviations from the designed GWS dimensions, mainly in the duty cycle. Consequently, the maximum diffraction efficiency was slightly blue-shifted and measured to be 97% at 2030 nm, i.e., lower than the 99% predicted theoretically. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of using NIL for large-area GWS fabrication with high diffraction efficiency.

items.title: Metrology-Driven Sample Preparation for Advanced Microelectronics Using TESCAN FemtoChisel with Intelligent Multigas Processing, LPL, and AI-Enabled Correlative Workflows
items.abstract: Advanced microelectronics metrology increasingly depends on how the sample is prepared before inspection. In heterogeneous packages, the region of interest may be buried beneath combinations of mold compound, silicon, copper, redistribution layers, dielectrics, underfill, and organic substrate materials. The measurement challenge is therefore not only one of imaging resolution, but also one of physical access: the sample must be opened to the correct level, the exposed structures must remain interpretable, and the preparation geometry must provide useful views of internal layers and interfaces. This paper presents a metrology-driven sample-preparation workflow using the TESCAN FemtoChisel ultrashort-pulsed laser platform. The workflow combines femtosecond laser machining, intelligent multigas processing, laser protective layer strategies, imaging feedback, and AI-enabled process development. The broader platform capability includes controlled package opening, layer exposure, access-window creation, cross-section preparation, and correlative workflows with optical, confocal, SEM/FIB, and X-ray imaging. In this paper, the experimental results focus specifically on demonstrations relevant to metrology access: controlled laser delayering. Specifically, it is shown that the laser process can expose selected package levels and provide intermediate inspection states. Through creation of inverted pyramid structures we demonstrate the ability to stop at the layer of interest. The results support a preparation-to-measurement framework in which laser machining is used not simply to remove material, but to create measurement-ready sample states. Intelligent multigas processing and protective-layer concepts expand the usable process window by improving debris management and boundary preservation. AI-enabled process development and correlative navigation provide a path toward more repeatable and target-aware preparation. Together, these elements position FemtoChisel as a platform for creating controlled access geometries that support advanced package metrology, failure analysis, and process development.

items.title: Memory Fit: Architectural Support for Page Placement by Learning Models of Good Behavior
items.abstract: Server main memory is increasingly heterogeneous, incorporating technologies such as zswap, CXL memory expanders, and emerging phase-change memories (PCM). To decide where to place pages, operating systems have to choose between efficient but coarse-grained access bits, out-of-band profiling, or costly runtime instrumentation. This paper proposes memory fit, a hardware abstraction that provides precise and accurate page placement information to an operating system. Memory fit measures how well a page "fits" each type of memory in the system. Memory fit separates the mechanism of measuring affinity between pages and memories from the OS policy of choosing which pages to move when. The paper describes soft trace matching (STM), a computationally and space efficient algorithm to compute memory fit. The key technical insight behind STM is that it can estimate memory fit by comparing accesses to a page with a learned model of "good" traces for a memory. We have implemented memory fit and STM in a BOOMv3 RISC-V processor running Linux 6.6. On extended GUPS, memory fit placements recover 2.2-3.8 times as much of the performance gap to optimal placement as Linux TPP. For Redis with equal DRAM and PCM capacities, placements selected by memory fit recover 80% of the performance gap, versus 19% for TPP, in a placement replay. Memory fit requires only 64 bits of state per 4 KiB page and can be updated on every main-memory access with only a 1.2% overhead of OS kernel notification processing.

items.title: MCUFlowNet: Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Optical Flow on Microcontrollers
items.abstract: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/emedia-research-lab/esat-stadius/mcuflownet/mcuflownet.

items.title: Low Thermal Damage Laser Lift-off (LLO) Enabling Multi-Cycle Carrier Wafers Reuse for Advanced Packaging
items.abstract: Fusion and hybrid bonding are becoming critical enablers in advanced packaging for die-to-wafer (D2W), high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Laser lift-off (LLO) employing short-pulsed IR laser beam provides a clean and efficient method to release permanently bonded Si carrier wafers without need of a glue layer or backside grinding processes. LLO enables multiple carrier wafer reuse cycles, offering significant cost reduction and environmental sustainability benefits. However, LLO may generate the thermal and mechanical stresses during LLO to impact device integrity. This study investigates thermal damage mechanisms and mitigation strategies for stacked structures during carrier wafer release. Metal silicide phase transitions were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect thermal exposure 200–500 °C, while tracer ion diffusion analysis via time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) identified thermal exposures in the 800–1000 °C range. These results were calibrated against 60-second rapid thermal annealing (RTA) references to establish a thermal budget for LLO induced energy exposure. The results of these thermal damage experiments were used to model a broader spectrum of stacked materials. The absorption through the stack and the resulting heat transfer were simulated. Since experimental measurements generally require orders of magnitude for longer timescales than laser exposure, it is challenging to compare the energy spike in LLO simulation to a thermal budget based on RTA processing. If for a given stack it has been demonstrated experimentally that the heat energy from the laser is at an acceptable level, then it is reasonable to assume that other stacks that show equal or less heat energy in simulation are also acceptable. This integrated experimental–simulation framework supports optimized stack engineering, ensuring device integrity and sustainable multi-cycle carrier wafer reuse for advanced packaging.

items.title: INSIGHT-X: Multimodal VLM Assistant for Artifact Localization, and Mitigation Guidance in X-ray Inspection
items.abstract: Advanced semiconductor packages rely on X-ray CT and laminography for non-destructive inspection of buried interconnects and internal structures. However, dense metal features and heterogeneous materials often introduce artifacts, including ring artifacts, beam-hardening streaks, geometric distortions, and missing-cone artifacts. These artifacts obscure critical features during inspection, reduce reconstruction fidelity, and complicate defect interpretation, requiring expert-driven and iterative troubleshooting. To address these challenges, we propose INSIGHT-X, a vision–language model framework for artifact diagnosis, localization, root-cause and mitigation in X-ray inspection workflows. INSIGHT-X formulates artifact analysis as a multimodal question-answering task by integrating reconstructed X-ray images, artifact annotations, and expert knowledge into an artifact-centric dataset. Through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the model learns to identify artifact types, localize affected regions, and generate interpretable explanations. The system also provides artifact-aware cause and mitigation recommendations, including general acquisition and reconstruction adjustments, and calibration guidance. By combining visual understanding, spatial localization with explainable answers, INSIGHT-X transforms expert knowledge into a scalable AI assistant for improving inspection consistency, accelerating troubleshooting, and supporting decision-making in advanced semiconductor manufacturing.

items.title: Hardware-Aware On-Chip Learning with a Scalable Single-Transistor-based Neuromorphic Platform
items.abstract: Abstract Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a promising paradigm for energy-efficient computing, yet enabling on-chip training in analog hardware platforms remains challenging because internal neuronal states are difficult to access. Here, we present a hardware–algorithm co-designed neuromorphic architecture for state-access-free learning using the accessible signals of a single-transistor (1T) platform. Current-based surrogate gradient (cSG) and eligible leaky integrate-and-fire encoder (eLIFE) modules generate learning signals from spike events without explicit membrane-potential readout. Co-integrated 1T-synapses, 1T-neurons, and 1T-cSG devices demonstrate synaptic weight storage, leaky integrate-and-fire neuronal dynamics, and surrogate gradient signal generation in a measured unit architecture. At the algorithmic level, simulations demonstrate competitive performance using small-scale networks on F-MNIST, S-MNIST, and SHD and large-scale networks on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10DVS, DVS128Gesture, ImageNet, and COCO. Furthermore, hardware-aware simulations of an analog on-chip continual-learning framework demonstrate learning of previously unseen classes with limited average accuracy loss on previously learned classes. Under the adopted model, estimated inference energy is more than 60\% lower than that of fully digital SNN baselines. These results provide a unified device–algorithm framework for state-access-free learning in adaptive neuromorphic systems.

items.title: Fluorination enhanced lithographic performance of sulfonium-based molecular nonchemically-amplified resist
items.abstract: BackgroundNonchemically amplified resists (n-CARs) have emerged as a promising candidate for the next-generation of resists. Sulfonium-based n-CARs exhibit the capability of forming patterns with high resolution and low LER. However, their practical application is severely hindered by the low sensitivity.AimIt is expected to improve the sensitivity of sulfonium-based n-CARs by enhancing the absorption of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) or electron irradiation, thereby increasing the yield of secondary electrons and promoting the subsequent chemical reactions.ApproachFluorine has a higher EUV absorption cross-section than that of carbon and oxygen elements. Introduction of F-C bonds to resist matrix will boost the EUV photons or electrons absorption and induce the occurrence of new photochemical reactions. We synthesized a multisulfonium-based molecular glass (MG) functionalized with pentafluorobenzylphenylmethylsulfonium (AD-4PF), together with the nonfluorinated MG of AD-4Ph. The lithographic performances of both resists were evaluated by electron beam lithography (EBL) and extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUVL).ResultsThe sensitivity of AD-4PF resist (2487 μC cm−2) was 30% higher than that of AD-4Ph model resist (3559 μC cm−2) in EBL, achieving well-defined 20 nm line/space (L/S) patterns at a dose of 2900 μC cm−2. A similar sensitivity improvement (112 versus 172 mJ cm−2) was observed in EUVL. Photochemical reaction confirmed that the solubility switch of both MG resist films originated from the cleavage of the bond of benzylic S+−CH2PF to form nonpolar methyl thioether.ConclusionsThe fluorinated AD-4PF molecular resist demonstrates high resolution and improved sensitivity, which has been confirmed by EBL and EUVL. The difference in sensitivity between the AD-4PF and AD-4Ph resists is mainly attributed to the significantly enhanced absorption cross-section, the reduced bond energy, and the additional possible dissociative electron attachment (DEA) process by fluorine incorporation.
items.venue: Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning Materials and Metrology

items.title: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving
items.abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.

items.title: Ferroelectric AlScN Four-Mode Reconfigurable Transistors Enabling Unified Logic, Memory, and Neuromorphic Computing
items.abstract: The increasing demand for data-centric and artificial intelligence workloads has intensified the need for device platforms that integrate logic, memory, and adaptive computing beyond conventional von Neumann architectures. Here, an aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN)-based nonvolatile four-mode reconfigurable field-effect transistor is demonstrated as a multifunctional device platform. By combining the large remanent polarization of AlScN with the ambipolar transport of the MoTe2 channel, the same transistor can be persistently programmed into logic nFET, logic pFET, memory-on, and memory-off states. These modes arise from polarization-controlled modulation of carrier injection and channel electrostatics, enabling a single device to function as a polarity-reconfigurable logic element, nonvolatile memory cell, and analog synaptic element. Programming is performed through voltage pulses applied to the source, drain, and back gate, while top-gate readout is decoupled from AlScN programming, enabling stable nonvolatile operation. Based on this device, a single-transistor ternary content-addressable memory cell concept and two-input reconfigurable multifunctional logic gates are demonstrated. The wide polarization-tunable memory window further supports multilevel cell memory and nearly linear long-term potentiation and depression for neuromorphic synaptic operation. These results establish ferroelectric AlScN as a robust platform for integrating reconfigurable logic, nonvolatile memory, associative search, and neuromorphic computing within a common device framework.

items.title: Exploring the sustainable scaling of AI dilemma: a projective study of corporations’ AI environmental impacts
items.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), raises environmental concerns extending beyond greenhouse gas emissions. Limited transparency from major providers hinders companies’ ability to evaluate their AI-related environmental impacts and achieve their net-zero targets. This paper proposes a methodology to estimate the environmental impact of a company’s AI portfolio, delivering actionable insights without requiring deep AI or Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) expertise. Using a modeling approach that incorporates increased AI usage, hardware efficiency, and electricity mix changes aligned with IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) scenarios, we forecast AI impacts through 2030. Under a high adoption scenario, driven by complex generative AI models and frameworks, AI electricity consumption could rise by a factor of 24.4. Mitigating this impact by 2030 demands coordinated efforts across the AI value chain. Isolated measures like hardware or model efficiency alone are insufficient. We call for standardized environmental assessment frameworks, increased transparency, and a “Return on Environment” metric to align AI development with sustainability goals.

items.title: Evaluating COTS components for the LIZARD payload on micropatterned dry adhesives
items.abstract: Abstract The Long-term Investigation of Zero-gravity, vAcuum, and RaDiation effects on geckomaterials (LIZARD) payload investigates the effects of the space environment on the adhesive properties of microstructured dry adhesives (MDA). MDA are elastomers with microstructured surfaces offering a promising solution for space applications. The LIZARD payload marks the first testing of MDA in real space conditions. A key focus during development was the pragmatic use of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components without compromising reliability. This paper details the challenging environment in low Earth orbit (LEO), COTS component selection and verification processes for the payloads deployment aboard the 12U AIOTY-CUBE satellite. A SPENVIS simulation determined that the majority of components will receive a total dose of 1.563 krad during the 1-year mission. A total ionizing dose test was conducted at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin. Critical components were subjected to $$\gamma$$ γ -radiation doses of up to 12 krad. All flight components passed the test unharmed. An ST890 MOSFET in the power supply of the designated microcontroller’s development board failed; presumably due to excessive charge build-up in its gate oxide. Thermal testing of the critical components confirmed an expected shift in the camera’s focus between temperature extremes; however, this does not affect the analysis results. AIOTY-CUBE’s lack of active stabilization necessitated an illumination test. Adversely oriented, incoming sunlight may significantly affect the built-in cameras’ image exposure. Adjusting the image exposure accordingly reliably mitigated the effect, ensuring accurate data collection and unaffected performance of image analysis tools. Redundancies for microcontrollers, non-volatile memory and file systems further enhance mission reliability. The conducted tests confirmed that the design decisions and component selections resulted in operational hardware capable of enduring the rigorous conditions encountered in LEO.

items.title: Engineering Energy‐Storage Interfaces With Atomic and Molecular Layer Deposition: From Surface Chemistry to Process Design
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The performance and lifetime of energy‐storage devices are determined at the interfaces between electrodes, electrolytes, and separators, where ion and charge transfer, parasitic reactions, and mechanical degradation originate within nanometers of the surface. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) and molecular layer deposition (MLD) enable precise engineering of these interfaces through self‐limiting surface reactions that produce conformal coatings with controlled thickness and composition, even on porous electrodes. Although ALD surface chemistry is well established on ideal oxide surfaces, energy‐storage materials present chemically and structurally complex surfaces, on which reaction mechanisms, growth per cycle, and coating function can differ. This Review develops a chemistry–process–structure–function framework that connects surface chemistry, precursor reaction pathways, and nucleation behavior with film structure, ionic transport, charge‐transfer kinetics, redox stability, and mechanical response. We examine growth on oxide, sulfide, metal, polymer, and carbon substrates and relate the films to their functions at cathodes, anodes, solid electrolytes, and separators in Li‐based and beyond‐Li batteries. We further assess process scalability in terms of precursor utilization, throughput, and energy consumption, and discuss in situ monitoring, post‐deposition characterization, and full‐cell test conditions needed to validate coating performance. These relationships are summarized as six design rules presented as a decision flow.

items.title: Energy-Time Optimal Decoding Using Expander-Graph LDPC Codes and Mesh Network Architecture
items.abstract: Within the Thompson VLSI model, the first energy optimal decoding schemes (up to polylogarithmic factors) that also reach clock cycle lower bounds are constructed. Let $N$ be block length. Then, there is an exponential error scaling function and a binary symmetric channel, such that for all $f(N)$ that scales to zero more slowly than this, there is a decoding scheme for this channel with error probability that scales as $O(f(N))$ that has number of clock cycles $T\le O(\sqrt{-\log(f(N)})\text{polylog}(N))$ and energy $E\le O(N\sqrt{-\log(f(N))}\text{polylog}(N))$. This matches fundamental lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. The technique uses expander-graph based LDPC codes, a mesh network architecture, and a parallelization technique. The key technical result needed for this is a lemma in graph theory. This lemma is used to show that communication graphs of bounded node degree can be routed through two- and three-dimensional mesh networks without overflowing the memory of any mesh node. Upper bounds are also extended to three dimensions.

items.title: Enabling Retraining-Free Accurate Inference in Analog Compute in Memory Accelerators
items.abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators compute matrix-vector products directly inside memory arrays, eliminating weight movement and promising order-of-magnitude gains in inference efficiency. However, converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on these arrays, and hardware-aware retraining is costly. We enable retraining-free, accurate inference of pretrained models on simple analog arrays with low-cost, shared calibration. Our key observation is that analog error depends on how each layer is represented on the array, and that this representation can be changed offline without changing the computation. We center the inputs and apply Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays, which keep shared reference errors spread and confine input mixing to each array. Across CNNs, vision transformers and LLMs up to 14B parameters on PCM and ReRAM, the method brings vision models and larger LLMs within a few points of floating-point accuracy and matches or approaches published hardware-aware training without training any weights. On ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, it restores ViT-B/16 from 37.4% to 82.9% and Phi-4 from 27.0% to 72.2%, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy.

items.title: Effect of photoacid generator loading and quencher on development pathways in a model chemically amplified photoresist
items.abstract: BackgroundThe development in photolithography proceeds through multiple steps that require precise monitoring to capture each procedure. Although standard sensitivity analysis defines the static dose-to-clear endpoint, these conventional metrics fail to resolve the time-dependent physical and chemical pathways that dictate final pattern quality.AimWe aim to determine the effect of photoacid generator (PAG) loading and quencher additives on the sensitivity and time-resolved development pathways of a model chemically amplified photoresist exposed under extreme ultraviolet (EUV).ApproachInitial sensitivity analysis on silicon substrates established a dose-to-clear reference window for all resist formulations. Using this defined exposure range, a quartz crystal microbalance with resistance monitoring tracked real-time dissolution kinetics from low doses through full clearance in a diluted developer.ResultsDevelopment behavior was categorized into four distinct modes based on resonant frequency and motional resistance. Increasing PAG concentration or exposure dose systematically shifted the observed development behavior from diffusion-dominated uptake toward rapid bulk dissolution.ConclusionsSamples exhibiting similar final thicknesses can evolve through fundamentally distinct time-resolved development pathways. Here, we report a model photoresist formulation that transitions from swelling (at 5 wt.% PAG) to nonswelling behavior (at 10 and 20 wt.% PAG) during dissolution in a diluted developer. In addition, resists containing a photo-decomposable quencher required a higher exposure dose than their quencher-free counterparts to achieve similar dissolution behavior. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that real-time kinetic measurements are essential to capture the critical, transient interfacial states that govern EUV resist dissolution.
