items.abstract: The synthesis of boron nanoparticles (BNPs) at different temperatures using the dual-pulsed laser ablation (DPLA) method was investigated. A Q-switched Nd: YAG laser with dual wavelengths of 532 and 1064 nm was used to ablate a solid boron target. BNP growth with 0.5% Ni and 0.5% Co catalysts was facilitated through a vapor-solid process in a quartz tube furnace under controlled temperature and pressure with flowing argon (Ar). X-ray diffraction (XRD) revealed diffraction features consistent with crystalline boron structures, with several reflections corresponding to α-boron. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) revealed nanoscale particles with temperature-dependent morphology. Image analysis showed mean particle diameters of 6.24, 3.68, and 1.49 nm for BNPs synthesized at 450, 550, and 650 °C, respectively. The corresponding lattice distances were 0.37, 0.35, and 0.33 nm, indicating potential relevance to hydrogen storage applications. Raman spectroscopy revealed characteristic vibrational modes associated with the BNPs. UV–Vis spectroscopy, Tauc analysis, and four-point probe measurements were used to investigate their optical and electrical properties. The optical bandgap increased from 3.72 to 3.80 eV with increasing synthesis temperature, while electrical conductivity increased from 0.198 to 0.249 S cm -1 , with approximately linear current–voltage characteristics. These results demonstrate temperature-dependent structural, optical, and electrical characteristics of the synthesized BNPs and their relevance to semiconductor-related applications. Furthermore, a resistive memory device incorporating the 650 °C BNPs into a PVP matrix exhibited an ON/OFF current ratio of approximately 7 × 10 4 , endurance exceeding 10 4 cycles, and retention of up to 10 6 s. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the synthesized BNPs for nonvolatile resistive memory applications.

items.title: TOMAS: Operation-Aware Hybrid of In-Memory AI Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Transformer Inference -- simulation code and data
items.abstract: Hybrid-IMC v2.0 Simulation code, results, and parameter provenance for "TOMAS: Operation-Aware Hybrid of In-Memory AI Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Transformer Inference." What's new in v2.0 Engine v2: one array, digital, and system model for all four configurations (digital baseline, ReRAM AIMC, FeFET CIM, and the hybrid of ReRAM AIMC and SRAM CIM). TOMAS-Map: derives subarray dimensions, input slicing, converter provisioning, engine balance, and the schedule from the model's shape, the device limits, and an area budget. Analog accuracy check (STEP 5.0b): SST-2 accuracy under programming noise and IR drop, over 5 seeds. New studies: context-length scaling, GPT-2 autoregressive decoding, subarray, DRAM, and converter-resolution sensitivity sweeps, and BERT-Large, GPT-2 XL, and ViT-Base workloads. Updated documentation: README, MANUAL.md, and PARAMETER_PROVENANCE.csv (every parameter traced to its source). Contents notebooks/Hybrid_IMC_CrossTech_Simulation.ipynb: the full pipeline results/: every output of the reported run (JSON), including phase4_analysis/manuscript_numbers.json PARAMETER_PROVENANCE.csv, MANUAL.md, requirements.txt, CITATION.cff, LICENSE (BSD-3-Clause) Key result (BERT-Base, 128 tokens) At equal logic area, the hybrid reaches 55.31 TOPS/W at chip level. That is 1.27x standalone ReRAM AIMC (3.87x at 2,048 tokens), 11.1x the 8-bit digital baseline, and 3.0x a 4-bit one. Citation See CITATION.cff. A DOI for this release is issued by Zenodo.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: THERMAL-AWARE MODELING OF PHYSICAL UNCLONABLE FUNCTIONS FOR RELIABLE HARDWARE SECURITY IN 3D INTEGRATED CIRCUITS
items.abstract: Three-dimensional integrated circuits (3D ICs) are intended to achieve high integration density and short vertical interconnections, however, with the stacking of active layers, power density, thermal gradient, and reliability sensitivity increase. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) are appealing choices for hardware-security primitives, as they rely on manufacturing variations that are not controllable to produce a device-specific response. The delays and device variations of the process, however, are also temperature sensitive, which is the source of the PUF entropy. In this paper, a thermal-aware modeling framework for PUFs embedded in 3D ICs based on TSV is developed. It integrates a vertically stacked thermal model with a temperature dependent PUF response model, allowing local temperature, vertical position, TSV proximity and process variations to be simultaneously taken into account for reliability evaluation. Ring-oscillators and Arbiter-type PUFs are considered representative structures and the variation caused by TSV is considered as an extra entropy source. The evaluation method is based on the main evaluation metrics: reliability, uniqueness, uniformity, bit-error rate, intra-chip Hamming distance, and thermal sensitivity. Existing 3D-IC PUF research shows that process variation from CMOS, TSV, can both introduce entropy, and recent reliability studies demonstrate that temperature and voltage variation can have a significant impact on PUF stability. The proposed framework is a systematic approach to the thermal-aware placement of PUFs, modelling of their responses, and optimization for reliability in a stacked hardware-security architecture.

items.title: Scheduling Data to Compute: Hierarchical Data Pipelining for LLM Training on AMD GPUs
items.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have been the key focus of recent machine learning breakthroughs. As the model size grows exponentially, the computation needed for training is astronomical. A GPU can do a huge amount of arithmetic. However, the data its compute units need is not always available when they are ready. This data may still be in slow memory or on another GPU. While the chip waits, expensive compute sits idle, and at scale even a small drop in utilization translates into substantial cost. In this paper, we treat this waiting time as the primary bottleneck. We focus on hardware features designed for explicit data movement. These features load data from off-chip memory onto the chip, rearrange it into the layout the computation requires as it is loaded, and transfer it between GPUs. By orchestrating them, we keep a steady pipeline of data flowing to the compute units so that they remain busy. We present kernel and framework implementations that address this bottleneck using three key data-movement instructions and hardware features. The Tensor Data Mover (TDM) moves tensor data from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into on-chip memory. Transpose-load instructions transpose tensor data into the layout that LLM computations require as it is loaded on-chip. Finally, System DMA (SDMA) and Remote DMA (RDMA) move data between GPUs over the scale-up and scale-out networks, respectively. Our results show that TDM and transpose-load provide on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level, respectively. The SDMA and RDMA lead to on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. This is the first AMD LLM training system to utilize all the GPU data pipelining features. Our implementation has been integrated into open source framework and library for AMD GPUs. https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus-Turbo https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus

items.title: Reliability and Lifetime Power Cycling Study of GaN HEMTs under Temperature Swings from 70deg C to 100deg C
items.abstract: Power devices in electric vehicle applications experience thermomechanical stresses that limit longterm reliability. The coolant temperature determines the lower bound of the devices' junction temperature swing, whilst package thermal ratings set the upper bound. The magnitude of the temperature swing strongly affects lifetime, and failures are commonly observed, not at the junction inside the actual die, but instead at the interfaces between the die and packaging. This paper investigates the lifetime of enhancement-mode GaN HEMTs as a function of lead-frame temperature swing. Temperature swings between 70deg C and 100deg C are evaluated, implemented by holding the upper bound constant at approximately 140deg C and correspondingly varying the lower temperature bound. An accelerated switching-loss-based AC power cycling method is used to achieve approximately 100,000 cycles per week. Switching parameters to obtain the relevant die-attach temperature swing are derived from a thermal-electrical equivalent model. A dependency of minimum cycle lifetime on temperature swing is apparent, thereby showing the significant impact of coolant temperature on reliability. However, deviceto- device variation appears to dominate and therefore higher numbers of cycling tests will be required to obtain statistically relevant results.

items.title: Reducing Test Response Volume and Test Time in Direct-Access-Based High-Bandwidth Memory Testing
items.abstract: In high-bandwidth memory (HBM) testing through the direct access (DA) port, the response-path bandwidth is far lower than the internal data bandwidth. Because most read responses are fault-free, transferring every response incurs substantial transfer overhead and test time. This paper proposes three fault-data transfer methods. Selective staggered read suppresses fault-free response transfers and overlaps faulty-response transfers with the subsequent read latency. Duplicate fault suppression replaces identical fault responses at consecutive addresses with a short duplicate code. Failing-bit indexing transmits only the positions of failing bits. The proposed architecture controls whether, when, and in which format each response is transferred without modifying the DA port interface or the March command and address sequence. Cycle-accurate simulation of an HBM2 test model shows that, across Random, Column-Correlated, and Row-Correlated Fault models with fault rates of 0.01–5%, the proposed method reduces the DA response data by 99.32–99.99% and the total test time by 44.86–45.01% compared with the conventional method. Synthesis shows that the added logic is smaller than that of on-chip fault collection and signature compaction schemes and independent of the memory capacity. The proposed architecture attains nearly the same test time as on-chip fault collection and signature compaction schemes while delivering every faulty response and its failing-bit positions to the tester, so that its diagnostic coverage is not bounded by on-chip storage.

items.title: Read-reference voltage adaptation for 3D NAND flash memory via RBER-aware few-shot transfer learning
items.abstract: Program/erase (P/E) cycling and retention drift alter the threshold-voltage distributions of 3D NAND flash, causing previously calibrated read-reference voltages to become mismatched to new operating conditions. To update read references when target measurements are limited, we propose a raw bit error rate (RBER)-aware few-shot transfer framework that adapts a Gaussian-parameter predictor from a single characterized source condition without requiring a pre-calibrated multi-condition voltage grid. The predictor is pretrained on source measurements and fine-tuned using a small set of target records, with mean squared error (MSE) as the parameter-training objective. Candidate checkpoints are selected using a restricted RBER metric over the measured programmed-state boundaries, aligning model selection with read-reference quality. Experiments on measurements collected from 3D NAND flash cover six target conditions and five random seeds, accounting for both training and validation measurements. With a total budget of two target wordlines, the proposed framework achieves an average reduction of 83.0% in the evaluated RBER relative to the evaluated training-from-scratch configuration (95% confidence interval 67.2–98.8%). In a paired experiment using 32 target training records and 13 validation wordlines, RBER-based checkpoint selection reduces RBER by 42.1% compared with MSE-based selection on the same fine-tuning trajectories (95% confidence interval 34.7–49.5%). Target-wordline interpolation achieves lower mean restricted RBER than the proposed framework in all 24 matched-budget comparisons. The checkpoint-selection benefit therefore concerns improvement within the learned framework, while direct interpolation provides higher accuracy under the tested budgets. By combining source-model reuse with RBER-based checkpoint selection, the proposed framework enables read-reference voltages to be adapted to changing P/E and retention conditions using limited target measurements.

items.title: Nanoscale etching characteristics for controlled AFM tomography of amorphous chalcogenide thin films
items.abstract: Amorphous chalcogenide materials are of increasing interest for phase-change memory and threshold-switching device applications. However, the fast-switching behavior in the nanoscale regime is difficult to confirm and characterize in terms of changes in conductivity. Understanding these electrical characteristics requires three-dimensional tomographic imaging capable of resolving structural and compositional changes across the film. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) is a powerful tool for obtaining such 3D tomographic imaging by alternating etching and imaging steps, and it also enables both electrical measurement and biasing during etching, ​which is essential given the volatile nature of Ovonic Threshold Switching (OTS) behavior. However, achieving accurate AFM-based etching for tomography requires a quantitative understanding of the tip-induced wear resistance of the chalcogenide film, since amorphous materials, lacking long-range structural order, make their wear resistance difficult to predict from local bonding configurations and surface-mediated contact mechanics alone. Here, we study a first-order framework for estimating the relative wear resistance of amorphous chalcogenide thin films from Raman spectroscopy and for selecting initial load​ in AFM etching and test it on depth-controlled AFM tomography.Etched depth as a function of applied load was measured for three amorphous binary films (Ge-Te, Si-Te, and Ge-Se) using AFM with a diamond-coated probe, and the probe state was monitored by force-distance pull-off measurements before and after etching. The load-depth data were analyzed within an Archard-DMT (Derjaguin-Muller-Toporov) framework to obtain a composite wear parameter ([Formula: see text]) that combines the wear coefficient and the effective hardness, allowing relative comparison of the films under nanoscale AFM contact conditions. This parameter follows the order Ge-Te > Si-Te > Ge-Se in both the low- and high-load ranges. To explain this order without independent nanoindentation, we introduce an effective bond enthalpy calculated from the composition and the Raman-resolved bonding configurations, which decreases monotonically with the wear parameter. Applied to an amorphous ternary Si-Ge-Te film, this relationship was used to select an etching load that yielded layer-by-layer tomographic imaging with an etched depth close to the target. These results suggest the Raman-derived effective bond enthalpy as a practical descriptor for selecting initial load​ in AFM-based nanoscale etching of amorphous chalcogenide films.

items.title: Modern analog computing for solving differential and matrix equations
items.abstract: Analog computing is gaining renewed interest from artificial intelligence and scientific computing demands. We term the evolving landscape modern analog computing, identifying three core primitives—solving differential equations, solving matrix equations, and performing matrix-vector multiplications—and exploring their interconnections and hardware implementations, from discrete components to integrated circuits and resistive memory devices. We then survey recent progress in solving differential and matrix equations using CMOS analog circuits and resistive memory arrays. Finally, we discuss applications, precision and scalability challenges, in-memory computing relationships, and the computational complexity of analog computing, providing a unified perspective on this emerging field.

items.title: Memristor‐Based Neuromorphic Computing for Intelligent Sensing and Edge Applications
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Memristor‐based neuromorphic computing has emerged as a promising hardware paradigm for energy‐efficient, scalable artificial intelligence edge applications. This review surveys recent progress in memristor‐based neuromorphic computing, in‐memory computing architectures, learning algorithms, and hardware implementations for edge intelligence. Volatile and nonvolatile memristive dynamics are discussed as key mechanisms for emulating biological neurons and synapses, providing foundational building blocks for crossbar‐based hardware neural networks. Moving beyond conventional neural‐network acceleration, this review examines the integration of memristive technologies into edge‐specific applications, focusing on emerging in‐sensor computing, optical in‐memory computing, and multimodal sensing frameworks. Furthermore, we outline the deployment of hardware‐compatible, brain‐inspired algorithms—including artificial, spiking, and recurrent neural networks—and evaluate their physical implementation within memristive architectures. The review also highlights the evolution of memristor‐based hardware from single‐device demonstrations to array‐level accelerators and CMOS‐integrated system‐on‐chip platforms, with the associated hierarchical challenges and solutions. By bridging the gap between individual device physics and full system engineering, this review provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing highly adaptive, low‐latency, and autonomous hardware platforms for the next generation of localized edge intelligence.

items.title: Leveraging Quantum Deficit Modeling for Scalable Multi-Tenant Resource Allocation on Advanced Cloud Datacenter Platforms
items.abstract: Multi-tenancy is fundamental to cloud storage, but efficient resource sharing with predictable performance remains challenging because SSD internals are opaque and shared-resource contention increases tail latency. As a result, to meet latency targets, existing host-side approaches rely on conservative over-provisioning, reducing utilization. In this paper, we present DILATON, a closed-loop Quality of Service (QoS)-aware scheduling framework for multi-tenant NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) SSDs (Solid State Drives). DILATON is motivated by the observation that QoS degradation arises from both back-end contention and the mismatch between issued and completed requests across domains. We leverage the submission–completion gap and resulting per-domain percentile-latency deficits as implicit feedback signals for dynamic request regulation. We develop a contention-aware QoS model that captures die-level collision probability and relates queue depth to bandwidth and latency. Using this model, DILATON adjusts per-domain queue depths to meet QoS targets, transforming conventional open-loop NVMe scheduling into a closed-loop framework that aligns host-side demand with SSD’s back-end capacity. We implement a multi-dimensional quantum-deficit scheduler with credit-based admission control and a feedback-driven controller for dynamic adaptation. We use a real-system testbed to evaluate open-loop control and demonstrate the submission–completion gap that motivates feedback, while closed-loop policies are evaluated in simulation. QD Control uses the submission–completion gap to balance resource allocations across domains, while QoS Control uses percentile-latency deficits to satisfy latency targets. The results show that DILATON meets its tail-latency targets across all priority classes in the configurations evaluated, allocating capacity adaptively rather than through static over-provisioning.

items.title: Interstellar Electromagnetic Matter Reconstruction (IEMR): A Soliton-Based Framework for In-Situ Atomic Matrix Beamforming
items.abstract: This paper introduces the theoretical foundation of Interstellar Electromagnetic Matter Reconstruction (IEMR), establishing a non-mechanical paradigm for in-situ resource assembly using electromagnetic soliton pulses. Interstellar Electromagnetic Matter Reconstruction (IEMR)A Soliton-Based Framework for In-Situ Atomic Matrix Beamforming and Field-AssistedAssemblyPrzemysław WodejskoIndependent Researcher • Theoretical Physics & Space ArchitecturesABSTRACTThis paper introduces the theoretical foundation of Interstellar Electromagnetic MatterReconstruction (IEMR), a non-mechanical paradigm for in-situ resource assembly indeep-space environments. By projecting phase-locked electromagnetic soliton pulses acrossinterstellar dust clouds, IEMR establishes spatially coherent electromagnetic potential wellsthat capture, ionize, and position ambient matter into structured atomic matrices. ExtremeUltraviolet (EUV) laser-plasma dynamics—exemplified in industrial lithography—serve as anempirical baseline demonstrating precision electromagnetic control over matter states. IEMRextends these dynamics into long-range, self-confined wavefield architectures, bypassingconventional logistics barriers in interstellar expansion.1. Introduction & Theoretical MotivationTraditional physical exploration beyond Earth is constrained by material transport logistics.The IEMR framework addresses this fundamental bottleneck by proposing anelectromagnetic beamforming architecture capable of structuring ambient cosmic particulatedirectly at destination targets. Rather than carrying static physical payloads, an IEMR systemprojects dynamic structural blueprints via coherent electromagnetic fields.2. Field-Plasma Interactions & Empirical Proof-of-ConceptThe physical feasibility of field-driven particulate control is grounded in high-intensitylaser-plasma physics. In advanced semiconductor manufacturing—specifically EUVlithography systems—high-frequency pulsed lasers interact with microscopic liquid metaldroplets, vaporizing and ionizing them into high-density plasma states controlled strictly byelectromagnetic boundary dynamics.IEMR scales these principles from micro-scale laboratory regimes to macro-scaleastronomical environments. The system uses coherent soliton wave packets designed toresist dispersion across long propagation distances:i ℏ ( ∂Ψ / ∂t ) = - ( ℏ² / 2m ) ∇²Ψ + V_EM(r, t)Ψ + g |Ψ|² ΨHere, V_EM(r, t) represents the targeted electromagnetic potential gradient configured toconstrain interstellar ions, while the non-linear self-interaction term g|Ψ|² maintains wavefrontstability across space.3. Architecture & Operational Phases• Phase I: Ionization & Trapping: Pulsed electromagnetic arrays scan ambient interstellardust, imparting targeted charges to create a localized plasma cloud.• Phase II: Soliton Beamforming: Intersecting phase-locked beams create stationaryinterference patterns, establishing 3D optical and magnetic lattice traps.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: In-Memory Computing Architectures for Accelerating Large-Scale Models: Principles, Devices, and System Challenges
items.abstract: Memory bandwidth is the binding constraint for large-model inference today. In-memory computing (IMC) addresses this limitation. This paper reviews where the technology stands. It compares analog and digital IMC implementations and find that analog arrays currently lead on energy efficiency, while digital designs maintain a substantial edge in precision and programming flexibility. Then it discusses three device candidates: Resistive Random-Access Memory (ReRAM), Ferroelectric Field-Effect Transistor (FeFET), and Spin-Transfer-Torque Magnetic Random-Access Memory (STT-MRAM). ReRAM offers the highest density but suffers from stochastic filament growth and conductance drift. FeFETs integrate cleanly with CMOS but are limited by ferroelectric switching variability. STT-MRAM is the most durable and stable, yet its modest tunnel-magnetoresistance ratio restricts analog precision. Finally, three limitations are pointed out: device variation under realistic workloads, peripheral-circuit overhead that can erase array-level energy gains, and scalable multi-chip orchestration for trillion-parameter models. IMC will succeed or fail based on cross-layer co-design—not on any single device breakthrough. Materials, circuits, compilers, and algorithms must advance together, and the compiler layer remains underdeveloped relative to device research. This paper provides development ideas for higher performance for IMC.

items.title: Hybrid Nanocomposite for Resistive Switching Memory
items.abstract: s, low operating voltage, stable ON/OFF state, and ease of device fabrication suggest that the PANI:ZnO nanocomposite is a promising candidate for non-volatile memory.

items.title: HyPAIC: Personal AI Computer with High Bandwidth Flash for High Performance Trillion-Parameter LLM Inference
items.abstract: LLMs have rapidly expanded from simple chatbots to agentic AI, where models directly use tools to solve complex problems. To improve problem solving, most frontier LLMs adopt an MoE architecture, pushing model sizes into the trillion-parameter regime. While cloud services have dominated large-scale LLM inference, cost and security concerns drive demand for on-premises deployment. Thus, GPU manufacturers have introduced personal AI computers (PAICs). However, existing PAICs with LPDDR-based unified main memory suffer from severe capacity limitations, restricting hostable LLM size on a single device. If most memory holds model weights, little remains for the KV cache, reducing supported context length. In this paper, we propose HyPAIC, a PAIC architecture incorporating HBF to overcome these memory constraints. HyPAIC stores read-only model weights in HBF and mutable runtime data in LPDDR. HBF offers over 10x the capacity of HBM with comparable TB/s-scale bandwidth. HyPAIC addresses HBF's access latency, limited write endurance, and page-level access granularity through prefetching, read-only weight placement, and coarse-grained weight accesses, respectively; power and cooling remain significant implementation challenges. Through simulation-based evaluation, we show that a single HyPAIC improves end-to-end system throughput by up to 1.04x and TDP-normalized throughput by up to 3.59x during 1T-parameter MoE inference versus the aggregate of eight baseline systems without HBF, one HyPAIC thus approaches the raw performance of eight baselines with far superior power efficiency. For small model inference, HyPAIC increases the maximum number of concurrent tasks sustaining at least 50 decode TPS per task by up to 4x, enhancing user experience and productivity. Although HBF specifications are still evolving, this study demonstrates strong architectural synergy between HBF and PAICs.

items.title: Hump modulation in Transfer Characteristics: Simulated Gate-all-around field-effect transistors — Supporting TCAD Simulation Data
items.abstract: A parasitic current path beneath the bottom nanosheet of a simulated triple-stacked silicon gate-all-around field-effect transistor (GAA-FET) accompanies a hump in the low-drain-bias transfer curve. In a separate punch-through stopper (PTS) simulation, both the hump and the drive current were reduced, indicating a substrate-side contribution. Without altering the substrate structure, the hump is also dependent on channel and source/drain conditions throughout 486 parameter combinations. For channel widths of 8 and 12 nm, the mean peak-to-valley logarithmic-current gradient difference was lower by 51.2% in the wider-channel case. At 0.05 V drain bias and 8 nm channel width, the interface trap density was changed from 1010 to 1012 cm-2 eV-1. Hump onset moved to more positive gate voltage for all 27 paired conditions, with a mean shift of 23.91 ± 0.49 mV. The change in gradient difference has a coefficient of variation (CV) of 24.3%. The onset shift has a CV of 2.1%. Different relative contributions from nanosheet and substrate currents can account for these responses. Channel and source/drain parameters may thus modify hump shape without additional substrate-isolation structures.

items.title: High-performance annealing-free wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors with ultrathin oxide semiconductors for neuromorphic computing
items.abstract: Wurtzite-structured aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN) ferroelectric materials are potential candidates for non-volatile memory (NVM) applications because of their high remanent polarization (Pr > 100 μC·cm−2) and compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes. However, achieving high-performance wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) remains a significant challenge because of their high interface trap density (Dit) and large threshold voltage (VTH) variation. Here we show the distinct polarization switching mechanisms of AlScN FeFETs based on an ultrathin indium gallium oxide (IGO) channel with three different structures. FeFETs with a metal–ferroelectric–metal–insulator–semiconductor (MFMIS) structure show high interface quality with low Dit and a stable VTH, achieving a large memory window (MW) of up to 20.6 V and a high endurance of 106. The stable 6-bit operation of our devices with 64 distinct states shows the feasibility of multilevel storage applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the FeFET in neuromorphic networks, with a high recognition accuracy of 93.02%. AlScN field-effect transistors for non-volatile memory are limited by high interface trap density and threshold voltage instability. Wang et al. demonstrate annealing-free AlScN ferroelectric transistors with low interface trap density and stable threshold voltage, enabling a large memory window and robust 6-bit operation.

items.title: Ferroelectric Hybrid Processor Family - Tier-1 Engineering Specification (HTML)
items.abstract: This document provides the complete engineering specification for the three Tier-1 products of the Ferroelectric Hybrid Processor Family: a standard premium phone chip (Ph-1), a high-end desktop chip (Pc-1), and an entry-level single-socket server chip (Dc-1S). The architecture combines an RV64GCVH out-of-order CPU core, a FeFET non-volatile L3 cache, and an analog AI crossbar on a standard N5 CMOS process with a hafnium zirconium oxide (HfZrO, HZO) back-end module. The document provides the complete engineering parameters for design, fabrication, test, and operation at the specification level: cell geometries, material compositions, fabrication steps, circuit designs, operating procedures, qualification tests, and acceptance criteria (Parts 3--16), plus the register map, firmware interface, interrupt assignments, device tree and ACPI bindings, full pin description, mechanical drawings, bring-up checklist, and security provisioning procedure (Appendices A--H). The advanced optimization promotion is in Part 17. The design is released as a public, patent-free engineering specification.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Emulating SiC Modules Using Electrically Representative PCBs to Investigate Die-Level Current Phenomena
items.abstract: Power modules with parallel-connected dies can exhibit significant current imbalance and inter-die ringing under various operating conditions, making it desirable to observe per-die currents during module and system development. However, measuring individual die currents in kV-rated modules is challenging due to the limited space for instrumentation and the dies being encapsulated with silicone gel. This paper presents methods to implement a PCB with parallel-connected SiC discretes, which emulates the relevant parasitic impedances of a given commercial SiC module. This facilitates per-die instrumentation, and thus a low-cost means to study die-level current phenomena. The relevant parasitic module impedances are extracted using a combination of geometric estimates, impedance measurements, and double-pulse tests. For some impedances, replication on a PCB is straightforward; for others, the TO-247 package imposes parasitic inductances that are too high. These are addressed through measures such as low impedance return paths, current mirror planes, and optimized drain connections. The methods are demonstrated on a 1200 V, 400 A SiC module; validation using a vector network analyser confirms the emulator PCB delivers module-like parasitics, and double-pulse tests at 800 V and 300 A show similar switching behaviours of the PCB and module being emulated.

items.title: Deployment-aware acceleration boundaries for Edge-IoT intrusion detection on Raspberry Pi 5 and Hailo-8
items.abstract: Edge-IoT intrusion detection systems must balance predictive performance with the throughput, latency, and resource constraints of embedded deployment. This study investigates when hardware acceleration is beneficial for tabular IoT intrusion detection on a Raspberry Pi 5 equipped with a Hailo-8 AI accelerator. We evaluate lightweight multilayer perceptrons, conventional 1D convolutional neural networks, and a quantization-friendly 1D-CNN across CICIoT2023 and Edge-IIoTset using ONNX Runtime, Hailo quantized-emulator evaluation, and physical HailoRT benchmarking. The results reveal an execution-regime-dependent acceleration boundary. For the evaluated MLPs, CPU throughput exceeds HailoRT streaming throughput under both reported CPU reference regimes, whereas the conventional 1D-CNNs achieve higher HailoRT streaming throughput than both CPU references. Relative to CPU batch-size-one execution, the CICIoT2023 and Edge-IIoTset 1D-CNNs reach streaming-throughput ratios of 10.34\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\times $$\end{document} and 9.61\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\times $$\end{document}, respectively; the corresponding ratios relative to buffered CPU execution are 1.88\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\times $$\end{document} and 1.82\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\times $$\end{document}. The quantization-friendly model reduces ONNX-to-quantized-emulator macro-F1 degradation by 7.66 percentage points relative to the standard Edge-IIoTset 1D-CNN while also reducing parameter count, HEF on-disk size, and accelerator-side hardware latency. These findings show that accelerator selection for Edge-IoT IDS should consider model structure, execution regime, runtime overhead, and quantization behavior jointly.

items.title: Co-Design of a Low-Power RISC-V Processor and a Reconfigurable Neural Network Accelerator for Edge AI Computing
items.abstract: The operational efficiency of the compact edge AI accelerator is susceptible to variations in network structure and data transmission speed. To address this issue, this study proposes a collaborative design scheme for digital integrated circuits. By adjusting the working mode of the computing array and coordinating with storage and power management, the operational efficiency of the accelerator is improved. The research tested three network models trained on the publicly available Digits dataset. The results showed that the average accuracy of integer reasoning ranged from 96.78% to 97.33%, and the average loss was at most 0.11 percentage points compared to floating-point reasoning. In a cost model with 64 processing units and 8 KiB memory, compared to a fixed array, this scheme reduced the inference delay by 14.83% to 18.74%, decreased the single-inference energy consumption by 6.86% to 8.81%, and increased the area by 7.58%. Further experiments demonstrated that reducing the waiting time between data transmission and computation plays a major role in improving operational efficiency. Allowing the computing array to flexibly adjust its working mode can also increase the utilization rate of processing units, but this improvement is still limited by data transmission capabilities. In the hardware resource allocation test, the scheme with 64 computing elements and 1 KB memory further reduced the area while keeping the power consumption basically unchanged. These results indicate that this design can balance operational efficiency and hardware overhead to a certain extent, but the specific effect still needs to be verified through actual hardware testing.

items.title: Bezier-GP: Bezier-Surface-Based Gaussian Process for Chips-on-Wafer Warpage Modeling
items.abstract: As the semiconductor industry transitions to the post-Moore paradigm, wafer warpage has become a critical quality issue in advanced packaging; particularly for 3D stacking and high-bandwidth memory manufacturing where die-level deformation can affect bonding quality, interconnect reliability, and yield. However, direct high-throughput measurement of individual chip warpage remains difficult in mass-production environments, while existing wafer-level metrology systems routinely provide dense 3D shape data at the wafer scale. This paper proposes a Bezier-surface-based Gaussian Process---known as Bezier-GP---for chips-on-wafer warpage modeling. The proposed framework combines wafer-level point-cloud metrology data with wafer-map layout information to construct chip-region-level Bezier surface patches, imposes continuity constraints between neighboring patches, and represents the resulting chips-on-wafer surface through a compact free-control-point vector. A GP is then introduced in this low-dimensional representation to model wafer-to-wafer variation, chip-region-level spatial dependence, and provide uncertainty quantification. Numerical experiments, using an ASC wafer-map layout, demonstrate that the proposed framework can reconstruct chips-on-wafer surfaces, preserve chip-region-level geometric interpretability, and recover population-level mean and covariance structures under a controlled multi-wafer simulation setting. The results suggest that Bezier-GP provides a measurement-driven statistical modeling foundation for connecting wafer-level metrology data to chip-region-level warpage analysis in semiconductor manufacturing.

items.title: Beyond parameter count: performance-latency-robustness trade-offs in compact neural OFDM channel estimation
items.abstract: Parameter count is often used as a proxy for deployment cost in neural OFDM receivers, although it does not measure kernel efficiency or channel-mismatch robustness. This paper evaluates a 754-parameter residual estimator that refines a discrete Fourier transform least-squares (DFT-LS) estimate. Baselines include LS, DFT-LS, oracle and stale-statistics LMMSE, a multilayer perceptron, and a convolutional network. Five training seeds and 1,000 OFDM symbols per condition cover six SNR values, three modulation orders, four within-symbol Doppler values, and five static channel scenarios. At 10 dB in the matched channel, the compact model reaches -11.29 dB NMSE, compared with -10.70 dB for DFT-LS and -12.11 dB for oracle LMMSE; the larger learned models are close to -12 dB. The compact model takes 0.293 ms per symbol, versus 0.027 ms for the MLP and 0.093 ms for the CNN. A uniform power-delay-profile shift produces a 1.34 dB gap between oracle and stale LMMSE, whereas normalized Doppler up to 0.1 causes modest degradation. Accuracy, parameter count, latency, and robustness therefore require separate reporting.
items.venue: International Conference on Wireless, Optical Communication, and Information Engineering (WOCIE 2026)

items.title: Avaliando a Estratificação de Memória na Inferência de LLMs somente em CPU
items.abstract: A capacidade de DRAM representa um fator limitante de custo e viabilidade para a execução da inferência com Grandes Modelos de Linguagem (LLMs) em ambientes sem aceleradores. Este trabalho investiga o impacto da alocação seletiva dos três principais componentes internos de um LLM (pesos de atenção, pesos da FFN e KV-Cache) entre DRAM local e uma camada de memória de maior capacidade e maior latência, em uma plataforma exclusivamente baseada em CPU. Utilizando o modelo LLaMA 2 7B quantizado em Q4 K M, avaliam-se oito estratégias de posicionamento em cinco cenários de uso que variam o tamanho do contexto e a proporção entre prefill e decode. Os resultados demonstram que não existe um componente universalmente mais tolerante à estratificação: a hierarquia de custos rotaciona ao longo do gradiente de contexto, sendo a KV-Cache o componente mais seguro sob contexto efetivo curto (−3,9% de degradação de decode) e o mais custoso sob contexto efetivo longo (até −46,8%). A decisão de alocação é formalizada como um problema bi-objetivo (DRAM liberada vs. vazão) resolvido por meio da fronteira de Pareto com um piso de aceitabilidade de vazão, do qual derivam-se diretrizes práticas de alocação sensíveis ao contexto.

items.title: Advanced Capacitor and Supercapacitor Structures Based on Functional Thin Films
items.abstract: Thin-film capacitors and supercapacitors are gaining increasing attention due to the rapid development of modern electronics, flexible devices, microsystems and wearable technologies. Their small size, low weight and compatibility with integrated electronic systems make them promising components for next-generation applications and energy-storage systems. In recent years, significant progress has been achieved in the development of thin-film structures with improved capacitance, higher energy density, lower leakage current and better thermal and electrical stability. Advances in thin-film engineering have also enabled the use of high-k dielectric materials, ultrathin insulating layers, oxide-based electrodes and advanced carbon materials to enhance device performance. This review presents recent progress in thin-film capacitor and supercapacitor technologies, focusing on device architectures, dielectric and electrode thin films and reliability-related challenges. Different configurations, including metal–insulator–metal (MIM), metal–oxide–semiconductor (MOS), interdigital, flexible and three-dimensional structures, are discussed. Special attention is given to oxide thin films, nanostructured electrodes, interface quality, defect-related phenomena and scaling effects influencing electrical performance. Current market trends and commercial perspectives are also discussed in the context of emerging electronic applications. Finally, key technological challenges and future development directions for thin-film capacitors and supercapacitors are highlighted.

items.title: A Resonant-Tunneling Quantum-Dot Demultiplexer for Scalable Cryogenic Single-Electron Routing
items.abstract: Scaling quantum electronic systems such as quantum-dot spin qubits and single-electron devices is increasingly limited by the wiring overhead between cryogenic devices and room-temperature control electronics. Multi-channel quantum-dot architectures that selectively route electrons using a few shared control lines, analogous to demultiplexers in classical networks, offer a promising solution. Here, we propose and theoretically investigate a gate-defined architecture of three parallel quantum dots sharing a common source reservoir and coupled to independent drain channels. Using an analytical electrostatic model and tight-binding quantum transport simulations, we show that the device can act as an on-chip single-electron demultiplexer based on resonant tunneling in the cryogenic regime. Closed-system eigenstate analysis reveals localized orbital states in each dot, and open-system transport calculations show resonant conductance peaks when these levels align with the incident electron energy, consistent with the closed-system eigenenergy evolution. By engineering the barrier-gate spacing and the relative plunger-gate dimensions, we obtain well-separated resonances with minimal overlap between channels. Bond-current density calculations show that transport is confined to the resonant channel with negligible leakage into neighboring outputs, yielding channel selectivity approaching unity for all resonant modes. The architecture is compatible with Si/SiGe and GaAs/AlGaAs platforms and can be extended to more channels, offering a route toward programmable quantum routing and resonant-tunneling-based quantum circuitry.

items.title: A RISC-V Simulator for the Tenstorrent Tensix Architecture
items.abstract: RISC-V based AI accelerators have become popular and not only for AI and ML, but also as vehicles for exploring HPC workloads more generally. Tenstorrent are one example, and whilst they document their Tensix architecture in detail and develop their software stack openly, running code has historically required a physical card, and their recently released simulator targets hardware equivalence rather than introspection. In this paper we present Wolfpine, a community developed RISC-V simulator for the Tensix architecture, supporting both the Wormhole and Blackhole generations and integrating seamlessly with the TT-Metal software stack. Constructed entirely from publicly available documentation, open source software and measurements on physical hardware, Wolfpine is written in pure Python for readability and ease of modification. An opt-in, provenance-tracked cost model adds timing fidelity incrementally, and typed event streams, per-component tracing and timeline export enable programmers to identify and diagnose performance bottlenecks that the hardware itself hides.

items.title: 3D integration of a hybrid quantum dot circuit-QED device for fast gate dispersive charge readout and coherent spin-photon coupling
items.abstract: Hybrid circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) aims at coupling various quantum degrees of freedom, among which are spin and charge degrees of freedom in gate defined quantum dots, phonons or magnons... with quantized electromagnetic fields in superconducting microwave cavities to investigate fundamental physics questions or for quantum computation and simulation. However, low microwave losses, key for many hybrid cQED experiments, are challenging to achieve given the often exotic and/or complex material stacks (e.g. semiconducting material, ferromagnets, or piezoelectric materials) required to host the various quantum degrees of freedom. In this work, we present a 3D-integration process to overcome this challenge for semi-industrial silicon MOS spin qubits. The process is based on dense indium bump interconnects at a pitch of 10 $\mathrmμ$m and superconducting thin films of Niobium Nitride (NbN). First, we report on DC and RF interconnect properties that demonstrate a high galvanic interconnection yield and internal quality factors above $10^{5}$ in the single photon regime for NbN resonators interrupted by a single indium bump interconnect. Eventually, we fabricated a 3D-integrated hybrid circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) device based on a semi-industrial MOS hole double quantum dot and a high impedance NbN resonator. For this device, we report a cavity internal quality factor above 10000 and demonstrate record sensitivity for gate-based dispersive readout of the charge degree of freedom with an SNR of 100 in 300 ns. Finally, we demonstrate strong spin-photon coupling of $g_{s}/2π$ = 75 MHz, which highlights the viability of 3D-integration for quantum dot based hybrid spin circuit quantum electrodynamics and opens to high-fidelity spin readout and microwave photon-based remote spin qubit entanglement.

items.title: qLevelPlace: A Level-Based Placement Framework for RSFQ Circuits
items.abstract: Rapid Single Flux Quantum (RSFQ) logic can operate at ultra-high clock frequencies; however, its physical design is complicated by explicit splitter trees and deep gate-level pipelines in which every logic gate is clocked. To address this challenge, we present qLevelPlace, a level-based placement framework for RSFQ circuits. We separate gate and splitter placement into two stages to better support levelguided gate-to-row assignment and use a timing-aware quadratic cost function to penalize long interconnects. Experiments on the benchmark circuits show that, on average, qLevelPlace achieves a $2.65\times$ higher clock frequency and a 51% reduction in layout area compared with the state-of-the-art RSFQ placer qPlace.

items.title: VF-SSD: High-Level Architecture Specification and Four-Phase Digital Pipeline Verification for Lossless Field-Processor Systems
items.abstract: Breaking Physical Boundaries in Solid-State Storage: The VF-SSD Architecture Conventional non-volatile flash storage is fundamentally limited by physical wear degradation (P/E cycle limits) and heavy error-correction (ECC) overhead. To overcome these barriers, we introduce the Vortex-Field Solid-State Drive (VF-SSD)—an independent hardware processor featuring conservative gauge field mapping and a deterministic 4-phase synchronous pipeline (IDLE, PROCESS, DECODE, DONE). Validated through rigorous Icarus Verilog hardware simulation, the VF-SSD core achieves absolute 1:1 lossless data parity with a zero bit error rate (BER=0BER=0), successfully bypassing traditional physical wear mechanisms. This publication establishes a legally binding defensive prior art timestamp on Zenodo, while delivering a verified, enterprise-ready IP core primed for FPGA synthesis and proprietary SoC integration.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. VI. Surface diffusion on a nonmetal-terminated surface
items.abstract: Ab initio calculations were used to simulate surface diffusion of adsorbates on the nonmetal-terminated surface of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. These surfaces are wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e. GaN(000-1) surface, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e. GaP(-1-1-1) gallium arsenide, GaAs (-1-1-1) and gallium antimonide GaSb (-1-1-1) surfaces. The mixed coverage consists of Ga adatoms in the first layer with a nonmetal atom attached above them forming a triangular-based pyramid. The pyramidal structures are stable during surface jumps involving rotations around one of the basal Ga adatoms. Thus, the diffusion proceeds via rotation (pivot) of the pair of the other basal Ga adatoms around an immobile Ga adatom moving them into new, originally empty sites. Using an energy-path determination procedure, the diffusion barriers were obtained as the difference between the initial site energy and the activated complex state energy. The detachment energy of the NM adatom was obtained assuming a final state in atomic and molecular form. The energy barrier for detachment to the atomic state is high for all atoms, on the order of 5 eV. For the molecular state these barriers are different: smaller for nitrogen, on the order of 1 eV, which is related to the high dissociation energy of the N2 molecule. For P and As the barrier is above 2 eV. For Sb it was not determined. Accordingly, the surface diffusion length is macroscopically large, indicating that all NM adatoms arrive at the steps.

items.title: Toward Deployable Hardware Roots of Trust for Edge AI: Software PUFs and Their Trade-offs
items.abstract: Deploying AI at the edge increases the need for security features on existing devices. When physical access to the device is available, storing secret keys in non-volatile memory is vulnerable. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) address this by exploiting the unique yet repeatable characteristics of each device, but conventional implementations require design-stage modifications, making them inapplicable to a vast number of existing devices already manufactured. Recently, software PUFs have emerged as an alternative approach, leveraging analog characteristics exposed through software-only interfaces to derive unique responses, without post-fabrication changes. Since edge AI hardware is bound to long operational lifespans, this offers clear economic and engineering value. Existing research on software PUFs remains fragmented. It lacks a holistic review of the trade-offs among choices of components used as entropy sources and software methods to expose analog characteristics. This gap hinders assessing feasibility, comparing approaches, and identifying open challenges towards a hardware root of trust in existing devices. This paper surveys 37 existing software PUF works and compares them against the requirements of on-device model protection: boot-time versus runtime key derivation, and response latency. It analyzes trade-offs, outlines four key challenges that current software PUFs face for edge AI deployment, and highlights promising directions for overcoming barriers to real-world adoption.

items.title: Thin Glass Substrates with TGV: Handling and Process Advances
items.abstract: Glass is a leading substrate for advanced electronics and photonics applications. In addition to its large bulk resistance, several variants of glass offer very low loss at radio frequencies. Glass interposers with through-glass vias have been demonstrated in wafer and panel formats, yet adoption especially for thin glass has been hindered by the need for robust fabrication processes. We use a novel temporary bond approach to handle thin glass (typically < 200 micron) with though glass vias. The bond is robust to temperatures exceeding 400 °C, and creates handle/glass stacks with total thickness variation (TTV) like that of a silicon wafer. The bonded wafer pair, combined with the smoothness and dimensional stability of glass, allows processes already mature for silicon to be translated to glass substrates, such as copper fill of TGVs and surface metallization. In order to demonstrate the capabilities of thin glass with our novel handling approach, we review the fabrication and performance of several relevant RF structures including passive and active devices that operate at greater than 50 GHz. We also review the performance of Cu-filled TGV and glass based RDLs upon exposure to thermal cycling and HAST tests.

items.title: The first-principles analysis of transition metal dichalcogenide electrodes in HfO 2 -based resistive random access memories
items.abstract: Abstract In this work, a comprehensive first-principles analysis of various transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDs) as top electrodes and an HfO 2 based resistive random access memory (RRAM) structure is explored, where performance and reliability are strongly influenced by the contacts. The following interfacial and transport phenomenon are investigated for optimizing the RRAM performances: (i) Strain mapping at the interface reveals the lattice distortions highlighting their contribution in stabilizing or destabilizing the memory; (ii) Total energy calculations quantifying the relative thermodynamic stability of the interfaces, establishing a direct link between strain relaxation and interfacial energy; (iii) Transport through the interface, near the Fermi energy (E f ), is analyzed with transmission spectra calculation, revealing that choice of TMD significantly modulates the available conduction pathways; (iv) Capturing the carrier dynamics, Shockley-Read-Hall (SRH) recombination rates are evaluated, showing a distinct variation across different interfaces, affecting the switching kinetics, and finally (v) Normalized spectral conductance binds all the analysis together, providing a comparative measure of transport, correlating interfacial strain, total energy, SRH and transmission. Together, these analyses establish a coherent picture of choosing the optimum RRAM structure using TMD-HfO 2 interface, offering valuable guidelines for next-generation memory devices.

items.title: Temperature-Independent Logarithmic Current Slope in Interdiffusion-Broadened Silicon pn Junction toward Low-Power Thermometry
items.abstract: With the development of cryogenic technologies such as quantum computing, there is an increasing need for low-power cryogenic thermometers that minimize self-heating. Here, we report an anomalous temperature-independent logarithmic current slope, $d(\ln J)/dV$, in heavily doped silicon p$^{+}$n$^{+}$ junctions with significant dopant interdiffusion and highlight the advantages of our device as a low-power, cryogenic thermometer. Electrical characterizations from 2 to 420 K reveal that, at low forward bias, $d(\ln J)/dV$ remains nearly constant, which yields a voltage-temperature responsivity that is nearly independent of bias current. The observed transport cannot be fully understood with conventional diffusion or direct band-to-band tunneling. Instead, the results suggest the contribution of trap-assisted tunneling. These results establish interdiffusion-broadened silicon p$^{+}$n$^{+}$ junctions as a route to low-power temperature sensors while providing insight into carrier transport in heavily doped semiconductor junctions.

items.title: Technical Challenges for Ultra Fine Pitch Hybrid Bonding
items.abstract: Hybrid bonding is rapidly emerging as a foundational technology for next-generation advanced packaging, enabling ultra-high-density interconnects required for heterogeneous integration of chiplets, logic, memory, and specialized accelerators. As the industry pushes toward ultra-fine pitch interconnects approaching single-digit microns and below, significant technical challenges must be addressed across the process flow. These challenges include achieving extremely tight wafer and die alignment tolerances, maintaining surface planarity and cleanliness at the nanometer scale, controlling copper dishing and dielectric erosion during CMP, and ensuring defect-free oxide and copper-copper bonding interfaces. In addition, scaling hybrid bonding to ultra-fine pitch requires improvements in metrology, defect inspection, thermal management, and yield control to support high-volume manufacturing. Integration with complementary technologies such as silicon interposers, wafer-to-wafer and die-to-wafer bonding architectures, and heterogeneous material stacks further increases process complexity. This presentation reviews the key technical barriers to ultra-fine pitch hybrid bonding and discusses emerging process solutions and equipment innovations required to enable reliable, high-density interconnects for future high-performance computing, AI, and advanced system-in-package applications.

items.title: TD-MSEFormer: temporal dependency multi-scale expert former for IGBT remaining useful life prediction
items.abstract: Accurate remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of insulated gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) is important for ensuring the reliability of power electronic systems. However, IGBT degradation sequences usually exhibit nonlinear evolution, mixed short-term and long-term dependencies, and stage-dependent degradation characteristics, which makes robust RUL prediction challenging. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Temporal Dependency Multi-Scale Expert Former (TD-MSEFormer). Specifically, a Sequential Dependency Calibration Module (SDCM) is introduced to enhance degradation-related temporal dependency representation. A Multi-Scale Temporal Expert Block (MSTEB) is designed to capture degradation patterns at different temporal scales, while a Temporal Dual-Attention (TDA) block further refines local temporal interactions. Extensive experiments on NASA IGBT Aging Dataset demonstrate that the proposed TD-MSEFormer consistently outperforms other methods, achieving the best overall RUL prediction performance with superior accuracy, robust generalization, and stable degradation representation under complex nonlinear aging conditions.

items.title: Spectroscopy of low-lying valley states in hot Si/SiGe quantum dots
items.abstract: The presence of low-lying valley states in Si may hinder the development of large-scale spin-based quantum processors. Rapid prototyping of novel Si/SiGe heterostructures and gate stacks will be central to identifying pathways that increase the valley splitting. We compare the performance of pulsed-gate spectroscopy (PGS) and detuning axis pulsed spectroscopy (DAPS) at temperatures up to 700 mK. We find that DAPS outperforms PGS, with DAPS resolving valley splittings as small as ∼86 μeV, while the energy resolution of PGS is only ∼210 μeV. Our work demonstrates that DAPS can be used to efficiently extract valley splittings at elevated temperatures in high throughput cryostats.

items.title: Scalable p-type Te 1-x Se x thin-film transistors and low-power complementary logic gates
items.abstract: Abstract Despite the promise of Te as a p-type channel material, realizing Te-based thin-film transistors (TFTs) with low off-state current and high on/off ratio is challenging due to its small bandgap and high background carrier density. Se-alloying offers a potential solution to mitigate these limitations, yet the device performance has remained suboptimal. In this work, through the synergy of stoichiometric control and thickness engineering, we achieve an optimal trade-off between charge transport and switching characteristics in Te1-xSex TFTs. The resulting devices exhibit an average field-effect mobility of 16.8 cm2 V-1 s-1, Ion/Ioff ratio of 1.3×105 and an ultralow off-state current of 10 pA μm-1. The fabrication process is fully compatible with established low-temperature TFT technologies, enabling high-yield production of transistor arrays with favorable electrical uniformity. Notably, the devices demonstrate exceptional environmental stability, retaining critical performance metrics after six months of storage without encapsulation. Complementary logic gates (NOT, NAND, and NOR) are fabricated by integrating p-Te0.63Se0.37 and n-IGZO TFTs. The inverter achieves a high voltage gain of 28, a noise margin of 92.3%, and a low static power consumption of 420 pW at 3 V supply voltage. This study highlights the potential of Te1-xSex as a scalable p-type channel material, advancing the development of TFT-based logic circuits.

items.title: Robust Power-Law Computing for Edge Intelligence Using Spin-Orbit Torque Magnetic Tunnel Junctions
items.abstract: Power-law transformations are widely used in edge perception, where compact implementations must balance numerical precision, circuit resources, and device variability. Here we demonstrate a stochastic power-law architecture based on spin-orbit-torque magnetic tunnel junctions (SOT-MTJs). An event-driven feedback loop adjusts the write voltage to regulate the probability of an all-1 event in an n-bit block. Under the fixed-point sampling model, this establishes a switching probability p=b1/n, from which m-bit event statistics yield the power-law target bm/n. Online probability locking removes the need for offline per-device probability-voltage characterization or stored calibration tables. Measurements on W-based SOT-MTJs, combined with digital analysis of the acquired bitstreams, demonstrate representative power-law operations with absolute deviations of 0.003 or less at the reported precision, as well as parallel decoding of multiple exponents from one source. A 4-bit gamma-correction example preserves dark-region image detail and reaches approximately 35 dB peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) relative to the theoretical gamma-domain reference near 1000 raw samples. A 5 Oe device-level field perturbation and a joint {plus minus}90% simulation centered on the measured parameter means of 25 devices examine adaptation and the safe-voltage operating boundary under the tested conditions. These results establish a nonlinear computing primitive with accuracy controlled by sampling depth and an operating point maintained through feedback.

items.title: Raw data for “Ferroelectric transistor and dipole-valve based on atomically thin α-In2Se3”
items.abstract: Ferroelectricity, characterized by the spontaneous ordering of electric dipoles arising from charge-center displacements, can be non-volatilely and efficiently controlled by an external electric field. In principle, this offers an electric analogue to its magnetic counterpart — the spin valve, in which two ferromagnetic metals are sandwiched by a non-magnetic tunneling barrier. However, most ferroelectric materials are intrinsically insulating, severely limiting their functionality to passive dielectric elements. Here, we show that, in an atomically thin ferroelectric semiconductor α-In2Se3, the ferroelectric polarization can be intrinsically coupled to semiconductor field-effect modulation, enabling a gate-programmable ferroelectric hysteresis loop. The coercive field is widely tunable with a factor of 400 % upon gating. We further realize a bilayer ferroic junction architecture in analogue to a spin valve, in which dipoles from each constituent layer can be tuned into parallel and anti-parallel configurations, leading to gate-tunable high- and low-resistance states (HRS and LRS). This establishes a ferroelectric dipole valve, demonstrating active control of dipole transport in a solid-state device. Our results bridge ferroelectricity and semiconductor electronics in the two-dimensional limit, and open a route towards non-volatile, electrically programmable device concepts based on dipole degrees of freedom.

items.title: Projected Disc-type Phase-change Memory for Analog In-Memory Computing
items.abstract: Abstract Resistive memory technologies offer a compelling advantage for in-memory computing. However, realizing a device architecture that simultaneously achieves high computational precision, efficiency, and density has remained elusive due to inherent trade-offs among these performance metrics. Here, we introduce a compact phase-change memory device architecture that combines an ultra-confined active switching volume for enhanced electro-thermal efficiency with a non-insulating thin film that suppresses temporal conductance fluctuations. We analytically model and back-end integrate these devices into crossbar arrays. Even with conventional, undoped phase-change materials, the device architecture enables a computational precision approaching 6 bits, low conductance values below 50 μS with an adequate conductance window, and a viable pathway toward sub-100 μA programming currents under nominal operating voltages.

items.title: Plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition of tungsten diselenide thin films using bis( tert -butylimido)bis(dimethylamino)tungsten and H2Se plasma
items.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides are promising for next-generation technologies due to their unique optical and electronic properties. Tungsten diselenide (WSe2) is especially attractive because of its ambipolar conductivity and high theoretical carrier mobility. However, conventional high-temperature chemical vapor deposition limits WSe2 growth on 3D nanostructured or thermally sensitive substrates. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) could enable large-area, conformal WSe2 synthesis at back-end-of-line compatible temperatures, though it remains underexplored for this material. In this work, we develop and characterize a plasma-enhanced ALD process for 2D layered WSe2 using bis(tert-butylimido)bis(dimethylamino)tungsten as the precursor and pure H2Se plasma as the coreactant at 300 °C. Surface saturation conditions for the precursor and coreactant were established using atomic force microscopy. At 300 and 400 °C, a growth rate of ∼0.3 Å/ALD cycle was obtained. An 8-in wafer map of films deposited at 300 °C demonstrates high thickness uniformity and process scalability. 10 nm thick films grown at both 300 and 400 °C are characterized using Raman, grazing-incidence XRD, XPS, AFM, and SEM. As deposited, the films are crystalline, stoichiometric, and have rough surface morphologies. Cross-sectional STEM and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy indicate crystalline 2D WSe2 layers that are aligned parallel to the surface. Some large amorphous tungsten selenide features are also present, likely caused by selenium contamination and related secondary-deposition processes in the reaction chamber.
items.venue: Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology A

items.title: Plasma etch process optimization for photonic-grade diamond-on-insulator substrates and thickness evaluation using colorimetry
items.abstract: Diamond qubits integrated with photonic circuits can be initialized, manipulated, entangled, and read out individually with high fidelity, making them attractive for large-scale quantum systems. However, the limited size of heteroepitaxially grown single-crystal diamond and photonic-grade diamond-on-insulator (DOI) remains challenging for integration with existing manufacturing processes. Here, we develop a plasma etch recipe to thin direct-bonded (100) single-crystal diamond ( < 50 μ m ) into large-area, thin-film DOI, and demonstrate free-standing photonic chiplets fabricated from the resulting DOI. The ICP-RIE recipe preserves bonding and provides sufficient micro-masking and surface-quality control. We thin a 10 μ m diamond bonded to SiO 2 / Si and obtain a photonic-grade DOI with diamond thickness ≤ 300 nm over 0.5 × 0.5 mm 2 with roughness < 0.5 nm . Diamond photonic chiplets are fabricated using a standard two-step lithography process, without complex thin-film transfer, under-etching, or pedestal formation. We also present a colorimetric study of diamond visibility and quantify color differences across thicknesses in common colorimetric spaces. This analysis enables automatic diamond-thickness extrapolation from standard optical microscope images with 5 nm resolution, in good agreement with white-light interferometry (WLI) measurements. The DOI substrate and colorimetric thickness-evaluation method provide an effective fabrication platform and reliable validation route for scalable manufacturing of diamond nanophotonic devices.

items.title: Physics-aware calibration neural network for automated TCAD-to-experiment modeling of carbon nanotube field-effect transistors
items.abstract: Abstract Low-dimensional semiconductor devices, including carbon nanotube field-effect transistors (CNT-FETs), require efficient calibration methods to reconcile numerical simulations with experimentally measured electrical characteristics. Conventional manual calibration is time-consuming, while purely data-driven surrogate models may provide limited physical interpretability and reduced reliability when applied to device geometries outside the training domain. In this work, we propose a physics-aware calibration neural network (PACNN) for supervised technology computer-aided design (TCAD)-to-experiment calibration of CNT-FET transfer and output characteristics. PACNN uses current–voltage curves generated by a two-dimensional intrinsic silicon TCAD model as a stable numerical reference. The architecture combines an anchor-preserving physical-affine module, which accounts for global variations in voltage alignment, current amplitude, slope, and extracted electrical parameters, with family-specific bounded residual modules that correct the remaining local discrepancies. Transfer characteristics are processed in the signed logarithmic current domain, whereas output characteristics are calibrated in the normalized linear current domain using separate amplitude and low-rank shape corrections. Model training incorporates curve-fitting, curve-level R 2 , slope consistency, device parameter, residual, and regularization objectives. Channel-length generalization was evaluated through out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation to $${L}_\mathrm{ch}$$ L ch = 4.5 μm and 5.0 μm. PACNN achieved macro-averaged curve-wise R 2 values of 0.947 4 and 0.876 0 for the transfer and output characteristics, respectively, with corresponding pooled pointwise R 2 values of 0.962 7 and 0.996 2. The predicted curves also preserved key electrical parameters, yielding a balanced physical consistency index of 0.918 3. These results indicate that PACNN provides an accurate and physically constrained framework for automated TCAD-to-experiment calibration of CNT-FET characteristics.

items.title: PagedMoE: Cross-Precision Expert Caching for Token-Level Dynamic Precision in SSD-Resident MoE Inference
items.abstract: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are promising for local inference because sparse routing allows the routed-expert pool to reside on SSD while DRAM caches recently used experts. However, under practical DRAM cache capacities, substantial SSD I/O remains on the critical path despite I/O-computation overlap. Token-level dynamic expert precision offers a natural way to reduce this data demand by allocating bits according to expert importance and quantization sensitivity. Nevertheless, treating each bit-width of the same expert as an independent object prevents cross-precision cache reuse, causing overlapping data to be fetched repeatedly. The key insight is that precision should instead denote the refinement depth of one shared expert state. Based on this insight, we present PagedMoE, which stores each expert once using a prefix-compatible tree codebook and bitplane layout. Lower-precision representations are valid prefixes of higher-precision ones, allowing cached data to be reused or extended by fetching only missing bitplanes. PagedMoE selects the required prefix length before I/O using current routing weights and offline expert-specific error profiles, and directly executes cached 1-8-bit prefixes without materializing full-precision experts. At an average routed-expert precision of 2.5 bits, PagedMoE achieves quality close to GPTQ-INT4 on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and to MXFP4 on most evaluated GLM5.2 tasks. With a 24 GiB expert cache, it reaches 8.89 tokens/s on Qwen3.5, 1.33x the throughput of the same dynamic requests using independent precision objects and 1.56x that of uniform 4-bit execution.

items.title: PRISM: Unifying multiphysics optothermal transport and identifiability-guided inference for nanoscale thermal metrology
items.abstract: Quantifying thermal transport across micro- and nanoscale heterostructures is critical for solid-state devices and relies on fitting heat-transfer models to thermal-wave spectra. When probing scales approach optical absorption depths, electron-phonon equilibration lengths, or phonon mean free paths, classical surface-heating Fourier models can match measured phase spectra while returning biased, measurement-dependent parameters. Here we introduce PRISM (Physics-Resolved Inference and Screening Meta-framework), an agentic framework coupling multilayer optical transfer-matrix electrodynamics, two-temperature electron-phonon relaxation, and nonlocal Guyer-Krumhansl phonon hydrodynamics within a unified admittance formalism, paired with singular-value-decomposition identifiability screening and knowledge-guided routing. Demonstrated with frequency-domain thermoreflectance across stacks relevant to microelectronic contacts and dielectric barriers, PRISM corrects a 24-28% interfacial conductance underestimation in Au/Si, recovers intrinsic silica conductivity in Au/Ti/SiO$_2$, and eliminates a 40% cross-plane conductivity underestimation in Au/MoS$_2$. In bimetallic Au/Ti/Si stacks, where all three non-classical mechanisms act simultaneously, nonlocal modeling reconciles the $116$-$137$ W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ local-fit scatter across spot sizes and frequency windows into a configuration-independent intrinsic silicon conductivity of $141$ W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. For ion-irradiated and graded media with continuous conductivity profiles, PRISM can autonomously construct and verify a deep operator network solver to reconstruct steep damage gradients. By uniting non-equilibrium transport physics and identifiability screening with autonomous model synthesis, PRISM establishes a generalizable paradigm readily extensible to broader optothermal and thermal-wave metrology modalities.

items.title: OoB reflections of Mo/Si multilayer EUV mirrors with carbon contaminations and surface oxidization
items.abstract: In EUV lithography, laser produced plasma light sources emit not only 13.5 nm radiation but also a broad spectrum of out-of-band (OoB) light (140–300 nm), which causes image contrast loss and reduces manufacturing yield. This study evaluates the relationship between surface modifications, including carbon contamination and oxidization, and OoB reflectance characteristics. Using carbon-contaminated Mo/Si ML mirrors exposed to resist outgas and Ru-capped mask mirror samples oxidized by ozone ashing, experiments were conducted at the NewSUBARU synchrotron radiation facility. Results from BL-3 and BL-10 beamlines, including X-ray absorption spectroscopy, reveal that both carbon contamination and oxidization modify OoB reflectance spectra, depending on surface condition and chemical composition.
items.venue: International Conference on Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography

items.title: Negative Feedback in Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 Resistive Memory: Feigenbaum Route Toward Two‐Terminal Pseudo‐Random Number Generation and Neural Network Instabilities
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Resistively switching metal‐insulator‐meal (MIM) structures are a strong contender for universal memory technologies and neuromorphic computing applications. Their ability to combine non‐volatility with analogue tuneability enables in‐memory computing, where both data processing and storage occur in the same physical location. A period‐doubling bifurcation was observed in endurance tests of TiN/ Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 /Au devices, where sequences of voltage pulses with constant amplitudes are supplied to the stack. Based on this, the memory cell's response to increasingly larger voltage pulses is measured. The extracted parameters are used to deduce a probabilistic non‐linear map describing endurance cycling of the MIM system. The investigation of the dynamics involves the identification of parameters that have been reported to be subject to change during continuous switching, and the investigation of how this drift affects the switching dynamics. The found model thus serves as a design framework to either deliberately develop systems exhibiting chaotic dynamics or circumvent them for classical memory applications.

items.title: Modeling and Analysis of Reliability Challenges in Nanoscale Transistors
items.abstract: To meet the speed, complexity, circuit density, power consumption, and ultimately cost requirements of many advanced applications, scientists have spent decades shrinking device feature sizes for better performance of metal-oxide semiconductor (MOS) technology. However, there are several disadvantages to switching to these nano size MOS devices.
