Most of the functional failure in nano-scale devices is caused by aging related phenomena such as negative bias temperature instability (NBTI), hot carrier degradation (HCD), and time dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB). However, Silicon devices’ dimensions and material capabilities are beginning to hit their limitations. Scientists and researchers have figured out how to replace the current silicon material with an emerging novel material like carbon nano tube. The goal of this research was to develop a drain current and threshold voltage model for carbon nanotube field effect transistors (CNTFETs) that can be used in the analysis and design of reliable integrated circuits, focusing on the reliability issues of conventional metal oxide semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) at the nanoscale. To develop this model, we investigated the atomic structure of carbon nanotubes and used the fundamentals of electrostatics to describe a field-effect transistor. By analyzing and defining the electronic structure of carbon nanotubes, we first arrived at analytical formulas for the carrier concentration in carbon nanotubes for various chiral vectors (n, m). By combining several chiral vectors, it is possible to determine the threshold voltage expression that is obtained throughout the procedure as well as the I-V characteristics for CNTFETs. The diameter and chiral angle of carbon nanotubes were shown to be significant determinants of the I-V characteristics and threshold voltage. In terms of the threshold voltage change CNTFET shows better performance 24% less than the conventional MOSFET in 45nm technology node.
items.venue: Saudi Journal of Engineering and Technology

items.title: Mixed-timestep spiking neural networks: a temporal alignment framework for high-efficiency neuromorphic computing
items.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are energy-efficient due to their event-driven computation and sparse spike-based communication. However, most existing SNN models adopt a uniform time-step across all layers, which limits temporal flexibility and leads to suboptimal accuracy latency trade-offs under low-latency inference. To address this limitation, we propose Mixed-Timestep Spiking Neural Networks (MT-SNNs), a paradigm in which different layers operate with different time-steps, enabling layer-wise temporal allocation for efficient inference. To construct MT-SNNs, we develop a quantization-aware ANN-to-SNN conversion framework. Specifically, we establish a theoretical relationship between ANN activation bit-width and SNN time-steps, showing that the SNN time-step T can be approximated by the activation quantization level 2 n of the source ANN. Based on this relationship, layer-wise activation bit-widths in ANNs can be mapped to layer-wise time-steps in SNNs. We then jointly optimize quantization levels and firing thresholds to obtain compact mixed-timestep configurations that reduce inference latency while preserving accuracy. Finally, we identify the temporal dimension mismatch issue caused by heterogeneous layer-wise time-steps and propose Scaled Synaptic Current Accumulation (SSCA), a fused temporal alignment mechanism that aligns inter-layer propagation in the synaptic-current domain without instantiating a standalone temporal-alignment kernel. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, CIFAR10-DVS, and DVS-Gesture demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. On ImageNet-1K, MT-SNNs based on ResNet-34 achieve 73.63% Top-1 accuracy with only 4.88 average time-steps, demonstrating a favorable accuracy latency trade-off for low-latency SNN conversion.

items.title: Methodology for determining interface-state density in AlGaN/GaN MIS-HEMT structures using sub-bandgap illumination
items.abstract: In this work, we present a methodology for determining the interface-state density distribution in metal-insulator-semiconductor (MIS) AlGaN/GaN heterostructures using sub-bandgap illumination. First, we discuss the electronic transitions that occur during sub-bandgap illumination of MIS AlGaN/GaN heterostructures. In particular, we show how these transitions can induce a threshold-voltage shift in MIS AlGaN/GaN HEMT structures and, consequently, lead to a completely erroneous interpretation of the results. In this context, we experimentally demonstrate that the interface-state density distribution can be significantly overestimated due to, for example, free-hole generation resulting from electronic transitions via interface states at the AlGaN/insulator interface and/or deep levels in the GaN buffer layer. Finally, we provide guidelines for the accurate determination of the interface-state density in MIS AlGaN/GaN heterostructures using sub-bandgap illumination, including detailed measurement and analysis procedures.

items.title: Memristor-Based In-Memory Computing for Artificial Intelligence Acceleration: A Review of Devices, Crossbar Architectures, Benefits and Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence workloads are dominated by multiply-and-accumulate operations on very large weight matrices. In conventional processors these weights must be moved repeatedly between memory and the arithmetic units, and this data movement, rather than the arithmetic itself, consumes most of the energy and time. Memristor-based in-memory computing (IMC) addresses this limitation by performing computation inside the memory array. A memristor is a two-terminal resistive switching device whose conductance can be programmed and retained, so it can store a weight. When memristors are arranged in a crossbar, Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's current law cause the column currents to equal the product of an input voltage vector and the conductance matrix, so a complete vector–matrix multiplication is obtained in a single analog step. This review explains the memristor concept and its physical realisations, the working principle of crossbar arrays, and the peripheral circuits and system architecture needed to build an accelerator. Representative device-level and system-level studies are compared. The benefits for AI inference and training are assessed against non-idealities such as device variability, limited precision, conductance drift, wire resistance and the cost of analog-to-digital conversion. Applications and research directions are identified.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Mechanical and Thermal Performance of CoWoS-S Using Glass-Core Substrate and Glass-Interposer
items.abstract: With the rise of the high-speed computing era and Artificial Intelligence (AI), Chip on Wafer on Substrate (CoWoS) package has become a mainstream package type. CoWoS-S (Si-interposer), with its high interconnection density and heterogeneous integration capabilities, is now the dominant CoWoS product on the market. However, as package size increase, the drawbacks of CoWoS-S have also emerged, such as high manufacturing cost of silicon interposers and the large stress and high warpage resulting from large reticle size. Glass interposer and glass-core substrate are currently seen as a solution to these problems, due to their lower cost compared to silicon and their excellent coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) adjustability. Therefore, this study explores the thermal stress, warpage and thermal performance of glass applied to interposer and substrate core, and compares them with normal CoWoS-S. This paper utilizes the finite element analysis software ANSYS to conduct simulations. First, the stress and warpage performance of CoWoS-S using a glass substrate versus a conventional organic substrate were compared. Under the same thickness, the glass substrate exhibited lower warpage but higher stress at the chip module (CM) corner. However, by reducing the glass substrate thickness to match the warpage of organic substrate, the glass substate demonstrated better stress performance. Furthermore, the stress and warpage behavior of a glass interposer versus a conventional silicon interposer were investigated. The results showed that the glass interposer performed better in both warpage and stress. When the silicon interposer size was fixed at 3.3X the reticle size, a glass interposer size of 5.2X yielded similar stress and warpage performance. This study also explored the thermal behavior of glass interposer and glass-core substrate, revealing that with a strong external cooling system, the difference between glass and initial materials was insignificant. However, as the cooling capability of the external cooling system decreased, the differences became more pronounced. This research explored the application of glass materials in different package structures through simulation, providing directions for structural improvement and confirming the differences in thermal behavior. Above all, the number of experiments was reduced, and design directions for future CoWoS-S applications using glass materials were provided.

items.title: Material optimization of interconnects and transistors for energy-efficient and high-performance cryogenic GAA technology
items.abstract: Abstract Unprecedented computational demand is reshaping the landscape of energy-efficient and high-performance computing. As Moore’s law approaches its physical limits, continued progress to meet this demand can no longer rely solely on transistor scaling. Cryogenic operation of CMOS circuits offers a promising path forward, enhancing the subthreshold slope (SS) of transistors while enabling certain materials to exhibit superconductivity. This dual advantage positions device- and material-level optimizations as a compelling solution for next-generation cryogenic computing. In this work, we demonstrate that unlocking the full potential of cryogenic CMOS requires strategic transistor and interconnect-level optimizations. We show that (1) material optimization for tuning transistor work function is vital for translating SS improvements into a significant increase in ON current, while (2) exploiting superconducting interconnect materials at cryogenic temperatures is essential to eliminate resistive parasitics and overcome interconnect bottlenecks. To quantify these benefits, we employ a cryogenic-aware 2 nm gate-all-around nanosheet digital design flow, incorporating calibrated device models along with a full standard cell library. Our evaluation results targeting the compute fabric of the AI accelerator circuit demonstrate that our optimizations provide a 3× increase in TOPS, 7.7× increase in TOPS/W, and 23× improvement in efficiency TOPS 2 /W.

items.title: Laser-transferrable GaN HEMTs based on high-quality AlN/GaN/AlN sacrificing templates
items.abstract: Laser lift-off (LLO) technology is an effective approach to fabricate transferrable GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) and address self-heating effects during device operation. However, conventional approaches struggle with precise control of LLO positions and structural integrity of devices, especially for those with AlN-based back barriers (BBs). Herein, we develop a laser-transferrable GaN HEMT with a μm-scale AlN BB, which is grown on a novel template including a GaN sacrificing layer (SL) and a metalorganic chemical vapor deposition-grown AlN nucleation layer (MO-AlN NL). The MO-AlN serves as the dislocation filtering layer to suppress dislocation propagation in the GaN SL, thereby creating an optimized nucleation template for the AlN BB. As such, the AlN-on-GaN epitaxy proceeds in a coherent 2D growth mode with largely reduced threading dislocations and preserved compressive strain. The devices fabricated on this AlN-BB/GaN-SL/AlN-NL tri-layer template can be integrally detached by a 266-nm UV laser, which only breaks the GaN SL and leaves an intact device active region. This work simultaneously resolves the critical challenges in μm-scale AlN-on-GaN epitaxy and laser transfer of GaN HEMTs with AlN-based BBs, offering a viable approach to laser-transferrable GaN power/RF devices with customized device structures toward improved device characteristics and thermal management.

items.title: Laser welding of dissimilar aluminum/copper joints: A review
items.abstract: Aluminum/copper (Al/Cu) laser-welded joints are increasingly used in lightweight and highly conductive interconnections, including battery tabs, busbars, and power modules. The pronounced differences between Al and Cu in thermophysical properties, optical absorptivity, and metallurgical compatibility promote the formation of Al–Cu intermetallic compounds (IMCs), heterogeneous reaction zones, pores, cracks, and lack-of-fusion defects. These microstructural features and defects can affect the load-bearing capacity, electrical resistance, current-induced temperature rise, and long-term stability of the joints. This review examines recent advances in interfacial reactions, weld-pool mixing, defect formation, process control, interlayer-assisted joining, process monitoring, and service reliability of laser-welded Al/Cu joints. The applicability of continuous-wave, pulsed, beam-oscillation, core–ring beam, short-wavelength laser, and external-field-assisted approaches is evaluated in relation to sheet thickness, stacking sequence, penetration requirements, electrical-resistance requirements, production cycle time, and interfacial gap. Multisensor monitoring can establish correlations between process signals and penetration depth, interfacial fusion width, or defect state. However, model performance should be validated using cross-sectional metallography, micro-computed tomography (μXCT), and service-performance data. Independent-weld validation and tests across processing conditions are needed to assess model transferability. Finally, a conceptual traceable quality-chain framework is proposed for Al/Cu electrical interconnections. The framework links processing parameters with interfacial microstructure, spatial defect distribution, effective current paths, and service-related performance drift, providing a basis for traceable quality assurance and reliability assessment.

items.title: LUPIN: A LUT-Based DRAM-PIM Accelerator for Feature Aggregation in Graph Neural Networks
items.abstract: Processing-in-memory (PIM) architectures have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional von Neumann architectures for accelerating memory-bound applications, such as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), by reducing data movement between memory and processing units, thereby improving energy efficiency and reducing computational latency. Feature aggregation is a fundamental operation in GNNs; however, the sparsity of graph data leads to poor spatial and temporal locality. This results in dynamic and irregular memory access patterns, ultimately limiting performance and increasing latency. To address this issue, we propose LUPIN, a look-up table (LUT)-based PIM architecture to accelerate GNNs. In this design, logic-based processing is replaced with precalculated results stored in LUTs to perform the required computations within the DRAM memory platform. The proposed LUPIN architecture achieves enhanced performance and markedly improved energy efficiency compared to conventional bitwise-parallel PIM designs. Moreover, it avoids the fabrication challenges associated with integrating logic circuits into memory. It leverages the extensive internal parallelism of DRAM to accelerate the execution of GNN models while maintaining high energy efficiency. Our results demonstrate that LUPIN achieves geometric-mean energy improvements of 32× and 51× on GCN and GIN, respectively, over the CPU and 15× and 19.5×, respectively, over the GPU. Moreover, LUPIN reduces latency by 35.8× and 25.7× on GCN and GIN, respectively, compared with the CPU and 29.6× and 20.5×, respectively, compared with the GPU. The proposed LUPIN architecture achieves nearly 10× higher energy efficiency and 5× speedup compared with the state-of-the-art PIM architectures.
items.venue: Journal of Low Power Electronics and Applications

items.title: Introducing Cluster Efficiency to LLM Serving: Pooling Economical Accelerators over Fast Interconnects
items.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) serving places substantial demands on compute, memory capacity, and memory bandwidth. Economical accelerators can offer these resources at lower cost, but their limited per-device capacity requires pooling across devices, making communication overhead critical. We study cluster efficiency, measured in tokens per dollar and per joule, and show how low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnects enable economical accelerators to retain their cost advantage. Guided by a characterization of coding-agent workloads and accelerator scaling, we realize this design on the Tenstorrent Galaxy, a cluster of Blackhole chips. The serving stack combines integrated communication engines, pipelined ring transfers, communication-computation overlap, and device-side decode replay to reduce collective overhead. Across three dense models in BF16 and 8-bit configurations with 8K-256K-token contexts, the Galaxy achieves 1.07-2.24$\times$ the tokens per dollar of an eight-GPU RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell server under a three-year acquisition-and-electricity cost model. Emulating TCP-class communication on the same chips reduces throughput by 23.5-67.4% and eliminates the cost advantage in every evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate how fast interconnects translate the per-dollar resource advantages of economical accelerators into cost-efficient long-context LLM serving.

items.title: Improved electrical and interfacial performance of HfO2-based gate stack on Si with Ga2O3-induced dipole dominated effect via laser spike annealing
items.abstract: In this work, metal–oxide–semiconductor (MOS) capacitors with a HfO2/Ga2O3/SiO2/p-Si structure were fabricated and treated with laser spike annealing (LSA) at 650, 850, and 1050 °C in order to investigate the effects on the electrical and interfacial performance of the devices. The p-type dipole dominated effect is demonstrated, although a fixed-charge contribution cannot be fully excluded. The Ga2O3 layer introduces a p-type dipole at the interface, resulting in a 1.03 V flatband voltage (VFB) shift with only a minor increase in equivalent oxide thickness. LSA can further strengthen this dipole dominated effect while improving the gate-stack quality by reducing the trap/detrap electron density (Not) and the interface trap density (Dit) at the same time. The time zero dielectric breakdown test indicates 850 °C as the optimal LSA temperature, yielding the highest breakdown voltage and operational stability. The physical mechanism is directly validated by x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, which correlates the VFB modulation with a systematic shift in the valence band offset. Our work indicates that the synergistic integration of a Ga2O3 dipole layer with LSA provides a promising strategy for large VFB adjustment and reliability enhancement in advanced MOS technologies.

items.title: High-Performance GaN HEMTs on an Ultrathin 4H-SiC/Diamond Engineered Substrate via Optimized Epitaxial Growth
items.abstract: Abstract GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) were fabricated on an ultrathin 4H-SiC/diamond engineered substrate using an optimized epitaxial growth scheme. Optimization of the epitaxial growth conditions improved epitaxial quality and carrier transport properties.The fabricated devices exhibited a maximum DC drain current density of approximately 1.25 A/mm and a peak transconductance of 367 mS/mm, demonstrating high current capability on the engineered substrate platform. Infrared thermography yielded a low-power thermal resistance of 0.92 K•mm/W, compared with 2.46 K•mm/W for a GaN-on-SiC reference device.The device on the engineered substrate sustained a maximum DC power dissipation density of 37.8 W/mm. These results demonstrate the potential of the optimized GaN-on-4H-SiC/diamond platform for high-performance GaN devices with enhanced thermal management.

items.title: Heterogeneous Integration for Direct RF Digitization: Packaging Strategies for Wideband Software Defined Sensor Systems
items.abstract: Direct RF digitization is reshaping the architecture of radar, EW, and wideband sensing systems by enabling direct sampling of multi‑GHz to millimeter‑wave (mmW) signals. However, translating the performance of advanced data converters and digital processing ICs into deployable, size-weight-and-power (SWaP)‑constrained modules requires better packaging architecture to gain improved module signal integrity power delivery and thermal performance. Today’s heterogeneous‑integration (HI) ecosystem imposes additional constraints that complicate module co‑design: chiplets arrive with fixed I/O functions, pre-defined bump maps and power‑pad distributions; interposer technologies offer limited routing granularity in redistribution layers (RDLs) and insufficient freedom to separate RF, digital, and power domains and to extract module heat efficiently; and packaging Process Design Kit / Assembly Design Kits (PDKs/ADKs) models remain immature, preventing robust co‑simulation of RF, mechanical, and manufacturing effects such as warpage, CTE mismatch, and process variation. These ecosystem limitations restrict the available “tuning knobs” needed to optimize wideband RF signal paths, mixed‑signal interfaces, high‑speed SerDes data movement, and multi‑hundred‑watt thermal extraction. To address the above HI system‑driven challenge exacerbated by current business models and manufacturing realities, an improved HI RF digitation module architecture is proposed—including function‑sensitive RDLs for RF/mmW routing, low‑loss power‑delivery architectures, multi‑tier thermal paths, and EDA/PDK innovations. Analytical modeling calculations and simulations demonstrate significant improvements compared to traditional HI architecture, including ~27 dB lower RF-digital isolation, ~45°C peak module junction temperature reduction and ~640 mV maximum module IR voltage drop improvement. These enhancements in signal integrity, thermal and power performance is crucial to stabilize data converter linearity, reduce clock‑jitter coupling, and improve FPGA digital timing closure, and enable next generation scalable, deployable direct‑RF digitization modules.

items.title: Enabling High‐Frequency Characterization for Dynamic Modeling of Schottky Barrier Field‐Effect Transistors
items.abstract: This work presents a comprehensive methodology describing static and dynamic characterization and compact modeling of an ambipolar Schottky barrier field‐effect transistor (SBFET) technology, taking into consideration the integration of specifically designed test structures necessary for accurate scattering parameter measurements. In this work, we demonstrate, for the first time, the complete design flow for this emerging technology, starting with design and fabrication of dedicated high‐frequency test structures for scattering‐parameter measurement up to 110 GHz. The high frequency data are then used to validate a physics‐based compact model for the ambipolar SBFETs. Physically meaningful results are obtained with a good agreement between the measured and compact model data, demonstrating the usefulness of such dedicated methodologies for the refinement of the emerging technology performance.

items.title: Emerging Heterojunction Memristors: Structural Design, Switching Mechanisms, and Advanced Computing Applications
items.abstract: The relentless demand for data‐intensive computing has exposed the fundamental bottlenecks of the conventional von Neumann architecture, driving the search for alternative processing paradigms. Memristors have emerged as compelling building blocks for next‐generation in‐memory and neuromorphic computing. Within this domain, heterojunction‐based memristors stand out as highly promising candidates, leveraging interfacial engineering to deliver exceptional device performance and multifunctional capabilities. This review provides a comprehensive and critical overview of recent advancements in heterojunction memristors. We systematically examine the material systems, structural classifications, and fabrication strategies that underpin these devices, followed by an in‐depth analysis of their underlying resistive switching (RS) mechanisms. Furthermore, we highlight their transformative potential across diverse application domains, spanning data storage, artificial synapses, neuromorphic biomimetic sensory perception, and advanced logic circuits. Finally, we address the prevailing technical challenges and propose viable strategies, offering a strategic roadmap for the rational design of high‐performance heterojunction memristors to power the future of neuromorphic hardware.

items.title: Dual-Fold Triggered Memory Elements for High-Speed Time-Encoded ADCs
items.abstract: The strength of mixed signal processors nowadays depends on the conversion speed of analog signals to digital. VCO-based ADC converters nowadays use counters and registers to meet the demands of the integrated era. This chapter proposes memory elements adapting DFT. The two have been developed differently, with one having 14 transistors (14-T) and the other having 12 transistors (12-T). Results are obtained by modeling the circuits at a 1.2 V supply voltage and 45 nm technology. The propagation delay of 14-T is seen to be 46.3% shorter than that of 16-T, and that of 12-T is 60.52% shorter than that of 16-T. When compared to 16-T, the area for 14-T decreases by 17.42%, and for 12-T it decreases by 37.16%. Examinations of dynamic power scattering are available for multi-bit registers with up to 64 bits and a variety of capacitive loads operating at different frequencies.

items.title: Distributed Charge-Trap Dynamics in Graphene Transistors Revealed by RF Impedance Dispersion
items.abstract: Abstract Charge trapping at the graphene/dielectric interface is a major source of instability in graphene transistors, yet its signature in the radio-frequency electrical response remains poorly understood and characterized. This work reports that trap-related charge exchange along the graphene channel produces a distinct, frequency-dependent dispersion in the transistor output impedance, observable from standard microwave measurements without dedicated stress or pulsed-bias protocols. This dispersion primarily affects the reactive part of the output impedance, particularly at low frequencies, and gradually diminishes toward the GHz range, consistent with a distribution of trap relaxation times along the channel. To capture this behavior, a non-uniform transmission-line model is developed that treats channel trapping as a spatially distributed process. An equivalent lumped circuit, consisting of a single RC branch in parallel with the channel resistance, reproduces the distributed response accurately, and explicit analytic relationships between both representations enable extraction of local distributed-model parameters from the lumped circuit. The equivalent capacitance converges to a stable value as the number of distributed trapping sections increases, whereas the effective time constant remains dependent on trap position, preserving information about the distributed nature of the phenomenon. Using the converged values, the extracted interfacial trap density is consistent with reported values for graphene/AlOx interfaces, and the extracted trap dynamics depend systematically on channel aspect ratio, identifying device geometry as a means of tuning the frequency range over which trap-induced dispersion is observable. Excellent agreement between model and experimental data is demonstrated across the full characterization frequency range, and the resulting trap-aware description further improves prediction of the device input reflection coefficient. This work establishes high-frequency electrical characterization, interpreted through a distributed-to-lumped framework, as a non-destructive, quantitative route to probe the density, spatial distribution, and dynamics of traps in graphene channels, with direct relevance to interface engineering and defect characterization of graphene devices.

items.title: Curvature-induced integrate-and-fire and burst firing in an antiferromagnetic skyrmion neuron
items.abstract: Antiferromagnetic skyrmions, owing to their zero skyrmion Hall effect, high stability, and low driving current, are promising information carriers for neuromorphic devices. Here, we propose an antiferromagnetic skyrmion artificial neuron based on a U-shaped curved nanotrack that emulates both integrate-and-fire and burst-firing neuronal functions through curvature-regulated skyrmion dynamics. The curvature-induced energy barrier traps antiferromagnetic skyrmions near the cutoff line, while the accumulating inter-skyrmion repulsive interactions collectively overcome this barrier, enabling a biological-like integrate-and-fire behavior. Further tuning of the driving current modulates the interplay between the curvature-induced barrier and inter-skyrmion repulsion, which allows multiple skyrmions to successively cross the cutoff line and gives rise to burst firing. By tuning the material and geometric parameters, both firing modes and threshold currents can be effectively regulated. Moreover, burst firing exhibits lower energy consumption per spike, while burst-based encoding achieves lower bit error rates and enhanced noise robustness. These findings establish antiferromagnetic skyrmion neurons as promising building blocks for energy-efficient and reliable neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Cu-Cu Hybrid Bonding for Chiplets Heterogeneous Integration
items.abstract: Cu-Cu hybrid bonding is an old packaging technology. It has been in high volume manufacturing (HVM) for more than 10 years. In this study, 21 different HVM or to be in HVM products and 12 new applications with Cu-Cu hybrid bonding will be briefly mentioned. Some recommendations will be provided. A brief history and fundamentals of Cu-Cu hybrid bonding will be presented first.

items.title: Crystallographic Alignment Reshapes the Electronic Landscape and Enhances Charge Transport in Indium Gallium Oxide Thin‐Film Transistors
items.abstract: Amorphous indium gallium zinc oxide thin-film transistors are widely used in high-end organic light-emitting diode displays. However, their intrinsic mobility-stability trade-off fundamentally limits further performance scaling. Crystallized oxide semiconductors have emerged as a promising pathway to overcome this constraint, yet the relative roles of crystallinity and crystallographic alignment remain unclear. Here, we systematically compare amorphous, random-polycrystalline, and highly aligned crystalline indium gallium oxide channels to elucidate the origin of enhanced charge transport. Temperature-dependent electrical analysis and multi-frequency capacitance-voltage spectroscopy reveal that crystallographic alignment sharpens and energetically stabilizes subgap states near the conduction band, indicating reduced energetic disorder. Spatially resolved potential analysis further shows that this alignment suppresses grain-boundary-induced potential barriers, producing a more uniform transport landscape. In contrast, random-polycrystalline channels retain broadened subgap states and spatially distributed grain-boundary barriers despite their crystallinity. These results show that crystallographic alignment, rather than crystallinity alone, governs charge transport in polycrystalline oxide semiconductors by concurrently optimizing the energetic and spatial aspects of the electronic landscape, while maintaining robust bias-stress stability.

items.title: Continuous Kinetic Model of Counterion-Mediated Redox Switching in 14-Bit Molecular Memristors for Analog In-Memory Computing
items.abstract: Kinetic molecular memristors offer a compelling path toward high-density analog in-memory computing by achieving 14-bit precision, wherein discrete redox transitions and counterion displacements dictate non-volatile conductance across a deterministic energy landscape. However, integrating these nanoscale kinetics into macroscale circuit simulators has remained bottlenecked by derivative discontinuities and solver convergence failures. Here, we present a physics-inspired continuous kinetic model that bridges microscopic molecular transport with scalable circuit architectures. By casting discrete intramolecular states, counterion relaxation dynamics, and Marcus-Hush-Chidsey electron transfer rates into continuously differentiable state variables, we derive a robust, Spectre-compatible compact model and a matching vectorized Python solver. This work culminates in a unified computational platform to reliably predict the behavior of complex circuits built on these molecular memristors.

items.title: Co-Engineering Packaging Architecture for Next Gen Data Center Xeon SoC
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of AI and High-Performance Computing (HPC) has driven the need for advanced modular packaging architectures (2D, 2D+ 2.5D, 3D & 3.5D). As workloads become more demanding and time-to-market (TTM) accelerates, robust, scalable, and efficient processor packages are needed. The innovations in advanced packaging architectures are intended to aid scalability and performance but also face challenges from increased SoC area, higher pin-counts, larger package form factors with more layers, higher packaging/assembly costs and lower manufacturing yields resulting from greater substrate stack complexity. This paper presents a comprehensive co-design methodology for multi-chiplet processor packaging that integrates physical design optimization, signal integrity enhancement and power delivery network improvements. Our approach addresses the fundamental challenge of maintaining performance while reducing package complexity and cost through innovative routing topologies, advanced via architectures, pinmap optimizations and optimized power distribution strategies. The integrated methodology demonstrates significant cost reduction while meeting next-generation performance targets, providing a scalable framework for future multi-chiplet processor implementations.

items.title: Brillouin comb line amplifiers for optical atomic clocks
items.abstract: Optical atomic clocks outperform the microwave clocks at the heart of current timing and navigation infrastructure by orders-of-magnitude, and recent progress in on-chip integration provides the opportunity to widely deploy them. Conventionally, a narrow linewidth laser interrogates the atomic transition, and an optical frequency comb divides its stabilised frequency (hundreds of terahertz) down to a microwave that is electronically countable. The laser(s) impose a significant size, weight, power and cost penalty, which is a current barrier to low-cost, scalable, fully on-chip optical clocks. Here, we position the frequency comb as the central engine of the clock by using Brillouin-amplified comb lines for atomic spectroscopy, which eliminates the need for stable clock lasers. Amplified comb lines reach an ultra-low frequency noise floor of $6\,\mathrm{Hz^2/Hz}$ at $30\,\mathrm{kHz}$ offset, an order-of-magnitude below a high-end commercial fibre laser. We realize a clock based on the $\mathrm{5S}_{1/2}\rightarrow\mathrm{5D}_{5/2}$ transition in $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$ with competitive fractional frequency stability of $2\times10^{-13}$ at $τ= 1\,\mathrm{s}$, averaging to $9\times10^{-15}$ at $τ= 1000\,\mathrm{s}$. Lastly, we demonstrate a photonic chip-integrated Brillouin amplifier with a record 62.9 dB gain and up to 40 dB transferred noise suppression when pumped with a simple, low-cost diode laser. This opens a new route to compact optical clocks and enables use of atomic transitions lacking low-noise lasers by broadening a comb to the required wavelength and amplifying single lines.

items.title: Accelerating LLM Decoding with In-DRAM Parallelism
items.abstract: Autoregressive decoding of large language models (LLMs) on edge devices is dominated by memory-bound general matrix--vector multiplication (GeMV) operations. Processing-using-DRAM (PUD) is a promising computing paradigm that can alleviate this bottleneck by reducing processor--memory data transfers and enabling massively parallel computation within DRAM (e.g., across 65,536 columns). However, weight matrices in individual LLM layers (e.g., a QKV matrix in Llama3 8B with 6,144 rows) are typically too small to fully utilize parallelism in PUD. To address this challenge, we propose an algorithm--system co-design for PUD-based LLM inference. At the algorithm level, we enable a subsequent projection to be packed with the current projection by reformulating it as a computation on the current residual state plus a correction for the residual update. Layer redundancy allows this correction to be approximated using fewer bit-serial steps. At the system level, we tailor data mapping and execution to improve utilization of either columns within DRAM subarrays (SIMD) or independently controlled banks (MIMD). Overall, we achieves up to $1.41\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over the PUD baseline, corresponding to a $2.45\times$ speedup over processor-based execution.

items.title: Accelerating Advanced Packaging and Interposer Design with AI-Based 3D Full-Wave Optimization
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of microelectronic technologies has led to increasingly compact, high density package designs that must accommodate for multiple high-speed die-to-die interconnects. With modern high-speed package deigns becoming increasingly complex, this presents a significant challenge in achieving the optimal path planning to maintain routing and signal integrity. This paper explores an advanced methodology of how Artificial Intelligence (AI) is being leveraged to help evaluate the best tradeoffs more efficiently. The approach enables designers to optimize inter-die connections in heterogenous multi-die packages, mitigating insertion loss, ensuring impedance matching, and reducing cross talk.

items.title: Abstract 8400: Parsimonious Models Integrating Routine Clinical Data and Artificial Intelligence-Derived Angiographic Phenotypes to Predict Acute Kidney Injury, Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events and Heart Failure After Cardiac Catheterization
items.abstract: Background: The coronary anatomy captured during cardiac catheterization is rarely used to predict subsequent complications. Acute kidney injury (AKI), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and heart failure (HF) affect ~8%, ~11%, and ~4% of patients, respectively, representing a substantial burden of preventable morbidity. No validated risk scores are routinely applied for MACE or HF, while the Mehran score for contrast-induced AKI depends on manual variable extraction: a laborious process blind to the angiogram. AI now enables automated angiographic reading at scale, opening the path toward efficient and clinically applicable risk models. Hypothesis: Automated AI angiographic reading improves complication prediction, and a compact model can rival validated manual scores. Methods: We linked a registry of coronary catheterizations (Montreal Heart Institute, 2017-2024) with pre-procedure laboratories, electrocardiograms, comorbidities, procedural data and automated deep-learning angiographic interpretations (ventricular function, stenosis, calcification, occlusion, SYNTAX). Outcomes were 48-hour KDIGO AKI, 1-year MACE (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke) and 1-year heart-failure (HF) hospitalization. For each outcome, clinical and AI variables were ranked by LASSO regression; sparse logistic models were assessed by AUROC and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) with 95% bootstrap CIs on a held-out test set. The compact AKI model was compared with the Mehran score, in an identical percutaneous coronary intervention subset, by paired DeLong test. Results (preliminary): Among 6 383 (AKI, 6%), 11 790 (MACE, 12%), and 11 292 (HF, 4%) patients, hybrid models using only 5-6 variables discriminated well: AKI AUROC 0.80 [0.78-0.82], AUPRC 0.26 [0.22-0.31]; MACE 0.82 [0.81-0.83], AUPRC 0.40 [0.37-0.43]; HF 0.82 [0.79-0.84], AUPRC 0.24 [0.19-0.28]. AUPRCs were 3-6x outcome prevalence, confirming strong precision for these rare events. A single AI-derived measure, predicted left ventricular ejection fraction, was the leading angiographic variable for MACE and HF, whereas AKI did not clearly benefit from AI input. The 5-variable AKI model equaled the Mehran score (AUROC 0.79 vs 0.79; p=0.96) without manual entry of hypotension, shock or heart failure. At a Youden threshold, NPVs reached 0.98-0.99 for AKI and HF, identifying a low-risk majority who could forgo prophylaxis and monitoring. Conclusion: Compact models combining routine variables with AI-generated angiographic measures accurately predict MACE, HF and AKI, even matching the Mehran score, without requiring manual data entry. At our center only (~5,800 catheterizations/year), these models could flag several hundred patients annually for targeted prevention, supporting prospective and calibration testing before point-of-care use.

items.title: A review of phase-change display: materials, architectures, driving, and applications
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of next-generation display technologies has driven an increasing demand for devices that simultaneously offer ultrahigh resolution, high refresh rates, and ultralow power consumption. Phase-change materials (PCMs) undergo reversible structural transitions between amorphous and crystalline states, accompanied by pronounced changes in optical constants. This process is inherently nonvolatile and requires no sustaining bias, resulting in near-zero static power consumption. These properties have established PCMs as a highly competitive platform for next-generation display technologies. However, several critical challenges remain, including limited color gamut coverage, insufficient cycling endurance, and difficulties in pixel-level addressing, all of which continue to hinder the practical deployment of PCM-based displays. This review provides a systematic overview of phase-change display technologies, organized along four interconnected dimensions: materials, device architectures, driving schemes, and applications. The microscopic mechanisms and optimization strategies governing switching speed, energy consumption, and cycling stability are first summarized. The optical modulation principles of thin-film interference structures, subwavelength metasurfaces, and multimodal hybrid devices are then reviewed. The multilevel grayscale control strategies of electrothermal and laser-based driving schemes are subsequently compared. Representative applications, including reflective, transmissive, and holographic displays, are also surveyed. This review aims to establish a coherent framework spanning from material fundamentals to device architectures and application development, providing a structured reference for advancing PCM-based displays toward high-performance and practical implementation.

items.title: A Low‐Overhead SEU‐Resilient and Highly Defect‐Testable Scan‐Test‐Aware Latch Design
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Sequential elements in nanoscale CMOS circuits are becoming increasingly susceptible to radiation‐induced soft errors. Many hardened latch designs utilize cell‐internal redundancy to achieve soft error tolerance. However, such redundancy masks not only soft errors but also physical defects, thereby degrading test quality. Furthermore, escaped defects may compromise the soft error tolerability of these designs. Existing scan‐test‐aware designs (STAHL and HIDER) use design‐for‐test (DFT) techniques to improve cell‐internal defect detectability and reduce the impact of these potential defects on soft error tolerability. However, these two designs incur higher area and power overheads than existing designs. To overcome the limitations of these two scan‐test‐aware hardened designs, this paper proposes a low‐overhead, highly defect‐detectable, and SEU‐self‐recoverable hardened (LDSH) latch. The LDSH design uses cross‐connection to mitigate the output‐coupling problem of dual‐output C‐element (DOC) and achieve high soft error tolerability. Simulation results demonstrate that, the proposed LDSH achieves the highest defect coverage (DC) of 84.4%, and the lowest post‐test vulnerability factor (PTVF) of 3.37%, indicating that these undetected defects have low impact on the soft error tolerability of the proposed LDSH design. Compared with the two typical scan‐test‐aware latch designs, LDSH reduces power consumption by 72.66%, delay by 85.45%, power‐delay product (PDP) by 96.26%. Furthermore, detailed process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) as well as Monte Carlo simulations verify the low sensitivity of the proposed LDSH latch under the variation of PVT.
items.venue: International Journal of Circuit Theory and Applications

items.title: 2D Material‐Based Photonic Devices for Optical Sensing and Computing
items.abstract: Photonic devices offer broad bandwidth, low‐power operation, and intrinsic parallelism for intelligent sensing and neuromorphic computing. Silicon photonics provides a mature foundation for integrated optical systems. The indirect bandgap and absence of an intrinsic bulk Pockels effect in silicon motivate complementary material integration. Selected two‐dimensional (2D) materials combine atomically thin geometries with strong light–matter interactions and tunable electronic and optical properties. Their diversity allows complementary properties to be combined through van der Waals integration, extending the functionality and dynamic tunability of established photonic platforms. This review summarizes the luminescent, optoelectronic, and nonlinear optical properties of representative 2D materials and discusses recent progress in 2D‐material‐integrated light sources, photodetectors, and optical modulators. Integration strategies based on micro‐transfer printing and in situ epitaxial growth are further examined. Prospects for multidimensional optical sensing and neuromorphic computing are assessed alongside challenges in device performance, interface quality, scalable integration, and complementary metal‐oxide‐semiconductor (CMOS)‐compatible manufacturing.

items.title: Unlocking Device Bias Instability at Extremely Scaled Contact-Length and Its Impact on Circuit-Level Behavior of BEOL-Compatible Oxide Semiconductor 2T0C DRAM
items.abstract: We report the systematic study of bias instability in back-end-of-line (BEOL)-compatible oxide semiconductor transistors with sub-50 nm channel length ( ${L}_{\text {ch}}\text {)}$ and ultra-scaled contact length ( ${L}_{\text {c}} =30$ nm), and its direct impact on circuit-level 2T0C DRAM operation. Scaling ${L}_{\text {c}}$ from 150 nm to 30 nm suppresses NBTI-induced degradation in the write transistor, resulting in over a $7\times $ improvement in 2T0C DRAM retention. The physical mechanisms underlying the reliability impact of ${L}_{\text {c}}$ and ${L}_{\text {ch}}$ scaling are comprehensively clarified through combined experimental characterization and TCAD simulations. We propose an asymmetric device design strategy that leverages contact engineering to simultaneously optimize retention, read current, and reliability, offering a practical pathway toward scalable oxide semiconductor memories for high-density monolithic 3D integration.

items.title: Ultra-Wide Band Gap Material Gallium Oxide, Technology, Properties, Characterization
items.abstract: Gallium oxide (Ga₂O₃) is a ultra wide-bandgap semiconductor (4.7 ~ 5.3 eV) that has garnered significant attention for its exceptional structural, optical, and electrical properties, which make it suitable for high-power electronics, UV photodetectors, and catalysis. Structurally, Ga₂O₃ exhibits polymorphism, with α-, β-, γ-, δ-, ε-, and κ-phases, among which β-Ga₂O₃ is the most thermodynamically stable under ambient conditions. Synthesis methods, including hydrothermal growth, sol-gel processes, RF/DC sputtering, atomic layer deposition (ALD) and molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) enable precise control over phase formation, crystallinity, and defect density. In the present work is demonstrated the reactive magnetron sputtering (DC) technology for formation β-Ga₂O₃. As substrate is used 2-inch, (0006) orientation and 400μ thickness sapphire wafer. Experiments are made in different condition (power, oxygen partial pressure, time, temperature etc.) for analyzing the best technological rout of growing Ga₂O₃ with good structural, optical and electrical properties. X-ray structural analysis (XRD) was measured and a small peak was identified at the diffraction angle 2θ=20.5°. In terms of optical properties, transmission spectra were measured. The calculated optical band gap was ~ 5 eV. Electrically, Ga₂O₃ behaves predominantly as an n-type semiconductor due to oxygen vacancies. Undoped β-Ga₂O₃ exhibits high resistivity (~10⁶ Ω·cm). Electrical measurements also were performed on an HP 4279A C-V Meter to obtain a C-V profile, and the thicknesses of the deposited films were calculated from the graphs and compared with the values measured on the profilometer.

items.title: Triple‐Level Content‐Addressable Vertical NAND Flash Memory (Adv. Sci. 61/2026)
items.abstract: Content-Addressable V-NAND Flash Memory A blue search beam illuminates the matching path through a towering, multilayer V-NAND array. The image represents triple-level content-addressable V-NAND, which stores and compares multilevel data in place for fast, energy-efficient memory searches and AI computing. More details can be found in the Research Article by Jong-Ho Lee and co-workers (DOI: 10.1002/advs.77390).

items.title: Triboelectric Sensory Intelligence: From Mechanical Information Encoding to In-Sensor Memory, Neuromorphic Computing, and Closed-Loop Interaction
items.abstract: Triboelectric interfaces are progressing beyond self-powered sensing toward integrated sensory systems capable of encoding, retaining, transforming, and responding to mechanical information. Yet, the rapid convergence of triboelectric transduction with memory, neuromorphic devices, and intelligent interfaces has also blurred the distinctions between signal generation, state modulation, physical computation, and task-level intelligence. This Review establishes an information-centric framework for triboelectric sensory intelligence, in which mechanical interaction is traced through electrical encoding, signal–device coupling, internal state evolution, sensory processing, perception, and ultimately closed-loop action. Sensory representations based on amplitude, polarity, temporal structure, spatial patterns, material-dependent responses, and multimodal signals are considered in terms of encoding fidelity, separability, and robustness. Stateful mechanisms based on resistive switching, charge storage, ferroelectric polarization, and ionic or electrochemical dynamics are then related to sensory memory, temporal filtering, synaptic plasticity, event-based transformation, and other physical computational primitives. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing structural integration from processing location, device dynamics from implemented computation, and hardware processing from downstream software inference. The Review further links these principles to tactile and material perception, gesture and motion interfaces, multisensory integration, and sensory–motor feedback, while introducing system-level considerations of reproducibility, energy, latency, scalability, and generalization. Looking forward, reliable source–receiver co-design, adaptive processing, scalable heterogeneous integration, and closed-loop operation will be central to translating triboelectric interfaces from isolated device demonstrations into persistent and autonomous sensory systems.

items.title: Tri-Mode Resistive Switching in HfOx-Based RRAM for Reconfigurable In-Memory Computing
items.abstract: The effect of switching layer thickness on achieving tri-mode switching in HfOx-based resistive random access memory (RRAM) has not been explored. Here, we systematically investigate Pt/HfOx/Ti RRAM with different HfOx thicknesses (5, 10, and 15 nm) and reveal that the device with 10 nm HfOx thicknesses can achieve tri-mode switching. Compared with devices with 5 and 15 nm HfOx thicknesses, the digital switching mode of the device with 10-nm HfOx thickness is controlled by the formed conductive filaments (CFs) and the HfOx/Ti interface. The interface-dominated analog switching mode is achieved by modulating the oxygen vacancy concentration at the HfOx/Ti interface under low bias voltage. The occurrence of the write-once-read-many switching mode is due to the continuous accumulation of Joule heating without compliance current (CC), resulting in the formation of an irreversible conductive channel. This work provides a concise and mechanism-clear route for integrating storage, computing, and security functions in reconfigurable in-memory computing applications.

items.title: Trace‐Impurity Behavior of Semiconductor Ultra‐High‐Purity Hydrogen: Comparison of Gaseous and Liquefied Hydrogen Feedstocks After Getter and Cryogenic Purification Using Multi‐Channel Gas Chromatography With Plasma Emission Detection
items.abstract: ABSTRACT As semiconductor manufacturing advances, ultra‐high‐purity hydrogen quality has become important for process reproducibility, equipment reliability, and contamination control. The emerging introduction of liquefied hydrogen alongside conventional gaseous hydrogen requires analytical criteria that account for feedstock‐dependent behavior after purification. An operating semiconductor hydrogen supply system was used as a field platform to compare argon, nitrogen, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane, and non‐methane hydrocarbons after getter and cryogenic purification using multi‐channel gas chromatography with plasma emission detection. Raw liquefied hydrogen showed lower impurity levels and narrower variability than raw gaseous hydrogen in the investigated deliveries, whereas gaseous hydrogen showed greater variation, particularly for argon, nitrogen, and methane. At the final supply line, most target impurities in liquefied‐hydrogen‐derived product were below the method detection limits, whereas residual signals in gaseous‐hydrogen‐derived product reflected both feedstock characteristics and purification pathway. The main contribution is a process‐resolved interpretation framework linking raw‐feed measurements, individual purifier outlets, and final endpoint signals. These results indicate that interpretation criteria derived from gaseous‐hydrogen operation may require verification before application to liquefied‐hydrogen‐based systems, especially when vaporization history and purification pathway differ.

items.title: Toward Understanding Moisture-Induced Failure in SiC MOSFETs Under High-Voltage Bias: Insights From Coupled Simulation and Micro-Raman Analysis
items.abstract: Reliability under humid conditions is a critical prerequisite for the deployment of silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFETs in harsh environments. The high-voltage, high-humidity, and high-temperature reverse bias (HV–H3TRB) test is widely used to evaluate the humidity reliability of SiC MOSFETs. This work reveals that under HV–H3TRB conditions, electrochemical corrosion and mechanical damage coexist at the failure region, while the underlying failure mechanism cannot be clearly identified through static electrical parameters during the aging process and conventional postfailure physical analysis. By further incorporating electrohygrothermal multiphysics simulations and micro-Raman spectroscopy into the conventional analysis framework, the dominant degradation pathway is identified. Cross-validation between simulation and experiment provides further insight into the degradation process. In particular, hygro–thermal stress together with device self-heating generates mechanical stress in the passivation layer, leading to crack formation. This facilitates electrochemical corrosion, thereby inducing localized electric-field enhancement at the SiC surface and ultimately triggering catastrophic breakdown. These results provide new insights into the failure mechanism of SiC MOSFETs under HV–H3TRB conditions through the proposed methodology.

items.title: Timing Yield-Driven Clock Skew Scheduling Based on Hybrid Distributions
items.abstract: Clock skew scheduling (CSS) is a cost-effective technique for enhancing synchronous digital VLSI systems. The technique simply involves adjusting the clock skew to meet signal path timing constraints in order to increase the clock frequency or timing yield (TY). Traditionally, Gaussian distributions have been assumed for path delays under process variations. However, this assumption may be inappropriate due to the notable asymmetry of actual path delay distributions. In this article, we propose the generalized extreme value (GEV) distribution as a potential alternative, along with a hybrid distribution approach that utilizes different distributions for different path delays to improve accuracy. We also analyze three parameter estimation methods: maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), linear-moments (L-moments), and the method of moments (MoM) to evaluate the accuracy of the fit. Our experimental results show that the GEV distribution more accurately approximates path delays in benchmark circuits, achieving an average improvement of 40% and 30% in the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) statistic compared to the Gaussian and Lognormal distributions, respectively. In addition, quantile–quantile (Q–Q) and probability–probability (P–P) plots are employed to visually validate the goodness-of-fit for different distributions. For TY-driven CSS, the hybrid method achieves the highest performance, improving yield by an average of 6% over the Gaussian model and by 2% over the GEV-based model. These results demonstrate that the hybrid distribution approach effectively captures heterogeneous path behavior and provides robust yield optimization.
items.venue: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems

items.title: Threshold voltage instability in Schottky p-GaN gate HEMTs under dynamic gate stress
items.abstract: This work investigates the threshold voltage instability of 650-V Schottky p-GaN gate HEMTs under dynamic gate stress (DGS). The effects of gate bias, temperature, switching frequency, and duty cycle on the threshold voltage shift (ΔV TH ) are experimentally analyzed. The results show that ΔV TH strongly depends on the applied stress conditions and arises from the interplay of multiple charge-trapping mechanisms within the gate stack. In particular, increasing gate bias enhances the negative threshold voltage shift, while higher temperature and switching frequency promote positive contributions that partially compensate for the negative drift. Duty cycle is also found to play a key role by modifying the effective positive-bias time and the balance between competing trapping mechanisms. A comparison with DC constant-voltage stress further highlights the importance of dynamic stress conditions in determining the threshold-voltage evolution. These findings provide further insight into the reliability behavior of p-GaN HEMTs under DGS conditions relevant to switching operation.

items.title: Thermal and Electrical Stress Differences of SiC MOSFET Under Active/Reactive Loads in AC Power Cycling Test
items.abstract: Thermal and electrical stresses are key factors influencing the reliability of silicon carbide (SiC) mosfets. The alternating current (AC) power cycling test (PCT) has emerged as a more representative reliability test method for applications compared to traditional direct current PCT. However, the distinction between thermal and electrical stress under active and reactive load conditions during AC PCT remains largely unexplored. This article presents a comparative study of active and reactive load AC PCT using a SiC inverter topology. Theoretical analysis and experimental verification show that under identical packaging and testing conditions, the differences in electrical stress (dv/dt at the gate and source, Vds overshoot) between the two loads are negligible. The difference in thermal stress between the two loads depends on the current and the modulation index. When an increased current causes the SiC mosfet to enter synchronous rectification, the thermal stress on the active load exceeds that on the reactive load. Moreover, the higher the modulation index, the greater the difference in thermal stress. These findings support the design of endurance testing for SiC mosfet under AC PCT.

items.title: Temporal Structure Encoding Drives Accurate and Robust Temporal Processing in Spiking Neural Networks [Research Frontier]
items.abstract: Neuromorphic computing, inspired by the fundamental structures and principles of biological neural systems, has emerged as a promising paradigm for achieving energy-efficient and robust artificial intelligence. However, effective temporal processing in dynamic scenarios remains a fundamental challenge, as neuromorphic systems must handle temporally varying signals and discriminate their underlying temporal structures over time, a capability that remains limited in existing spiking neural networks (SNNs). To address this challenge, we propose Temporal-structure Encoding spiking neural networks (TE-SNNs), a framework equipped with a Temporal-structure Encoding (TE) module that explicitly encodes salient rhythmic and non-rhythmic temporal structures. By leveraging TE to modulate neuronal dynamics, TE-SNNs substantially enhance the capability to discriminate various temporal structures in cognitive timing tasks. Extensive experiments on sequential benchmarks further reveal that this temporal discrimination supports accurate and robust temporal processing. Finally, we demonstrate the practical significance of TE-SNNs in a closed-loop autonomous driving task, where they are implemented on neuromorphic hardware to generate optimized driving strategies with orders-of-magnitude improvements in energy efficiency.

items.title: THz-TSI: A Terahertz Wireless Through-Silicon Interconnect Module for Advanced 3-D Integration Applications
items.abstract: By vertically stacking device layers, advanced 3-D integration overcomes traditional planar scaling limits, delivering the bandwidth and power efficiency essential for modern artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) integrated systems. However, continued scaling of conventional through-silicon vias (TSVs) and microbumps presents critical bottlenecks due to inherent thermo-mechanical stress, complex manufacturing, and poor heat dissipation. Consequently, wireless interconnects based on electromagnetic (EM) coupling have emerged as a robust alternative. By pushing operating frequencies into the terahertz (THz) band, these wireless links exploit abundant spectrum to support the massive data throughput requirements. In this work, a THz through-silicon interconnect (THz-TSI) module for advanced 3-D integration is presented, which achieves a record-high data rate of 264 Gb/s and efficiency of 0.33 pJ/bit with the help of an offline equalization. Both bidirectional point-to-point link and broadcast mode are successfully demonstrated. This scheme offers highly competitive bandwidth and density with significantly simpler fabrication and lower cost. Furthermore, its high flexibility enables real-time adjustable interconnect topology to effectively reduce AI/HPC system latency.

items.title: T-2T SRAM: A CMOS 8-bit T-2T SRAM Ladder-Based Analog Current-Domain Compute-in-Memory (CIM) Architecture
items.abstract: This paper presents a CMOS 8-bit T-2T SRAM ladder-based analog current-domain Compute-In-Memory (CIM) architecture for multi-bit neural network applications. A 1-to-2 ratio CMOS 8-bit T-2T SRAM ladder structure was implemented across the entire Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) macro, where the area scales linearly (~N) with N-weight, while the power consumption scales sub-linearly (~2(1 - 1 / $2{^{\text {N-1}}}$ ), enabling area- and power-efficient multi-bit CIM operation. The proposed T-2T SRAM ladder-based Successive Approximation Register Analog-to-Digital Converter (SAR ADC) effectively reuses the memory read and write peripheral circuits for asynchronous SAR operation, removing the need for dedicated SAR logic and register, thereby improving silicon area efficiency. Pre-distortion technique was implemented within input Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) stage, to compensate for the non-linearities within the Synaptic T-2T bitcells. The proposed T-2T SRAM architecture exhibits PVT tolerance through an inherent differential tracking and compensation mechanism between the main and reference computing paths, effectively suppressing PVT-induced variations and preserving MAC linearity. Fabricated using TSMC 65nm GP CMOS process, the proposed T-2T SRAM chip achieved a peak energy efficiency of 4.99 TOPS/W, a peak throughput of 1.5 GOPS/Kb, and a peak compute density of 0.114 TOPS/mm2. Using the hardware-aware neural network analysis framework, we achieved 92.11% classification accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset with a VGG-9 model, and 67.43%/90.28% Top-1/Top-5 accuracy on the CIFAR-100 dataset with a ResNet-20 model.
items.venue: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems Part 1: Regular Papers

items.title: System-In-Magnetics-Based Compact DAB Converter Module With Leakage-Integrated High-Frequency Transformer and Co-Packaged SiC MOSFETs
items.abstract: This work presents a compact and unified dual-active-bridge (DAB) converter module enabled by a system-in-magnetics (SiM) structural concept featuring a hexagonal high-frequency transformer (HFT) and co-packaged SiC MOSFETs. Unlike conventional DAB or resonant CLLC converters that require bulky auxiliary inductors and multiple discrete passive components, the proposed architecture eliminates external inductors entirely by precisely controlling the HFT’s leakage inductance through strategic core placement and adjustable winding gaps. Instead of employing large, heavy, and expensive core pairs, the HFT is constructed using multiple small, lightweight, and cost-effective U26/22/16 ferrite cores in a hexagonal configuration. This geometry enables tunable leakage inductance through adjustable segment spacing and provides a central hollow region that accommodates the entire electronic system, resulting in a compact and unified DAB converter module. The HFT design is validated through COMSOL magnetic simulations, confirming the effective integration of leakage inductance for DAB converter operation. Finally, a physical prototype of the SiM-based DAB module has been fabricated, incorporating the hexagonal HFT along with co-packaged SiC MOSFETs, thermal management elements, the controller, gate drivers, and the main PCB within a single consolidated package. Experimental testing verifies the effective operation, feasibility, and advantages of the proposed architecture for versatile bidirectional power management applications.

items.title: Synaptic Transistors With Photoresponsive and Light-Shielding Properties for Optical Password Lock
items.abstract: With the goal of addressing the security flaws and high power consumption of traditional software-based password locks, a hardware-level optical password lock strategy inspired by biological visual neural networks is proposed. The essence of this approach is organic synaptic transistors with combined sensory and computing functions, with optical signals acting as security keys for identification and encryption. Initially, a light-sensitive organic synaptic transistor is designed using a pentacene semiconductor film combined with polystyrene (PS) as the charge-trapping layer. It offers excellent photoelectric performance due to the influence of photogenerated excitons and charge-trapping processes, especially in response to different light irradiations. Moreover, to address the most critical problem of ambient light interference, a synaptic transistor with light-shielding functionality is constructed using a PSSH electrolyte layer. Based on the exciton-polaron quenching caused by the electric double-layer (EDL) effect and photogenerated excitons, the devices can effectively block RGB visible light with an intensity of up to 12 mW/cm2 (red light), yielding a shielding efficiency higher than 94%. Finally, through the combination of both these functional devices, a scheme of optical password lock is formed that allows precise recognition, verification, and unlocking operations using specific optical wavelength keys. This work validates the feasibility of hardware encryption with photoresponsive and light-shielding synaptic transistors, which show significant benefits in terms of anti-interference performance, ultralow-power consumption, and improved security.

items.title: Subarray-Based Victim-Centric Per-Row Counting for Mitigating RowHammer
items.abstract: RowHammer remains a critical security and reliability challenge in DRAM, despite numerous mitigation techniques. Existing solutions face limitations depending on their implementation: memory controller (MC)-based approaches lack visibility into internal DRAM mappings, hindering precise victim row identification, while DRAM-based methods are limited by interface constraints that prevent timely mitigation. Recently, per-row activation counting (PRAC) and alert-back-off (ABO) protocol have been introduced as a JEDEC standard, enabling MC-DRAM interaction to track and mitigate vulnerable rows. However, most existing tracking-based solutions, including PRAC, enforce aggressor-centric counting, leading to degraded mitigation efficiency. In this article, subarray-based victim-centric per-row counting (SAVER) is proposed as an advanced RowHammer mitigation technique. In SAVER, a counter subarray is implemented in each bank using low-cost DRAM cells, allowing vulnerable rows to be deterministically tracked. By leveraging subarray parallelism, count updates are performed concurrently with row activation, ensuring that DRAM timing constraints are preserved. Additionally, victim-centric counting is enabled by this structure, improving mitigation efficiency. To further address the interface-related limitations, the ABO protocol is utilized in SAVER to mitigate the identified vulnerable rows. Experimental results demonstrate that SAVER deterministically mitigates RowHammer while reducing performance overhead compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions.
items.venue: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems

items.title: Strategies to Improve Efficiency of Select-Gate Voltage Floating During GIDL-Assisted Erase in 3-D NAND Flash Memory
items.abstract: This study addresses the issue in 3-D nand flash memory where, during gate-induced drain leakage (GIDL)-assisted erase, the floating (FT) select-gate (SG) cell approach induces uncertainty in SG voltage ( $V_{\mathrm {SG}}$ ) rise due to the parasitic capacitive suppression (PCS), degrading SG cell reliability. First, technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulations were performed to elucidate the mechanism of $V_{\mathrm {SG}}$ rise in the FT approach ( $V_{\mathrm {SG,FT}}$ ), and a physics-based compact model capable of quantitatively predicting $V_{\mathrm {SG,FT}}$ variations was developed. Strategies to mitigate the degradation of $V_{\mathrm {SG,FT}}$ rise were proposed, ultimately achieving both SG cell reliability and GIDL erase efficiency while offering a scalable approach. The validity of the proposed strategies was confirmed through a Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE)-based Monte Carlo (MC) simulations using the developed compact model, evaluated from the perspective of threshold voltage distribution.
items.venue: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems

items.title: SpikeLet: Empowering Multichiplet Neuromorphic System With Hierarchical Interconnect and Spatial–Temporal Parallelism
items.abstract: As spiking neural networks (SNNs) scale, their neuron counts exceed the capacity of a single chip, necessitating multichip integration. Multichiplet systems provide dense, high-bandwidth interconnects but suffer from inefficient interchip spike transmission, limited parallelism, and the lack of transmission-aware mapping. We present SpikeLet, the first multichiplet neuromorphic system tailored for large-scale SNNs. SpikeLet employs a hierarchical transmission interconnect with an extend-AER protocol to aggregate spikes and decouple intrachiplet and interchiplet communication, an event-driven spatial–temporal-parallel dataflow that enables cross-layer and cross-timestep parallelism, and a communication-aware hierarchical mapping based on cooperative co-evolution to balance computation and communication across chiplets and cores. On a $4\times 4$ -chiplet prototype, SpikeLet reduces transmission latency by 74.2%, improves throughput by $36.6\times $ , and boosts energy efficiency by $39.2\times $ over a 2-D multichip baseline, demonstrating a compact and scalable platform for next-generation neuromorphic computing.
items.venue: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems

items.title: Sound‐Activated Liquid‐Metal Networks for High‐Performance Stretchable LEDs
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The development of flexible and stretchable light emitting diode (LED) circuits requires conductive materials that maintain electrical continuity during repeated mechanical deformation. However, the reliability of liquid metal conductors is limited due to insulating oxide layers and disrupted particle contacts. This work investigates elastomer‐embedded eutectic gallium‐indium (EGaIn) particle networks for flexible LED interconnects. Conductive pathways are realized based on the combination of sonication‐assisted particle synthesis, screen printing and acoustic activation, photopatterning, and localized laser treatment. Acoustic activation induces nanoscale (∼100 nm) bridges between micrometer‐sized (∼2‐3 µm) particles. The obtained network has an electrical conductivity of 2.10 × 10 6 Sm −1 at 74.4 vol% liquid metal content. Interparticle separations < 2 nm suggest that hopping or tunneling may contribute to charge transport. The electromechanical measurements present stable electrical behavior over 2000 stretching cycles with resistance stabilization and recovery times of 145 and 187 ms, respectively. The relative resistance change is linearly dependent on the applied strain in the range studied ( R 2 = 0.989). The integrated LED circuit is powered at 3 V and remains lit during bending and light stretching. These results show the promise of acoustically activated EGaIn networks as conductive interconnects for mechanically adaptive electronic devices.

items.title: Solution Processed PDBT-co-TT-Based OFET Using Asymmetric Work-Function Source--Drain Electrode for Enhanced Ammonia Sensing
items.abstract: This study presents the fabrication and characterization of an asymmetric work-function source–drain (S–D) electrode-based organic field-effect transistor (OFET) for enhanced ammonia (NH ${}_{{3}}$ ) gas sensing by utilizing poly{2, 2’-[(2, 5-bis(2-octyldodecyl)-3, 6-dioxo-2, 3, 5, 6-tetrahydropyrrolo[3, 4-c] pyrrole- 1, 4-diyl)]dithiophene-5,5’-diyl-alt-thieno[3, 2-b] thiophen-2, 5-diyl} (PDBT-co-TT) polymer as a semiconducting channel. The sensing film was deposited via the floating film transfer method (FFTM), a low-cost, room-temperature, and solution-processed technique that yields uniform and crystalline thin films. A bottom-gate top-contact (BGTC) device configuration incorporating asymmetric S–D electrodes composed of LiF/Al and MoO x /Ag was employed to enhance the sensing response. The fabricated device exhibited a significant improvement in electrical performance, achieving a higher on / off current ratio, a reduced subthreshold swing, an optimized threshold voltage (V ${}_{\text {TH}} \approx -1.53$ V at 0 ppm NH ${}_{{3}}$ ), and charge carrier mobility ( $\mu \approx ~2.8\times 10^{-{1}}$ cm 2 /V $\cdot $ s). Upon exposure to increasing NH 3 concentrations (2–15 ppm), a gradual reduction in drain current and mobility, along with an increase in threshold voltage, was observed due to charge trapping in the p-type PDBT-co-TT channel. The device demonstrated a maximum sensing response of 60.4% at 15 ppm NH 3 with a low limit of detection (LOD) of 238 ppb. The average response and recovery times were measured to be approximately 9 and 34 s, respectively, indicating a fast and reversible operation. Excellent selectivity, a low LOD, and fast response/recovery characteristics make the proposed asymmetric FFTM-based OFET a promising, scalable gas sensor for environmental monitoring applications.

items.title: SPEC-TTA: A Lightweight Spectral Adaptation Framework for Self-Correcting Consumer Edge AI
items.abstract: Deep learning models deployed on consumer edge devices for time-series forecasting degrade due to distribution shift caused by changing user behaviors, environmental fluctuations, and sensor degradation. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables on-device self-correction, but existing methods require backpropagation through large backbone networks: full backbone fine-tuning exceeds the typical static random-access memory (SRAM) budget of the host microcontroller (MCU), even embedded-friendly variants retain 3– $4\!\times \!$ the activation memory of the proposed approach, and standard MCU neural-network (NN) toolchains provide no backward kernels. We introduce SPEC-TTA, a parameter-efficient spectral adaptation framework that models distribution drift as amplitude scaling, phase shifts, and temporal misalignment in the frequency domain. SPEC-TTA wraps a frozen backbone with three lightweight modules: 1) sparse spectral adapter applying learnable gains to the top- $K$ Fourier bins; 2) time-shift head leveraging the Fourier Shift Theorem with a single delay parameter $\tau _{c}$ per channel; and 3) affine trend head for bias correction. Drift-triggered proximal updates conserve energy by adapting only upon detecting a distribution shift. Across 8 datasets and 4 backbones (96 dataset–backbone–horizon configurations), SPEC-TTA is the selected single winner in 34 cases, a plurality among seven TTA methods, and is best-or-tied in 41 cases, with gains concentrated on datasets exhibiting both strong spectral concentration and non-trivial residual structure (ETT family, Weather), matched-but-not-improved performance on the weakly-periodic Exchange-Rate stress test, and a near-saturation case on Electricity suggesting that high spectral concentration alone is insufficient when the frozen backbone already captures the dominant mode. The full adaptation pipeline fits within 84.3 KB SRAM and adds 1.1% per-window latency overhead on triggered full-adaptation windows (0.4% on non-trigger windows; $\approx 0.7$ % steady-state at the default 41% trigger rate) under Cortex-M7 (Renode) emulation, with 469 trainable parameters for the profiled 7-channel PatchTST configuration (general count: $C(2K{+}3)$ for $C$ channels and $K$ selected Fourier bins).
