items.title: Fixed-Bias Stream Computing in Filamentary RRAM Crossbars: A Measurement-Calibrated Device–Circuit Study
items.abstract: Filamentary metal–oxide RRAM conducts through a tunneling gap for which the current grows exponentially with bias, so its Read-range I–V characteristic follows a sinh(V/V0) law. This introduces a systematic, input-dependent multiply–accumulate (MAC) error when used in analog Compute-in-Memory (CiM) accelerators with inputs encoded as voltage amplitudes. Because the nonlinearity also varies with resistance state, a single correction factor cannot generally compensate for all programmed weights. We present a measurement-calibrated device-to-circuit study of this error and show how it can be mitigated by replacing voltage-amplitude inputs with fixed-bias time-domain inputs, as in Asynchronous Stream Computing (ASC), which uses constant-amplitude sigma–delta streams. RRAM samples from two independent processes, Pt/Ti/HfO2/Ta/Pt and Al/TiO2/Au/Ti, are characterized, and the Stanford compact model is calibrated to each process. Together with two published parameter sets, the fitted nonlinearity coefficient V0 spans 0.29–0.55 V across four stacks and varies with resistance state within individual devices. In 65 nm circuit simulations, voltage-amplitude encoding incurs up to 30% relative error in a single cell and approximately 8.5% full-scale-normalized error in single-bitline crossbars of 4 to 256 rows. At a 5 ms accumulation window, ASC reduces the array error to 0.4–0.8% with ideal-integrator readout and 0.8–2.3% with transistor-level AΣΔM readout. Under measured device variability, group-balanced Monte Carlo simulations yield 7.6–9.2% analog error versus 0.5–0.7% ASC error. Wire resistance reduces the fixed-bias advantage but does not eliminate it within the simulated conditions. First-order energy estimates identify accumulation time and cell read current as important costs, while practical implementation also requires wordline drivers and high-ratio current division.

items.title: Exploring optimal PSF modeling: requirements for MPC under bulk-sleeve dose modulation in high-NA EUV
items.abstract: With the advancement of High-NA EUV lithography, the minimum feature size on photomasks is approaching the sub-30 nm regime, where pattern miniaturization increasingly leads to pronounced edge roughness and degradation of dimensional uniformity. In this context, contrast enhancement through over-dose correction has emerged as an effective approach for mitigating edge roughness and improving uniformity on the mask. Recent multi-beam mask writers support bulk-sleeve type dose correction, which is a conventional method for contrast enhancement, enabling improved uniformity even for complex curvilinear patterns. To properly implement such fine and localized dose modulation, it is necessary for Mask Process Correction (MPC) to accurately account for dose-dependent dimensional variations and to simultaneously apply appropriate bias correction. In particular, under bulk-sleeve-like dose control at nanometer-scale granularity, the accuracy of the point spread function (PSF) describing electron-beam forward scattering becomes a critical factor in determining correction performance. In conventional MPC frameworks, the forward scattering component is typically approximated by a Gaussian distribution. However, prior studies have indicated that the actual scattering behavior cannot be sufficiently captured by a simple Gaussian approximation. Historically, this limitation has not posed a significant issue, as the dose corrections were applied over relatively large spatial scales and the correction target was the post-etch pattern. However, with the introduction of curvilinear patterns and high-resolution dose modulation in the High-NA EUV era, inaccuracies in forward scattering modeling can no longer be neglected and may significantly impact mask fidelity. In this study, we systematically evaluate the impact of forward scattering model accuracy on mask pattern fidelity and contrast representation, with the goal of identifying the required PSF accuracy for MPC in production environments utilizing bulk-sleeve writing. Specifically, we compare several forward scattering models, including the conventional Gaussian as well as arbitrary distribution. The evaluation employs a variety of test patterns, including edge-segmented patterns mimicking bulk-sleeve dose assignment with sufficient variations in edge width and dose allocation, two-dimensional rectangular patterns to analyze corner rounding behavior, and diverse curvilinear patterns ranging from ellipses and sine-wave geometries. Particular attention is given to deformation behavior in high-curvature regions, where the impact of forward scattering is expected to be most pronounced. As evaluation metrics, edge placement error (EPE) distributions are analyzed by comparing model predictions with contours observed in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images, enabling quantitative assessment of pattern fidelity. In addition, the correlation between energy distribution gradients and edge roughness is examined to evaluate not only dimensional prediction accuracy but also the fidelity of contrast representation across different PSF models. This work clarifies the requirements for forward scattering modeling in achieving high-accuracy MPC for the High-NA EUV era and provides insights that contribute to the advancement of dose correction methodologies in next-generation mask manufacturing.

items.title: Evaluating OPC performance on novel EUV masks: Mo/Si vs Ru/Si multilayer effects on high-NA random logic via designs
items.abstract: EUV imaging performance strongly depends on exploration in mask absorber and multilayer materials. This study evaluates molybdenum / silicium (Mo/Si) and ruthenium / silicium (Ru/Si) multilayer mirror masks for imec random logic via patterning at sub-30 nm pitch. Both bright-field and dark-field mask tones are investigated using resolution enhancement techniques (RET), including optical proximity correction (OPC) and source–mask optimization (SMO). Metal-oxide resist (MOR) with negative tone development (NTD) is applied for bright-field exposures, while chemically amplified resist (CAR) with positive tone development (PTD) is used for dark-field exposures to pattern contact holes on wafers. Experimental results, supported by simulations, show that Ru/Si multilayers provide improved image contrast and reduced mask 3D effects. Based on combined wafer and simulation data, optimal process conditions are identified, and recommendations are provided for mask selection, RET configuration, and OPC strategy for advanced EUV via patterning.

items.title: Enhanced dielectric properties and alignment behavior of ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals in the non-polar nematic phase.
items.abstract: Abstract Ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals (FNLCs) combine long-range orientational order with macroscopic polarization. While their ferroelectric nematic phase has attracted considerable attention, the extent to which its polar character influences the non-polar nematic phase is not yet fully understood. Here, we investigate the non-polar nematic phase of the ferroelectric nematic mixture (MIX NF-P1) that emerges above 44 $$^\circ$$ C. In particular, we determine this liquid crystal interaction with alignment substrates by characterising the pretilt and polar anchoring. The pretilt is found to decrease with increasing temperature, while the polar anchoring remains strong throughout the non-polar nematic phase. Through dielectric and optical characterization, we also extract the dielectric coefficients, birefringence, voltage threshold, and the splay and bend elastic constants as a function of temperature. The voltage threshold is shown to be up to 20 times lower than in the conventional nematic liquid crystal E7, because the large dielectric anisotropy is retained in the non-polar nematic phase. The birefringence monotonically decreases with increasing temperature, while the elastic constants show temperature dependent behaviour consistent with trends reported for other FNLCs. This behavior differs markedly from those observed in conventional nematics, with the splay elastic constant remaining relatively constant. Thus, we demonstrate that the nematic phase of FNLCs cannot be regarded as a conventional nematic state and instead retains signatures of the underlying polar interactions. The combination of strong dielectric response and a low threshold voltage highlights the potential of these materials for high-speed electro-optic and photonic applications.

items.title: Enabling high-NA EUV masks for 18A and 14A with MBMW301 and MBMW401
items.abstract: High-NA EUV lithography tightens photomask requirements on patterning quality, throughput, and data-path scalability at the same time. This paper reviews how multi-beam mask writers (MBMWs) meet these requirements for Intel 18A and 14A. MBMW301, with an 11 nm aperture, has been in production for three years and enables 22 nm isolated line-and- space patterning for high-NA EUV high-volume manufacturing (HVM). MBMW401 extends this with an adjustable aperture down to 9 nm, about 1.5 times the beam-current density, and improved electron-source and stage designs. These changes lower the total effective blur and shorten write time by 10–15%. The first production-relevant MBMW401 print with the standard resist reaches a minimum feature size of about 18 nm. Compared with MBMW301, MBMW401 also shows lower edge-placement error (EPE) and better critical-dimension uniformity (CDU). A negative-tone chemically amplified resist (NCAR) for bright-field masks is being co-developed to reduce background exposure, dose latitude, line-edge roughness (LER), and resist heating. On the data side, the P49 Multigon-compatible MBW4.0 format cuts data volume by up to 50% relative to MBW3.0 and enables online bulk-sleeve edge-dose enhancement. The MBMW401 datapath bandwidth increases from 450 to 675 Gbit/s, which keeps margin as the aperture size shrinks and curvilinear layouts become more complex. The results make the case for optimizing writer optics, resist, correction, and datapath together as one manufacturing system to extend high-NA EUV mask patterning to 14A and beyond.

items.title: Electrical Modeling and Experimental Validation of Sub-5 μm GSG-TSV Interconnects Under Combined Electrothermal Coupling and Parasitic Surface Conduction for 3D ICs
items.abstract: Through-silicon via (TSV)-based 3D ICs continue to scale with advanced CMOS technology nodes. TSV interconnects therefore operate over a wide operating-temperature range, set jointly by the ambient temperature and by self-heating under rising power density. As a result, the temperature dependence of their electrical behavior can no longer be neglected. To address this, a temperature dependence equivalent circuit model for ground signal ground through silicon vias (GSG-TSVs) is proposed in this paper. The model simultaneously incorporates electrothermal coupling effects and the parasitic surface conduction (PSC) effect. The model is validated against HFSS simulations for three geometries (2.5/12.5, 3.5/25 and 5/50 μm) and against measurements of a fabricated 3.5/25 μm GSG-TSV from −40 °C to 100 °C and from DC to 50 GHz. Good agreement and scalability are achieved from −40 °C to 100 °C and from DC to 50 GHz. The influence of TSV size variations is further investigated. The results demonstrate that GSG-TSVs become increasingly susceptible to electrothermal effects as the diameter scales below 5 μm. This work provides a modeling methodology for analyzing the temperature-dependent behavior of TSV interconnects, including electrothermal coupling, over a wide temperature range.

items.title: Effects of DBC Copper Layer Thickness on the Electrical, Thermal, and Thermo-Mechanical Performance of Parallel SiC Chip Power Modules
items.abstract: Direct Bonded Copper (DBC) substrates simultaneously provide current conduction, heat spreading, and structural support in multi-chip power modules, making Cu thickness a key trade-off variable. This study investigates the effects of DBC Cu thickness on the electrical, thermal, and thermo-mechanical responses of a 300 A parallel SiC chip power module. Thermal-coupling analysis was performed to distinguish the temperature effects of chip spacing from those of top Cu thickness. Electro-thermal simulation showed that conduction loss and maximum chip temperature increased as the top Cu thickness decreased, with a pronounced change between 0.175 and 0.160 mm under the 300 A condition. Thermo-mechanical analysis showed that reducing the symmetric top/bottom Cu thickness from 0.30/0.30 to 0.15/0.15 mm decreases reflow warpage of the baseplate from 183.930 to 30.091 μm. Thermal-cycling analysis showed that the cycle increment in volume-averaged inelastic strain energy density in the evaluated solder region decreased by 17.2%. The results showed distinct thickness-dependent responses: reducing the top Cu thickness increased conduction loss and maximum chip temperature, whereas symmetrically reducing both the top and bottom Cu thicknesses decreased reflow warpage and solder inelastic strain energy density in simulation.

items.title: Effect of Rapid Thermal Annealing on the Superconductivity of ALD-Grown TiN thin films
items.abstract: Titanium nitride (TiN) is a promising superconducting material for scalable quantum technologies owing to its tunable kinetic inductance and compatibility with CMOS thin-film processing. However, the superconducting performance of atomic-layer-deposited TiN can be degraded by oxygen incorporation, off-stoichiometry, and crystallographic disorder. In this work, we investigate rapid thermal annealing (RTA) in high-purity nitrogen as a post-deposition strategy to improve polycrystalline TiN films grown by RF-biased plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition. Grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction reveals reduced peak broadening, a smaller lattice parameter, and a stronger (111) preferred orientation with increasing annealing temperature. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy depth profiling shows reduced oxygen-related bonding and a shift toward a Ti--N-dominated chemical environment after annealing. These structural and chemical changes result in a 25% increase in the superconducting transition temperature and a significant narrowing of the transition width. Annealing also reduced the sheet resistance and the estimated sheet kinetic inductance, increased the residual resistance ratio, and improved the magnetic-field tolerance. Together, the structural, chemical, and transport results are consistent with reduced material disorder and improved superconducting uniformity. Because RTA is a relatively low thermal budget and is a semiconductor fabrication compatible process, it offers a practical route to improve the quality of ALD-grown TiN for superconducting applications.

items.title: Dynamic evolution and lifetime modeling of EUV CNT pellicles under hydrogen exposure
items.abstract: Carbon nanotube (CNT) is one of the most promising materials for pellicle applications due to their high extreme ultraviolet (EUV) transmittance. However, while promising, issues such as lifetime require improvement, largely stemming from the CNT's inherently weak durability to hydrogen when exposed to EUV. The resulting lifespan of a CNT pellicle is closely linked to its structural integrity. Thus, understanding of CNT structural dynamics under hydrogen attack, in a quantitative way, can in turn help to identify the structures that have an enhanced hydrogen resistivity. In this study, we unravel the dynamic failure mechanism of CNTs under conditions mimicking EUV exposure, detailing the CNT membrane's structural evolution and degradation under the combined influence of varying temperatures and hydrogen. Utilizing TEM imaging and a previously published, self-developed image analysis method, we quantified the rate of CNT degradation under hydrogen exposure at various temperatures. From this, three key indices (porosity, bundle size distribution, and total carbon loss) were identified as lifetime indicators. Furthermore, combining simulation and experimental data, we established a molecular dynamics model for lifetime prediction that incorporates diverse CNT membrane structural characteristics. This work provides valuable insights into CNTs' hydrogen durability, crucial for enhancing CNT pellicle lifetime.

items.title: Dual-Gate IGZO Transistor-based Time-Varying Reservoir Computing for Highly Efficient Human Action Processing
items.abstract: Abstract Physical reservoir computing (PRC), which leverages the intrinsic dynamics of materials, offers significant advantages for time-series processing with its low training complexity. However, most reported PRC systems suffer from fixed characteristic timescales, which limits their applicability to scenarios involving widely varying temporal dynamics. To address this issue, we demonstrate an on-chip PRC system based on a dual-gate IGZO transistor. In this device, a modulation gate is introduced to electrically control the relaxation timescale by tuning the ionic relaxation of the electric double layer (EDL). As a result, the device enables ~3.3-fold tunable timescales and is feasible for monolithic integration. A 5 kb IGZO transistor array is fabricated and integrated with a custom FPGA board, providing an array‑level and FPGA‑based demonstration of a time-varying reservoir computing (TV-RC) system. This TV‑RC system enables multiple time-series processing tasks, including electrocardiogram (ECG) and speech signal classification. Furthermore, human action recognition, which has not been accomplished by previous on-chip PRC systems, is validated in this system using the UTD-MHAD dataset. The system achieves an average recognition accuracy of 91.85% across 27 actions. It consumes 5.15 mJ/action for inference, with only 3.99 J/action for reservoir state generation. Our design would be of profound significance for extending the boundaries of physical reservoir computing, especially for vision-based intelligent tasks.

items.title: Development of bright field EUV masks for high-NA lithography: challenges and progress in negative-tone patterning
items.abstract: High-volume manufacturing of the 2 nm node has begun, while development toward next-generation nodes, including A16 and A14, is actively progressing. In EUV lithography, mask technology is a key enabler for fully utilizing the performance of exposure tools. DNP has been developing EUV masks for more than 20 years and has contributed to the EUV supply chain through advanced mask fabrication technologies. Recently, bright-field (BF) masks have been discussed as a promising option for High-NA EUV lithography. However, further improvement in negative-tone patterning performance is required for practical application. DNP has therefore focused on BF masks and investigated improvements in resolution, pattern fidelity, and local critical dimension uniformity (LCDU) using negative-tone processes. This paper discusses the lithographic advantages of BF masks, the progress of BF mask fabrication using negative-tone development (NTD), and the applicability of BF and DF masks to future High-NA EUV nodes.

items.title: Design and evaluation of novel capping layers for advanced EUV masks
items.abstract: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography has played a critical role in the continued scaling of semiconductor devices, driving extensive research into EUV mask technologies. Recently, phase-shift mask (PSM) using absorber materials with a low refractive index and a mid-to-high extinction coefficient has attracted considerable attention because of their potential to further improve lithographic performance. However, these absorber materials are difficult to process and require aggressive repair conditions. Ensuring sufficient repair durability of the capping layer therefore remains a major challenge. In this study, we developed a new capping layer with improved durability under the aggressive repair conditions required for these absorber materials. The capping-layer microstructure was controlled through an advanced deposition process, resulting in significantly improved repair durability. Plan-view transmission electron microscopy revealed fewer void-like regions at grain boundaries in the developed capping layer than in the other evaluated capping layers. The observed correlation between grain-boundary void density and repair-induced damage suggests that reducing these voids is important for improving repair durability. These findings provide a new design guideline for enhancing the repair durability of EUV mask capping layers and demonstrate the potential of the developed capping layer for application to next-generation EUV PSMs.

items.title: Delta-Seeker: Closed-Loop Generative Search for Novel Circuit Design Discovery
items.abstract: Generative models are increasingly used for circuit synthesis and optimization by proposing topologies, sizing devices, and exploring large design spaces. We investigate whether they can instead support design discovery, where generated structures must depart from known designs while producing reproducible electrical behavior. We propose Delta-Seeker, a closed-loop circuit search framework that combines discrete diffusion for topology generation and mutation with structural checking, SPICE-in-the-loop sizing, Pareto selection, and feedback from prior search outcomes. The search controller uses progress and recurring structural failures to allocate evaluation effort and steer subsequent topology generation, while independent re-sizing and operating-corner analysis are performed only after search. In generator-only experiments, cross-generation feedback increases structurally valid children from 143 to 945 and reduces the faulty-candidate fraction from 0.925 to 0.761. In op-amp topology discovery at matched sizing cost, Delta-Seeker yields 54 designs that remain feasible in at least three of four independent re-sizings and 18 that additionally pass device-level checks and supply-temperature corner analysis, compared with 38 and 10 under fixed control. Removing cross-generation memory reduces independently robust discoveries from 54 to 43 and seven-corner robust discoveries from 40 to 27. In DC-DC converter search, nearest-parent analysis identifies a corpus-absent topology whose generated switching current path changes its nearest training-corpus parent from infeasible at all four operating corners to feasible at all four, while increasing median efficiency from 31.2% to 98.96%. These results show that closed-loop generative search can support circuit discovery beyond structural novelty by identifying new topologies with independently verified changes in circuit operation.

items.title: DC , Small Signal and Noise Analysis of Graded‐ AlGaN /ε‐Ga2O3 Barrier GaN HEMT on β‐Ga2O3 Substrate for LNAs
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This work presents detailed analysis of a graded‐AlGaN/‐GaO/GaN HEMT on a ‐GaO substrate. The incorporation of ‐GaO as a barrier layer significantly enhances the DC, RF, small‐signal and noise performance of the device. TCAD simulation results demonstrate a positive shift in threshold voltage and suppression of OFF‐state leakage current due to enhanced polarization effects and the formation of a two‐dimensional hole gas (2DHG) at the ‐GaO/AlGaN interface. A peak transconductance of 570.55 mS/mm is achieved, marking a 61.69% improvement over the graded‐AlGaN/GaN HEMT. The proposed device exhibits reduced gate–source and gate–drain capacitances, leading to improved electrostatic control and minimized parasitic effects. As a result, 39.98% enhancement in cut‐off frequency (79.08 GHz) and a 42.93% increase in maximum frequency of oscillation (151.14 GHz) is obtained. Small‐signal analysis based on S‐parameters reveals lower input and output reflection coefficients ( & ), enhanced forward gain () and improved RF stability factor (k) which ensures superior impedance matching and signal amplification capability of the proposed device. Furthermore, noise analysis confirms improved low‐noise performance of proposed bilayer barrier HEMT. The device exhibits a 70.31% reduction in noise conductance compared to graded AlGaN barrier HEMT and offers a minimum noise figure of 1.25 dB. It also exhibits improved auto‐correlation of 244.64% (real) and 61.50% (imaginary) and cross‐correlation of 111.10% (input) and 460.49% (output), which is attributed to reduced scattering effects. These results highlight the graded‐AlGaN/‐GaO barrier architecture as a promising alternative for advancing GaN‐based HEMT technology for designing Low noise amplifiers (LNAs).
items.venue: International Journal of Numerical Modelling Electronic Networks Devices and Fields

items.title: Convolutional neural network approach to enhance mask registration accuracy on arbitrary design patterns
items.abstract: Mask registration metrology is highly sensitive to the design and corrections applied to measurement features. With advanced nodes such as High-NA EUV, mask registration capability requirements are evolving and require greater design flexibility and new targeted applications at critical mask regions, while improving tool-to-tool matching capability in a hybrid fleet. In this work, we describe the development of a convolutional neural network approach to enhance mask registration measurement using die-to-database capability at Intel Mask Operation and present results demonstrating improved capability with reduced sensitivity to feature type variations.

items.title: Control-Noise Trade-offs in Industrially Integrated ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ Spin-1/2 Qubits
items.abstract: Scaling silicon spin qubits to fault-tolerant processors requires semiconductor foundry integration, yet it remains unclear how industrial fabrication and dense device integration affect qubit control and noise. Here we study ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ electron spin-1/2 qubits fabricated using Intel's industry-compatible 300 mm process and incorporating micromagnets for electrically driven spin resonance, using a high-performance device fabricated in the RIKEN research cleanroom as a reference. Primitive $π/2$-gate fidelities reach the 99.99% level in the Intel devices, which also exhibit longer idle coherence, weaker low-frequency correlations and reduced qubit-to-qubit variability across several measured characteristics. In the present Intel devices, the micromagnets are integrated inline with the back-end-of-line (BEOL) contact routing, with their separation from the quantum well set through the vertical stack design. Relative to the reference, their larger separation contributes to weaker longitudinal and transverse magnetic-field gradients. The weaker longitudinal gradient suppresses the conversion of charge noise into qubit-frequency fluctuations, whereas the weaker transverse gradient reduces electrically driven spin-resonance efficiency and makes drive-dependent errors relevant at lower Rabi frequencies. Additional BEOL routing and metal levels required for two-dimensional arrays make such placement decisions increasingly consequential when scaling. These results establish an integration-level control-noise trade-off linking micromagnet placement within densely routed layouts to achievable gate performance, while very high-fidelity operation remains possible in industrially fabricated devices.

items.title: Characterisation of vertical gate-all-around tunnel FET using modulation-doped InGaAs nanowire/Si junction on SOI wafer
items.abstract: Tunnel field-effect transistors (TFETs) utilising quantum tunnel transport are expected as promising candidates for low-power switching applications, primarily due to their potential to overcome the thermionic limit of 60 mV/dec in subthreshold slope (SS) of conventional FETs. Despite this potential for low-voltage switching operation, TFETs face serious challenges for practical circuit integration, most notably low on-state currents and a narrow gate voltage window for maintaining steep SS characteristics. In this report, we characterised selective-area growth of modulation-doped core-multishell (CMS) nanowires (NWs) consisting of an InGaAs/InP/AlInAs/δ-doped AlInAs/AlInAs/InGaAs heterostructure on InGaAs NW sidewalls on silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates and vertical gate-all-around (VGAA) TFETs using the CMS NW-channels on SOI. The TFET devices exhibited robust gate modulation of the tunnelling current at the n-InGaAs/p-SOI junction, achieving a minimum SS of 35 mV/dec at a low drain-source voltage. While the TFETs are promising, the enhancement of the on-state current was constrained by an unintentionally thick InP barrier layer and over-etching to reveal the contact layer, both of which induce a non-ideal distribution of the internal electrical field. These findings underscored that precise dimensional control of the CMS architecture and moderate junction engineering at the InGaAs/Si heterointerface were critical for achieving high-performance VGAA-TFETs in practical applications.

items.title: Area-Selective Plasma-Enhanced Atomic Layer Deposition of a Silicon Oxycarbide Low-k Dielectric via Dynamic Surface Passivation
items.abstract: In advanced integrated circuit manufacturing, back-end-of-line (BEOL) patterning techniques such as fully self-aligned through-silicon vias required precise area-selective deposition (ASD) of low-dielectric-constant (low-k) materials to suppress parasitic capacitance and enable continued device scaling. However, conventional ASD approaches were often limited by the poor thermal and plasma stability of organic inhibitors, which restricted their reliability during extended deposition processes. Here, a plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PEALD) strategy was developed for the selective growth of silicon oxycarbide (SiOC) thin films using octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane (OMCTS) as the precursor. Plasma-induced ring-opening of OMCTS enabled the formation of Si-O-Si networks on hydroxylated dielectric surfaces, while selective inhibition on Cu was achieved using n-dodecyl mercaptan (DDT) self-assembled monolayers (SAMs). A cyclic surface passivation strategy was further introduced, where hydrogen plasma enabled in situ modulation of the SAM layer to maintain inhibition capability during repeated cycles. This approach achieved selective SiOC growth of at least 2 nm while effectively suppressing nucleation on Cu surfaces. The resulting SiOC films exhibited a dielectric constant of 3.2-3.4, confirming their suitability for advanced interconnect applications. The results highlighted the critical role of dynamic SAM stability in regulating selective deposition and suppressing parasitic growth on metal surfaces.

items.title: Uniformity Enhancement in 3D NAND Etch Processes via N₂ Bubbling Si₃N₄ Removal and Poly-Si Etch-Back
items.abstract: The push for increasingly large-capacity non-volatile data storage necessitates an improvement in NAND flash memory technology. It challenges high volume manufacturing (HVM) to incorporate more complicated three-dimensional structures, such as gate line and channel hole architectures, that have ever-increasing aspect ratios. Consequently, in advanced NAND flash memory manufacturing, the etch back of the polysilicon (poly-Si) film in channel holes and the selective removal of Si 3 N 4 /SiO 2 film stacks in the gate line, are two crucial processes that help determine device performance. However, as the specifications of wet etch processes evolve, these two key process steps suffer issues of poor etch uniformity and serious by-product regrowth. Herein, we present an advanced N 2 bubbling technology incorporated in an ACM Ultra C wet bench (WB) tool, that addresses these concerns. The performance of the poly-Si etch back and selective silicon nitride (SiN) removal steps on blanket film wafers (BW) both showed significant improvements, which were ultimately demonstrated on patterned wafer (PW). Keywords: NAND flash memory manufacturing, gate line, channel hole, N 2 bubbling technique, etch uniformity, byproduct regrowth

items.title: Understanding MOR pattern density sensitivity and its mitigation through process optimization
items.abstract: Metal oxide resists (MORs) are considered key enablers for high-NA EUV lithography in high-volume manufacturing due to their high EUV absorption and suitability for thin resist processes. However, compared to chemically amplified resists (CARs), MORs exhibit significantly higher sensitivity to pattern density variations, with critical dimension (CD) changes reaching up to two times larger for equivalent density variations. In this work, we investigate the underlying mechanisms driving this enhanced density sensitivity and explore potential mitigation strategies. Experimental results demonstrate that MOR CDs vary as a function of surrounding mask pattern density, even when the corresponding features do not print on the wafer, indicating that the effect is primarily governed by optical interactions rather than resist chemistry alone. To understand the origin of this behavior, we analyze the aerial image sampling characteristics of different resist processes. Our findings show that MOR processes sample the aerial image farther from the iso-focal region compared to CAR processes, resulting in operation at a lower effective aerial-image slope. This reduced slope increases sensitivity to density-induced flare variations, leading to enhanced CD variability. Finally, we demonstrate that improving either aerial image contrast or resist process conditions can effectively reduce density-induced CD variation. These results provide a physics-based understanding of MOR pattern density sensitivity and offer practical pathways for its mitigation in advanced EUV lithography processes.

items.title: Ultra‐Efficient Memristive Voltage‐Resistance Logic Framework With Integrated Readout Strategy Based on Hafnium Zirconium Oxide
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The integration of logic operations and data storage is regarded as a promising strategy for enabling edge computing, a key requirement for real‐time, data‐intensive scientific and industrial applications. Achieving edge‐capable computing, however, requires exceptional spatiotemporal efficiency, and many previously proposed logic schemes still face substantial limitations. Here, we introduce a memristive voltage–resistance (V–R) logic strategy that infers output resistance states without additional incurring area or latency penalties. The approach relies on integrated readout of the discharge behavior into programming of a two‐terminal capacitor‐type memristor. Implemented in an HfO 2 ‐based ferroelectric tunnel junction (FTJ) device with multiple resistive states, this strategy enables a half adder to be computed using a single device in a single step, and a 1‐bit full adder using only three FTJs in three steps—achieving previously unattainable spatiotemporal cost for execution of standard benchmarking tasks. Our work provides a pathway to edge computing by maximizing the spatiotemporal efficiency achievable with memristor‐based logic‐in‐memory.

items.title: TiN Stepwise Etch for CFET Replacement Metal Gate Module
items.abstract: A TiN digital stepwise etch process is reported that could significantly simplify the monolithic Complementary Field Effect Transistor (mCFET) flow within the Replacement Metal Gate (RMG) Module. The process consists of repeated cycles of controlled TiN oxidation followed by selective oxide dissolution step. Various chemistries were screened for enabling controlled and selective TiN recess. Furthermore, we demonstrate that TiN cyclic etch does not damage the seam in between the nanoSheet (NS) in the CFET patterned structures.

items.title: Thickness‐Programmable Opto‐Memristive Dynamics in 6‐In Wafer‐Scale Atomic‐Layer‐Controlled WS 2 for Reservoir Computing
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Neuromorphic optoelectronic hardware requires 2D channels whose thickness, and therefore band structure, is reproducible across an entire wafer, yet atomic‐layer control of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) must reconcile precision, uniformity, and scalability simultaneously. Here, 6‐inch wafer‐scale atomic‐layer control of WS 2 is reported by integrating low‐temperature plasma‐assisted synthesis with a three‐component mixed‐gas (Ar+O 2 +CF 4 ) reactive ion etching process. WS 2 synthesized from electron‐beam‐evaporated W seed layers preserves structural integrity and achieves uniform atomic‐layer control across the wafer, whereas sputter‐derived WS 2 etches non‐uniformly with rougher surfaces and partial lattice disruption, as confirmed by ellipsometry, atomic force microscopy, Raman mapping, and cross‐sectional transmission electron microscopy. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations qualitatively support the experimentally observed optical band gap according to the number of layers and provide insight into the layer‐dependent electronic properties of WS 2 . The layer‐controlled WS 2 was subsequently employed to fabricate opto‐memristive devices, which exhibited pulse‐history‐dependent photocurrent modulation at zero read bias. The 4L‐WS 2 device balances optical sensitivity against inter‐pulse memory, resolving 16 four‐pulse optical histories into distinguishable analog states. A dual‐state recursive model calibrated from the measured device dynamics achieved a mean waveform‐classification accuracy of 95.8 ± 1.69%. Atomic‐layer control thus provides a manufacturable route from wafer‐scale TMD processing to band‐structure‐programmed neuromorphic optoelectronics.

items.title: The particle removal tool: dry cleaning of advanced photomasks
items.abstract: Mask defectivity is a critical concern in semiconductor lithography, particularly due to the stringent requirements for advanced photomasks, including their cleaning durability. To enable the use of advanced lithography in high-volume manufacturing, it is essential to develop a reliable cleaning method that does not degrade photomasks, thereby facilitating efficient wafer fabrication operations. Currently, the challenges associated with dry-cleaning steps involve removing sticky particles of various sizes without necessitating subsequent inspection, qualification, or additional cleaning steps. The introduction of High-NA EUV lithography presents new challenges, as smaller particles can print, and anamorphic High-NA photomasks exhibit higher structural complexity. We introduce an advanced nano manipulator based dry-cleaning process, enhanced by live SEM imaging for process supervision. Our innovative approach allows for the repair of a broad range of particle defects on advanced photomasks using defect optimized manipulator tips. Additionally, electron induced chemistry can be used to augment particle manipulation and removal, ensuring cleaning without compromising mask integrity. Optional in-situ material analysis of the particle facilitates expeditious particle defect analysis for the identification of the particle source in case of production excursion, and production line commissioning. Our process is ready to match the demands of HiNA EUV lithography, where precision and efficiency are paramount.

items.title: Test Vehicle and Metrology for Defectivity Study in Wet Processes
items.abstract: Controlling defectivity is critical for achieving high yield and performance in advanced CMOS fabrication. Wet processing presents key challenges such as pattern collapse, non-uniform etching, and incomplete cleaning in high-aspect-ratio (HAR) structures. To effectively optimize single-wafer wet process conditions with good across-wafer uniformity, well-designed test vehicles and advanced metrology are indispensable. This paper provides an overview of 300 mm patterned wafer test vehicles, as well as recent developments in advanced metrologies. Together, they offer a robust framework for quantitatively assessing process performance, thereby enabling more efficient and reliable single-wafer processing.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Systematic study of vector- and pixel-based MPC for curvature control in high-NA EUV masks
items.abstract: The continuous advancement of semiconductor device performance is driving increasingly stringent requirements for pattern fidelity in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. Curvilinear patterns are becoming more critical as design complexity grows, and their accurate transfer onto photomasks is essential for maintaining imaging performance. This challenge is further intensified in High-NA EUV systems, where 4:8 anamorphic scaling changes the effective curvature representation on the mask, making curvature preservation a key factor in mask fabrication. However, the mask manufacturing process inherently suffers from curvature loss due to resist blur, which acts as a low-pass filter and degrades high-frequency geometric components. Previous studies have addressed this issue through bias-based corrections that effectively enhance high-frequency content, while recent advances in multibeam mask writers enable fine, pixel-level dose modulation as a new pathway for curvature compensation. The primary advantage of dose correction is its ability to improve contrast through edge enhancement. It can be implemented in two distinct ways. One approach is vector-based, in which the pattern is segmented, and a higher dose is assigned to regions near the edges. The other is pixel-based, where the optimal exposure dose distribution is directly solved at the pixel level. In the vector-based method, the segmentation width and the assigned dose are typically fixed values for each pattern. In contrast, pixel-based dose optimization enables a higher degree of freedom in the correction, allowing more flexible and locally adaptive solutions. While this approach can more effectively enhance contrast, it also carries the risk that corrections exceeding the limits of process capability may result in instability, potentially leading to artifacts such as isolated features or local pattern loss. In this study, we investigate vector-based and pixel-based correction as approaches to mitigate curvature loss and clarify their respective advantages. The objective is to determine the most suitable mask process correction (MPC) strategy for fabricating high-end curvilinear mask patterns, particularly in response to variations in local curvature. To systematically evaluate curvature-dependent behavior, two representative pattern types are examined. Elliptical patterns are used to observe systematic trends in curvature by varying aspect ratio and overall dimensions. In addition, sine-wave patterns are employed to analyze differences between convex and concave regions, including inflection points. Three correction methods are compared. The first is a conventional vector-based MPC without dose enhancement. The second is also a vector-based method with dose enhancement through bulk and sleeve segmentation. In this scheme, a higher dose is assigned to the sleeve region and a lower dose to the bulk region to enhance the energy profile contrast. The third is a pixel-based correction, assuming fully optimized dose modulation map. In this method, constraints are imposed to match the target contour while maintaining high contrast in the energy profile. Performance is evaluated using a rigorous resist model to assess the distribution of edge placement error (EPE), as well as resist contrast and lineedge roughness, to identify an optimal correction framework for maintaining curvature fidelity in advanced EUV mask fabrication.

items.title: Surface Preparation Challenges for Direct Bonding in 3D Integration
items.abstract: The relentless advancement of microelectronics, historically driven by Moore’s Law, faces increasing challenges as device scaling approaches fundamental physical and economic limits. To overcome these constraints, the semiconductor industry has adopted the "More than Moore" approach, emphasizing heterogeneous integration of diverse functionalities within compact 3D architectures. Central to this evolution, bonding techniques, particularly direct and hybrid bonding, enable the assembly of high-density, high-performance multilayer systems. This article reviews the critical role of surface preparation in direct bonding processes, highlighting its influence on bond strength, defectivity, and reliability. Key factors such as surface roughness, contamination, and chemical activation are examined, alongside the impact of particle-induced voids and their correlation with bonding void size and adhesion energy. Advances in low-temperature bonding enabled by plasma and chemical treatments are also discussed. Furthermore, challenges specific to die-to-wafer bonding, including dicing-induced damage and volatile organic compound contamination, are addressed. This comprehensive overview underscores the necessity of meticulous surface engineering to unlock the full potential of direct bonding for next-generation 3D integration, facilitating the development of reliable, multifunctional semiconductor systems.

items.title: Supplementary code and data: ML surrogate for memory-window variability in multi-granular 3-D FeFET
items.abstract: Supplementary material for the manuscript “Machine Learning-Driven Surrogate Modeling of Memory Window Variability in Multi-Granular 3-D Ferroelectric FETs” (Micro and Nanostructures, MICRNA-D-26-01886). Contents: Python code (Poisson–Voronoi grain generator, signature extraction, Seq2Seq LSTM/GRU/MLP surrogate, cross-validation, Monte Carlo and statistics); raw 3-D TCAD I–V data of 400 multi-granular FeFETs (5-nm and 10-nm films, with and without grain boundaries) and their grain-structure files; Sentaurus read sweeps, structure decks and logs; all computed results and figure data. Running “python run_all.py” reproduces every number and figure of the paper. TCAD data from the study of N. Pandey et al., ICEE 2022 (doi:10.1109/ICEE56203.2022.10118356).

items.title: Study of copper bottom-up filling method for through silicon via
items.abstract: This study investigated copper electroplating conditions for void-free filling of high-aspect-ratio through-silicon vias (TSVs). Seed-layer reinforcement using copper pyrophosphate plating improved seed coverage at the via bottom, promoting stable copper nucleation during subsequent sulphate copper electroplating and enhancing bottom-up filling behaviour. For TSVs with an aspect ratio of 5, filling behaviour was strongly influenced by the concentration balance of SPS and DAP in the presence of PEG. An appropriate SPS concentration promoted uniform bottom-up filling, whereas non-optimised additive compositions resulted in reduced bottom growth and pinch-off. For TSVs with an aspect ratio of 10, conventional plating conditions led to severe void formation because of restricted transport of electrolyte and additives within the vias. The application of jet-flow plating improved mass transport and additive supply, enabling successful void-free filling. These results demonstrate that seed-layer quality, additive balance, and hydrodynamic conditions are key factors governing copper filling behaviour in high-aspect-ratio TSVs.

items.title: Si Thinning in Alkaline Solutions for 3DDRAM Applications
items.abstract: This work investigates silicon (Si) thinning by wet alkaline etching to enable vertical bit lines (VBL) and monocrystalline silicon Gate-All-Around (GAA) architectures for 3D DRAM integration. Two etchants—tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH) and ammonium hydroxide (NH₄OH)—were systematically studied. Process screening was initially performed on blanket Si to identify conditions offering controlled etch rates and low surface roughness. Optimal conditions were then applied to wagon wheels and 3D patterned test structures, revealing strong anisotropic behaviour influenced by Si crystallography. To mitigate this directional dependence, wafers with a 45° notch rotation were explored to align vertical sidewalls along the orientation, promoting isotropic etching in the desired directions. In TMAH, rotated wafers initially exhibited suppressed lateral etch rates, but prolonged etching exposed fast-etching planes, leading to undesired lateral etching. NH₄OH demonstrated a similar evolution, though boron-doped Si showed partial etch-stop behaviour and increased surface roughness. Blanket etch tests on epitaxially grown boron-doped Si further corroborated these observations. These insights provide critical guidance for integrating scalable GAA devices in next-generation 3D-DRAM architectures.

items.title: Si Etchants for Si Thinning for 3D DRAM Application
items.abstract: We developed a novel etchant designed to suppress Si (111) facet formation while maintaining a high etch rate for Si (100) surfaces. Screening of additive candidates was performed using bare silicon substrates and etch rates of different crystal planes were evaluated. As a result, one specific formulation (FORM B) was found to achieve both suppression of Si (111) facet formation and a high etch rate for Si (100). Further investigations revealed that the dissolution rate of each plane exhibited different sensitivity to the amount of additive B. This is attributed to differences in surface reaction site density and the selective adsorption behavior of the additive. The optimized etchant also showed good compatibility with patterned Si/SiGe substrates, suppressing facet formation similarly to bare Si substrates. These results indicate that the developed etchant is a promising candidate for advanced 3D DRAM processes.
