items.title: Self Assemble Monolayer for Area Selective ALD
items.abstract: In advanced semiconductor devices, shrink of critical dimension increases via resistance which reduces device performance. In order to decrease the interconnect via resistance, use of Self-Assembly-Monolayer (SAM) is proposed [1]. SAM works as Atomic-Layer-Deposition (ALD) blocking layer and enable to have Area-Selective-Deposition (ASD). In this study, we studied selective adsorption and ALD inhibition performance of SAM on W and Mo metals [2,3].
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Reversing amorphous aging associated with resistance drift in phase-change memory via atomistic rejuvenation
items.abstract: Resistance drift in the amorphous RESET state limits phase-change memory (PCM) for multilevel storage and neuromorphic computing. Most mitigation strategies slow drift rather than reverse the structural aging that develops after programing. Here, we use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations with a Y-Sb-Te neuroevolution potential to examine atomistic rejuvenation in Sb-Te based glasses. Aging and rejuvenation are quantified using potential energy, radial distribution functions, global Steinhardt order parameters, ring statistics, and homopolar bonding, which track short-range relaxation, topological ordering, and bond rearrangement. Binary Sb-Te models first establish competing thermal pathways: low-temperature annealing promotes energetic relaxation and ordering, whereas high-temperature reheating followed by requenching restores higher-energy, less-aged amorphous states while avoiding prolonged residence in the crystallization-prone window. In Y-doped Sb2Te3, Y suppresses energetic relaxation, delays four-membered-ring ordering, and reduces bonding fluctuations while preserving reversible rejuvenation. Device-scale simulations further show that rejuvenation pulses reset key aging-sensitive descriptors in a 6.5 × 10⁵-atom mushroom-cell PCM model. These results demonstrate that atomistic rejuvenation can reverse aging-sensitive structural features in Sb-Te-based PCM glasses, providing a structural route toward mitigating resistance drift.

items.title: Resolving the Kay–Dunn limit and the speed–endurance dilemma in ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 for DRAM-class sub-volt capacitors
items.abstract: Abstract Ferroelectric hafnium zirconium oxide can increase charge density in scaled capacitors, but its high coercive field limits the low-voltage, high endurance switching required for dynamic random-access memory and embedded ferroelectric memories. Here we show that plasma-engineered (111)-textured TiN electrodes with N-rich, oxidation-resistant surfaces suppress interfacial oxidation and enable robust switching in 5 nm Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 capacitors. The devices exhibit saturated hysteresis at 0.6 V, with 2 P r = 31.5 μC cm −2 and E c = 0.62 MV cm −1 , and no hard electrical breakdown through 10 12 bipolar cycles. Their nucleation-limited switching kinetics extrapolate to sub-nanosecond polarisation reversal at DRAM-relevant capacitor areas. At 1.1 V, circuit simulations of a common plate 1T–1 C cell yield short- and long-term stand-by sensing margins of 482 and 201 mV under a 20 fF bit line load. Electrode texture and interface engineering therefore enable low-voltage, high speed switching without compromising endurance, mitigating the practical Kay–Dunn scaling penalty and the speed–endurance dilemma.

items.title: Reconfigurable Nanofluidic Synapses Based on Polyaniline Protonation-Deprotonation Chemistry for Potential Bio-Integrated Computing
items.abstract: Polyaniline (PANI) has been extensively studied for decades, yet its reversible protonation-deprotonation (PDP) chemistry has remained unexploited in nanofluidic neuromorphic computing. Here we show that a porous PANI membrane, prepared by simple spin-coating, functions as a volatile ionic synapse whose short-term plasticity is chemically reconfigurable. Acid and base treatments reversibly switch the same device between paired-pulse facilitation and paired-pulse depressionopposing forms of synaptic behaviorthereby achieving chemically reconfigurable plasticity. Taking the base-configured state as a model system, the device exhibits spike-frequency, spike-amplitude, spike-duration, and spike-number dependent plasticity, revealing rich temporal dynamics. When integrated into a reservoir computing framework for handwritten digit recognition, this synaptic element achieves a classification accuracy exceeding 90%. Our work repositions PANI from conventional electrochemistry to reconfigurable nanofluidic synapses, where its PDP chemistryonce merely governing conductivity and surface chargenow enables history-dependent ionic dynamics under nanoconfinement. This convergence of classical polymer chemistry with neuromorphic iontronics establishes an unexpected materials platform for aqueous-based, bio-integrated computing systems.

items.title: Recent Developments in AI Technology and Its Application to Wet Process Optimization
items.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have increased the need for high-performance, high-capacity semiconductors. Consequently, cutting-edge semiconductor structures have become increasingly complex, requiring highly precise optimization in manufacturing processes, and achieving high yield rates within short periods has become challenging. This study focuses on the use of various yield improvement and process development methods using AI in semiconductor manufacturing and development to address these challenges. Specifically, we report that Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (MOBO) can be used in the phosphoric acid etching during the word line formation of 3D NAND Flash, to determine optimal etching conditions and hard parameters for a batch-type wet etching bath without experimental verification using wafers.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Phosphoric Acid Reuse for High-Selectivity Silicon Nitride/Silicon Dioxide Wet Etching via Fixed Automated Process Control in Memory Devices
items.abstract: In this study, a Batch Fix APC(Automated Process Control) system was implemented to address etch rate instability issues in the selective Si3N4/ SiO2 wet etching process of DRAM devices using phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) baths. The etch rate instability was primarily attributed to the accumulation of silica residues and chemical concentration fluctuations induced by bath aging, which resulted in increased variability in the SiO2 etch rate. To mitigate this, the lower limit of the SiO2 etch rate was defined based on XPS analysis, considering the impact of native oxide formation on the Si3N4 surface, and an appropriate bath condition was established. Notably, the Batch Fix APC system played a critical role in maintaining stable Si3N4/SiO2 selectivity and etch rates by precisely controlling the etch time at each process step according to a predefined lookup table, using bath concentration, temperature, and life count as input parameters. This approach ensured stable process performance despite bath aging and real-time chemical concentration fluctuations. The system also reduced the frequency of chemical replacements, resulting in a 5.52% increase in productivity, and improved chemical reuse efficiency, achieving a 33% cost reduction per cycle.Furthermore, by integrating Batch Fix APC with real-time in-line thickness monitoring, this approach can be extended to patterned DRAM device processes, contributing significantly to process stability and yield management in high-volume manufacturing environments.

items.title: Non-Volatile Memory Devices for Neuromorphic Computing
items.abstract: This chapter explores the critical role of emerging non-volatile memory (eNVM) devices in advancing neuromorphic computing. Inspired by the human brain's remarkable ability to perform complex tasks like pattern recognition and adaptation, neuromorphic computing offers immense potential for implementing complex neural networks (NNs) in real hardware. Despite ongoing research into the brain's complexities, its fundamental operation relies on neurons (processing units communicating via electrochemical signals) and synapses (junctions between neurons). The modifiable strength of the synapse is key to learning and memory functionality, allowing the brain to adapt and rewire itself. For dense and low-power circuits in neuromorphic computing, these eNVM devices are ideal due to their synaptic-like behavior and non-volatile information storage. Properties such as conductance modulation of these devices emulate synaptic plasticity, which is crucial for learning, and their scalability makes them promising for large-scale neuromorphic architectures. This chapter will delve into the various types of eNVM devices such as resistive RAM (ReRAM), phase-change memory (PCM), spintronics-based memory devices, and their applications in neuromorphic computing, discussing their challenges and opportunities, and highlighting recent advances in their integration within neuromorphic systems.

items.title: NORmal: Architecting 3D Ferroelectric NOR Flash as Main Memory -- From Co-Fabricated BEOL Arrays to 200B-Class Multi-Agent LLMs in a Smartphone
items.abstract: Smartphone agents increasingly work as teams, in which a large planner directs parallel workers across long sessions. Running such a team on the device requires 200B-class models and contexts that exceed phone DRAM many times over, yet existing tiers treat flash as storage: UFS starves per-token weight streaming, and mobile High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) needs a redesigned SoC and cannot absorb continuous KV writes. We show that a non-volatile memory can join an unmodified LPDDR6 bus as a plain rank only if its access latency fits the DRAM timing window, a condition no NAND tier meets. We present NORmal, to our knowledge the first main-memory architecture for 3D ferroelectric NOR flash. We have fabricated and experimentally characterized back-end-of-line (BEOL) 3D FeNOR arrays that co-integrate dense 3-bit MLC and fast, high-endurance in-place-writable SLC with sub-7.5 ns sensing. NORmal turns these co-fabricated arrays into a byte-addressable, deterministic-timing load/store rank on an unmodified LPDDR6 interface through an under-array DRAM-emulation bridge, staggered bank reads with zero-cycle weight swizzling, and posted SLC writes. Across this rank and DRAM, NORmal places agent state by mutability and lifetime rather than by hotness, serving 200B-class models and persistent planner contexts in place while dynamically partitioning subchannels across agent phases. In serving-level simulation on production agent traces, NORmal is 8.9$\times$--28.0$\times$ faster than UFS offloading, within 0.4% of an unlimited-DRAM ideal, and 2.8$\times$--6.3$\times$ faster than HBF on sessions beyond 256K tokens, with 8.1$\times$--17.8$\times$ less memory energy per token.

items.title: Metal-oxide resist height variations through pitch in EUV lithography
items.abstract: EUV photolithography patterns are often characterized by 2D top-down metrics such as pitch or pattern placement. However, also the photoresist height and height variations are an important aspect to consider for later processing steps. To quantify resist height under different lithography conditions, this work combines physics-based resist modeling, ellipsometry measurements on resist blanket films, and atomic force microscopy (AFM) measurements on line/space patterns across a range of pitches. From the ellipsometry measurements we find that both the EUV exposure as well as post-exposure bake (PEB) cause significant height loss. This height loss can be attributed to entirely to photoresist shrink. As expected, increasing the PEB temperature decreases the dose-to-gel (D0). However, the resist height is independent of PEB within the studied temperature range if a hardbake step after development is included. The resist height above D0 is then quite stable with only a small dose-dependence of less than 1 nm over a range of 60 mJ/cm2. For the developed patterns measured with AFM, we observe a bifurcation of the resist line profile. The result is a height profile variation for the largest pitch (96 nm) with a center height that is equivalent to a large, fully relaxed resist surface, but distinct height peaks towards the line edges. The origin is exposure-driven stress, which causes an accumulation of material at the feature edges. This is confirmed by linear elastic strain simulations using a physics-driven resist model. For the smaller pitches of 28 to 40 nm the line height is constant, and the bifurcation is much less pronounced, providing a high degree of pattern height uniformity.

items.title: Mask technologies: active controller for the semiconductor business
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence is fundamentally reshaping global industries and daily life, necessitating continuous advancements in advanced semiconductors to power this AI-driven transformation. Historically, the realization of high-volume manufacturing and stable yield for highly scaled devices has been underpinned by the evolution of lithography, where innovations in mask technology played a pivotal role in establishing the prevailing architectural paradigm of semiconductor fabrication. Key enabling technologies—including Phase Shift Masks, Pellicles, full-pattern mask inspection, advanced data formats, e-beam writing, and the optimization of mask sizes—have collectively allowed the industry to push the limits of resolution and productivity. Today, this trajectory continues with the transition to Extreme Ultraviolet lithography and the strategic preparation for High-NA and beyond. While Moore’s Law has guided the industry for over half a century, the emergence of Advanced Packaging is expanding this paradigm toward ‘More than Moore,’ driving innovation through heterogeneous integration and system-level scaling. As masks remain indispensable to both ‘More Moore’ and ‘More than Moore’ eras, the mask industry must evolve to support both pathways simultaneously. However, the current industry structure for advanced chips reveals a precarious trend: an increasing reliance on a few captive mask shops and a shrinking number of merchant shops in high-end mask industry, which in turn exacerbates the R&D burdens and technical risks for equipment and material suppliers. Based on a comprehensive survey of 16 leading stakeholders in the mask ecosystem, this paper analyzes the increasing complexity of R&D, prolonged ROI cycles, and the systemic uncertainties facing the industry. To mitigate these risks and ensure sustainable innovation, this paper proposes the establishment of a ‘Mask Roadmap Committee’ as a strategic framework for co-opetition and collective growth.

items.title: Machine-learning-based 3D sidewall reconstruction of line/space patterns from 2D SEM images
items.abstract: Critical-dimension scanning electron microscopy (CD-SEM) is a fast metrology tool for pattern features, but a top-down SEM image remains a two-dimensional view of a three-dimensional sidewall morphology. We present a virtual-metrology workflow that links Monte Carlo-based SEM image simulation with convolutional neural network (CNN) regression to recover 3D sidewall roughness descriptors directly from image data. Synthetic resist line/space patterns with controllable roughness are generated from Fourier-filtered stochastic fields parameterized by RMS and ξ, rendered into realistic Monte Carlo-based SEM images with Nebula, and sampled with Latin Hypercube Sampling over the experimental EUV line/space geometry. The sampled ranges are chosen to cover representative EUV line/space pattern metrics. A validation-optimized stacked ensemble of ResNet CNN regressors predicts RMS and ξ from the image inputs. On a held-out test set of 75 samples, the ensemble achieves R2 = 0.936 for RMS and R2 = 0.902 for ξ. Applied to the SEM image, it predicts (0.547nm, 9.060nm), showing that Monte Carlo-based CNN inference can estimate key 3D sidewall roughness descriptors directly from top-down SEM images.

items.title: MBMW-401: high-performance multi-beam mask writer for high-NA EUV
items.abstract: Over the past decade, multi-beam mask writer (MBMW) technology has become the industry standard for advanced photomask, EUV mask, and NIL master template production, successfully overcoming the throughput limitations of variable shaped beam (VSB) writers [1,2]. The transition to High-NA EUV lithography necessitates simultaneous improvements in Critical Dimension Uniformity (CDU), resolution, and placement accuracy, while maintaining economic viability through high-volume manufacturing (HVM) [3]. In 2025, we introduced the MBMW-401 [4], designed to meet the rigorous mask requirements of the A10 node. The system utilizes 590,000 individually controllable electron beams with a beam size down to 7.5 nm. To achieve HVM throughput, a new electron source delivering a total current of up to 4.2 μA was developed. To leverage this increased current without compromising lithographic precision, the MBMW – 401 incorporates several key technological advancements: Higher currents intensify stochastic blur and electron optical distortion due to Coulomb interactions between the individual electron beams. A novel space-charge compensation technique has been developed that mitigates these effects for layouts with a high write density. In addition, an increased current leads to substantial local thermal loading, causing write-density-dependent CD variations. To overcome this hurdle, we have implemented a Resist Heating Correction (RHC), which dynamically adjusts the exposure dose to eliminate the impact on global CDU. Experimental results are presented, demonstrating the feasibility of the MBMW – 401 tool for High-NA EUV Mask pattern writing, highlighting sub-nanometer CD control and significantly improved placement precision.

items.title: LAMP: LLM-Driven Analog Placement through Adaptive Tool Composition
items.abstract: Analog placement requires circuit-specific trade-offs among area, matching, routability, and electrical performance. Balancing these trade-offs through predefined objectives and fixed placement flows remains difficult. In this paper, we propose an analog placement framework in which a large language model (LLM) acts as a layout engineer through composable placement components. These components support constraint management, placement and legalization, and lightweight evaluation of routability and electrical performance. Using multimodal checkpoints of the initial and evolving design, the LLM selects and combines components to construct and revise its own placement flow. It also adapts the placement hierarchy by reopening modules or partitioning and regrouping devices, allowing local layouts to respond to global design needs. An experience skill provides reusable design knowledge to guide these decisions. Evaluation on two SMIC 180 nm circuits shows that the framework reduces placement area and improves most measured post-layout performance metrics.

items.title: Investigation of anamorphic reductions in hyper-NA EUV
items.abstract: As the first high NA (0.55) EUV systems (EXE) begin deployment in semiconductor manufacturing cleanrooms, ASML and ZEISS are preparing to meet future industry demands by exploring a further increase in numerical aperture (NA) as the next stage of EUV lithography development [8][9][10][11][12]. A hyper NA EUV system, featuring an NA increased to 0.75 and offering a potential resolution approaching 5 nm for dense line/space patterns, builds upon and advances the design principles established for high NA EUV systems. The adoption of anamorphic optics was a key innovation that enabled high NA EUV lithography. By employing different reduction factors in the slit (along x) and scan (along y) directions, the optical design maintains compatibility with the existing 6-inch EUV reticle blank quality area while providing a half-field exposure format with sufficient throughput [1][2]. Several alternative anamorphic reduction options satisfy the same reticle and wafer field-size constraints [3][4][5], with each involving distinct imaging and system-level tradeoffs. The anamorphic reduction factors play a fundamental role in defining the angles of incidence at the mask and, consequently, the magnitude of mask 3D effects and their impact on imaging performance. Changing the anamorphic reduction also affects the scanner architecture, requiring internal design adaptations by ASML and ZEISS, and has user-visible consequences, particularly in the reticle layout. In this study, we reassess, in the context of hyper NA EUV lithography, the anamorphic reduction options previously evaluated for high NA EUV [3][4][5]. Two alternative options are compared with the baseline 4×/8× configuration, while accounting for the emerging low-n absorber materials. The investigation focuses on line/space patterns and regular contact holes near the resolution limit. Three mask absorber materials are evaluated across a range of absorber thicknesses. The lithographic metrics assessed include normalized image log-slope (NILS), exposure threshold, mask error enhancement factor (MEEF*), best-focus shift, and pattern displacement through focus (non-telecentricity). While the reticle blank quality area remains unchanged, departures from the baseline anamorphic reduction option require adjustments to the reticle layout, including the placement and sizing of the alignment marks and the 2D barcode, as previously identified for high NA scanners [3]. Consequently, reticle-layout concepts are presented to illustrate the modifications and implementation challenges associated with the considered anamorphic reductions.

items.title: Inversion-layer quantization and hot-carrier effects in ultrathin-gate MOSFETs: impact on channel thermal noise
items.abstract: Abstract Below approximately 2 nm equivalent oxide thickness, gate tunnelling and inversion-layer quantization modify carrier statistics and energy dissipation in metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) channels, yet their effect on microscopic thermal fluctuations remains unresolved. By treating the channel as an open quantum-transport system, tunnelling-induced energy loss is embedded into the electron energy-balance equation to obtain quantum-corrected hot-electron temperature and mobility degradation. Inversion-layer quantization is further accounted for through surface-potential elevation and threshold-voltage shift, yielding a self-consistent drain-current description and a corresponding channel thermal noise framework. Monte Carlo simulations provide trend comparisons. The results show that omitting quantum effects overestimates the thermal noise, the correction being governed almost entirely by inversion-layer quantization while the tunnelling contribution is negligible. The hot-carrier effect, strengthened by high fields and short channels, enhances the thermal noise and outweighs this quantization-induced suppression, leading to a net increase relative to the thermal-equilibrium baseline.
items.venue: Journal of Physics D Applied Physics

items.title: Imaging near the resolution limit: from Abbe’s theory on microscopy to high-NA EUV lithography
items.abstract: We summarize Abbe’s theory of image formation in the microscope which he formulated in 1887 at the latest. The smallest resolvable pitch for one-dimensional structures, 0.5𝜆NA⁄ with 𝜆 being the wavelength and NA the numerical aperture of the imaging optics, was stated by Abbe even earlier, in 1873. The resolution equation for projection lithography, min.half pitch=𝑘1𝜆NA⁄ with 𝑘1≥0.25 for lines and spaces, is consistent with Abbe’s theory. Progress in projection lithography used in semiconductor manufacturing follows closely this resolution equation in reducing 𝜆, increasing NA, and gradually lowering 𝑘1. For optical lithography, this progress began with unit-magnification all-reflective projection imaging using a mercury arc lamp and culminated in 193-nm immersion lithography with NA=1.35. For extreme ultraviolet lithography, thirty-five years of research and development led us all the way to the present-day NA=0.55 high-NA scanners with the capability to pattern sub-30-nm-pitch two-dimensional features with good contrast. As with Abbe in microscopy, resolution of projection imaging in lithography is best understood by analyzing diffraction patterns in the pupil plane of the projection optics . The larger the NA, the higher the spatial frequencies that can pass through the aperture, resulting in better resolution and fidelity of printed patterns on the wafer, especially two-dimensional patterns.

items.title: IMPLEMENTATION OF OPTIMIZED RECONFIGURABLE BUILTIN SELF-REPAIR SCHEME FOR RAMS IN SOCS
items.abstract: Random Access Memory (RAM) is a critical component of modern System-on-Chip (SoC) designs, and its reliability directly affects overall chip performance and manufacturing yield. As VLSI technology advances, memory circuits become more susceptible to manufacturing defects and operational faults, making efficient testing and repair mechanisms essential. Conventional Built-In Self-Test (BIST) techniques can detect memory faults but may require additional hardware resources and may not provide an effective repair mechanism for different memory configurations. This project presents an optimized Reconfigurable Built-In Self-Repair (ReBISR) scheme for embedded RAMs in SoCs. The proposed approach integrates memory testing, fault detection, redundancy analysis, and repair configuration to improve memory reliability. A reconfigurable BuiltIn Redundancy Analysis (ReBIRA) circuit is designed to support different RAM sizes and redundancy organizations, while an adaptive fusing methodology aims to reduce repair setup time. The document also describes Cellular Automata Linear Feedback Shift Register (CA-LFSR)-based test pattern generation as an alternative to conventional LFSR-based testing, along with FPGA-based design verification using hardware description languages and simulation tools. The proposed approach aims to reduce hardware area overhead, improve fault detection and repair efficiency, and increase memory yield and reliability. It can be useful in embedded systems, automotive electronics, consumer devices, aerospace applications, and other SoC-based systems where dependable memory operation is essential. Overall, the project emphasizes the importance of reconfigurable memory testing and self-repair techniques in developing reliable and cost-effective VLSI systems.
authors: K. Gouthami,Dr. N. Suresh,Mr. Ch. Sreedhar
items.venue: International Journal of Engineering Research and Science & Technology

items.title: Highly Selective Si3N4/SiO2 Etching for 3D NAND Manufacturing with H3PO4- Free Etchant
items.abstract: Si 3 N 4 film could be selectively removed by novel H 3 PO 4 -free etchant (PFE). Instead of H 3 PO 4 , another type of nucleophile is needed for selective etching of Si 3 N 4 . In order to increase Si 3 N 4 etching rate and Si 3 N 4 /SiO 2 etch selectivity, additives were optimized in the H 3 PO 4 -free etchant. Much faster etch rate of Si 3 N 4 with no oxide regrowth was achievable in the high number Si 3 N 4 /SiO 2 layer by using this etchant.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: High-Performance and Safer Wet Stripper for 50 to 400 µm-Thick Negative Photoresists and Laminated Films in Wafer Level Packaging
items.abstract: Thick negative-tone photoresists are increasingly used to fabricate high-aspect-ratio structures such as copper pillars, which are critical in advanced packaging technologies. However, their high film thicknesses and strong crosslinking make complete removal particularly challenging. This study presents the development of a new photoresist stripper formulation, free of N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) and tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH), designed to address both efficiency and material compatibility requirements in advanced packaging environments. Through a systematic formulation approach, including each formulation components screening, an optimized stripper was developped. Compared to conventional TMAH-based strippers, this new formulation enables significantly faster stripping of thick resists, up to 400 µm, and laminated films, while maintaining excellent compatibility with sensitive materials. The results validate its performance across a range of advanced applications, while offering substantial safety and environmental benefits.

items.title: High precision curvilinear metrology and design-based metrology technologies for Advantest’s mask CD SEM
items.abstract: Curvilinear mask architectures are becoming increasingly important for advanced EUV lithography. For curvilinear masks, contour-based metrology using edge placement error (EPE) is essential. While EPE is often summarized by global statistics such as mean, 3σ, and worst-case values, these statistics do not explain where the deviation occurs or why it occurs. To address these challenges, we propose a curvilinear metrology framework that combines interpretable and curvilinear-aware metrics with a metrology infrastructure consisting of state-of-the-art mask CD-SEM hardware and novel metrology algorithms in this paper. This framework enables geometry-aware and width-aware interpretation of contour variation.

items.title: Hardware-Aware Model Inversion in Memristive Spiking Neural Networks
items.abstract: Hardware-accelerated spiking neural networks (SNNs) implemented on memristive crossbar arrays offer significant gains in energy efficiency, while device variability and analog noise are sometimes assumed to hinder information extraction. However, whether these hardware effects improve, preserve, or degrade privacy after deployment remains largely unexplored. Therefore, we ask whether model-inversion leakage characterized on an SNN remains representative after the same model is mapped to a non-ideal memristive substrate, and how hardware non-idealities and reliability faults affecting synapses, neuron thresholds, and spike processing reshape that leakage. To study this problem, we introduce Spiking Domain Model Inversion (SDMI), an inversion method that combines Expectation over Transformation (EOT) with surrogate gradients to optimize inputs through stochastic analog behavior and non-differentiable spiking dynamics. We use SDMI consistently across the SNN model, its memristive SNN, and the same memristive SNN under additional hardware perturbations. Across four datasets, reconstruction leakage does not vary monotonically with model accuracy or hardware variability. At comparable accuracy levels, neuron-threshold perturbations increase reconstruction fidelity, measured by SSIM, by up to 51.8%, whereas spike-level perturbations primarily degrade utility without consistently improving reconstruction. Weight noise, in contrast, reduces leakage under the same inversion procedure. These results show that hardware variability is not inherently privacy-preserving: model inversion leakage in memristive SNNs depends on the hardware state and cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone.

items.title: Flexible Control of Si Etching and Si/SiGe Selectivity for Advanced 3D Integration
items.abstract: Si/SiGe etch selectivity was controlled through surface passivation, oxidation, and digital etching. NH₄OH showed high selectivity toward Si, further enhanced by (NH4)2S-induced suppression of SiGe etching. H2O2-assisted surface oxidation enabled preservation of Si pattern integrity during the thinning process. In addition, by incorporating acidic environments and fine-tuned digital etching, Si/SiGe selectivity was modulated with increased flexibility. These approaches offer flexible etch control for advanced Si/SiGe integration.

items.title: Enhancing SiOx Protection during SiGe Selective Wet Etch in CFET Integration Using Oxide Surface Functionalization
items.abstract: This work describes the OSF concept (Oxide Surface Functionalization) as being a pre-treatment before a wet SiGe removal within the CFET integration. The SiGe is removed with an HF_H₂O₂ formulated chemistry that induces some oxide loss in the CFET structures (hard mask and STI). The OSF consists in a selective coating that occurs on the oxide surfaces and not on the SiGe surfaces that need to be removed. The selective coating prevents the oxide surface of being significantly etched during the wet SiGe removal.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Enhancements of EUV optics at ZEISS and future developments
items.abstract: Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography is crucial for high-volume semiconductor manufacturing. The 0.33 NA optics family has been essential in delivering high-quality imaging for critical layers. ZEISS and ASML have continuously refined this technology to meet demands for higher throughput, cost-effectiveness, and improved optical performance. This contribution highlights the latest enhancements in EUV optics, focusing on 0.33 NA improvements that boost throughput and imaging quality. We will discuss ZEISS's efforts to enhance transmission and support higher source power. We will provide updates on 0.55 NA optics and advancements in Starlith® optics, demonstrating how ZEISS and ASML are supporting next-generation semiconductor nodes and ensuring the ongoing relevance of NA 0.33 optics in future manufacturing processes.

items.title: Enhanced SiGe/Si Selective Etching by Acetic Acid in HNA Solutions
items.abstract: Selective SiGe etching process is crucial for the fabrication of Gate-all-around field-effect transistors (GAAFET) and three-dimensional dynamic random access memory (3D-DRAM). A mixture of HF, HNO 3 , and CH 3 COOH (HNA solution) is the etchant traditionally used to etch Si, but can also be used to etch SiGe. The effect of adding various concentrations of CH 3 COOH to HF/HNO 3 solutions on the selective etching of SiGe over Si was investigated in this study. It was found that addition of CH 3 COOH can enhance the selective etching of SiGe over Si, while an excessive amount causes etching of Si. In addition, concentration optimization of HNA solution was conducted to further increase the etching selectivity of SiGe over Si.
items.venue: Diffusion and defect data, solid state data. Part B, Solid state phenomena/Solid state phenomena

items.title: Energy-Efficient Memristor Accelerator for Depression Detection with a CNN-LSTM Hybrid Model
items.abstract: Early screening of depression requires efficient analysis of audio and speech data, while conventional CPU and GPU platforms incur high latency and energy consumption for CNN-LSTM inference. To address this challenge, we propose a unified resistive RAM (ReRAM) processing-in-memory accelerator for a CNN-LSTM attention workload. The architecture integrates convolutional, recurrent, attention, and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) stages within a crossbar-based framework, reducing intermediate data movement between spatial and temporal branches. CNN operations are mapped through im2col-based vectorization, while LSTM gate computations are reformulated using concatenated input-state vectors and mapped onto ReRAM crossbars. We further provide module-level workload breakdown, parameter sensitivity analysis, and matched-workload context against representative ReRAM/PIM accelerators. Experimental results show 32.1 times and 9.3 times latency reduction over CPU and GPU baselines, respectively, with about 160 times and 140 times energy reduction. Simplified weight-perturbation tests characterize ASLF sensitivity in an untrained pipeline with synthetic spectrogram-shaped inputs. Task-level prediction accuracy and robustness remain to be evaluated.

items.title: Elitho: an open-source high-NA EUV lithography simulator
items.abstract: Lithography simulation is essential for optimizing and evaluating lithography processes. However, available open-source simulation tools are limited to optical lithography, and no open-source simulator exists for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. Although commercial EUV simulators are available, they are often costly and implemented as black boxes, which limits their flexibility and may make them unsuitable for downstream applications such as Source-Mask Optimization (SMO) and Inverse Lithography Technology (ILT). This paper proposes Elitho, an open-source, Python-based EUV lithography simulator designed to support both standard-NA and high-NA systems. Elitho enables flexible implementation and evaluation of EUV lithography simulation. Elitho is available at https://github.com/takahashi-edalab/elitho.

items.title: Edge Chemical Passivation Engineering of Armchair MoSi 2 N 4 Nanoribbon PMOS Field‐Effect Transistors: A First‐Principles DFT–NEGF Investigation
items.abstract: Edge chemical passivation provides an effective strategy for tuning the electronic and transport properties of two‐dimensional semiconductor nanoribbons. Here, the effects of hydrogen (H), chlorine (Cl), and fluorine (F) edge passivation on armchair MoSi 2 N 4 nanoribbon PMOS field‐effect transistors are systematically investigated using density functional theory combined with the nonequilibrium Green’s function (DFT–NEGF) approach. The electronic band structure, density of states (DOS), transmission spectrum, transfer characteristics, and transconductance are analyzed to elucidate the impact of edge termination. All passivation configurations improve the electronic and transport characteristics relative to the pristine nanoribbon. The electronic bandgap increases from 1.80 eV for the pristine structure to 1.88, 1.95, and 2.03 eV for H‐, Cl‐, and F‐passivated structures, respectively, while the DOS gap increases from 1.16 to 1.34, 1.38, and 1.56 eV. These changes indicate effective suppression of localized edge states. Among the investigated configurations, F passivation yields the highest ON‐state current and I ON / I OFF ratio, while maintaining a comparable OFF‐state current. The enhanced performance is attributed to the high electronegativity of F, which promotes edge charge redistribution and carrier confinement.

items.title: EUV mask defectivity assessment through PDM characterization study (Part I)
items.abstract: Industry has made significant progress advancing Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography (EUVL) technology the past several years leading to its full adoption starting at N7 node and volume production through N3 node. EUVL is a cornerstone technology for advanced semiconductor manufacturing and key enabler for advanced technology nodes, where stringent pattern fidelity and defect control are essential for achieving high yield and reliability, yet mask defectivity remains a critical challenge that directly impacts yield, device reliability, and overall process control. Mask defectivity remains one of the most critical challenges in this domain, as even minor defects can propagate to waferlevel failures. This paper presents a comprehensive Program Defect Mask (PDM) characterization study specifically designed for DRAM technology, addressing defect mechanisms from mask design through wafer printability. The PDM design incorporates representative DRAM features to enable systematic evaluation of defect sensitivity across critical geometries. Our methodology integrates precise defect measurement and high-resolution SEM image analysis with contour extraction and characterization to compare actual mask features against design intent. Inspection results are correlated using complementary strategies – actinic inspection and optical 193nm-based inspection – to assess detection sensitivity, classification accuracy, and inspection coverage for DRAM-specific patterns. Furthermore, wafer-level printability studies quantify the impact of mask defects on critical dimensions and edge placement error, establishing robust correlations between mask inspection data and wafer performance. The study highlights key trends in defect mechanisms, inspection tool capabilities, and their combined effect on DRAM pattern fidelity. By leveraging PDM-based analysis, we provide actionable insights for optimizing mask design, refining inspection strategies, and mitigating defect-related risks in high-volume DRAM manufacturing. These findings establish a practical framework for EUV mask quality control and process improvement, supporting the continued scaling of DRAM technology nodes.

items.title: EUV holography: a new patterning mode for the PSI interference lithography facility
items.abstract: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) interference lithography (IL) at the XIL-II beamline of the Swiss Light Source (SLS) has long supported photoresist development for advanced semiconductor nodes, but its grating- and mirror-based exposure modes are restricted to periodic patterns. To extend the facility toward arbitrary, non-periodic structures, we have implemented EUV holographic lithography as part of a substantial upgrade of the lithography end station. In this approach, a transmissive mask carrying a computer-generated hologram (CGH) diffracts the EUV illumination to reconstruct a target aerial image on the wafer plane. We describe the new end station and the suite of writing modes it will support and present the first results obtained with a holographic mask fabricated by e-beam lithography in a 200 nm hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) layer on an 80 nm silicon nitride membrane. The mask was designed with a fast convolutional simulation method to reconstruct the target image at a stand-off distance of 200 μm. Exposures performed at the BL05U-A1 beamline of the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) demonstrate the printing of arbitrary patterns with critical dimensions (CDs) of 40 nm, opening a path toward high-resolution, holographic EUV patterning of non-periodic structures.

items.title: Dynamic Wafer Curvature Engineering Toward Ultraflat and Highly Uniform 8‐Inch GaN Heteroepitaxy
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Large‐area GaN heteroepitaxy is essential for next‐generation electronic and optoelectronic systems, yet simultaneously achieving low wafer bow and high epitaxial uniformity remains challenging due to the dynamic evolution of thermo‐mechanical stress during growth and cooling. Here, we develop a dynamic wafer curvature engineering strategy based on a thermal‐cycling stress‐loading (TCSL) layer to regulate curvature evolution throughout epitaxy and suppress residual bow after cooling. The TCSL layer consists of a hydrogen‐rich SiO 2 film deposited on the backside of sapphire substrates, where hydrogen‐driven viscoelastic relaxation and dehydrogenation‐induced network densification generate asymmetric stress evolution. Applying this strategy to AlGaN/GaN HEMT epitaxy, we realize ultraflat and highly uniform 8‐inch wafers on 1‐mm‐thick sapphire substrates, achieving a bow of 7.4 µm, a warp of 17.2 µm, and relative standard deviations of 0.82%, 1.2%, and 1.8% for epitaxial thickness, Al composition, and sheet resistance, respectively. The AlGaN/GaN heterostructure preserves high crystalline and interfacial quality, enabling a high‐quality two‐dimensional electron gas with a sheet density of 7.0 × 10 12 cm −2 and an electron mobility of 2040 cm 2 /V·s. This work establishes a scalable approach for simultaneous control of wafer flatness and epitaxial uniformity in large‐area GaN heteroepitaxy, paving the way toward highly integrated GaN‐based electronic and optoelectronic technologies.

items.title: Dislocation-controlled reverse leakage and temperature-dependent transport in quasi-vertical GaN-on-Si Schottky barrier diodes
items.abstract: Abstract Temperature-dependent reverse leakage in quasi-vertical GaN-on-Si Schottky barrier diodes was investigated and linked to material growth conditions through structural characterization. The NH 3 pre-dose prior to AlN nucleation was varied from 60 to 190 s, modifying the total threading dislocation density (TDD), relative proportions of dislocation types and wafer bow. An intermediate NH 3 pre-dose resulted in the lowest atomic force microscopy (AFM)-derived TDD of (1.5 ± 0.4)× 10 9 cm −2 , the lowest proportion of edge-type dislocations and desirable convex wafer bow. This correlated with the lowest reverse leakage (mostly invariant to measurement temperature) and the highest breakdown voltage of ∼ − 160 V. Conversely, lower NH 3 pre-dose resulted in higher AFM-derived dislocation density ((2.3 ± 0.5)× 10 9 cm −2 ), a reduced breakdown voltage (∼ − 140 V), an undesirable concave bow of ∼2 μ m, and increased thermally-activated leakage paths. This behaviour is consistent with trap-mediated transport such as Poole–Frenkel-type emission from electrically-active dislocation-related states. The highest NH 3 pre-dose resulted in the highest AFM-derived dislocation density of (3.0 ± 0.4)× 10 9 cm −2 , anomalous forward IV characteristics associated with surface v-pits, the highest leakage and the lowest breakdown voltage of ∼ − 50 V. The temperature dependence of this sample indicates additional contact/interface or localized shunt leakage contributions. Our results demonstrate that even a narrow distribution of total TDD and small changes to dislocation type strongly impact the electrical characteristics and alter the dominant physical transport mechanisms. This highlights how targeted epitaxial growth optimization can enable low-cost GaN-on-Si platforms to approach the performance metrics required for high voltage, mass market power electronics.
items.venue: Journal of Physics D Applied Physics

items.title: Detecting Hidden Trap States from Adjacent Dwell Times in FinFET Random-Telegraph Noise
items.abstract: Random-telegraph noise from a single defect has been usually characterized by the distributions of its filled and empty dwell times. If a charge state hides several structural configurations, different Markov models can produce exactly the same two distributions, making the order in which the dwells occur an important source of information. We ask when the correlation between a dwell and the one that follows it is sufficient to detect that hidden structure. For a reversible model with two hidden sub-states per level, the covariance of adjacent dwells is a product of three factors. It vanishes only when the joint dwell distribution factorizes, with or without transitions inside a level. With more sub-states, the answer changes. When (n_E − 1)(n_F − 1) ≥ 2, where n_E and n_F count the hidden sub-states of the empty and filled levels, reversible models can have the same one-dimensional dwell laws, exactly zero correlation, and a joint distribution of higher rank. We construct such models explicitly and show that zero-correlation models with higher-rank joint distributions also occur on a published six-state defect topology. A Pearson chi-squared test on quantile-binned pairs of adjacent dwells detects these dependencies, but its cost depends mainly on the separation between sub-state time constants. Across 300 constructions, the median record length required for 90% power at five-sigma significance decreases from approximately 7 × 10⁸ dwell pairs when sub-state exit rates span less than a factor of two to approximately 6 × 10³ when they span more than a factor of sixteen. Simulated continuous trajectories match these independent-pair benchmarks to within 1.5 percentage points of power. A BSIM-CMG sample card is used only to confirm that the threshold-shift parameter acts as a rigid gate-voltage offset over the simulated range.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: Decoupling mask and EUV lithography scanner contributions to contact-hole stochastic LCDU
items.abstract: On-wafer local critical dimension uniformity (LCDU) in contact-hole patterning contains coupled contributions from the mask, metrology, resist, and scanner. Conventional ANOVA-based decomposition separates systematic and stochastic terms. However, the mask-induced intrafield fingerprints affect the apparent stochastic LCDU metric. This limits the interpretation of intrinsic scanner performance and complicates cross-tool benchmarking. We used a direct, physics-based correction method in which mask reflectivity variations measured by mask reflectivity maps and mask critical-dimension (CD) variations measured by reticle SEM (RSEM) are used to model the mask contribution to LCDU. The model is based on the stochastic scaling relation LCDU_stoch ∝ 1/(NILS√CD), allowing mask-induced image perturbations to be translated into expected LCDU variation through sensitivity terms. The calculated mask contribution is subtracted from the normalized measured stochastic LCDU after removal of metrology noise, yielding a scanner-related residual. Validation on two masks across twenty NXE:3800E scanners shows strong reduction of intrafield fingerprints, and more than a twofold reduction of through-scan variation. The method demonstrates mask-independent behavior and provides a robust basis for scanner benchmarking, while indicating that separation of residual resist stochastic effects remains a next step toward a fully intrinsic scanner metric.

items.title: Deconstructing the Nanoscale Electromechanical Response of Mixed Conductors
items.abstract: Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) techniques, which probe nanoscale electromechanical coupling, are often difficult to interpret. For ferroelectric mixed conductors useful for computation elements, this becomes more difficult due to non-piezoelectric electromechanical effects. The measured PFM signal can have tip-local and nonlocal contributions associated with multiple coupling mechanisms, and it is often unclear what material property is truly being probed. Here, using antimony sulfide (Sb2S3) as a model system, an emerging phase change material for optical and electrical memory and computation elements, we show that the PFM signal can be separated into a fast, capacitive contribution, and a slow, ionic contribution whose time-domain characteristics match well with diffusion-controlled kinetics. This ionic contribution, rather than ferroelectric switching, leads to electromechanical hysteresis in Sb2S3, with no clearly measurable ferroelectric switching effects. Uniquely, electromechanical behavior has a very clear spatial contrast that is decoupled from surface topography, showing that the signal arises from surface charging that reflects bulk-like properties and allowing a self-consistent interpretation in terms of dielectric behavior. This protocol establishes a clear interpretation of a non-piezoelectric signal, often mischaracterized as an indication of the ferroelectric state. Additionally, because all electromechanical experiments show a strong, low-frequency electric relaxation in crystalline Sb2S3 while the response of glassy Sb2S3 is static, we conclude that the crystalline phase of Sb2S3 is a mixed conductor, while the amorphous phase remains strictly insulating.

items.title: Curvilinear MRC mask verification methodology
items.abstract: Recent advances in free-form, high-throughput multiple-beam mask writer (MBMW), GPU-accelerated inverse lithography technology (ILT), and curvilinear (CL) contour metrology have enabled CL masks to deliver clear lithographic benefits, including improved process windows and reduced cost through mask-count reduction [1,2,3,4]. A key remaining challenge, however, is the establishment of a robust curvilinear mask rule check (CL-MRC). Such a framework is essential for defining design rules, identifying potential hotspots, supporting optical proximity correction (OPC) and enabling CL-mask qualification through accurate CL-mask metrology, ultimately enabling CL-mask insertion into EUV lithography HVM for advanced technology nodes. In this work, we present a methodology of CL MRC framework that defines mask manufacturing limits on minimum area, curvature, spacing and width to systematically identify potential hotspots. A representative set of features is verified up to the actual mask level, by manufacturing the mask, characterizing the mask features by mask CD-SEM, and analyzing the mask and design data using contour extraction software. Single-gauge-based edge placement error (EPE) measurements confirm whether they fall outside fabrication capability [5]. A test mask is fabricated as a dark field mask using the reference Ta-based mask process with a positive tone chemically amplified resist (PCAR). The analysis shows that the mask design contour maximum convex curvature of 0.11nm-1 corresponds to a mask contour convex maximum curvature of 0.08 nm-1 at the given EPE. There were not enough design variations of the ellipse feature on the test mask to provide maximum concave curvature and minimum area on the test mask. Finally, improvement strategies, including mask process correction (MPC), increasing vertex density in high-curvature regions, enhanced OPC recipes, and the adoption of multigon SEMI P49 format, are discussed. This methodology establishes a practical path toward robust CL mask qualification for advanced EUV lithography.

items.title: Corrosion-Free Copper Pad Recess Enabled by Wet Acid Etching and Functional Water Rinse for Hybrid Bonding Applications
items.abstract: This study presents a novel cyclic wet etching process based on citric acid for the controlled recessing of copper (Cu) pads, aimed at improving wafer-to-wafer (W2W) and die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding in advanced packaging applications. Conventional chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) struggles to prevent corrosion and excessive recessing of the Cu pads, particularly when they are connected to long metal lines. These issues compromise the quality and reliability of interconnects. To address these challenges, we propose an alternative strategy. The proposed citric acid-based approach enables nanometer-scale precision of Cu pad recess without causing corrosion. The work includes detailed investigations into the formation and aging of native Cu oxide, the kinetics of Cu oxide etching, and the interaction of citric acid with both Cu and silicon carbon nitride (SiCN). A stable etch rate of 24.6 nm/min is achieved using 0.05 wt% citric acid. Furthermore, a cyclic process involving ultraviolet (UV) exposure and wet etching enables controlled Cu pad recessing by approximately 1.5 nm per cycle. Optimized rinse chemistries such as functional water (ultra-dilute NH 4 OH) are also developed to improve surface quality and minimize Cu corrosion in connected pads. This method offers a robust and reliable solution for precise Cu pad height control and reduces Cu corrosion, contributing to enhanced performance in hybrid bonding with high-density interconnects.

items.title: Conformal Silicon Nitride Etching in Superdeep and Narrow Patterns
items.abstract: Despite the silicon nitride (SiN) etching in both narrow critical dimension (CD) and high aspect ratio feature requires extreme precision for the structural integration of NAND Flash device, pattern dimension-dependent chemical kinetics and thermodynamics cause fluctuation in the SiN etch rate. Here we tackle both wet and gaseous process control methods to achieve the conformal SiN etching in superdeep and narrow pattern. Firstly, we studied the boundary layer and electric double layer in nanoconfined patterns to understand their significant impact on CD-dependent wet etching. Additionally, gaseous etching in Knudsen flow regime has been discussed to address the CD independent etching. Next, we investigated thermodynamic strategies to minimize the accumulation of byproducts during phosphoric acid-based SiN wet etching, which can reduce the etch rate lag at the bottom of superdeep holes. These strategies were experimentally validated, supported by computational calculations. Furthermore, we investigated the improvement in local etch rate lag within the top layer of superdeep holes, with a particular emphasis on the effusion of SiN gaseous etching products. This led to the demonstration of excellent top-bottom uniformity, characterized by a ratio of nearly ~1.
