items.title: Group-IV semiconductor physics and technologies for next-generation electron-photon-spin integrated devices on silicon
items.abstract: Abstract This paper reviews group-IV semiconductor physics and technologies for realizing ultra-low-power electron-photon-spin semiconductor systems on a silicon platform. First, some technologies for high-speed CMOS and silicon photonics devices are introduced on the basis of heteroepitaxy of Ge, SiGe, and GeSn alloys on Si. Next, aiming to integrate logic and nonvolatile memory, electrical spin injection and detection technologies for spin transistors are explained using Ge on Si. Also, recent progress of the studies of spin-related physical properties such as spin relaxation time and spin diffusion length is introduced for Ge. Meanwhile, recent research progress on low-temperature-formed gate stack structures, Ge-on-Insulator (GOI) structures, and Ge/SiGe multi-heterostructures will be presented to combine CMOS technology with spintronic and/or spin-photonic devices on a Si platform. Finally, the possibilities of spin-tunnel FETs, vertical spin FETs, GeSn-based spin devices on the Si platform will be described for future applications.

items.title: FPGA-DSP Tightly Coupled PHM Architecture with Radiation-Tolerant Mechanisms for Spaceborne NOR Flash
items.abstract: The growing demand for low-cost, high-reliability onboard storage in commercial aerospace missions poses significant challenges for industrial-grade NOR Flash memory, which must contend with gradual total-ionizing-dose (TID) degradation and potentially abrupt single-event effects (SEEs) in space radiation environments. This paper proposes an FPGA–DSP tightly coupled Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) architecture for spaceborne NOR Flash. The architecture is implemented with a TMS320F28335 floating-point DSP and an A3PE3000 Flash FPGA, establishing a complete “sensing–evaluation–decision–execution” closed loop. The time-domain evaluator uses sliding-window least squares for online remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, while the spatial-domain evaluator performs dynamic wear leveling through minimum-error replacement. A Dual-Domain Collaborative Arbiter (DDCA) fuses both assessments to schedule adaptive refresh, dual-mode Reed–Solomon (RS) coding, backup pre-switching, and eFuse isolation. The experimental claims in this study are limited to laboratory 60Co γ-ray TID irradiation at 1 rad(Si)/s; the SEE-oriented functions are architecture-level mitigation provisions and have not yet been validated by heavy-ion, proton, or neutron beam tests. Using four control groups, the proposed scheme reached an observed failure total dose of 24.7 krad, compared with 12.3 krad for the unprotected baseline. Under the tested control group definitions, this corresponds to a 100.8% improvement and a 4.9 krad excess over the additive estimate from the two single-domain groups. Because independent device-level repeats were not available, these dose values are reported as observations rather than population means. The complete PHM decision loop executes in under 60 μs.

items.title: Experimental Characterization of SMD Inductors for Cryogenic Power Conversion at 4 K
items.abstract: With the increasing complexity and scalability demands of cryogenic electronic systems, such as quantum computing platforms, conversion of power within the cryogenic environment has become a primary concern. Magnetic inductors are among the key components affecting converter performance, as their electrical and magnetic properties can change significantly at low temperatures. In this paper, five commercially available Vishay SMD power inductors are experimentally characterized down to 4 K: DC resistance is measured continuously during cooldown, while frequency-dependent AC inductance and resistance are measured up to 2 MHz at both room temperature and 4 K. The results show substantial DC resistance reductions of 25x-58x at 4 K, while the inductance degrades by only about 5-5.5%. Although cryogenic operation slightly increases the AC resistance (due to the intensified skin effect) and raises core losses, converter-level analysis shows an inductor-only efficiency improvement of approximately 5.3-6.9 percentage points at 1 A, and up to 22.8 points at 3 A. The measured frequency-dependent impedance of each inductor is imported into Cadence and a complete single-phase 24 V-to-1 V buck converter with GaN power devices is simulated at 1, 2, and 3 A at 4 K. The full-converter efficiency at 4 K is shown to improve by 3.0-5.2 percentage points at 1 A and by up to 22.5 points at 3 A for the AC-characterized devices. These findings indicate that commercially available off-the-shelf power inductors remain operationally viable under cryogenic conditions and can simultaneously increase inductor efficiency and reduce the overall power loss in cryogenic power conversion systems.

items.title: A Multiplexed Range-Resolved Interferometry-Based Virtual Metrology Frame for Planar Deformation Compensation in a Nanopositioning Machine
items.abstract: This dataset records structural deformation in a nanopositioning system (NPS6D200) with 6-DOF control under non-ideal thermal conditions. It was collected to support the validation of the Virtual Metrology Framework (VMF), a measurement-driven architecture that replaces passive mechanical rigidity metrology frame with real-time, distributed sensing and compensation. Measurements from six range-resolved interferometry (RRI) channels are syncronized with a laser focus sensor (LFS) signals and environmental sensors (temperature, relative humidity, and atmospheric pressure), recorded over a continuous period of approximately 5 days. The system was operated under typical laboratory conditions with insufficient air conditioning and uneven heating sources, inducing local temperature gradients that led to both uniform and non-uniform thermal expansion across the machine base. Key variables include: RRI phase signals (raw and unwrapped), Ciddor-corrected optical path differences (OPD), LFS sum and difference signals, Environmental parameters (temperature, humidity, air pressure), VMF-reconstructed coordinates (X and Y), Residual errors between VMF and reference interferometer readings. All individual RRI data are provided in CSV format. Machine measurements (including LFS and environmental data) are stored in a MATLAB .mat database files. Timestamps are synchronized to UTC. The origin reference point is defined as the position of the machine when the sample center is aligned with the optical axis of the LFS, and the corresponding laser interferometer values are recorded as the baseline for coordinate reconstruction. Obs.: The main script requires the air_index.m file, which is available from the MATLAB File Exchange: Air Refractive Index.

items.title: A Hybrid GPU and Processing-Near-Memory Architecture with Shared DRAM for Efficient Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
items.abstract: The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) has significantly increased the compute and memory demands of inference serving. A key challenge arises from the mismatch between compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decoding: when executed together, the two phases interfere, while separating them via prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation leads to substantial resource underutilization. Specifically, prefill leaves memory bandwidth underutilized, whereas decoding underutilizes compute resources. Prior approaches, such as GPU Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) partitioning, attempt to improve utilization by spatially dividing GPU resources. However, these approaches remain fundamentally limited, as memory-bound decoding still requires a large number of SMs to saturate bandwidth, reducing the compute resources available for prefill and resulting in an inherent trade-off. To address this limitation, we propose DuoPD, a hybrid PD-disaggregation architecture that integrates lightweight Processing-Near-Memory (PNM) units into the HBM logic die. Unlike prior PIM/PNM designs that rely on costly internal bandwidth scaling and offload only partial decoding operations, DuoPD enables full decoding execution on PNM by leveraging bandwidth sharing with the GPU over a shared HBM interface. This allows compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decoding to execute concurrently with minimal interference, improving both compute and memory utilization. To realize this design, we develop a compact PNM microarchitecture, a TSV-level bandwidth sharing mechanism, and a hierarchical data mapping scheme tailored for hybrid GPU-PNM execution. Evaluations on server-scale LLMs demonstrate that DuoPD achieves up to 2.23x higher end-to-end throughput than conventional PD-disaggregation.

items.title: Tailoring Dielectric Relaxation and Charge Transport in Amorphous Ge-Te-Se Phase-Change Materials through Yttrium Incorporation
items.abstract: The Te(1-x)(GeSe0.5)Yx (x = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15) alloys were prepared by a melt-quenching method and characterized using dielectric spectroscopy. The dielectric parameters and electrical conductivity were evaluated to assess their potential for phase-change memory and other electronic applications. The temperature and frequency dependence of the dielectric constants, ac conductivity, and dielectric loss of prepared chalcogenide glassy alloys were investigated over the frequency range 1 Hz - 1 MHz, and the temperature range 302 - 422 K, below the glass transition temperature. Both dielectric loss and dielectric constant were found to decrease with increasing frequency and decreasing temperature. The observed dielectric loss change was interpreted using the Guintini model of dielectric dispersion, correlated barrier hopping (CBH) model, and orientation polarization. The Cole-Cole analysis confirmed a distribution of relaxation times and yielded activation energies consistent with the CBH conduction mechanism. The frequency dependence of the ac conductivity follows the power law (Aωs), where the frequency exponent (s < 1) decreases with increasing temperature, further supporting the CBH conduction mechanism. The incorporation of Y increases the density of localized tail states, resulting in enhanced ac conductivity. These findings suggest that the investigated materials are promising candidates for future phase-change memory and other electronic device applications.

items.title: Virtual metrology for process perturbation prediction in lithographic alignment marks using a physics-guided directed attention network
items.abstract: Process perturbations in lithographic alignment marks deform multilayer profiles, break mark symmetry, and introduce alignment position uncertainty. Although alignment position deviation (APD) and wafer quality (WQ) responses contain process-dependent information, retrieving the underlying perturbations remains challenging because the inverse relationship is nonlinear and strongly coupled. We formulate this task as alignment mark virtual metrology, in which process perturbation values are estimated from paired APD/WQ response matrices. To solve this inverse problem, we propose a physics-guided directed attention network (PG-DAN). PG-DAN uses diffraction limit masked attention (DLMA) to inject wavelength, diffraction order, propagation, locality, and identity priors into APD/WQ attention logits, enabling the model to use physically meaningful token relations rather than unconstrained data correlations. A directed decoder further follows multilayer coupling during prediction. Evaluated on a rigorous coupled wave analysis (RCWA) dataset, PG-DAN achieves a mean R 2 of 0.999875, a mean range-normalized RMSE of 0.34%, and a mean range-normalized MAE of 0.23%, with lower estimation errors than conventional neural inverse models. These results support physics-guided inverse modeling for alignment mark process perturbation estimation.

items.title: UnO-NeSy: Optimizing Neuro-Symbolic Computing with Unified FeFET Based In-Memory System
items.abstract: Neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence (NeSy AI) combines neural perception with symbolic reasoning, enabling logical reasoning. Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is promising for NeSy AI, owing to its high parallelism and strong robustness to noise. However, the dense neural operations and memory-intensive symbolic inference in NeSy impose a severe "memory wall" bottleneck. Existing NeSy accelerators either focus solely on symbolic kernels or rely on conventional digital architectures, lacking a unified and energy-efficient hardware substrate. Moreover, exploring optimal hardware design configurations often requires costly trial-and-error. In this work, we propose UnO-NeSy, a unified CiM framework for optimizing NeSy computing. UnO-NeSy consists of UnO-CiM, an ultra-low-power NeSy architecture based on a homogeneous 2FeFET--2R compute-in-memory (CiM) array that supports both neural computation and HDC reasoning, and UnO-Sim, a cross-workload, end-to-end CiM simulator that models device non-idealities, neural quantization effects, and HDC execution behavior for accurate system-level evaluation. Built on UnO-Sim, we further develop an automated optimizer to identify workload-specific operating points under coupled energy, accuracy, and hardware constraints. By optimizing the operating configuration of the baseline 2FeFET--2R design, UnO-NeSy achieves $61.8\%$ higher energy efficiency and $38.2\%$ lower full-system inference energy. Across seven RAVEN configurations, UnO-NeSy achieves $96.2\%$ average reasoning accuracy under hardware non-idealities, demonstrating a practical and scalable path toward ultra-low-power NeSy hardware.

items.title: Ultrathin BiO x Charge-Transfer Doping for Cross-TMD Electronic Modulation and Homogeneous WSe2 Inverters
items.abstract: Charge-transfer doping provides a nondestructive route to tune two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), but selectively patterned n-type dopants effective across different TMD channels remain limited. Here, ultrathin bismuth oxide (BiOx) is used as an n-type charge-transfer doping and passivation layer for monolayer MoS2 and WSe2 transistors. In MoS2, 2 nm BiOx preserves the channel structure and yields a TLM-extracted effective contact resistance of 0.71 ± 0.06 kΩ·μm at n2D = 1.8 × 1013 cm-2. Thicker BiOx strengthens n-type modulation but reduces gate controllability. The modulation remains stable after ambient storage and air annealing. BiOx also enhances electron transport in WSe2 and enables homogeneous WSe2 inverters with MoOx-doped p-FETs, achieving a gain of ∼19 and a total normalized noise margin of 0.895 VDD at VDD = 2 V. These results establish BiOx as a cross-TMD n-type charge-transfer dopant for contact, threshold-voltage, and polarity engineering.

items.title: Two-step oxygen treatments for low-resistance ohmic contacts on p-NiO
items.abstract: As an important p-type wide-bandgap oxide semiconductor, NiO exhibits promising prospects for application in wide-bandgap power devices. However, owing to its high work function, strong Fermi-level pinning effect, and large hole injection barrier, it is challenging to realize low-resistance ohmic contacts on p-NiO. In this work, a synergistic surface engineering strategy combining oxygen plasma treatment (OPT) and oxygen rapid annealing (ORA) is proposed to optimize the Ni/NiO ohmic contact. Mechanistic studies demonstrate that this synergistic treatment process can introduce interstitial oxygen into the NiO surface layer to increase the hole concentration, narrow the interfacial depletion width, and enhance carrier tunneling transport. Meanwhile, it can effectively reduce the interface state density, thereby alleviating Fermi-level pinning, lowering the surface barrier, and significantly improving interface uniformity and stability. After the OPT+ORA treatment, the specific contact resistivity ρc of Ni/NiO is reduced from 2.55 × 10−3 to 8.01 × 10−5 Ω cm2. By applying this process to a p-NiO/n-Ga2O3 heterojunction diode, the specific on-resistance RON,sp decreases from 5.28 to 3.08 mΩ cm2. This approach provides an effective pathway for achieving low-resistance ohmic contacts on p-type NiO and realizing high-performance NiO-based wide-bandgap power devices.

items.title: Thermal-history encoding through ionic-state programming in a monolithic organic thermosynapse
items.abstract: Abstract Encoding thermal history directly in soft ionic matter requires a material in which temperature controls not only ion transport but also the persistence of the resulting ionic state. Here we report a bio-inspired monolithic thermosynapse that encodes thermal history through ionic-state programming within a single organic electrochemical transistor. A zwitterionic gel with an upper critical solution temperature regulates ion confinement and release across its phase transition, producing an approximately 922% relative increase in ionic conductivity. Field-induced polarization further stabilizes the written ionic state after bias removal, increasing memory retention by 69.7% relative to a conventional hydrogel and, unusually, making retention more persistent as temperature rises. This coupling of thermally regulated ion transport and post-stimulus state retention allows prior thermal exposure to be stored within the ionic material and translated into history-dependent electronic responses. As a proof of concept, the retained state regulates robotic recontact, suppressing cumulative heating and thermal drift in a co-located pressure sensor.

items.title: Sustainable Processing-in-DRAM Integration and Replacement for Transformer Inference Servers
items.abstract: Processing-in-DRAM (PID) accelerators are emerging as a sustainable alternative to GPUs for transformer model inference. They bring compute to data, mitigate the memory bandwidth limitation, and reduce the overall energy footprint. Yet, carbon analysis of PID accelerators is covered for only a limited set of hardware and workloads. In this work, we present a carbon modeling framework for PID-enabled inference servers that captures embodied carbon along with idle and active operational carbon. Our evaluation spans three GPU baselines, six PID architectures, and eight transformer workloads. Additionally, we propose an aging-aware model that finds the carbon-optimal replacement period for PID accelerators over a 10-year horizon. Across evaluated configurations, our analysis shows that including PIDs in AI inference servers increases the total embodied carbon by at most 2.5\%, while the total carbon is reduced by up to 1.14$\times$ for encoder and 1.04$\times$ for decoder transformer workloads. The results also depend on GPU selection for pairing, where introducing PID modules in high-end HGX-H100 servers incurs 5.4--5.9$\times$ higher total carbon compared to A100 and H100 servers, due to their larger idle and embodied carbon. Introducing PID modules in higher-end GPU servers, compared to the A100-only baseline, increases (decreases) the total carbon-delay product (CDP) for encoder workloads (decoder workloads).

items.title: Superposed analog memory for vector storage in neural networks
items.abstract: The growing memory demands of artificial neural networks pose a major challenge for energy-efficient computing, particularly for models that rely on large collections of high-dimensional weight and embedding vectors. Conventional memory architectures store these vectors individually, requiring many memory cells per vector and limiting achievable storage density. Here we demonstrate an analog memory architecture that encodes multiple vectors in a distributed superposition within a single memory array. Individual vectors are recovered through in-memory matrix-vector multiplication, allowing the degree of superposition to be tuned to balance storage density against recall fidelity. This approach introduces a new scaling dimension for analog memory, in which effective storage density can be increased without a corresponding increase in the number of physical memory cells. The distributed representation also provides resilience to device-level noise. We implement the architecture on a prototype phase-change memory chip and experimentally evaluate it using embedding tables from deep learning recommendation models and large language models. The results demonstrate inference accuracy comparable to full-precision software baselines, establishing analog superposition as a promising route towards dense, energy-efficient memory for artificial intelligence.

items.title: Strain-Induced Interfacial Bond Evolution and Facet-Dependent Strain Response of Electronic Properties in Oxidized Silicon Nanowires
items.abstract: Abstract Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation nanoelectronic devices due to their tunable electronic properties, and compatibility with aggressive scaling requirements. The integration of strain further enhances their performance by modulating carrier mobility, band structure, and transport behavior without altering material chemistry. Within the NW, the silicon–silicon dioxide (Si–SiO2) interface serves as a critical region where strain redistribution and suboxide bonding collectively influence the mechanical and electronic response. Here, we combine reactive force field molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations to investigate how oxidation-induced interfacial structure and crystallographic facet orientation govern strain-dependent bond evolution and facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties in oxidized Si NWs. Simulated dry thermal oxidation generates chemically realistic Si–SiO2 interfaces, enabling direct characterization of bond order redistribution and stress gradient development across the interface under tensile strain. Interfacial Si–Si bonds exhibit elongation and reduced bond order associated with partial oxidation states, leading to localized stress concentration and preferential bond rupture. Complementary density functional theory calculations on facet-specific models reveal that orientation-dependent interfacial bonding modulates facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties. Together, these results establish a direct coupling between interfacial suboxide chemistry, mechanical deformation, and electronic structure, providing atomistic insight into strain-modulated behavior at oxidized silicon interfaces in faceted NWs.
items.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C

items.title: Strain-Engineered Giant Tunneling Magnetoresistance in Fe-Intercalated MoS2 van der Waals Magnetic Tunnel Junctions
items.abstract: Abstract This work proposes an all-two-dimensional magnetic tunnel junction consisting of Fe-intercalated MoS2 ferromagnetic electrodes and a pristine bilayer MoS2 tunneling barrier. We systematically investigate the modulation mechanism of out-of-plane tensile strain on the spin-transport properties of the device using quantum transport simulations. The results reveal that Fe intercalation induces a semiconductor-to-ferromagnetic-metal transition in MoS2 and the magnetic moment increases progressively under tensile strain. Under an applied tensile strain of 3%, the MTJ achieves an ultrahigh tunneling magnetoresistance of 1.67 × 105% accompanied by a spin injection efficiency of 90%. The enhancement of spin-dependent tunneling efficiency under tensile strain originates from a Fermi level shift of the electrodes and modulation of the spin asymmetry of the interfacial Schottky barrier. By integrating atomic intercalation with strain engineering, this work establishes a new paradigm for designing high-performance, low-power two-dimensional spintronic devices.

items.title: South Korea’s AI Power Under Uneven Interdependence: Semiconductor Depth, National Conversion, and the KIC Model-Selection Case
items.abstract: This policy brief examines South Korea’s AI power under uneven technological interdependence. It argues that Korea combines globally consequential semiconductor and high-bandwidth-memory capabilities with growing domestic models, public compute programs, cloud and telecommunications capacity, and industrial and administrative AI applications, but these strengths do not constitute a nationally controlled end-to-end AI stack. The brief distinguishes AI National Power, AI Boundary Power, Boundary Autonomy, and Systemic Influence, and evaluates Korea’s capacity conversion across memory, compute, domestic models, industrial AI, and public-sector deployment. It uses the Korea Investment Corporation as a diagnostic case of mixed-origin institutional AI, where Chinese-developed Qwen3 and BGE-M3 reportedly operate alongside U.S.-developed models for differentiated internal functions. The case does not establish foreign control, strategic realignment, or durable dependence; instead, it highlights the importance of deployment architecture, continuing control rights, switching costs, security review, and function-preserving substitution. The brief concludes that South Korea’s future AI power will depend on converting specialized technological depth into sustainable national functions, exercising effective control at consequential interfaces, and preserving credible alternatives under disruption.

items.title: Resolving the Thermal Labyrinth inside 3D-IC Stacks
items.abstract: The heat pathways in 3D-ICs have long been a labyrinth lacking experimental investigations into spatial distribution of thermal properties, severely limiting study of internal thermal management inside chips. For the first time, we established a methodology for 3D thermal characterizations of advanced 3D-ICs, implemented through a systematic workflow that enables layer-resolved thermal property extraction and the construction of a location-specific thermal database. We demonstrated its application to an advanced sample featuring 2.2-μm-diameter TSVs and ~2-μm-pitch face-to-face hybrid bonding (HB). Time-domain and steady-state thermoreflectance were used to extract the thermal conductivities (TCs) of Al traces, TSV, BEOL interconnects and HB pads, indicating HB structure enables efficient thermal transport with 9 W/m-K TC. Further, we mapped and visualized the TC distribution of TSV structures and RDL Cu wires with small step sizes down to 0.2 μm. Utilizing these results, we proposed an experiment-based thermal model to reveal that co-evolution of interconnect and substrate TCs is essential for thermal design and fabrication towards effective cooling optimization.

items.title: Reliability Analysis of Isolation Structures for Integrated Circuits Based on the Beta Generalized Weibull Distribution
items.abstract: The reliability analysis of integrated circuit (IC) isolation structures (ISs) faces two challenges: how to accurately describe the distribution of time-to-failure (TTF) data, and how to obtain the TTF distribution under actual working conditions (AWCs). To address these issues, this paper introduces the flexible five-parameter Beta Generalized Weibull (BGW) distribution, which can represent the five characteristic failure-rate shapes (IFR, DFR, CFR, BFR and UBT). The sign of the hazard derivative is analyzed through Glaser’s eta-function theorem together with the asymptotic behavior of the hazard rate at the origin and at infinity; this yields exact, necessary-and-sufficient parameter conditions for each shape, with the origin controlled by the product aγω and the tail controlled by γ. A TTF model based on the BGW distribution is then proposed to predict the TTF distribution under AWCs, and it is proved analytically that a change of stress affects only the scale parameter δ, leaving all shape parameters unchanged. Because this invariance was previously stated as an assumption, it is verified empirically on the time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) data using per-level Weibull shape estimates with bootstrap confidence intervals, a Kruskal–Wallis test on standardized failure times, and a parametric-bootstrap likelihood-ratio test within the BGW family; all three tests support stress-invariant shapes. The reliability function is recast as a convergent infinite series, with the correct beta-integral kernel and an explicit ratio-test bound. Finally, the effectiveness and superiority of the method are verified using TDDB TTF data, and the untested 3800 V condition is predicted from the fitted linear voltage-acceleration model.

items.title: Rare Gases
items.abstract: FORTUNE GAS has extensive experience in supplying our customers with rare gases. We use advanced technologies and processes to extract noble gases such as argon, neon, helium, krypton and xenon from feed stock gases. It has the characteristics of advanced technology, high recovery rate, and safety and reliability Krypton / Xenon Typical Projects: Rare Gases Extraction Unit for Industrial Gases Field Add: Hebei, China Helium / Neon / Krypton / Xenon Typical Projects: Rare Gases Extraction Unit of GOX40,000Nm³/h(1400TPD) ASU Add: Hubei, China Application: Steel Making Complex Helium Extraction and Liquefaction Fortune Gas Rare Gas Spectrum Rare gases (often grouped under noble gases or inert gases) are chemically stable, which makes them ideal for high-precision industrial environments where contamination is unacceptable. Krypton & Xenon: Critical for Advanced Semiconductor Processes While neon krypton and helium xenon have legacy uses in specialty lighting, their strategic importance today is strongly tied to semiconductor manufacturing, including: 3D NAND etching processes that require tightly controlled gas chemistry High-value, purity-sensitive operations where gas consistency can impact yield Key procurement concern: supply reliability and reproducible purity across lots—especially for fabs. Neon: The “Buffer Gas” Behind DUV Lithography Lasers Neon is a crucial component in excimer laser gas mixtures used in deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography—a foundational step in advanced chip production. When neon supply tightens, downstream impacts can ripple through the semiconductor value chain. Helium: Cooling, Leak Detection, and Aerospace Reliability Helium is essential in: MRI cooling (cryogenic applications) Aerospace and high-vacuum leak detection Purging and inerting where ultra-low reactivity is required Technical Data Table: Boiling Points & Atmospheric Concentrations (Quick Reference) Why it matters: these large boiling point differences are what make cryogenic separation feasible—and what drive the design of a high-efficiency rare gas recovery system. How Rare Gas Recovery Works — From ASU Tail Gas to High-Purity Product The ASU Connection: Where Rare Gases “Hide” Large-scale ASUs primarily produce oxygen and nitrogen. Rare gases do not disappear—they concentrate in specific side streams during cryogenic processing: Krypton/Xenon tend to concentrate with oxygen-rich fractions (often linked to LOX handling routes) Neon/Helium are typically found in non-condensable fractions associated with nitrogen stream handling and tail gas management This is why the most cost-effective rare gas production often comes from recovery, not “primary” manufacturing. Process Deep-Dive: Two Main Recovery Pathways 1) Krypton/Xenon Recovery (Often Associated with LOX-Related Streams) A typical route includes: Concentration of Kr/Xe-rich mixtures Multi-step fractional separation Purification to industrial or semiconductor specifications This is the basis for solutions commonly described as xenon/krypton recovery from ASU tail gas (implementation varies by ASU configuration and operating objectives). 2) Neon/Helium Recovery (Non-Condensables from Nitrogen Handling) Because helium and neon are extremely volatile, they are often recovered from: Non-condensable fractions Tail-gas or purge routes designed for controlled separation and purification Fortune Gas Rare Gas Recovery Systems: Designed for Yield, Purity, and Integration A modern rare gases cryogenic system is not just a “bolt-on box.” It must be engineered around: Existing ASU flows and cold box interfaces Contaminant profiles (including moisture, hydrocarbons, and trace impurities) Target product slates (Ne/He vs. Kr/Xe) and required purity Fortune Gas focuses on cryogenic system solutions that aim to maximize: Recovery rate (economics) Product stability (quality) Operational uptime (reliability) Why Source Rare Gases from China? The Fortune Gas Advantage In today’s volatile sourcing environment, buyers are actively diversifying supply chains. China has become a major player in rare gas separation and supply—especially when the procurement requirement includes technical coordination, consistent output, and scalable delivery. Supply Security for Industrial and High-Tech Buyers For procurement managers and engineers, stable availability is often as important as price. A qualified supplier must demonstrate: predictable production planning consistent batch quality export and documentation readiness Purity Standards: 5. and 6. items.title: Photo-synaptic organic light-emitting transistors (PS-OLETs): new frontiers for neuromorphic computing
items.abstract: In-memory and neuromorphic computing based on organic synaptic transistors promise to overcome the speed, energy, and bandwidth limitations of von Neumann architectures, yet electrically driven devices remain constrained by the same bottlenecks affecting purely electronic transistors. Photonic synaptic devices, using light as both input and output carrier, offer signal transmission, which is anti-interference, long-distance, low-loss, massively parallel and with no need for impedance-matching between computing units, positioning photonic neuromorphic hardware as a natural evolution of information technology. Building on organic photonic synaptic transistors (OPSTs), which combine electrical and optical stimulation with an electrical readout, this perspective introduces the photo-synaptic organic light-emitting transistor (PS-OLET), that merges optical sensing, in-device information processing, synaptic plasticity, and light emission within a single, scalable, planar transistor architecture. We review the material and device strategies used to achieve optical triggering in OPSTs and describe how the intrinsic light-generation capability of organic light-emitting transistors can be merged with these synaptic mechanisms to realize a genuinely dual-output optoelectronic device relevant for intelligent-display applications. We further propose PS-OLETs as physical nodes for photonic Reservoir Computing: by integrating electrical and optical input, nonlinear processing, and electrical and optical output within one device, PS-OLETs can act as low-loss, low-latency optoelectronic reservoir units, overcoming the need for external light sources and the spatial constraints of memristor- or waveguide-based architectures. Within the appropriate signal bandwidth, the PS-OLET-based reservoir can operate with intrinsic timescales matched to the input temporal features, enabling optimal memory capacity. We also discuss how PS-OLET networks could support fully analogic, reconfigurable reservoir computing systems combining high state richness and massively parallel, distributed processing. Extending the spectral response to the visible and near-infrared range, exploiting circularly polarized light for chiro-optical synaptic functions, and integrating additional sensing modalities are expected to establish PS-OLETs as a foundational technology for next-generation photonic neuromorphic hardware.

items.title: One-dimensional structural boundaries in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides: physics, engineering, and functional electronics
items.abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) materials, including graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), provide atomically thin platforms for next-generation electronic, optoelectronic, and van der Waals heterostructure devices. In realistic materials, however, device-relevant properties are often governed by one-dimensional (1D) structural boundaries that arise during crystal growth, grain coalescence, or layer assembly. Unlike point defects, these boundaries remain structurally continuous while introducing localized changes in crystallographic orientation, symmetry, or stacking registry, giving rise to characteristic atomic motifs and boundary-confined electronic states. In this topical review, we establish a unified conceptual framework for understanding 1D boundaries in 2D TMDs by classifying them according to their governing structural order parameters: grain boundaries (GBs) defined by crystallographic misorientation, mirror twin boundaries (MTBs) by symmetry transition, and domain walls (DWs) by stacking-registry variation. For each class, we discuss the relationships among formation mechanisms, atomic structures, electronic properties, deterministic synthesis strategies, and emerging device concepts. By comparing these boundaries in TMD monolayers and in Moiré and sliding-ferroelectric TMD bilayers, with bilayer graphene as a reference system for stacking DWs, we show that their electronic functionalities are governed by distinct physical mechanisms, including atomic stitching, defect-core motifs, symmetry-defined metallicity, stacking topology, strain relaxation, and local electrostatic reconstruction. Finally, we highlight recent progress in deterministic boundary engineering and demonstrate how GBs, MTBs, and DWs provide complementary design concepts for programmable switching interfaces, atomically precise metallic interconnects, correlated quantum wires, and electrically reconfigurable functional devices. We conclude that the field is undergoing a transition from defect engineering toward boundary architecture engineering, in which the arrangement, interaction, and functionality of 1D boundaries become programmable design elements for next-generation 2D electronics.

items.title: ORCA: Oracle-less CNN-based Structural Attack on Hardware Obfuscation and Reverse Engineering to RTL
items.abstract: In this paper, we propose ORCA, an oracle-less, CNN-based structural attack methodology that circumvents logic locking by predicting the key of a locked gate-level netlist and reversing it to RTL. The proposed methodology learns the features of a local gate near the root node in the obfuscated design to predict the key of the locked netlist. This methodology is evaluated on different standard benchmark suites such as ISCAS-85, ITC-99, and EPFL. ORCA predicts the key with an average accuracy of 96.69%, outperforming the state-of-the-art deep learning oracle-less attacks SAIL, SnapShot, OMLA, and LIPSTICK by 21.28%, 15.43%, 9.11%, and 0.75%, respectively. To check the effectiveness of ORCA in real scenarios, it is evaluated on netlists synthesized using the complete technology libraries of different foundries, such as TSMC (40nm, 65nm, and 90nm) and GlobalFoundries (40nm), unlike the limited standard cells used in the state-of-the-art attack methods. In the case of a complete technology library, our attack methodology predicts the correct key with an average KPA of more than 70%, demonstrating that it can perform well even when the locked netlist is synthesized using the entire technology library. In addition to traditional Random Logic Locking (RLL), the proposed methodology is also tested on the ML-resilient DECOR logic locking scheme, which predicts the key with an average KPA of 69.61%, outperforming OMLA by 17.18%. In addition to key prediction, the locked netlist is converted to RTL, making ORCA a complete reverse engineering attack flow.

items.title: Noise‐Driven Functionality in Neuromorphic Materials, Devices, and Systems
items.abstract: Neuromorphic hardware turns the physical dynamics of functional materials into computation, enabling dense in‐memory and probabilistic architectures beyond digital abstraction. Yet this advantage also makes neuromorphic systems highly sensitive to noise and variability, because analog device states directly encode synaptic weights, neuronal thresholds, membrane currents, and spike signals. While device‐to‐device variation, cycle‐to‐cycle variation, and drift have been widely discussed as critical non‐idealities, temporal noise, particularly read‐current fluctuations during sensing of analog states, has received less systematic attention. This review addresses this gap by positioning temporal noise within the broader landscape of device variability and by highlighting low‐frequency noise spectroscopy as a mechanism‐resolved tool for identifying fluctuation origins, spectral signatures, time scales, and computational consequences. We establish a framework that classifies neuromorphic noise according to its role: suppression, tolerance, and utilization: (1) noise suppression reduces intrinsic fluctuation sources to secure multilevel precision and computing accuracy; (2) noise tolerance maintains robust operation through device‐to‐system strategies; and (3) noise utilization transforms intrinsic stochasticity into primitives for stochastic neurons and synapses, entropy generation, probabilistic bits, Bayesian inference, and reinforcement learning. Across neuromorphic materials, devices, and systems, this review reframes temporal noise from a reliability‐limiting imperfection into a hardware‐native resource for adaptive neuromorphic intelligence.

items.title: N2/O2 Plasma-Tuned Hydrogen-Bonding Configurations for Suppressed Charge Trapping in PEALD SiON Films
items.abstract: Hydrogen incorporation in silicon oxynitride (SiON) dielectric films plays a dual role by passivating electrically active defects while simultaneously acting as a potential source of charge trapping, depending on the chemical-bonding configuration. In this study, plasma-enhanced atomic layer-deposited (PEALD) SiON thin films were fabricated using diisopropylaminosilane and a mixed N2/O2 plasma, and the hydrogen-bonding states were systematically engineered by controlling the N2:O2 plasma flow ratio. Increasing the N2:O2 ratio progressively transformed the SiON network from oxide-rich to nitrogen-rich, resulting in an increased dielectric constant from 4.95 to 6.67 while decreasing the induced trap density from 6.15 × 1011 to 1.84 × 1011 cm–2. An optimized N2:O2 ratio of 250:1 yielded the lowest capacitance–voltage hysteresis (0.10 V), whereas the N2-only plasma process caused a substantial increase in hysteresis (1.85 V) despite its highest hydrogen concentration. Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry analyses revealed that hydrogen incorporation shifted from O–H-dominated to Si–H/N–H-dominated bonding environments as the nitrogen content increased. Density functional theory calculations further demonstrated that Si–H and Si–N bonds have lower bond dissociation energies than O–H and Si–O bonds, thereby explaining the instability of oxygen-deficient SiNx-like networks under electrical stress. These results demonstrate that the charge-trapping behavior of PEALD SiON films is governed not by the total hydrogen concentration but by the hydrogen-bonding configuration and the structural stability of the Si–O–N network, thereby providing an effective strategy for defect passivation and suppressed charge trapping in dielectric films for advanced semiconductor devices.

items.title: Multilevel charge fluctuations in a Si/SiGe double quantum dot device
items.abstract: Discrete charge fluctuations, routinely observed in semiconductor quantum dot devices, may contribute significantly to device drift and errors resulting from qubit miscalibration. Understanding the nature and origins of these discrete charge fluctuations may provide insights into material improvements or means of mitigating charge noise in semiconductor quantum dot devices. In this work, we measure multi-level charge fluctuations present in a Si/SiGe double quantum dot device over a range of device operating voltages and temperatures. To characterize the parameter-dependent dynamics of the underlying fluctuating degrees of freedom, we perform a detailed analysis of the measured noise timeseries. We perform algorithmically assisted drift detection and change point detection to detrend the data and remove a slow fluctuator component, as a preprocessing step. We perform model comparison on the post-processed time series between different $n$-level fluctuator ($n$LF) factorial hidden Markov models (FHMMs), finding that although at most sweep values the independent pair of 2LFs model would be preferred, in a particular region of voltage space the 4LF model outperforms the other models, indicating a conditional rate dependence between the two fluctuators. By tracking fluctuator transition rates, biases, and weights over a range of different device configurations, we estimate gate voltage and conductivity sensitivity. In particular, we fit a phenomenological, detailed balance model to the extracted independent 2LFs rate data, yielding lever arm estimates in the range of $-2 μ$eV/mV up to $4 μ$eV/mV between the two 2LFs and nearby gate electrodes. We expect that these characterization results may aid in subsequent spatial triangulation of the charge fluctuators.

items.title: Migrate Computation, Not Data: Fault Recovery in Neuromorphic Many-Core Systems
items.abstract: As neuromorphic systems scale to thousands of near-memory cores, aging-induced permanent faults in neuron-update datapaths become an important obstacle to long-term deployment. Existing online recovery methods typically retire a faulty core and migrate its neurons, along with their weights and membrane states, to healthy cores. This whole-core treatment incurs high recovery traffic and makes recovery depend on scarce destinations; at high utilization, there may be enough surviving compute capacity but insufficient free storage to copy the affected neuron context. This paper presents SpikeRelay, an online recovery framework for diagnosed compute-unit faults. SpikeRelay exploits the fact that, in many neuromorphic cores, the compute datapath, local SRAM, and router are distinct modules: a compute fault need not destroy stored weights and states or disconnect the core from the NoC. Instead of retiring a faulty core and migrating its neuron data, SpikeRelay converts the faulty core into a storage-and-forwarding node while offloading neuron-update computation to a healthy rescue core. This decoupling of storage and computation eliminates recovery-time data migration and greatly reduces spare-SRAM requirements. Consequently, SpikeRelay sustains 100\% recovery at 92.2\% SRAM utilization and a 50\% fault rate, whereas the best baseline achieves only 22.1\%.

items.title: Mechanistic enhancement of mapping in layered-semiconductor-based reservoir computing devices for neuromorphic computing
items.abstract: We investigate Bi2Se3-based reservoir computing devices fabricated via a rubbing-induced site-selective deposition process, focusing on the role of grid density in governing dynamical behavior and computational capability. Devices with identical footprints but different network structures—including a grid-free 1 × 3 channel and cross-linked 3 × 3, 6 × 6, and 9 × 9 grids—are systematically studied. Step-forward dynamical modeling confirms that all devices exhibit stable, state-dependent responses characteristic of physical reservoirs. Dynamic prediction results show that increasing grid density significantly improves prediction accuracy for Mackey–Glass dynamics, demonstrating enhanced computational capability. Additional analysis reveals that increasing the number of output terminals further improves prediction performance, indicating that both structural complexity and readout dimensionality contribute to reservoir effectiveness. These results establish that grid-density-controlled structural connectivity governs reservoir performance and provide practical design guidelines for layered-semiconductor neuromorphic hardware.

items.title: M3D-FLOW: A Monolithic 3-D-Stackable Processing-Near-DRAM Architecture for Generative Normalizing Flow Applications
items.abstract: Normalizing Flows (NFs) have shown strong results in generative modeling, recently reaching state-of-the-art image generation performance. However, their repetitive, sequential operations limit the computational and memory efficiency achievable with GPUs and TPUs. We propose M3D-FLOW, a novel monolithic 3D-stackable (M3D) DRAM-based processing-near-memory (PNM) architecture that eliminates memory bottlenecks using a Cu-Cu hybrid-bonded logic die integrated with an M3D DRAM die. The M3D DRAM provides dense bank integration and a tiered organization with variable access latencies that M3D-FLOW exploits for the efficient processing of different NF workloads. To maximize compute density while minimizing area, energy, and thermal overhead, M3D-FLOW employs hybrid binary--stochastic floating-point multipliers, performing mantissa multiplication in the stochastic domain and exponent operations in the binary domain. A pipelined execution strategy maps sequential NF stages across dynamically partitioned PE groups, and together with the stochastic hardware, enables M3D-FLOW to achieve at least $6.6\times$ higher performance and $3\times$ better energy efficiency than prior PNM accelerators, with only a 2.2% bits-per-dimension (BPD) increase over bfloat16 and 4.1% over FP32. An analysis of stochastic hardware variants further shows that shorter stochastic bitstreams reduce execution time by up to $3.3\times$ at the cost of higher approximation error, providing a concrete design guide for latency--accuracy trade-offs.

items.title: Green Light: Carbon-Aware Design of Photonic Transformer Accelerators at the Edge
items.abstract: Migrating transformer inference to the edge requires sustainability considerations that encompass both operation and manufacturing, rather than operational energy alone. Silicon photonics enables high-bandwidth, low-energy matrix multiplication; however, existing microring-resonator-based Dot Product Unit (DPU) organizations have been tailored to convolutional computations and evaluated using analog signaling without accounting for embodied carbon footprints. We adapt three DPU organizations (AMW, MAW, and MWA) to transformer inference workloads and extend each organization to stochastic signaling, yielding six organizations in total. We then calculate their embodied and operational carbon per inference. Across five transformer models and four foundry grids, the photonic system achieves improvements of four, four, and six orders of magnitude in Energy-Delay, Carbon-Delay, and Carbon-Energy Product, respectively, relative to CPUs, while also being compared against H100 SXM5 GPU and TPU v5p baseline systems. Analog-to-stochastic conversion increases die area by 4.3-4.6x and embodied carbon by 4.4-4.8x, while reducing operational energy by approximately 91% and causing embodied carbon to equal or exceed operational carbon per inference. Importantly, the DPU organization and signaling scheme, rather than the foundry grid, are the key determinants of carbon impact. Consequently, the fastest organization (MWA) is not necessarily the most carbon-efficient, whereas MAW-Stochastic offers a favorable balance between sustainability and performance.

items.title: Framework Tecnico per Memoria Unificata Ibrida 3D [V1.0]
items.abstract: Questo repository ospita il Memoria Unificata su Materiali Abbondanti – Rapporto tecnico consolidato (Rev. 2.1), un framework per una nuova architettura di memoria ibrida a tre livelli progettata per integrare tecnologie mature con materiali sostenibili ed abbondanti. Il sistema propone una gerarchia innovativa composta da: (L0) cache SRAM + SOT-MRAM non volatile; (L1) memoria FeRAM 3D su HZO; e (L2) Computing-in-Memory (CIM) basato su array Crossbar di materiali bio-based (LIG da biomassa, ossido di grafene funzionalizzato, silicati d'argento e di calcio, argille). L'architettura affronta le criticità dell'integrazione verticale tramite un piano termico attivo in nitruro di boro esagonale (h-BN) per mitigare gli hot spot, e utilizza un controller ibrido per l'orchestrazione dei carichi di lavoro, il wear-leveling e la gestione dinamica delle code CXL. Il rapporto applica un protocollo di verifica rigoroso basato su fonti primarie: tutte le specifiche quantitative (latenza, energia per bit, endurance) sono ancorate a dati sperimentali verificati, scartando affermazioni non documentabili o prive di tracciabilità bibliografica. Non vengono inclusi stime economiche o modelli commerciali; l'attenzione è esclusivamente alle metriche fisiche e alla compatibilità di processo BEOL (<400 °C). items.title: Electron injection in tunneling-oxide-less charge-trap flash memories
items.abstract: This paper presents a physics-based technology computer-aided design framework for electron trapping in tunneling-oxide-less Al2O3/Si3N4 (AN) charge-trap devices and its extension to Al2O3/Si3N4/SiO2 (ANO) stacks. Unlike conventional ANO devices with a SiO2 tunneling oxide, AN devices place the Si3N4 layer in direct contact with the poly-Si channel, requiring a different electron injection model. The model combines Fowler–Nordheim tunneling through Si3N4 with direct channel-to-nitride injection caused by the tunneling-oxide-less gate stack. These two mechanisms are represented using shallow and deep trap-energy levels in the nitride layer. The trap energy Et, trap density Nt, tunneling effective mass m*, and spatial distribution are calibrated by matching simulated programming transients and ID–VG characteristics to measurements from fabricated AN devices. The measurement-calibrated framework accurately predicts the threshold-voltage shift ΔVth and trapped-electron distributions as functions of programming voltage and temperature. It also clarifies how Et, Nt, m*, and the spatial distribution determine the trapping rate, stored charge, and trapping location. Using the same nitride trap parameters, the model is applied to ANO devices with different tunneling-oxide thicknesses and accurately predicts their trapped-electron density distribution and ΔVth characteristics. These results establish tunneling-oxide-less AN devices as effective platforms for extracting intrinsic nitride trap parameters applicable to conventional ANO flash stacks and more complex tunneling-stack designs.

items.title: Dual‐Timescale 3D Synaptic Pillars: Monolithic Integration of Volatile and Nonvolatile Functions for Advanced Neuromorphic Computing
items.abstract: The rapidly growing demand for neuromorphic computing has driven extensive research shifting from software algorithms to hardware implementations. Among three‐terminal synaptic device candidates, 1T‐DRAM exhibits high‐speed operation but suffers from poor retention, whereas SONOS memory offers long retention but requires high power. To address these limitations, this study proposes a 3D vertically integrated synaptic device utilizing an n–p–n–p–n stacked channel structure that consolidates both volatile and nonvolatile functionalities into a single cell, achieving an ultra‐dense footprint of 4F 2 . By adopting a 3D vertical architecture, the proposed device demonstrates superior integration efficiency compared with conventional planar structures. Furthermore, the unique performance merits of this hybrid structure become particularly pronounced under extended holding times, where transferring stabilized weights from the volatile tier to the nonvolatile SONOS layer eliminates continuous refresh power overhead. To optimize weight modulation, an adaptive dynamic pulse scheme is introduced to secure high state linearity and symmetry across 32 training steps. NeuroSim V3.0 simulations successfully validated its learning capability, demonstrating a high MNIST classification accuracy of approximately 87%. Consequently, the proposed 3D vertical synaptic device serves as a highly promising candidate for next‐generation hardware‐based neuromorphic computing systems.

items.title: CGLLR: Classification-based Graded LLR Quantization Scheme for 3D TLC NAND Flash
items.abstract: low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are extensively utilized in triple-level cell (TLC) NAND flash memory due to their robust data error correction capability, with their performance dependent on the decoder’s iterative computation of the Log-Likelihood Ratio (LLR) messages transmitted by the NAND flash memory channel. However, implementing LDPC decoding algorithms in hardware necessitates the quantization of LLR messages due to limited hardware resources, which inevitably diminishes LLR accuracy and subsequently affects LDPC decoding performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose a classification-based graded LLR Quantization Scheme for 3D TLC NAND Flash, termed CGLLR. By employing the k-means clustering algorithm to categorize the quantized initial LLR messages from the channel, we apply distinct quantization factors to different categories of LLR values while preserving the relative magnitudes among the original LLR. This CGLLR strategy significantly enhances the resolution of LLR messages, thereby improving decoding performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CGLLR scheme reduces the average number of decoding iterations by 26.3% compared to the standard algorithm.
items.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems

items.title: Achieving Robust Ferroelectric Properties of Hf0.6Zr0.4O2 Thin Films through the Pseudofield-Inducing Effect of Al0.85Sc0.15N Bottom Electrode
items.abstract: Although ferroelectric (FE) Zr-doped HfO2 (HZO) is a promising material for ferroelectric random-access memory (FeRAM), achieving high remnant polarization (Pr) with a low coercive field (EC) at film thicknesses ≲10 nm remains challenging. This work demonstrates a multifunctional bottom electrode (BE) strategy by inserting a pristine, down-poled ferroelectric Al1-xScxN (ASN) layer into the BE, thereby inducing high mechanical stress and an internal field during HZO crystallization. The pristine down-polarization of ASN increased the c-axis preference of the overlying HZO film, as indicated by the contrast in the electrical characteristics and surface potential responses depending on the ASN poling direction. The ASN-containing BE imposes additional in-plane tensile stress on HZO due to ASN's low thermal expansion coefficient, facilitating orthorhombic phase formation. Consequently, 9 nm-thick HZO on the ASN-containing BE exhibits a large 2Pr of 81 μC/cm2 by conventional polarization-electric field (P-E) measurement and 68 μC/cm2 by positive-up-negative-down (PUND) compared with that of the TiN BE (43 μC/cm2, and 41 μC/cm2) with a pristine negative-bias imprint. These effects enable a high 2Pr/EC ratio without a significant increase in EC after wake-up, resulting in faster switching characteristics. Furthermore, it also enables the 5 nm-thick HZO film to overcome the pristine pinched hysteresis associated with tetragonal-phase stabilization, thereby achieving robust ferroelectric performance while suppressing wake-up behavior.

items.title: AceTherm: Accelerated Thermal Analysis of Chiplet Integration Using Non-Conformal FEM
items.abstract: As advanced process nodes continue to scale, heterogeneous integration technologies such as 2.5D/3D packaging, chiplets, and high-bandwidth memory have been widely adopted. However, these advances introduce substantially higher power densities, more complex interconnection structures, and increasingly diverse material systems. The resulting localized hotspots raise reliability concerns such as electromigration, thermomechanical stress, and structural warpage, making layout-driven thermal simulation with balanced accuracy and efficiency essential for rapid design iterations. This paper proposes AceTherm, an automated thermal simulation framework driven by Graphic Data System (GDS) layout and Process Design Kit (PDK) process parameters, which integrates non-conformal finite element method with customized sparse-matrix solvers. By exploiting the layered structure of the chip architecture, the simulation domain is sampled and discretized with a non-conformal mesh and high-resolution material mapping, significantly reducing degrees of freedom (DOFs) while preserving accuracy. The mesh division and sampling resolution provide a two-level control for trading off accuracy and speed, and the convergence and error behavior are analyzed to characterize the discrete scheme of AceTherm. Exploiting the structural properties of the resulting coefficient matrix, AceTherm employs supernodal sparse Cholesky factorization to accelerate the solution process. Notably, the symbolic factorization can be reused across multiple thermal load scenarios when the mesh pattern remains unchanged. Numerical experiments show that the proposed method achieves a 104.6 × speedup over the conventional COMSOL solution and reaches up to 539.2 × in repeated or preset-parameter simulations, while maintaining the average temperature error below 1 K. The combination of high computational speed, layer-aware modeling, and sub-Kelvin accuracy positions AceTherm as a practical tool for thermal analysis and optimization in heterogeneous IC back-end design.
items.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems

items.title: A 105 MS/s 4.18 nJ/inference 0.765 $\text{mm}^\text{2}$ Mixed-Signal Streaming ML Engine for Wireless Baseband in 12LP+ FinFET
items.abstract: We present SIXPPAC, the first streaming machine-learning engine for real-time integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) in wireless systems. SIXPPAC integrates two SAR ADCs and a digital binary-weight six-layer neural network (NN). The 0.765 mm$^\text{2}$ 12 nm FinFET engine stores all NN parameters on chip, enabling sustained 105 MS/s processing of 8b I/Q baseband samples at 0.8 V. By deploying bipolar inner products using AND instead of XNOR gates, SIXPPAC consumes 4.18 nJ/inference (0.42 POPS/W) at 0.8 V. We evaluate SIXPPAC on three example applications to demonstrate its versatility.

items.title: 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
items.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic. To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.

items.title: VS-Flash: Harnessing Vector Search with Computational Memory-Semantic Flash
items.abstract: As generative AI continues to evolve, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are driving rapid growth in vector database capacity requirements. As datasets outgrow host DRAM, vector databases rely on MMap-based serving over SSDs to extend capacity. However, high-fan-out ANN searches generate concurrent irregular accesses that contend for host memory and storage resources, degrading bulk throughput and inflating tail latency under mixed workloads. In this paper, we address these challenges through memory-semantic capacity and workload-aware compute placement. VS-Flash exposes flash as a large-capacity memory-semantic space and dynamically selects the execution engine according to runtime query and workload characteristics. It offloads throughput-oriented large-batch queries to a Computational Memory-Semantic Flash (CMS-Flash) device, while executing latency-sensitive small-batch queries on the host CPU. Both paths access the same resident segments, avoiding a separate host-DRAM replica. Across three billion-scale datasets, VS-Flash improves bulk-search throughput over vanilla Milvus by 36.8X on average, with up to a 57.4X improvement. Under mixed workloads, VS-Flash reduces the p99 latency of latency-sensitive requests by up to 24.8X while sustaining device-side bulk search. These results show that VS-Flash delivers scalable vector search beyond host DRAM capacity while jointly improving bulk throughput and small-request tail latency.

items.title: SRAM-PUF Response Recovery and Key Reconstruction for Intelligent Metering Terminals
items.abstract: With the continued development of new-type power systems and intelligent metering infrastructures, field devices such as smart meters, power information acquisition terminals, and fusion terminals have become essential components for energy metering, state sensing, and data interaction. SRAM-based physical unclonable functions (SRAM-PUFs) exploit intrinsic device variations in on-chip SRAM to generate device-specific responses and provide a lightweight hardware basis for terminal identification and key generation. However, variations in operating conditions can cause SRAM response instability and reduce key reconstruction reliability. To address this issue, this paper proposes a SRAM-PUF response recovery and key reconstruction method for intelligent metering terminals. A Bidirectional Temperature-Task Continual Learning (BTCL) mechanism is developed to continuously learn response evolution patterns under different operating conditions. Local consistency constraints and SRAM-cell reliability priors are further incorporated to recover disturbed responses, while spatial interleaving and concatenated error correction are employed to improve key reconstruction stability. Experimental results show that the proposed method reduces the mean pre-ECC bit error rate (BER) to 2.14%, corresponding to reductions of 35.93% and 26.33% compared with the raw SRAM-PUF and B-Spline Continual Learning, respectively. After spatial interleaving and concatenated error correction, the mean post-ECC BER is further reduced to 8.45 × 10−4%, while the mean key error rate (KER) decreases to 2.70 × 10−2%. These results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively improves SRAM-PUF response consistency and key reconstruction reliability under varying operating conditions, providing a reliable hardware-response and key-reconstruction basis for subsequent terminal authentication applications.

items.title: QUANTUM-SENSOR-GUIDED NANOLITHOGRAPHY AT THE LIMIT English Publication Description This monograph develops a falsifiable research architecture for integrating eligible quantum-sensing channels into nanolithographic process monitoring and safe feedback. Its central question is whether a physically qualified quantum observable contributes information about scanner drift, imaging state, materials response, or pattern-transfer conditions that cannot be recovered by optimized classical metrology at matched measurement time, power, calibration, computation and throughput. The volume is structured as 30 mathematical derivation plates, 82 research chapters, 410 individually paginated research sections, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. It examines nonclassical measurement eligibility, sensor-reference dependence, conditional process information, EUV imaging and resist stochasticity, inverse identifiability, robust feedback, independent after-pattern dimensional metrology, functional acceptance, cross-tool reproduction, and responsible scientific succession. The proposed five-layer architecture moves from operationally defined wafer observables to calibrated quantum-classical measurements, controlled discrimination among competing process mechanisms, authorized control decisions, and external reconstruction. The research emphasizes causal contrasts, blind wafer tests, physically meaningful uncertainty, rigorous classical baselines, complete resource accounting, and unambiguous stopping conditions. A gain in sensor sensitivity does not by itself demonstrate improved critical dimension, overlay, rare-defect performance, throughput or device yield. Four previously developed STARLI research monographs provide intellectual provenance, while a separate evidence ledger identifies 19 externally verifiable DOI-bearing publications concerning semiconductor metrology, EUV lithography, quantum sensing, photon loss, stochastic resist mechanisms, and interferometric baselines. The new hypotheses are clearly distinguished from established methods and prior demonstrations. The reader can move between research chapters, mathematical arguments, independent Gates and citation anchors without treating author-proposed integrations as proven experimental outcomes. The monograph is written as a prospective research atlas and an interdisciplinary invitation to future human and AI investigators. It presents no new wafer experiments, no certified industrial control recipe, and no confirmed universal quantum advantage. Its scientific contribution is the articulation of testable comparisons, explicit limits, negative-result preservation, and reproducible pathways by which the proposed architecture might be revised, rejected or eventually qualified. STARLI Research Works | Feng Cheng-en 33 | Institute XXIV | Flagship 01

items.title: QUANTUM INTERFEROMETRIC WAFER INSPECTION AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Works | Institute XXIV | Flagship 06 This prospective research monograph explores a single deceptively difficult question: can a nonclassical interferometric readout identify more weak physical defects on patterned semiconductor wafers than the best available classical inspection, without increasing throughput cost or false alarms? The investigation treats optical fringe visibility as an incomplete physical observable, not as a surrogate for defect detection performance. The three coupled research axes are interference visibility, sparse-defect localization and inspection economics. The book combines forward electromagnetic scattering, pattern-dependent background models, quantum and classical receiver statistics, sample and tool drift, preregistered blind testing, independent microscopy-based defect adjudication and the opportunity cost of factory review. Crucially, ideal quantum phase-information limits do not establish a real-world improvement in defect ROC, false-alarm risk or completed wafers per hour. Its architecture contains 30 large mathematical research plates, 82 research chapters with five single-page sections apiece, 200 independently paginated Research Gates and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger separates established semiconductor metrology, actinic mask inspection, EUV microscopy and quantum optics from the original hypotheses proposed here. Four earlier STARLI mother monographs are credited as intellectual lineage rather than independent evidence. Each Research Gate preserves a falsifiable alternative, a minimal experiment and a stop condition. Every candidate quantum advantage must survive loss accounting, optimized classical competitors, fixed false-positive rates, independent physical confirmation and genuinely unseen material and wafer lots. Null results, better classical methods and unsuccessful nonclassical prototypes remain legitimate research outcomes. This is a large experimental-design and conceptual research atlas, not a report of newly conducted experiments, a peer-reviewed industrial qualification, or evidence that a quantum interferometric wafer inspection product has achieved manufacturing advantage. Its purpose is to leave transferable, auditable and revisable research questions for future human and AI investigators.

items.title: Magnetoelectric Multiferroics for the Next‐Generation Ultralow‐Power Electronics
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Magnetoelectric multiferroics enable voltage control of magnetic states for low‐energy, non‐volatile memory and logic. Their practical value, however, depends on the complete device pathway, not coupling strength alone. This Review evaluates materials, switching mechanisms, and devices against these requirements, distinguishing measured performance from projected targets. We compare three magnetoelectric random‐access memory (MeRAM) routes with ferroelectric RAM and spin‐transfer torque magnetic RAM, and assess magnetoelectric spin–orbit (MESO) logic alongside complementary metal‐oxide‐semiconductor (CMOS) technology and current‐driven spintronics. MeRAM combines electric‐field writing, magnetic storage, and nondestructive readout, with prospects for low write energy and closer memory–logic integration. However, no integrated device has yet combined these benefits with competitive speed, retention, endurance, read margin, and density. For magnetoelectric logic, projected low‐voltage, non‐volatile operation has yet to be matched by experimental demonstrations of the full conversion path, gain and fan‐out. Results from BiFeO 3 , room‐temperature hexaferrites and other platforms identify deterministic switching, interface quality and thin‐film integration as central to closing the gap between projections and experiments. Magnetoelectric devices are therefore more likely to complement CMOS than replace it, particularly in logic‐in‐memory, compute‐near‐memory and normally‐off systems, where non‐volatility and reduced data movement could support next‐generation ultralow‐power electronics.

items.title: Defect-Mediated Van der Waals Epitaxial Growth of WS2 Nanosheets at Low Temperatures for Back-End-of-Line Integration
items.abstract: Epitaxial growth plays a crucial role in the current state-of-the-art semiconductor technology, providing a path for processing complex and high-quality thin films, heterostructures, and nanomaterials, which are used in a wide range of applications. Similarly, van der Waals (vdW) epitaxy, the epitaxial growth of layered compounds on top of a different 2D material, is recognized as a promising method to synthesize high-quality atomically thin films and their heterostructures. Indeed, research on vdW epitaxy has been intense, resulting in very promising results for many different material systems. Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) and molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) are the leading synthetic methods used for this purpose, operating at a growth temperature above 500 °C. Reducing the thermal budget and processing temperatures below 450 °C is essential for integrating these materials in many technologies, such as back-end-of-line (BEOL) silicon processing and flexible electronics, to name a few. Here, we demonstrate vdW epitaxial growth of nanodomains of WS2 on previously deposited MoS2 monolayers at a temperature range of 295−420 °C. The resulting heterostructures were characterized by means of high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), selected area diffraction (SAD), and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), in which the registry between the transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) shows a clear epitaxial relation. With the help of Raman spectroscopy and processing variations, defect-induced vdW epitaxial growth was revealed. Finally, a proof-of-concept photodetector was fabricated on the WS2/MoS2 and on pristine WS2 and MoS2 references, clearly showing an improved performance for the heterostructure device. A twelve-fold increase in the photoresponsivity is explained in the context of the WS2/MoS2 heterostructure band offsets and surface passivation. This work may lead to further research on the low-temperature vdW epitaxial growth for integrating a wide range of 2D materials within BEOL Processing, i.e., monolithic 3D integration (M3D) and ultra-thin diffusion barriers.
