items.title: Cryogenic Recharacterization of a Commercial 22 nm FD-SOI Foundry Standard-Cell Library
items.abstract: Wiring and bandwidth bottlenecks between a quantum processor and room-temperature electronics can be reduced by placing digital control at the cryogenic stage, but commercial foundry standard-cell libraries are not specified for operation at 4 K. A cryogenic recharacterization flow is therefore developed for a commercial 22 nm FD-SOI foundry standard-cell library using commercially available cryogenic compact-device models, while retaining the original cell circuits, layouts, logic functions, and implementation semantics and remaining compatible with the commercial synthesis, place-and-route, and signoff methodology used at room temperature. Body-bias dependence is quantified over 38,640 matched slew/load points at zero, +/-0.9 V, and +/-1.8 V body bias. Relative to full bias, zero-bias operation increases the median rising and falling delays by 38.6x and 33.0x, while approximately 90% of transitions exceed the foundry-defined maximum-transition envelope. The 0.8 V-to-0.4 V level shifter is even more sensitive to body bias: its worst-case falling delay decreases from 30.6 ns at zero bias to 0.56 ns at +/-1.8 V. For the outbound 0.4 V-to-0.8 V crossing, driving the 0.8 V receiver without a level shifter dissipates 57.7 uW of static power per bit at full bias, against 0.196 nW when level-shifted. In post-route analysis of the unchanged extracted physical database of a fabricated 32-bit ALU, the register-to-register setup boundary increases from 1.3 MHz at zero bias to 37.9 MHz at +/-0.9 V and 132.9 MHz at +/-1.8 V.

items.title: CLOSED-LOOP QUANTUM NANOLITHOGRAPHY AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Works | Institute XXIV | Flagship 07 This prospective research monograph investigates whether quantum-sensitive process metrology can add independent, operationally useful information to a qualified lithographic feedback system. Its three linked domains are lithographic process control, quantum readout, and counterfactual scientific validation. The work explicitly distinguishes sensor-assisted control from quantum-state exposure of photoresist: neither direct quantum lithography nor production-ready quantum advantage is assumed. The central research question is causal and industrial rather than merely optical. If a nonclassical readout reduces phase noise, does its incremental information—after accounting for photon loss, technical correlations, maintenance and latency—change an allowed exposure, focus or development action? Does that changed action improve independently qualified critical dimension, overlay, yield or scrap over the strongest available classical APC? Under what conditions does the quantum channel make no difference and a conservative classical fallback remain preferable? The atlas organizes 30 mathematically distinct research derivations, 82 formula-linked chapters with five independent single-page sections each, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 rebuildable Phoenix Answer Embryos. It proposes identifiable state-space models, conditional quantum information and Fisher analysis, chance-constrained and robust MPC, preregistered sensor-on/sensor-off experiments, HIL fault injection, cross-resist and cross-mask transfer testing, economic accounting, and traceable research succession. External DOI literature covers probabilistic lithography process windows, EUV manufacturing, classical semiconductor advanced process control and virtual metrology, quantum-estimation theory and constrained MPC. Four earlier STARLI monographs appear only as author-supplied intellectual lineage, not independent experimental proof. The complete study architecture insists on optimized classical comparators, independent final-wafer endpoints, strict safety constraints, transparent negative results and externally reproducible protocols. The document is a falsifiable research-design monograph. It does not report newly performed experiments or demonstrate that a quantum-assisted semiconductor manufacturing controller outperforms qualified classical process control. Its aim is to provide future human and AI investigators with a rigorous, transferable and revisable research foundation.

items.title: Breaking the Boltzmann Limit: A Review of Emerging Ultralow‐Power Transistor Technologies
items.abstract: As complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology scales down to the sub-2 nm node, the dramatic surge in power density has emerged as a fundamental bottleneck. Conventional metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) are constrained by the 60 mV/dec Boltzmann thermal limit, rendering further supply voltage reduction exceedingly challenging. To surmount this fundamental limit, various novel sub-60 mV/dec steep-switching devices have been proposed, including tunnel field-effect transistors (TFETs), negative-capacitance field-effect transistors (NCFETs), and cold-source field-effect transistors (CSFETs). A comprehensive review of the evolution of sub‑60 mV/dec technologies is presented, with particular emphasis on the three mainstream approaches: TFETs, NCFETs, and CSFETs. The underlying physical principles, recent research advances, optimization strategies, and remaining challenges of these devices are thoroughly analyzed. Finally, prospective directions for future breakthroughs are discussed, encompassing novel materials exploration, the synergistic integration of multiple physical mechanisms, and the experimental verification of integration with advanced CMOS nodes.

items.title: Atomic layer etching of diamond using argon and oxygen
items.abstract: The ability to remove surface defects of diamond by dry etching methods is of high importance for applications that make use of shallow color centers in diamond. Here, we present an atomic layer etching process, making use of oxygen as dosing gas and argon as etching gas, in order to achieve controlled etching of the surface without creating additional defects by sputtering. We demonstrate a process window, where quasi-self-limiting atomic layer etching takes place with an etch per cycle of (1.909 ± 0.004) Å/cycle, corresponding to about 2 atomic layers of the {100} oriented diamond sample. The process is able to reduce the rms surface roughness down to (0.15 ± 0.01) nm. Furthermore, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicates only a small amount of sp 2 bonded carbon on the diamond surface after the atomic layer etching process.

items.title: Multilevel Resistive Switching and Synaptic Functionality in an Energy Efficient Ferroelectricity Assisted Memristor Guided by Ionic Dielectric Barrier
items.abstract: A solution‐based method is used to fabricate a multilevel memristive device, in which the ferroelectric polarization of the LiNbO 3 layer is controlled by the ionic‐polarization of the Li 5 AlO 4 barrier layer. The high resistance state (HRS) to low resistance state (LRS) ratio in this LiNbO 3 /Li 5 AlO 4 /LiNbO 3 stacked configuration is approximately 10 4 . The device exhibits exceptional reliability, retaining steady performance over 10 3 switching cycles, sustaining ∼ 10 6 pulse operations, and preserving data retention beyond 10 5 s with an ON/OFF ratio close to 10 3 . Excellent device uniformity (±3%) and ReRAM‐like behavior demonstrated across 50 devices, confirming reproducibility. The device has the potential to create compact and multifunctional neuromorphic systems due to its reliable resistive switching behavior and support for basic logic operations. Oxygen‐vacancy‐assisted filament formation produces polarization‐modulated conduction pathways that govern the resistive states and allow for tunable multilevel switching under different compliance currents. Apart from its memory capabilities, the device successfully simulates synaptic processes like potentiation and depression, which reflect biological learning mechanisms. These neuromorphic features are further applied in the training of a convolutional neural network, achieving a training accuracy of about 98%. The study shows that polarization‐assisted transport and vacancy‐mediated switching work well together, providing a promising path toward high‐performance and scalable neuromorphic computing architectures.

items.title: GUMPIM: Unitary and Malleable Memory for Processing-in-Memory with Guaranteed PIM Pages
items.abstract: DRAM-based Processing-in-Memory (PIM) addresses the "memory wall" by executing computations directly inside main memory. However, memory interleaving and virtual memory limit contiguous data size visible to PIM units, constraining PIM task granularity. To mitigate this, existing PIM systems drastically isolate PIM memory or disable memory interleaving. These design choices, however, decrease the CPU memory bandwidth and introduce extra data transfer, leading to an additional "system memory wall" that must be resolved to realize PIM's full potential. In this work, we propose GUMPIM, a PIM system that allows interleaved CPU pages and non-interleaved PIM pages to coexist in a Unitary and Malleable memory space with Guaranteed PIM page allocation. GUMPIM enables zero-copy during PIM task offloading and maintains CPU memory bandwidth while ensuring low PIM offloading overhead. First, we propose a dual-track memory management mechanism consisting of independent page allocation and address translation for CPU and PIM pages. Second, we design GUMPIM interface hardware on PIM-enabled DRAMs to provide a dynamic address mapping for the different data layouts of CPU and PIM pages. Third, we propose a PIM-assisted page migration mechanism that transparently migrates pages while preserving CPU access bandwidth, thereby enabling guaranteed and accelerated PIM page allocation. GUMPIM requires no changes to commodity DRAM standards; all hardware modifications are limited to the DRAM side, ensuring full compatibility with existing CPUs and enabling immediate deployment on current HBMx- and LPDDRx-based PIM platforms. Our results show only <0.1% performance degradation for CPU workloads on GUMPIM. For PIM workloads, GUMPIM reduces memory allocation and CPU-part computation times by 2.7x and 4.93x, respectively, yielding an end-to-end 2.3x speedup over a state-of-the-art baseline system.

items.title: Understanding and Mitigating Charge‐Trapping Induced Transfer Curve Drift in Electrolyte‐Gated Graphene Field‐Effect Transistors
items.abstract: Electrolyte-gated graphene field-effect transistors (EG-gFETs) have great potential for chemical and biosensing applications and are increasingly attractive platforms for synaptic or memristive elements in neuromorphic computing. However, EG-gFETs exhibit drift in their electrical response, a phenomenon that remains poorly understood. An in-depth understanding of EG-gFETs' responses is essential for fully exploiting their behavior in applications and to open a much-needed discussion and standardization of practices within the community. In this work, we show that drift is ubiquitous across all tested devices and experimental conditions, and present evidence indicating that it is driven by progressive charge trapping in the insulating layer beneath the graphene channel. We then discuss potential strategies to mitigate drift, including alternative interrogation schemes and fabrication processes. Additionally, we propose approaches to enhance signal readability and facilitate discrimination of the signal from noise and false-positive responses in biosensing applications.

items.title: TileDRAM: Compiler-Controlled Tile-to-DRAM Layouts for 3D DRAM GPGPUs
items.abstract: Modern GPU compilers expose rich layout abstractions for mapping tensors to threads and on-chip resources, but compute-unit-local (CU-local) 3D DRAM architectures lack a corresponding abstraction for specifying how operand-tile data are arranged within the DRAM address space. Without such an abstraction, conventional placement under the existing DRAM address mapping can subject structured tile accesses to severe row-buffer conflicts. We present TileDRAM, a compiler-runtime toolchain that introduces tile-to-DRAM layouts as a compiler-visible abstraction for DRAM placement. TileDRAM extends the GPU Linear Layout abstraction from compute-side mapping targets to DRAM placement coordinates and selects layouts per tile access signature, using recurring tile-local access behavior as the specialization unit. Since row-buffer locality depends on ordered request history, TileDRAM evaluates candidate layouts through their row-buffer behavior under fixed DRAM address mappings. Accesses under the selected layouts are realized through ordinary address arithmetic, without new address-remapping hardware or ISA support. In full-trace replay on Accel-Sim/Ramulator2 across 108 mixture-of-experts (MoE) feed-forward network (FFN) cases, TileDRAM reduces the request-weighted row-conflict rate from 75.7% to 15.2% and achieves a 1.77x geomean speedup. Retargeting six traces to six 3D DRAM organizations yields a 2.20x geomean speedup under the same compiler abstraction. On an RTX 3090, address transformation adds 0.17% geomean overhead over identity.

items.title: Simulation Study of Short-Channel Effects in GAIA and GAA MOS Devices Operated in Weak-Inversion Regime Down to Deep Cryogenic Temperatures
items.abstract: This work investigates and compares the weak inversion behavior and drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL) of conventional Gate-All-Around (GAA) MOSFETs and the recently proposed Gate-All-Inside-and-Around (GAIA) devices from room temperature down to deep cryogenic conditions (≈5 K). A physics-based electrostatic and transport framework is developed to analyze short-channel effects in the subthreshold regime, where cryogenic operation significantly modifies carrier statistics, threshold voltage, and subthreshold slope. Results show that while both architectures benefit from improved electrostatic control compared to planar devices, GAIA MOSFETs exhibit a systematically reduced DIBL over the entire temperature range due to an additional insulating barrier that weakens drain-to-channel electrostatic coupling. At cryogenic temperatures, DIBL is found to be primarily governed by electrostatic effects rather than thermally activated transport, remaining nearly constant over a broad temperature range before exhibiting a moderate increase below approximately 30 K. A compact analytical model is proposed, capturing the combined effects of geometry and temperature phenomena on DIBL and subthreshold conduction. The results provide new insights into the role of device architecture in mitigating short-channel effects in cryogenic CMOS technologies for quantum and ultra-low-power applications.

items.title: Role of trap position variation on electrical parameters in hetero-dielectric double gate TFET
items.abstract: This work is a statistical reliability study of the Heterojunction Dielectric Double Gate (HDDG) tunnel field-effect-transistor (TFET) with respect to the randomized location of interface traps. The device configuration consists of a Ge source, and a p + pocket to increase the tunneling probability. Using TCAD Sentaurus, the impact of various interface trap localizations arising from the random nature of the interface is examined through a comprehensive variability analysis. A comprehensive variability study is conducted to evaluate the sensitivity of the device to interface trap localization. Of particular interest is how the device parameters change due to the incorporation of Gaussian-distributed traps in 5 nm segments of the oxide semiconductor interface. The statistical analysis of 100 devices is performed over four unique cases; (i) no traps, (ii) traps localized in the oxide/n+ channel region, (iii) traps localized in the oxide/p+ pocket region, and (iv) traps distributed across both regions. The typical behavior of the devices is examined and the statistical variation of the following parameters is discussed; On-Current (I ON ), Off-Current (I OFF ), Threshold Voltage (V th ), Band-to-Band Tunneling (BTBT) generation rate, electron velocity and subthreshold swing (SS).

items.title: Reconfigurable Floating‐Gate van der Waals Phototransistor With Asymmetric Contact Geometries for Bio‐Inspired Multi‐Stage Visual Tasks
items.abstract: Bio‐inspired optoelectronic devices with in‐sensor neuromorphic computing capability are promising for artificial visual applications. However, the biological visual system possesses simultaneous sensing and multi‐stage processing capability through the retina and visual cortex. Different device types and materials are required to emulate specific visual functions, which will unavoidably pose complexity in integration and limit the scalability. Herein, we report a WSe 2 /h‐BN/Graphene reconfigurable floating‐gate van der Waals phototransistor (RFGPT) featuring a laterally asymmetric contact geometry. The device exhibits reconfigurable optoelectronic functionality via gate voltage modulation, including photodetection mode with bipolar photoresponse and optoelectronic synapse mode with short‐term memory. The RFGPT fulfills versatile neuromorphic image processing functions, including retina‐level pre‐processing (edge extraction) and cortex‐level processing (image recognition). The RFGPT provides a fundamental unit to develop artificial visual hardware with reduced fabrication complexity and enhanced scalability for efficient in‐sensor computing.

items.title: REVIEW: ELECTRICAL PROPERTIES OF SILICON CARBIDE-BASED COMPOSITE MATERIALS
items.abstract: Silicon carbide (SiC) is a wide-bandgap semiconductor that is widely used in power electronics, automotive industries, and aerospace applications due to its high thermal conductivity and breakdown field. This review examines both the fundamental physics and the practical applications of SiC. We analyze its major crystal structures (polytypes), specifically 4H-SiC, 6H-SiC, and 3C-SiC, and discuss how these structures affect electrical performance. The paper also covers new developments in SiC functional ceramics, metal-matrix nanocomposites, and quantum defects used for quantum information science. By analyzing research literature from 2006 to 2026, we show how the industry transitioned from basic crystal growth to 8-inch wafer manufacturing and automated defect classification using neural networks. Finally, this review discusses the main technical problems that still limit SiC devices, such as high interface trap density (Dit), high contact resistance in p-type doping, and bias temperature instability (BTI). By comparing theoretical material properties with real device performance, this paper identifies key research priorities for the next generation of semiconductor technology.

items.title: MIXED-SIGNAL IN-SENSOR COMPUTING AND COMMUNICATION TECHNIQUES FOR ULTRA-LOW-POWER VIDEO SENSOR NODES
items.abstract: Video Sensor Nodes (VSNs) for Internet-of-Things (IoT) and Internet-of-Bodies (IoB) applications operate under severe energy and form-factor constraints imposed by continuous sensing, high data rates, and limited energy availability. These challenges become particularly critical in wearable and implantable systems, where miniature batteries restrict operating lifetime and frequent battery replacement may be impractical. At the same time, continuously acquired visual information introduces significant energy overhead from analog-to-digital conversion, computation, storage, and communication. This dissertation addresses these challenges through mixed-signal and time-domain techniques that reduce energy across the sensing--computation--communication chain, together with wireless power delivery for energy-constrained biomedical systems. The first part of this dissertation addresses the energy associated with front-end digitization and communication. Conventional Video Sensor Nodes typically digitize analog pixel values using an ADC before performing subsequent processing and communication. To eliminate this conversion overhead at the power-constrained sensor node, an Analog-to-Time Converter Transmitter (ATC-Tx) directly converts analog pixel voltages into pulse-width-encoded time-domain signals. Implemented in 65-nm CMOS, the ATC-Tx supports 5~MSps with 3-bit resolution while consuming \(110~\mu\mathrm{W}\), corresponding to an energy efficiency of 21.9~pJ/sample (7.3~pJ/bit). The resulting time-domain information is transmitted using broadband Time-Domain Body Communication (TD-BC), enabling an asymmetric node--hub architecture in which energy-intensive decoding and processing are transferred to a higher-power receiver. While ATC-Tx reduces the energy required to digitize and communicate individual sensor samples, communication energy ultimately scales with the amount of information transmitted. The next part of this dissertation therefore investigates in-sensor compression before conventional digitization. A switched-capacitor-based direct analog-to-MJPEG compressor (dAJC) performs 2D-DCT, quantization, and associated JPEG processing directly on analog pixel values. The 65-nm implementation operates at 50~Mb/s while consuming 2.02~mW. By exploiting the sparsity of the compressed transform coefficients, a dynamically activated ADC digitizes only significant samples, reducing ADC conversion energy by approximately \(20\times\). This architecture demonstrates that moving compression ahead of the ADC can simultaneously reduce conversion, computation, storage, and communication overhead. Building on the direct analog compression approach, the dissertation next explores time-domain computation to improve scalability, throughput, and energy efficiency. The proposed TD-dAJC architecture represents fixed DCT and quantization coefficients using pulse-width-based time weights generated by a multi-phase PLL, while retaining the image-sensor input in the voltage domain. Multiplication is performed through time-controlled current integration, avoiding the large capacitor arrays, capacitor-ratio matching requirements, and calibration overhead associated with switched-capacitor implementations. TD-dAJC operates at up to 100~MS/s and achieves approximately 2~pJ/pixel, enabling real-time 4K video compression at 12 frames/s. The architecture provides more than an order-of-magnitude improvement in energy efficiency over the switched-capacitor implementation while also improving throughput and active-area efficiency. The dissertation then addresses the complementary challenge of supplying energy to severely constrained and battery-less biomedical systems. A dual-mode inductive--capacitive wireless power-transfer architecture is developed using temporally reconfigurable rectifiers, load-isolation techniques, and an orthogonal cuboid-based coupling structure. The architecture improves charging speed by approximately \(3.4\times\), reduces leakage during energy accumulation, and enables orientation-tolerant operation under highly attenuated implantable channels. This approach provides a compact wireless-powering solution for miniature and implantable systems where conventional batteries are undesirable or impractical. Finally, this dissertation establishes the channel conditions required for reliable multi-level time-domain communication through and around the human body. Unlike conventional communication systems in which information is primarily represented by voltage amplitude, TD-BC encodes information in signal-transition timing. Circuit models, full-wave simulations, and measurements show that channel attenuation determines edge detectability, available bandwidth determines transferable pulse width and edge formation, and group-delay variation determines temporal distortion. A 64-level pulse-width representation supports 6 bits per 100-ns symbol, corresponding to 60~Mb/s. End-to-end transmission of a 6-bit video frame through the measured body channel achieves an SSIM of 0.9791, demonstrating high-fidelity preservation of visual information despite substantial amplitude attenuation. Collectively, these works establish a system-level framework for ultra-low-power Video Sensor Nodes by reducing front-end digitization and communication energy, compressing information before digitization, exploiting time-domain representations for computation and communication, and improving wireless energy delivery. The resulting mixed-signal architectures enable scalable and energy-efficient visual sensing for next-generation wearable, biomedical, and Internet-of-Bodies systems.

items.title: Impact of plasma conditioning-state evolution on Cl2/Ar plasma-assisted Si atomic layer etching
items.abstract: Plasma-assisted atomic layer etching (ALE) requires tightly controlled plasma conditions to achieve reproducible self-limiting material removal; however, the temporal stability of conditioned plasma environments and their influence on etching behavior remain insufficiently understood. In this work, the influence of conditioning state on plasma-assisted Si ALE using Cl2/Ar plasma chemistry is systematically investigated through in situ optical emission spectroscopy correlated with etch characterization. Time-resolved plasma diagnostics reveal strong idle-time-dependent evolution of the plasma environment, where oxygen-related emission initially dominates after extended idle periods before gradually transitioning into a stabilized chlorine-active regime associated with effective etching-related plasma–surface interactions. Corresponding cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy demonstrates a clear correlation between plasma conditioning state and etching characteristics, including negligible etching during early conditioning stages, rough and nonuniform etching during transitional stages, and smooth self-limiting etching under fully stabilized conditions with an etch per cycle of ∼13.5 Å/cycle. In contrast, continuous Cl2 plasma reactive ion etching exhibits comparatively stable plasma characteristics and etching behavior regardless of prior conditioning history under the present conditions. These results demonstrate that plasma-assisted ALE exhibits substantially greater sensitivity to conditioning history and plasma-environment evolution than conventional continuous plasma etching due to its self-limiting surface-reaction nature. The findings further highlight the critical importance of controlling conditioning-dependent plasma dynamics for achieving stable and reproducible atomic-scale etching processes.
items.venue: Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology A Vacuum Surfaces and Films

items.title: Hybridization–Ionicity Mapping for Descriptor-Guided Design of Amorphous Ge–Sb–Se Selector-Only Memory
items.abstract: Abstract Quantitative relationships among composition, bonding, and functional properties are essential for the rational design of amorphous chalcogenides. Here, we examine whether hybridization and ionicity, established composition-derived bonding descriptors, can guide selector-only memory (SOM) design. Mapping of reported SOM compositions reveals systematic correlations with the read-window margin (RWM) and identifies a favorable region for threshold-state differentiation. Guided by these trends, amorphous Ge–Sb–Se compositions with increasing Sb content were fabricated and evaluated, and all exhibited programmable SOM behavior with nonmonotonic electrical and reliability trends. Up to an intermediate Sb content, higher ionicity within an appropriate hybridization range increased polar heteropolar bonding, enlarged trap-energy separation and RWM, and improved threshold-voltage stability and endurance. Further Sb incorporation increased hybridization beyond the favorable range and promoted Sb–Sb-rich homopolar bonding, reducing trap-state differentiation and memory performance. X-ray photoelectron and Raman spectroscopy confirmed the corresponding bonding evolution, while temperature-dependent transport analyses linked these changes to trap energetics. These results establish a composition–bonding–trap–property relationship and show that hybridization–ionicity mapping can narrow candidate compositions before extensive fabrication and characterization.

items.title: HBFSim: A Simulator for Exploring HBF in Memory Hierarchies for LLMs
items.abstract: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising technology that provides terabyte-scale accelerator-local capacity at bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost-per-bit advantage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency, out-of-place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance and lifetime difficult to predict. To study this emerging design space, we present HBFSim, an LLM-aware event-driven simulator for heterogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application-level memory semantics while modeling flash-internal behavior. HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host-managed flash translation, and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a calibrated serving frontend. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does not fit in HBM 11.0--19.0$\times$ faster than host DRAM; HBM is better used to hold the running sequences' KV cache than as a cache for HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes. The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available.

items.title: Gate-defined quantum dot and charge noise analysis in a Forksheet transistor
items.abstract: We report the cryogenic characterization of a 14-nm nMOS Forksheet transistor down to 10 mK. We demonstrate that the device retains transistor operation with improved characteristics at cryogenic temperatures, while also forming a gate-defined quantum dot that can be tuned to the single-electron regime. In the quantum-dot regime, we perform low-frequency charge-noise measurements across different charge occupations and observe an average charge-noise amplitude of $\langle S_0\rangle = 10\;μ\mathrm{eV}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ at 1 Hz, with a minimum measured value of $3.3\;μ\mathrm{eV}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$. These results highlight the potential of Forksheet technology for the monolithic cointegration of quantum and classical CMOS functionalities in future quantum processors.

items.title: From Surface Reactions to Inhibitor Coverage: A Machine-Learning-Assisted Computational Study of Area-Selective Atomic Layer Deposition
items.abstract: Area-selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD) enables selective material growth for the fabrication of nanoscale semiconductor devices. Predicting inhibitor coverage is essential for understanding and optimizing surface blocking in AS-ALD. Here, we present a computational workflow combining a pretrained universal machine-learning interatomic potential with off-lattice grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations and apply it to inhibitor adsorption and precursor blocking on amorphous SiO2. Realistic surface models reveal substantial site-dependent variations in reaction energies and activation barriers, with silanol groups serving as the primary adsorption sites for aminosilane and related inhibitors and metal precursors. Coverage simulations show that inhibitors producing identical adsorbed fragments can yield different coverages because the intact molecules impose distinct steric constraints, leading to different accessible site densities and blocking capabilities. Beyond coverage, we highlight the importance of the reactivity of adsorbed inhibitor fragments toward precursors in determining inhibitor stability and blocking performance. Together, these findings demonstrate the need to consider both steric effects and chemical reactivity on realistic amorphous surfaces. Our calculations connect local reaction chemistry with inhibitor coverage and provide a computational basis for understanding inhibition mechanisms and selecting suitable inhibitor-precursor combinations for AS-ALD.

items.title: From Billion-Scale to Million-Scale Language Models: Operational Capabilities for Embedded Post-Exploitation
items.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for resource-constrained environments due to their low computational footprint. These characteristics also make them candidates for future autonomous malware, where connectivity, latency, privacy, or operational constraints may preclude cloud-based inference. Yet the ability of ultra-compact models to support malware during post-exploitation remains poorly understood. We systematically evaluate seven open-source SLMs (20M-1.5B parameters) on two post-exploitation code-generation tasks: Directory Enumeration and Backdoor Generation. We compare Python (high-resource) and Lua (low-resource) across prompting strategies, task formulations, iterative reasoning, grammar-constrained decoding, and execution-feedback loops. Results show that offensive code-generation capabilities do not increase linearly with model size. Successful execution depends on the interaction of model capacity, task formulation, and prompting strategy, with task formulation exerting a greater influence than prompt engineering alone. Algorithmic formulation combined with few-shot prompting enables Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B to reach Pass@5 of 100% in both Python and Lua for Directory Enumeration, 100% in Python for Backdoor Generation, and 99.2% in Lua. Although the evaluated models remain too computationally demanding for widespread deployment in contemporary malware, rapid progress in compact models may reduce this barrier. These findings help anticipate AI-assisted malware and inform future countermeasures.

items.title: Dynamic Ferroelectricity in Antiferroelectric Hafnia-Zirconia Thin Films at Cryogenic Temperatures
items.abstract: Abstract We report a novel, dynamic, ferroelectric response in ultrathin tetragonal-phase-rich antiferroelectric (AFE) Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 (HZO) films at cryogenic temperatures. At room temperature, AFE switching in these films arises from a field-induced tetragonal-to-orthorhombic (t-to-o) transformation followed by rapid o-to-t back-switching during each switching cycle, retaining little-to-no polar o-phase after applied electric field removal. However, upon cooling, the o-to-t back-switching during each bipolar voltage cycle becomes kinetically suppressed, allowing the field-induced polar o-phase to persist over the measurement timescale and at zero bias, resulting in dynamic ferroelectricity. At 12.5 K, the switchable polarization exceeds 20 µC/cm 2 , despite quasi-static tetragonal phase structure of the films at this temperature, verified by capacitance–voltage measurements. In-situ cryogenic grazing incidence X-ray diffraction confirms no structural transformation at cryogenic temperatures. Unlike conventional polarization “wake-up”, this high-polarization state is reversible upon thermal cycling and remains stable after 10 10 polarization reversals at 12.5 K. Temperature- and frequency-dependent measurements link the enhanced polarization to the kinetics of o-to-t back-switching rather than an irreversible structural transformation. These results establish a novel mode of dynamic ferroelectricity achieved in nominally antiferroelectric hafnium zirconium thin films and tunable by temperature and operating frequency. We report a novel dynamic ferroelectric response in ultrathin tetragonal-phase-rich antiferroelectric (AFE) Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 (HZO) films at cryogenic temperatures. At room temperature, AFE switching arises from field-induced tetragonal-to-orthorhombic (t-to-o) transformation followed by rapid o-to-t back-switching during each switching cycle, retaining little-to-no polar o-phase after field removal. Upon cooling, o-to-t back-switching becomes kinetically suppressed, allowing the field-induced polar o-phase to persist over the measurement timescale and at zero bias, resulting in dynamic ferroelectricity. At 12.5 K, switchable polarization exceeds 20 µC/cm 2 despite a quasi-static tetragonal structure, verified by capacitance-voltage measurements. In-situ cryogenic grazing incidence X-ray diffraction confirms no structural transformation. Unlike conventional “wake-up”, this high-polarization state is reversible upon thermal cycling and remains stable after 10 10 polarization reversals at 12.5 K. Temperature- and frequency-dependent measurements link enhanced polarization to o-to-t back-switching kinetics rather than irreversible structural transformation, establishing a novel mode of dynamic ferroelectricity, tunable by temperature and operating frequency.

items.title: A surface potential-based compact model for I–V and C–V characteristics in GaN HEMTs
items.abstract: A simple analytical expression describing the Fermi level Ef variation with the two-dimensional electron gas density ns in a GaN-based high electron mobility transistor is proposed. This expression is introduced to analytically describe Ef(Vg) and ns(Vg) using the Lambert W function. The calculated Ef is then used to derive a surface potential-based model for predicting I–V and C–V characteristics while incorporating various physical effects present in practical devices. The proposed model is validated through comparisons with numerical calculations, experimental data and TCAD simulations demonstrating good agreement over the entire bias range and for various device parameters.

items.title: Where the SRAM Goes: Per-Symbol Attribution of Static Memory in FreeRTOS-C and Embassy-Rust IoT Firmware on a 64 KB RISC-V Microcontroller
items.abstract: Selecting a firmware stack for a memory-constrained microcontroller is usually guided by aggregate binary sizes, which report how much SRAM a build consumes but not where it goes or why. We address that gap with a per-symbol attribution method that decomposes static RAM into architectural categories - scheduler heap, network buffers and pools, task stacks, and linker-reserved regions - by bounding sized ELF symbols to the .data, .bss and .stack section ranges. The method is validated by reconciling every category sum exactly against the size-based totals for all sixteen builds. We apply it to eight cumulative firmware milestones, from a bare task scaffold to a full MQTT-over-Ethernet client, implemented twice, in FreeRTOS-C and in Embassy-Rust, on the CH32V203RBT6, a RISC-V microcontroller with 64 KB SRAM and an on-chip Ethernet MAC and PHY, with functional parity verified on hardware at every milestone. The decomposition shows that both stacks spend a nearly identical share of their RAM on networking (63.8% versus 63.9%), yet the absolute cost differs by 4.4 times: 40,719 bytes for lwIP against 9,316 bytes for smoltcp. FreeRTOS task stacks grow linearly at roughly 1 KB per task while Embassy async state grows with state-machine complexity. We also report that lwIP could not be integrated under an all-static discipline on this platform, requiring a 20 KB arena that smoltcp does not. The measurement harness, the attribution tool, and the sixteen firmware implementations are released as artefacts.

items.title: Vertical Gate‐All‐Around SiGeSn/GeSn/SiGeSn Nanowire Transistors for Energy‐Efficient Electronics
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Conventional Si Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor (CMOS) technologies face increasing challenges in improving energy efficiency while maintaining device performance. Here, SiGeSn/GeSn heterostructures are employed as a unified Group‐IV platform for complementary vertical nanowire gate‐all‐around (GAA) MOSFETs and tunnel field‐effect transistors (TFETs) fabricated on Si wafers. The wider‐bandgap SiGeSn source/drain regions introduce band offsets to the GeSn channel, enabling heterostructure band engineering for leakage suppression and tunneling‐pathway control. Compared with all‐GeSn reference devices, the SiGeSn source/drain architecture suppresses drain‐induced barrier lowering and off‐state leakage without modifying the GeSn channel. The same heterostructure platform also enables complementary TFET operation, where the n‐TFET exhibits a subthreshold swing of 60 mV dec − 1 and a two‐order‐of‐magnitude enhancement in on/off current ratio. The performance difference between p‐ and n‐TFETs provides experimental evidence of the different efficiencies of indirect Γ‐to‐L and direct Γ‐to‐Γ tunneling processes. These results demonstrate that SiGeSn/GeSn heterostructures can be used to suppress leakage currents and engineer tunneling pathways, establishing SiGeSn/GeSn heterostructures as a unified Group‐IV platform for future energy‐efficient CMOS technologies beyond conventional Si.

items.title: Thermal Boundary Resistance as the Emerging Reliability Bottleneck in Wide-Bandgap Power Converters for Renewable Energy Integration
items.abstract: Title: Thermal Boundary Resistance as the Emerging Reliability Bottleneck in Wide-Bandgap Power Converters for Renewable Energy Integration Authors: 1. Lawal David Abdullahi 2. Dada Samuel Abiodun 3. Oladimeji Opeyemi Emmanuel 4. Atobatele Malik Williams Institution: Yaba College of Technology, Yaba, Lagos, Nigeria Department: Electrical / Electronic Engineering - Power Electronics Paper ID: 1723614 Journal: IRE Journals (Iconic Research and Engineering Journals) - Accepted October 2026, Volume 10, Issue 4 ISSN: 2456-8880 | Impact Factor: 5.904 Abstract: Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) wide-bandgap (WBG) power devices are displacing silicon in the converters and inverters that connect solar, wind, and storage assets to the grid. This paper reviews how thermal boundary resistance (Kapitza resistance) at material interfaces has become the limiting factor for device lifetime, rather than bulk material properties. It proposes practical mitigations including silver sintered die-attach, interface-aware thermal modeling, and coordinated thermal-electrical-mechanical qualification for renewable energy converters designed for 20+ years field service. Keywords: Wide-Bandgap, SiC, GaN, Thermal Boundary Resistance, Kapitza Resistance, Power Converters, Renewable Energy Integration, Reliability, Power Electronics This work is a student research paper accepted by IRE Journals for publication.
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.title: The Dormant Spiking Neuron: A State-Driven Mechanism for Efficient Spiking Neural Networks
items.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a compelling pathway toward energy-efficient artificial intelligence, fundamentally anchored in presynaptic input-driven sparsity. However, a substantial yet chronically overlooked source of computational overhead persists: the continuous subthreshold dynamics of postsynaptic neurons. Quantitative analysis reveals that up to 44% of neurons in an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18 model reside in a deeply inhibited state, imposing a persistent computational burden despite having a negligible probability of firing. To address this inefficiency, the Dormant Spiking Neuron (DSN) model is introduced. By incorporating a state-driven dynamic gate, the DSN allows a neuron to enter a dormant state when its membrane potential falls below a predefined negative threshold, dynamically pruning redundant computations at the instance level. Crucially, this dormancy mechanism is directly integrated into the neuronal dynamics and trained end-to-end via backpropagation through time using surrogate gradients, enabling the network to actively learn a robust dormancy policy that adaptively preserves critical information flow. Extensive experiments across static and neuromorphic datasets demonstrate that the DSN framework consistently reduces computational energy by 40% to over 70%. Notably, on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, the DSN outperforms state-of-the-art static pruning techniques at comparable reported cost reductions and simultaneously improves the corresponding baseline SNN accuracy by 1.34%. By establishing a trainable, state-driven sparsity paradigm orthogonal to conventional input-driven methods, the DSN unlocks synergistic efficiency gains, presenting an effective approach for advancing neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Revealing the influence of multiple process factors on 2D field-effect transistors performance
items.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) materials hold great potential for next-generation electronic devices due to high mobility and excellent interface quality. However, device fabrication processes significantly influence the final device performance, in which the photoresist residue could increase the carrier scattering and contact resistance, and the metallization process would damage the ultrathin channels. Our study aims to optimize fabrication techniques for reducing the multiple process factors to achieve the desired performance of 2D materials. By comparing the performance of devices fabricated using double-layer and single-layer photoresist processes, we demonstrate the critical role of interface cleanliness between the metal and 2D material in improving device characteristics. A strong correlation between evaporation rate and contact resistance was systematically investigated by thermal evaporation of metals at various deposition rates, which confirmed the thermal radiation generated during evaporation can be largely reduced, under the selection of an appropriate evaporation rate to minimize such damage. Additionally, we investigate the different device configurations and find that the extent of gate coverage over the channel and clearer interface between electrode and dielectric layer in 2D field-effect transistors (FETs) significantly affect transfer characteristics. The approaches presented in this work facilitate the realization of high- performance 2D FETs and promote the integration of 2D materials into electronic circuits and devices.

items.title: Reliability prediction of ESD and electro-thermal degradation in SiC MOSFETS for energy storage
items.abstract: Abstract Representative 1200 V planar SiC MOSFET and Si-IGBT cells are compared within a common device-level TCAD reliability-prediction framework, spanning sub-microsecond pulse electrothermal response and long-duration bias-temperature-induced interface degradation. Under a 10 A, 100 ns current pulse, the SiC cell exhibits a 4.70% lower peak terminal voltage (2392 V versus 2510 V) but an approximately 40% higher local peak lattice temperature (1313 K versus 938 K). After 180 h at 150 °C with V GS = 15 V and V DS = 0 V, the simulated on-state-current reductions are 21.65% for the SiC MOSFET and 4.64% for the Si-IGBT. Under off-state blocking stress at V GS = 0 V and V DS = 1200 V, the corresponding reductions are 0.12% and 10.87%, reversing the degradation ordering. Spatially resolved electric field, carrier energy, impact ionization, lattice temperature, and interface-trap distributions explain these stress- and metric-dependent responses. By covering both stress regimes, the framework addresses a gap in device-level TCAD reliability analysis for SiC power devices. Its modeling workflow can be transferred to other structures by updating device parameters and electrical and thermal boundary conditions, providing a reusable basis for reliability prediction, device design, and process optimization.
items.venue: Journal of Physics D Applied Physics

items.title: Range: Decoupling KV-Cache Reuse Granularity from Storage Work
items.abstract: LLM serving reuses cached key-value (KV) state to skip prefill, and growing contexts push that state past GPU HBM and CPU DRAM onto NVMe SSDs, placing prefix restore on the critical path of time-to-first-token (TTFT). We find that on a well-configured host-issued path the SSD is not the bottleneck: restoring the same 6 GiB of KV takes 2.1 s as 192 objects but 3.0 s as 6,144 objects, and more under layerwise loading, because every layer of the storage stack - lookup, allocation, I/O submission, GPU delivery, store, index - charges per logical object while the bytes stay the same. This cost grows with the KV footprint: longer contexts, deeper models under layerwise loading, and tensor parallelism each multiply the object count. Prior systems move this per-object work from the CPU to the GPU; the work remains per object. This paper presents Range, a KV-cache storage engine for vLLM and LMCache built on one principle: every cost on the storage path scales with bytes or physical batches, never with logical objects. Range tickets replace per-key lookup and ownership with token metadata and physical leases; byte stripes make the on-media layout independent of reuse granularity; completion-owned GPU transfer banks batch delivery and extraction and release each layer to attention as it lands. Range keeps the kernel cuFile path and changes four lines of vLLM. On a fixed 6 GiB restore, Range's median TTFT stays at 1.79-1.80 s across a 32x range of object counts and under layerwise delivery, within 70 ms of the prefix already being resident in GPU memory, while tuned in-process LMCache rises from 2.12 s to 3.01 s. Range improves on the fastest multiprocess DRAM-bounced path by 0.44 s at coarse granularity while moving no payload through host memory, and holds layerwise reuse at the cost of coarse-grained reuse, where the best stock path takes 2.24 s.

items.title: REUSE: Recurrent Subgraph Exploitation for ReRAM-Accelerated Graph Processing
items.abstract: Graph accelerators have emerged as a promising solution for accelerating the processing of large-scale sparse graphs by leveraging the in-situ computation capabilities of ReRAM crossbars. However, existing designs incur substantial memristor access overhead due to the large number of graph partitions, increasing execution time and energy consumption while reducing circuit lifetime. This paper presents REUSE, a ReRAM-based graph accelerator that exploits recurring subgraph patterns to minimize memristor write operations. REUSE identifies frequent patterns and maps them to static graph engines whose crossbar configurations are preserved throughout execution, while less frequent patterns are assigned to dynamic engines at runtime. To support efficient mapping, REUSE employs a lightweight host-side processing scheme that operates directly on the graph's coordinate list, avoiding costly dense matrix reconstruction. Patterns are then distributed across multiple crossbars within each graph engine to balance the workload and maximize utilization. Furthermore, we develop analytical execution-time and energy models and use them to explore key architectural parameters, including the allocation of static and dynamic graph engines. REUSE is evaluated on diverse real-world graph datasets using BFS, SSSP, and PageRank, with BFS as the common workload for comparison against four state-of-the-art ReRAM-based accelerators. It achieves average speedups of 6.9 × over SparseMEM, 4.2 × over RPBFS, and 2.5 × over TARe, and improves on GraphR by 76 ×. The corresponding energy-delay product reductions are 7.5 ×, 70 ×, and 4.9 × against the same three designs, and approximately five orders of magnitude against GraphR. Circuit lifetime is extended by 2 × over SparseMEM and by two orders of magnitude over GraphR.
items.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems

items.title: R$^{2}$PIAC: A Runtime Reconfigurable Photonic Interconnect Architecture for Chiplet-Based DNN Accelerators
items.abstract: The continued scaling of deep neural networks (DNNs) is driving accelerator architectures toward chiplet-based integration. However, conventional fixed and workload-level optimized topologies do not track fine-grained, time-varying communication during DNN inference, resulting in multi-hop latency and link congestion. To address this challenge, we propose R $^{2}$ PIAC, a runtime-reconfigurable photonic interconnect architecture for chiplet-based DNN accelerators. R $^{2}$ PIAC uses an electro-optic Mach–Zehnder interferometer (EO-MZI) switching fabric to establish high-bandwidth, single-hop lightpaths on demand. To enable runtime reconfiguration, R $^{2}$ PIAC adopts a two-stage heuristic scheduler. The scheduler combines capacity-aware topology matching with utility-driven holding-time selection and uses a cost-aware static fallback to avoid low-benefit reconfigurations for long-tail traffic. We validate R $^{2}$ PIAC through cross-layer hardware–software co-design using a custom $8\times 8$ EO-MZI switch controlled by a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and optimized receiver alignment and header qualification. Parallel all-offset alignment and 32-header qualification restore Ethernet packet service within $2.0352\;\mu \mathrm{s}$ after an optical-circuit reconfiguration. Across five DNN workloads on a four-board, eight-chiplet FPGA prototype, R $^{2}$ PIAC reduces mean aggregate inter-chiplet service time by 28.22%–63.43% relative to three baselines. The corresponding mean reduction in end-to-end inference latency is 6.14%–18.89%.

items.title: Quasi-Ballistic Thermal Transport in Vertically Aligned h-BN
items.abstract: Abstract Hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) has attracted significant interest in the semiconductor industry due to its wide bandgap (5.95 eV), high anisotropic thermal conductivity, and low dielectric constant. However, the formation of crystalline h-BN conventionally requires high processing temperatures, which are incompatible with back-end-of-line (BEOL) integration and advanced packaging processes that must remain below 400 °C to avoid degradation of front-end devices. In this work, trichloroborazine (TCB) was systematically investigated using ammonia as the nitrogen co-reactant under both plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PEALD) and atomic layer annealing (ALA) conditions. In the ALA process, low-energy inert ions are shown to enable in situ crystallization at temperatures well below those required for conventional MOCVD. As a result, highly ordered, vertically aligned polycrystalline h-BN films were deposited within a BEOL-compatible temperature window of 300–400 °C. The as-deposited ALA h-BN films exhibited clear signatures of cross-plane quasi-ballistic phonon transport over a thickness range of 20–50 nm, characterized by a thickness-independent effective thermal resistance of ∼6–9 m2 K GW–1. This invariance with film thickness indicates that phonon mean free paths exceed the film thickness, confirming quasi-ballistic heat transport enabled by the high crystallinity and preferential vertical alignment of the h-BN domains.

items.title: PAHT: Process-Aware History Tracking for Fast Read Retry in High-Capacity 3D NAND SSDs
items.abstract: While NAND flash memory has continuously increased its storage capacity, capacity-centric techniques have also exacerbated reliability problems. Conventionally, SSDs address reliability issues by incorporating read-retry operations that search for the optimal read reference voltage (VOPT). Read-retry reduces raw bit error rates (RBERs), but it significantly degrades read performance because multiple read iterations are required to complete a single host read request. To minimize this overhead, we propose Process-Aware History Tracking (PAHT), a novel technique that eliminates unnecessary read iterations during read-retry. PAHT is motivated by two observations: (i) VOPT does not need to be updated for a long interval, and (ii) the VOPT offset between wordlines (WLs) is identical across blocks in a chip. Our proposal integrates two optimizations. First, when a read on a given WL succeeds, we record and reuse the VOPT for future reads to the same WL. Second, we keep only one VOPT per block. For other WLs, we determine the VOPT using a predefined offset table that accounts for process variability in 3D flash memory. Based on comprehensive characterizations using 160 real 3D flash chips, system evaluations show that PAHT improves SSD performance by 58.3% on average by reducing read-retry invocations.

items.title: Oxygen Vacancy Engineering for Enhanced Remanent Polarization and Memory Window in a-IGZO/HZO Ferroelectric Field-Effect Transistors
items.abstract: HfO2-derived ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) are promising for nonvolatile memory and logic-in-memory applications owing to CMOS compatibility and low-voltage polarization switching. Amorphous InGaZnO (a-IGZO) is attractive for back-end-of-line compatible FeFETs, but inverted bottom-gate devices suffer from incomplete switching under negative gate bias, especially in the nonoverlap metal/ferroelectric/semiconductor (MFS) region where depleted a-IGZO becomes effectively floating and weakens voltage coupling across HfZrOx (HZO). Here, we demonstrate oxygen vacancy (VO)-mediated activation of negative-bias switching in a-IGZO FeFETs. The oxygen-deficient state of the bottom a-IGZO layer was controlled by sputtering oxygen flow ratio and rapid thermal annealing oxygen partial pressure. Depth-profile X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirms VO modulation near the a-IGZO/HZO interface. Positive-up-negative-down measurements and area-engineered capacitor test element groups show that VO-rich a-IGZO enhances reversible MFS switching by supplying compensating positive charge under depletion, thereby enlarging the memory window and improving switching behavior. This approach directly mitigates geometry-induced switching loss in practical oxide-semiconductor FeFET architecture.

items.title: Optoelectronic Synergy and Multimodal Neuromorphic Computing in SnS 2 /h‐BN/NbOCl 2 Van Der Waals Floating Gate Architecture
items.abstract: The kinetic basis by which a single charge‐storage layer supports both short‐term plasticity (STP) and persistent long‐term plasticity (LTP) remains unresolved. Using a SnS 2 /h‐BN/NbOCl 2 van der Waals floating‐gate architecture, we provide three complementary lines of evidence. Removing NbOCl 2 reduces the memory window from 92.2 to ∼2 V, identifying NbOCl 2 as the dominant charge‐storage medium. Variable‐temperature post‐stimulus relaxation (310–330 K), analyzed by biexponential fitting and Arrhenius regression, resolves two kinetically distinct components: a weakly activated component (WAC, E a,1 ≈ 0.026 eV) with fast relaxation, consistent with transient STP conductance modulation, and a thermally activated component (TAC, E a,2 ≈ 0.111 eV) with much slower relaxation, consistent with persistent LTP retention. Their approximately 4‐fold effective activation‐energy difference provides quantitative kinetic evidence for two distinct temperature‐dependent relaxation behaviors associated with the same NbOCl 2 layer. Sigmoidal fitting of the memory index yields a crossover power density P c = 26.49 µW/cm 2 , separating a predominantly volatile response at P P c (Path B). Transient electrostatic screening and tunneling‐assisted charge neutralization are proposed as the underlying processes. The device achieves 92.81% MNIST and 93.2% spoken‐digit recognition accuracy, demonstrating promise for multimodal neuromorphic computation.

items.title: Nanoscale domain structures with a feature size down to 5 nm in lithium niobate thin film on silicon substrate
items.abstract: By employing the tip-field-induced domain direct-writing technique based on atomic force microscopy, periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) with a periodicity of 40 nm was successfully fabricated in a 30 nm-thick, z-cut congruent lithium niobate thin film on silicon substrate. Simultaneously, ferroelectric dot-domain arrays with a lateral dimension of a single dot domain of ∼5 nm and a minimum dot-to-dot domain spacing of ∼26 nm were also achieved, demonstrating an information-storage density of 3.7 Tbit/in2. In addition, in MgO-doped lithium niobate thin films, PPLN with a period of 50 nm and dot domains with a lateral dimension less than 40 nm were obtained. These achievements effectively facilitate the device miniaturization and performance improvement for domain-based applications such as ferroelectric domain memories in lithium niobate.

items.title: MemLLM: End-to-end In-Storage Acceleration of On-device Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Precomputed KV Caches
items.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices enables personalized large language model (LLM) inference while preserving privacy. However, RAG's inherent length asymmetry makes the prefill phase the dominant bottleneck. While precomputing the KV caches offline alleviates the prefill cost on server systems, the multi-gigabyte caches over the narrow interconnect create a severe I/O wall for on-device systems. To mitigate this, we propose MemLLM, an end-to-end in-storage processing (ISP) architecture that executes the complete attention pipeline based on precomputed KV caches within the SSD. MemLLM utilizes per-channel accelerators to fully utilize the aggregated NAND channel bandwidth and accelerates all KV cache-related computations on the storage-side to minimize PCIe transfers. To efficiently handle the sparse updates required by RAG, MemLLM introduces a fused recomputation-query kernel paired with a hardware-based filter logic to halve the NAND read volume and eliminate write-back penalties. Furthermore, MemLLM's global SRAM-based stateful reduction engine enables a completely DRAM-less dataflow, thereby removing the internal memory bottlenecks and bounding the PCIe egress to an $O(1)$ footprint. A full-stack software stack allows asynchronous, zero-copy transfers from the ISP to the host and provides transparent execution within modern ML frameworks. Evaluated across eight real-world RAG datasets and six on-device LLM models, MemLLM achieves an average end-to-end speedup of 4.06$\times$ over the GPU baseline.

items.title: Long-Lived Charge Trap Characterization for Rare-Event Searches with Skipper-CCDs
items.abstract: Skipper Charge-Coupled Devices (Skipper-CCDs) are detectors with sub-electron resolution, allowing them to play a critical role in rare-event searches. A major challenge in experiments using these detectors is understanding and mitigating low-energy backgrounds which impact the single-electron rate. One potential component of the single-electron rate could arise from single-electron charge traps caused by lattice defects. In this work we use a new in-situ technique for generating uniform charge known as ``pixel-pumping''across the CCD to study single-electron traps in a SENSEI sensor placed underground in the MINOS cavern at Fermilab, which enables sensitivity to long-lived traps with emission times $>10^3$ seconds, a regime that was previously not accessible. We fully characterize 1787 traps and use this information to estimate their contribution to the single-electron background in SENSEI. Through simulation, we find the characterized population of traps does not significantly impact the single-electron rate. We further identify the energies and cross-sections for traps to which this analysis is sensitive, and compare this with the values that could impact the single-electron rate. This analysis probes a large fraction of this region. However, we also see that a sufficiently numerous hidden population could contribute significantly to the single-electron rate, and new measurement techniques will have to be devised in order to fully rule out this population.

items.title: High-performance WSe2 Ferroelectric Memory Device with Charge Trapping
items.abstract: This study demonstrates a non-volatile p-type FeFET device utilizing a silicon-compatible ferroelectric HZO/WSe2 structure, where ferroelectric polarization and defect trapping mechanisms synergistically enable superior memory performance. The fabricated device exhibits remarkable characteristics, including an exceptionally wide memory window of 4.91V at ±4V operation, ultrafast switching speed of 10ns, and excellent current switching ratio of ~107. Furthermore, it demonstrates robust endurance exceeding 105 cycles and stable retention properties lasting up to 104s. This integration of CMOS-compatible ferroelectric defect layers presents a promising pathway for next-generation high-density memory computing systems, offering significant improvements in both operational speed and energy efficiency.

items.title: High-Performance Enhancement-Mode Ultra-thin ALD-Grown InWSnO Transistors Enabled by W/Sn Co-Engineering and Back-Channel Passivation
items.abstract: We report atomic layer deposition-grown indium–tungsten–tin oxide (IWTO) thin-film transistors that effectively circumvent the conventional on-current–threshold voltage (ION–VTH) trade-off in atomically thin oxide semiconductors. A W/Sn co-engineered IWTO channel is developed by systematically varying the W concentration from 1 to 3 at.% while maintaining a fixed In/Sn cycle ratio, enabling balanced charge transport and threshold-voltage (VTH) stability in ∼2 nm channels. To ensure long-term reliability, an ozone-based back-channel passivation (BCP) process was implemented, suppressing environmental instability without compromising the intrinsic electronic properties. Devices optimized with a 1 at.% W concentration with BCP exhibit superior electrostatic control, characterized by a steep subthreshold swing, negligible hysteresis, and ultra-low leakage current. Notably, these performance advantages persist upon scaling the channel length (LCH) down to 200 nm, maintaining a high-drive current of 338 μA/μm (at VDS = 1 V) with the enhancement-mode operation (VTH > 0 V) and robust bias-stress stability. This work establishes a scalable material platform for high-performance oxide electronics compatible with back-end-of-line applications.

items.title: Comparative investigation of extended-gate GaAsSb/InGaAs HTFET biosensors for label-free biomolecule detection
items.abstract: Abstract The dielectric-modulated heterostructure tunnel FET (HTFET)-based nano-cavity integrated biosensors are emerging as energy-efficient, ultra-sensitive label-free detection platforms. This study investigates and compares three GaAsSb/InGaAs-based biosensor architectures: single cavity dual material double composite gate HTFET (SC-DM-DG HTFET), dual cavity dual material double composite gate HTFET (DC-DM-DG HTFET), and single cavity dual material extended double composite gate HTFET (SC-DM-EDG HTFET). The III–V heterostructure in the SC-DM-EDG HTFET enhances tunnelling probability, gate control, and on-current ( I O N ), thereby providing higher sensitivity than previously reported GaAsSb/InGaAs-based HTFET and FET biosensors. Sensitivity and selectivity parameters for I O N , transconductance ( g m ), and threshold voltage ( V t h ) were evaluated for various neutral and charged biomolecules. Under the standard bias condition ( V DS = 1.5 V, V GS = 1.3 V), the SC-DM-EDG HTFET exhibits the highest I O N of 3.02 × 10 −4 A/ μ m among the three structures; under a separately re-optimized bias ( V DS = 0.9 V, V GS = 1 V), the same structure instead achieves maximum sensitivities of 3.35 × 10 6 ( I O N ) and 3.49 × 10 5 ( g m ) for K = 12, at a correspondingly reduced I O N of 1.91 × 10 −4 A/ μ m. The maximum V t h sensitivity of 0.49 is achieved by this structure under the standard bias condition. In biomolecule differentiation, the SC-DM-DG HTFET demonstrates peak I O N and g m selectivity values of 9.55 and 4.64 for K = 12, respectively, while the peak V t h selectivity value of 0.3 appears in the SC-DM-EDG HTFET also for the same biomolecule. Furthermore, the SC-DM-EDG HTFET achieves superior I O N , g m , and V t h sensitivities for charged biomolecules, confirming its robustness, selectivity, and potential for next-generation, high-performance biosensing applications.

items.title: Carbon Dots Enable Low-Voltage Memristor Based on CsPbBr3 for Artificial Synapses
items.abstract: Optoelectronic memristors show significant potential for neuromorphic computing but are often limited by high operating voltages. Here, we constructed a low-voltage Ag/CsPbBr3/CDs/FTO photonic memristor by incorporating carbon dots (CDs) as a regulatory medium within the CsPbBr3 perovskite layer. The CDs significantly enhanced memristive performance: their surface defect states and localized electric field regulation enabled stable conductive filament formation and rupture at low voltages. This yielded favorable operational characteristics, including low set/reset voltages (0.72 V/−0.60 V) and preliminary cycling endurance with state retention. Leveraging the device’s continuously tunable conductance, we successfully emulated key synaptic learning behaviors such as paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) and long-term potentiation/depression (LTP/LTD). Implementing its weight-updating characteristics in an artificial neural network (ANN) achieved 92.17% accuracy in handwritten digit classification. This work demonstrates the effective role of CDs in enabling low-voltage, high-performance perovskite photonic memristors, providing a viable strategy for developing low-power neuromorphic hardware.

items.title: Can SOLARBURST go silicon? A systematic analysis on software supply chain attacks for VLSI design flows
items.abstract: An attacker targeting the software supply chain (SWSC) of VLSI tools can fully subvert the VLSI design pipeline through purely software level compromises. However, cur- rent literature on both SWSC and VLSI hardware security has not explored how software can be used to subvert the security of the VLSI design flow. In order to bridge this gap, this paper presents a systematic analysis of the vulnerable surface of VLSI from a SWSC standpoint. We carry this anal- ysis through three major activities. First, we did an empirical analysis of VLSI software suites, focusing on their software composition, security features, and tool interactions within the VLSI design flow. Second, we develop a VLSI-SWSC attack taxonomy model that links software supply chain at- tacks and their mechanisms to the VLSI attacks they enable, the design-flow stages they affect, and their resulting security outcomes, allowing us to identify 717 possible new attacks, including 60 high feasibility attacks supported by evidence collected in our empirical analysis. Third, we identify what possible security outcomes can be achieved by an attacker from these attacks and produce a comprehensive VLSI SWSC threat model. We evaluate the feasibility of the attacks identi- fied by our taxonomy across VLSI design stages and assess existing defenses to determine which attacks are mitigated and which remain unaddressed. In addition, we present case studies using a reference VLSI design flow consisting of open- source VLSI tools and highlight attacks identified through our taxonomy on the VLSI SWSC uniquely from a software perspective.

items.title: Beyond Word-Local ECC: A Bounded-Residual Certified Post-Failure Recovery Architecture for Clustered Upsets in Interleaved SRAM
items.abstract: Physical faults can cross error-correcting code (ECC) word boundaries even when static random-access memory (SRAM) protection remains word-local. This work proposes a bounded-residual certified post-failure recovery architecture for interleaved single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SEC-DED) SRAM. Once a complete one- or two-tile recovery window is acquired—either immediately upon a demand-path word-local detected-uncorrectable error (DUE) or during periodic integrity scrubbing—ordinary word syndromes and the known reverse interleaving map generate bounded physical fault hypotheses, while independently protected tile metadata alone authorizes memory write-back. We show that finite randomized testing is insufficient for selecting that certificate: a standard 16-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC-16) baseline passes extensive adversarial fault-injection campaigns without observed false corrections, yet exact algebraic residual analysis exposes deterministic silent data corruption (SDC) aliases and an explicit silent-correction witness. A parity-split residual-support lemma proves that under the weight-one/two per-word error model, distinct syndrome-equivalent explanations agree on every odd-parity single-error-correcting (SEC) word and can differ only on even-parity double-error-detecting (DED) words. This structural property yields two explicit authorization policies: a strict Commit-Exact mode that bounds active DED words per checked tile so that every authorized write-back lies inside the unrestricted exact one- and two-word residual domain, and a Commit-Env mode that retains the full frozen supported topology envelope, whose complete one-, two-, three-, and four-word candidate-difference space and two-tile boundary extension exhibit zero supported collisions under a fixed 32-bit Castagnoli cyclic redundancy check (CRC-32C) profile. Conditional on complete observation-window acquisition under the reference evaluation, the architecture recovers all template-exhaustive in-support, unseen-connected, and boundary-crossing failures and a high proportion of perturbed-shape failures while committing zero false corrections at modest metadata storage overhead. All formal safety and recovery guarantees remain explicitly conditional on the active commit mode (Commit-Exact or Commit-Env), complete observation-window acquisition, and the stated fault-model assumptions, namely bounded per-word candidate multiplicity, valid and coherent protected metadata, and complete candidate enumeration.

items.title: All‐Sputtered Oxide n‐p Heterojunction Anti‐Ambipolar Transistors for Semantic Segmentation Networks
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Neuromorphic vision provides an efficient route for extracting meaningful information from visual inputs and supporting intelligent perception in dynamic environments. However, visual scenes acquired under excessive or insufficient illumination often contain distorted contrast, weakened boundary information, and shifted input distributions, which degrade semantic segmentation accuracy before network computation. Conventional synaptic or neuromorphic hardware systems usually require additional normalization or preprocessing steps to compensate for such input distortion, limiting the direct integration of signal regulation at the device level. In this work, an all‐sputtered oxide anti‐ambipolar transistor (AAT) based on an IGZO/TeSeO x heterojunction is introduced as a device‐level preprocessing element for illumination‐robust neuromorphic vision. IGZO/TeSeO x AAT exhibits a well‐defined Gaussian‐like anti‐ambipolar transfer characteristic, with a peak‐to‐valley current ratio of 1.17 × 10 3 and a maximum negative transconductance of −240.8 nS, enabling effective attenuation of excessive input signals. The resulting Gaussian‐like anti‐ambipolar response is used to construct Gaussian smoothing and Laplacian of Gaussian filtering kernels. Applied to semantic segmentation under overexposed and underexposed conditions, the proposed preprocessing scheme improves pixel‐wise classification consistency and achieves 86.1% pixel accuracy.

items.title: All-SiC integrated process platform: development roadmap and challenges
items.abstract: Abstract With exceptional high-temperature tolerance and radiation hardness, Silicon carbide (SiC) integrated circuits (ICs) have emerged as a promising candidate for extreme-environment applications in automotive, aerospace and deep-well drilling. This paper provides a comprehensive review of monolithic SiC IC platforms, encompassing a low-voltage (LV) IC platform incorporating exclusively LV devices and a power IC platform featuring concurrent integration of high-voltage (HV) and LV devices. Fundamental components evolve from bipolar junction transistors (BJTs) to junction field-effect transistors (JFETs), and subsequently to metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs). A systematic review is conducted on the state-of-the-art and key technical hurdles for each device platform, with a focus on high-temperature and radiation-hardened applications. Finally, critical challenges confronting MOSFET-based integration process platforms are delineated, namely threshold voltage ( V th ) mismatch between NMOS and PMOS devices and radiation reliability issues, necessitating focused research initiatives to propel the industrialization of SiC monolithic ICs.

items.title: A 0.6 V Complementary Self-Referenced R-2R SAR-Based Temperature Sensor
items.abstract: This article presents a 0.6 V complementary self-referenced R-2R successive approximation register (SAR) temperature sensor for very large scale integration (VLSI) thermal management. With a digital-like architecture that uses only a comparator as its active analog block, the proposed design reuses complementary R-2R resistor ladders to implement temperature sensing and SAR quantization simultaneously. By virtue of the mutual referencing between the positive and negative temperature coefficient ladders, it requires no high-precision or high-frequency external reference clock or voltage biasing. Compared with the single-sided counterpart, this architecture nearly doubles the effective thermal sensitivity and achieves a low supply sensitivity of $0.74~^{\circ } \text {C/ {V}}$ . To ensure reliable operation under sub-1 V supply, a low-voltage dynamic comparator integrated with a partial feedback bulk adaptive floating inverter amplifier (PFBAFIA), output offset storage (OOS), and a body-driven latch is proposed in this work. Benefiting from the digital-like structure, the chip area, energy consumption, and conversion time of the sensor scale linearly with the number of bits. The proposed design is verified by postlayout simulations in 55 nm CMOS technology: it covers a wide temperature range from $- 40~^{\circ } \text {C}$ to $125~^{\circ } \text {C}$ , and achieves a ${3}\sigma $ inaccuracy of $\pm 0.45~^{\circ } $ C after two-point calibration. Meanwhile, it features a single conversion energy of only 0.7 nJ and a resolution figure of merit (RFoM) of 15.1 pJ-K 2 .

items.title: Understanding and Mitigating Interlayer Thermal Crosstalk in 3D Vertical Phase‐Change Memory
items.abstract: Three‐dimensional vertical phase‐change memory (3D vertical PCM) provides a device‐level route toward vertically integrated phase‐change storage, yet vertical stacking converts cell‐level thermal confinement into a stack‐level reliability constraint. Here, interlayer thermal crosstalk is investigated in a dual‐layer Hf‐doped Ge─Sb─Te 3D vertical PCM device by constructing an operation‐ and state‐dependent disturbance matrix. The monitoring cell is initialized in either the crystalline low‐resistance state or the amorphous high‐resistance state, while READ‐, SET‐, and RESET‐level pulse trains are applied to the adjacent programming cell. READ and SET produce limited disturbance, whereas RESET dominates interlayer thermal perturbation. The amorphous high‐resistance state exhibits the highest susceptibility, showing a pronounced resistance decrease under adjacent RESET excitation. Qualitative electrothermal simulations attribute this selectivity to localized RESET heating and transient vertical heat spreading across stacked layers. Paired‐pulse programming temporally redistributes the RESET thermal budget by decoupling rapid selected‐layer heating from delayed interlayer heat spreading. This strategy preserves the thermal response required for selected‐cell programming while suppressing heat transfer to the monitoring layer.
