The performance and properties of these network architectures are compared, with the results showing that SNNs possess a desirable combination of low relative neuron count, high accuracy and low output delay.

items.title: CoDPlacer: A Fast Approach for Digital IC Placement via Consistency Distillation
items.abstract: Modern digital IC placement requires methods that balance placement quality, legality, and runtime as circuit sizes continue to grow. Learning-based generative placers provide a promising alternative to analytical and sequential approaches, but they remain computationally expensive because high-quality generation requires large number of steps. This paper presents CoDPlacer, a consistency-distilled framework for accelerating generative chip placement. The method distills a pretrained diffusion placer into a consistency model for faster macro- and cluster-level placement. Two full-chip placement flows are evaluated: macro placement followed by DREAMPlace standard-cell refinement (conventional method), and a hierarchical flow using standard-cell clustering, boundary-aware expansion, local DREAMPlace optimization, and final assembly. Experiments on 18 IBM benchmarks and five ISPD2005 circuits evaluate inference-step sensitivity, macro placement, and downstream detailed placement. The 128-step consistency model achieves 4.1×, 3.11×, and 7.82× generation speedups relative to the strongest evaluated baseline on clustered IBM, macro-only IBM, and macro-only ISPD2005 benchmarks, respectively, while maintaining competitive HPWL. In conventional full-chip placement, the consistency-distilled model achieves the lowest average HPWL among the evaluated baselines. These results show that consistency distillation provides an effective quality-runtime tradeoff and useful initialization for downstream analytical placement.

items.title: A UTILIZAÇÃO DO MÉTODO PILATES COMO RECURSO TERAPÊUTICO NA REABILITAÇÃO DA DIÁSTASE ABDOMINAL: UMA REVISÃO SISTEMÁTICA
items.abstract: Diastasis of the rectus abdominis muscles (DRAM) is characterized by separation of the rectus muscles along the linea alba and may be associated with changes in abdominal wall function and stability. The Pilates method has been used as a physiotherapeutic resource because it involves exercises aimed at strengthening, controlling, and stabilizing the trunk musculature. This study aimed to analyze the evidence on the use of Pilates in the rehabilitation of DRAM. This systematic literature review was conducted using PubMed, SciELO, LILACS, PEDro, and Google Scholar. Primary studies published between 2015 and 2025 in Portuguese, English, and Spanish, directly related to Pilates and abdominal diastasis, were included. After identification, screening, and eligibility assessment, four studies were included. Three studies observed a reduction in inter-recti distance, whereas one study conducted during pregnancy did not identify a reduction in diastasis. Improvements in abdominal muscle strength and endurance and a reduction in low back pain were also observed. The findings indicate that Pilates was effective in reducing inter-recti distance in most studies and may be considered a physiotherapeutic resource applicable to the management of DRAM, although study heterogeneity limits the generalization of the results.
items.venue: Revista Ibero-Americana de Humanidades, Ciências e Educação

items.title: VLSI Design for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Applications
items.abstract: Unlock the next generation of AI chip design with this comprehensive guide to overcoming VLSI challenges, combining state-of-the-art nanomaterials, semiconductor modeling, and low-power circuit design into an essential roadmap for researchers and engineers. Very large-scale integration (VLSI) is the interdisciplinary science of utilizing advanced semiconductor technology to create various functions of a computer system. By combining VLSI technology, a very powerful computer architecture is possible to overcome the problems at different design stages. AI techniques such as knowledge-based and expert systems first define the problem and then choose the best solution from a range of possible approaches. This book comprehensively covers nanomaterials, semiconductor devices, and modeling and simulation techniques used to address the challenges of low-power VLSI chip design. It explores process variability, device sizing, power supply scaling, conventional and emerging materials, leakage mitigation techniques, and critical design tradeoffs. The book presents state-of-the-art research in nanomaterials and semiconductor technologies alongside practical design considerations for low-power VLSI circuits, making it an essential resource for scientists, researchers, and postgraduate students interested in AI hardware, semiconductor devices, modeling, and simulation.

items.title: Toward Intelligent Chemical Mechanical Polishing: Integrating Multiscale Modeling and Machine Learning
items.abstract: Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) remains the cornerstone planarization technology in advanced semiconductor manufacturing. As device architectures transition toward FinFETs, gate-all-around structures, heterogeneous integration, and wide-bandgap semiconductors, CMP must simultaneously deliver angstrom-level flatness, high selectivity, low damage, and improved sustainability. Against this background, research in CMP is moving beyond empirical trial-and-error toward a more integrated paradigm that combines consumables design, physics-based modeling, and data-driven intelligence. This review systematically summarizes recent progress in CMP from four interrelated perspectives. First, we examine advances in slurry and abrasive design, including morphology engineering, porous and core-shell abrasives, defect-controlled ceria systems, and environmentally friendlier chemical formulations, together with the emergence of photo-, electro-, ultrasonic-, plasma-, and gas-assisted CMP. Second, we review the multiscale modeling landscape, spanning macroscale planarization and profile evolution, mesoscale contact mechanics and slurry transport, and atomistic simulations based on first-principles calculations and reactive molecular dynamics. Third, we assess the rapidly growing role of machine learning in CMP, with emphasis on material removal rate prediction, surface quality evaluation, process monitoring, virtual metrology, and intelligent run-to-run control. Fourth, we discuss sustainability-oriented CMP, including source reduction, wastewater treatment and recycling, and the use of modeling and digital control to reduce non-productive resource consumption. By synthesizing developments across these areas, this manuscript highlights the current gaps in cross-scale model integration, physics-informed intelligent control, transferability across tools and materials, and life-cycle-oriented process design. We conclude by outlining how a closed-loop CMP ecosystem-linking materials innovation, mechanistic understanding, in situ sensing, and intelligent optimization-may support the next generation of high-efficiency, green, and manufacturable planarization technologies.

items.title: SSRESF-OPT: A Sensitivity-Aware Framework for Single-Particle Radiation Effects Simulation and Optimization in SoC Platforms Using Machine Learning
items.abstract: The increasing scale of System-on-Chip (SoC) architectures exacerbates the reliability risks of single-particle radiation effects, rendering traditional exhaustive gate-level fault injection prohibitively slow. To address this, we propose SSRESF-OPT, an end-to-end simulation and optimization framework combining accelerated dynamic fault injection with machine learning-driven prediction. The framework first introduces a cross-layer static binding mechanism to eliminate runtime string resolution, reducing per-injection simulation overhead to \(\mathcal {O}(1) \) complexity. Building on this optimized engine, an SVM-based classification pipeline, guided by structural clustering, accurately predicts the radiation vulnerability of unsimulated circuit nodes using netlist-derived features. To maximize resource efficiency, an OPT-based top- k hardening strategy is then employed to prioritize critical architectural bottlenecks. Evaluations across 15 gate-level netlists, including massive AES subsystems and RISC-V PULP SoCs, demonstrate the framework’s efficacy. The model-assisted approach achieves an average end-to-end runtime speedup of 6.35 × over the highly optimized simulation baseline while maintaining a 94.58% prediction accuracy. Furthermore, hardening only the top 10% of ranked nodes reduces system Soft Error Rate (SER) by 85%, providing a fast and actionable methodology for radiation-hardened microprocessor design.
items.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems

items.title: SGAnalog: An End-to-End Circuit Benchmark from Open-Source Silicon Tapeouts
items.abstract: Existing analog integrated circuit design benchmarks make two questions hard to answer: whether a model has learned transferable circuit skills rather than recalled familiar examples, and whether its output works under defined process and test conditions. We introduce a benchmark built from human-designed, open-source circuits associated with Tiny Tapeout manufacturing shuttles. The collection contains 273 topologically distinct top-level designs. Every source is retrieved at the revision recorded for its shuttle submission and processed in a fixed containerized environment. The pipeline exports each eligible schematic image and its SPICE netlist from the same source file, giving transcription an exact structural reference. Commit dates support model-specific training-cutoff analysis, while author testbenches provide the simulation context for sizing. The benchmark evaluates schematic-to-netlist transcription and device sizing. Across seven models on a fixed set of 66 transcription tasks, the strongest model reaches 56.1% exact graph isomorphism, and six of seven models drop sharply from the small to the medium tier. For one frontier model, removing author-chosen labels reduces exact matches while preserving aggregate structural F1, suggesting that labels can aid connectivity tracing. On the 17 sizing tasks, the leading model converges on all 17 proposals and reaches 91.2 out of 100 against the human reference, while the two newest Claude models refuse 4 and 11 of the same prompts they transcribe without objection; a proposal without sizes scores zero. The two tasks produce different model rankings, exposing distinct visual and design capabilities and, in one family, a policy rather than capability limit.

items.title: Reversing the Clock: Layout-Aware Recovery of Design Intent from Clock Distribution Networks
items.abstract: Hardware reverse engineering supports competitive analysis and hardware assurance by recovering information about an integrated circuit (IC) from its physical implementation. While existing techniques primarily recover the gate-level netlist, which represents logical functionality, they often overlook physical design decisions such as placement, routing, delay insertion, and interconnect optimization. The clock distribution network encapsulates many of these decisions; however, no prior published work has recovered this network from a fabricated IC to infer design intent. We present a layout-aware methodology that recovers and analyzes the clock distribution network by integrating a recovered gate-level netlist with layout information extracted from scanning electron microscope imagery. Our four-phase pipeline recovers clock-tree topology, buffering, gating and switching, interconnect delay, and crosstalk-mitigation measures. We demonstrate our methodology on a commercial 450 nm IC, recovering a global H-tree backbone with local X-tree-like branching, identifying an independent clock tree and global clock gating, quantifying latency, skew, and routing lengths, and confirming the absence of dedicated crosstalk mitigation. Together, these findings let us reason about the designer's intent. To encourage further research and support reproducibility, we release our clock tree recovery algorithm as open source.

items.title: RaBitQ-SSD: Split Codes and Pipelined I/O for SSD-Resident Vector Search
items.abstract: SSD-resident approximate nearest-neighbor search is essential when vector collections exceed DRAM capacity. The challenge is to reduce SSD reads and hide I/O latency through concurrent reads and overlap with computation. However, for graph-based search, progressive candidate discovery limits advance I/O planning while IVF search reads inverted lists in full, incurring unnecessary SSD reads. In this paper, we present RaBitQ-SSD, an extension of IVF-RaBitQ for SSD-resident vector search. Specifically, we propose Split-RaBitQ, which retains a configurable prefix of each binary code in DRAM, allowing in-memory code storage below one bit per dimension. Using this partial representation, it provides an unbiased distance estimator with a probabilistic error bound. Once the in-memory coarse quantizer identifies candidate lists, this bound supports pruning individual candidates within them, enabling finer-grained SSD access. We also design an asynchronous search pipeline that coordinates candidate pruning with SSD read scheduling to reduce unnecessary reads while overlapping I/O with computation. On datasets ranging from $5$ million to $1$ billion vectors, RaBitQ-SSD delivers up to $1.74\times$ the throughput of graph-based baselines at $90\%$ recall, while reducing SSD page reads by up to $3.8\times$. Its on-SSD indexes are up to $7.0\times$ smaller and $10.0\times$ faster to build than DiskANN. We also build and search an index of $10$ billion vectors on a single machine with one SSD, achieving over $3{,}000$ queries per second at $90\%$ recall.

items.title: Overcoming the Resistance Penalty in Large-Bandgap Carbon Nanotube Electronics via Synergistic Interfacial Engineering
items.abstract: High-pressure carbon monoxide (HiPCO) carbon nanotubes (CNTs) offer superior ION/IOFF ratios due to their larger bandgap (EG), yet they suffer from high series resistance limiting drive currents. Here, we demonstrate a synergistic dual-engineering strategy to simultaneously minimize channel and contact resistance in top-gate HiPCO CNT field-effect transistors (FETs). A 200 °C forming gas annealing (FGA) process effectively scavenges organic residues, reducing the intrinsic channel resistance to 318 Ω·μm for specific 50 nm gate-length devices. Furthermore, localized p-type contact doping using contact-defined self-aligned MoOx nanoparticles deposited selectively within the source/drain windows reduces the effective Schottky barrier height from 233 meV to 66 meV. Optimized HiPCO CNTFETs exhibit a record-high on-current density of 2.5 mA/μm at VDS = -0.5 V while maintaining excellent off-state suppression. Our devices outperform existing benchmarks and exceed the IRDS 2039 conductance projections by 4×. This synergistic approach provides a robust pathway for high-performance, low-power carbon-based nanoelectronics.

items.title: Optimization of Gate‐All‐Around Field‐Effect Transistors Design Using Genetic Algorithm
items.abstract: Gate-all-around field-effect transistors (GAAFETs) have come to the fore as a hopeful replacement for fin field-effect transistors in leading-edge semiconductor technology with better electrostatic control, shorter short-channel effects, and increased scalability for sub-3-nm nodes. GAAFETs utilize a surrounding gate geometry, allowing larger drive currents and smaller leakage relative to conventional transistor structures. Optimizing the design of GAAFETs remains a serious problem due to intricate interactions between structure parameters, material characteristics, and process variability. Design optimization of GAAFETs consists of several challenges, such as nanowire or nanosheet dimension selection being optimal, gate dielectric engineering, strain engineering, and managing variability. Accurate but time-consuming and computation-intensive physics-based simulations and traditional process optimization strategies are not practicable. Machine learning (ML) methods are very useful and efficient tools in speeding up the design and optimization process as they can quickly predict important electrical parameters like threshold voltage, subthreshold swing, and drive current. Unsupervised learning methods help to determine important design parameters and process variations. Using ML with physics simulations, one can effectively survey the large design space, minimize fabrication cycles, and improve device performance.

items.title: Negative‐Capacitance FET
items.abstract: The negative-capacitance field-effect transistor (NC-FET) enables effectively lowering of the power supply voltage (VDD) of conventional metal oxide semiconductor field effect transistor (MOSFET) because of its super steep switching feature, i.e., sub-60-mV/decade subthreshold swing (SS) at room temperature. The idea of overcoming the Boltzmann limit(S=60 mV/decade) by negative-capacitance (NC) lies in the fact that in a series combination of a negative and a positive capacitor, the total capacitance becomes larger than its constituent positive capacitor. Interestingly and particularly, this is just the opposite of two positive capacitors, where the total capacitance is always reduced. For a ferroelectric gate FET, the negative gate capacitance can make the total capacitance, looking into the gate, larger than the semiconductor capacitance. Thus, to induce the same amount of charge in the channel, the ferroelectric gate FET would require a smaller gate voltage than what required for a traditional FET. That is to say, the gate voltage could be reduced below the Boltzmann limit(S<60 mV/decade). Very recently, it has been demonstrated that temperature is an effective tuning parameter for the ferroelectric negative capacitance. The NCFET requires an additional ferroelectric layer in its gate stack. In this chapter, a negative-capacitance field-effect transistor (NC-FET) is designed with their added ferroelectric layer over SiO2 under the gate, having unique negative-capacitance behavior, which enables steeper subthreshold slopes and less power dissipation compared to traditional n-channel MOSFET (NMOS) devices. The examined performance parameters are threshold voltage, subthreshold slope, leakage current, and on-off current ratio to show that the NC-FET indeed offers all the advantages coupled with some limitations. Simulated results are found to be showing a better power consumption reduction and improvement in switching efficiency than NMOS transistors for NC-FETs. The focus here is on the potential of NC-FETs for energized VLSI circuits with insight into integrated applicability to future low-power digital designs. The conventional NMOS transistor performance is compared and analyzed with NC-FETs in terms of important parameters, such as power consumption, switching speed, subthreshold swing, and device efficiency. In this comparison, the potential advantages of NC-FETs over conventional devices is examined in terms of eliminating scaling barriers, increasing energy efficiency, and scaling the threshold voltage so that they allow for more efficient and compact VLSI designs for next-generation semiconductor applications.

items.title: Nanowire, Nanotube FET, and CNTFET
items.abstract: The evolution of today's electronics will remain directly associated with the improvisation in Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) technology, which is the building block of present computing and communication systems as well as intelligent electronic devices. The semiconductor devices are being ultra scaled down into nanometer regime, the industry is experiencing a shift from planar CMOS to advanced device structures. As traditional CMOS shrinks, short-channel effects increase (SCEs) increment in leakage current. For solving CMOS conventional scaling limitations Carbon Nanotube Field-Effect Transistor (CNTFETs) utilize a one-dimensional (1D) nanotube channel, which provides better electrostatic control over the channel, minimizing short-channel effects (SCEs) and lowering static power consumption. The CNTFETs alos offer ballistic transport, leading to high driving capability, 18 times faster switching speeds, and roughly less power consumption compared to bulk silicon. The CNTFETs are necessary in VLSI design to surpass the physical limitations of silicon CMOS at sub-10nm nodes, offering higher electron mobility, superior electrostatic control, and near-ballistic transport. This chapter has described the progress in nanowire field-effect transistors, nanotube field-effect transistors, and carbon nanotube field-effect transistors (CNTFETs) according to their structural, electrical, and functional properties. The chapter explains the fabrication process, performance optimization methods, and the influence of scaling on these transistor technologies. The use of one- dimensional nanostructures, i.e., nanowires and carbon nanotubes, in contemporary electronic devices provides enhanced electrical conductivity, increased mobility, and energy efficiency. Moreover, this chapter also suggests the advancement in dual-gate CNTFET geometries, thermoelectric nano transistors, and novel applications in high-speed logic circuits. The potential of these nanodevices in next-generation electronic and optoelectronic devices is evaluated critically in the future, which opens new areas of thrust in nanoelectronics.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning on the Design of Systems and the Future
items.abstract: Adoption artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) transformative impact on the design, development, and operation of systems across various industries. In this chapter impact of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) on the design, development, and operation of systems across various industries. The artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have evolved from rule-based expert systems to dynamic, data-driven architectures, enabling machines to learn from data, make intelligent decisions, and automate complex processes. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine Learning (ML) into system design offers enhanced automation, improved decision- making, personalization, and scalability, addressing the limitations of traditional rule-based approaches. The artificial intelligence (AI) and machine Learning (ML) are becoming essential in VLSI design to overcome the bottlenecks of exponential design complexity, power optimization, and manufacturing variability, replacing traditional, time-consuming manual EDA processes with automated, high-speed, and intelligent algorithms. They enable superior performance in physical design, specifically in placement and routing optimization, by analyzing vast data sets to predict timing, power, and yield. This shift has led to significant advancements in sectors such as e-commerce, healthcare, finance, and manufacturing, with artificial intelligence (AI) - driven innovations like personalized recommendations, fraud detection, and predictive analytics. Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems’ performance depends on data quality, diversity, real-time processing, and ethical considerations like fairness, privacy, and security. AI's full potential requires addressing challenges including data privacy, algorithm bias, and need for computational resources. Looking ahead, artificial intelligence (AI) and ML will continue to drive innovation in system design, with emerging trends like Artificial Intelligence (AI) -augmented design, explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI), and increased human-machine collaboration shaping the future.

items.title: High‐Speed Continuous‐Time Linear Equalizers for AI and Machine Learning Hardware
items.abstract: The rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have resulted in a significant increase in data transfer rates, requiring high-speed and energy-efficient communication systems. In high-speed wire line and optical links, signal degradation due to channel loss and inter-symbol interference (ISI) poses a significant challenge, impacting system performance and accuracy. Continuous time linear equalizers (CTLEs) are crucial in compensating for these distortions, enabling reliable high-speed data transmission for artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) hardware. The continuous-Time Linear Equalizers (CTLEs) are essential in high-speed VLSI serial link receivers to counteract frequency-dependent channel attenuation and eliminate Inter-Symbol Interference (ISI). Unlike digital equalizers (like Feed Forward Equalizers), analog CTLEs operate without a clock signal. This minimizes power consumption and saves chip area, making them highly efficient for receivers. This chapter focuses on the design, optimization, and linearity enhancement of high-speed continuous time linear equalizers (CTLEs) to meet the stringent requirements of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) systems. Linearity-improved continuous time linear equalizers (CTLEs) architecture enhances circuit linearity by replacing traditional current sources with high-linearity poly resistors. The core innovation of this design is the implementation of a voltage-to-current (V2I) converter in place of the conventional current source within the continuous time linear equalizers (CTLEs) biasing circuitry. The primary advantage of this innovative modification is a substantial improvement in the circuit's linearity, resulting in a notable reduction in total harmonic distortion (THD). The standard 65-nm complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology and a 1-V power supply were used to design and implement the continuous time linear equalizers (CTLEs). The overall active area occupied by the circuit is 0.023 mm², demonstrating an efficient and compact layout suitable for modern high speed transceiver applications. The performance evaluations indicate that the continuous time linear equalizers (CTLEs) delivers superior signal equalization when applied to a 12-inch transmission channel at a data rate of 12.5 Gb/s. The simulation results reveal an eye width of 71.24 ps and an eye height of 98.82 mV, ensuring a clear and distinguishable data signal. The measured jitter is also 8.63 ps, further validating the circuit's ability to maintain signal integrity and reduce timing uncertainty. In terms of power efficiency, the linearity-improved continuous time linear equalizers (CTLEs) consume only 3.29 mW, achieving a figure of merit (FoM) of 0.26 pJ/b. These advancements represent a significant step forward in developing high-performance continuous time linear equalizers (CTLEs) circuits.

items.title: Gate‐All‐Around Transistors Transforming Future‐Generation VLSI Scaling
items.abstract: The semiconductor industry has long been dominated by Moore's Law, which states that conventional CMOS transistors packed on a single silicon chip will double in size every 2 years approximately. As conventional CMOS technology scaling results in smaller and smaller transistor sizes, existing CMOS technology starts to encounter certain fundamental physical limitations. These limitations can potentially result in drastic reduction in performance and energy efficiencies of these transistors, which could make it untenable to continue scaling them. This in turn, would severely limit the benefits of further innovations in IC design. However, as devices go into the micro-sized zone, conventional planar semiconductor layouts face significant difficulties. The short-channel effects (SCEs) and leakage current are the result of insufficient gate control, which limits the scaling capabilities of traditional planar transistors. At transistor level, the scaling-in-duced performance degradation originated from short channel phenomena. The combination of strong gate length reduction and the shortening of the conduction channel led to an increase in leakage current, even when no voltage was applied to the gate. Similarly, the impact of source and drain on the shrinking channel region grew dramatically. These short channel effects drove the chip industry to transition from planar MOSFET to FinFET, and recently, to gate-all-around (GAA) transistors for high-performance computing applications. These architectural innovations allowed the gate to regain electrostatic control over the conduction channel. These issues are resolved by gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, which offer improved performance and superior electrostatic control. The gate-all-around (GAA) devices transform transistor design by completely encasing the channel with a gate, improving electrostatic control, drive current, and scalability. They function effectively at reduced voltages, minimizing power consumption and heat generation, rendering them suitable for artificial intelligence, Internet of Things, and 5G/6G applications. Their adaptable architecture accommodates high-performance computing; yet, intricate fabrication necessitates exact lithography and etching. Overcoming these challenges is crucial for their widespread adoption and impact on the semiconductor industry. The demand for novel design methods and assets for efficiently utilizing the advantages of gate-all-around (GAA) devices creates an additional challenge. Because gate-all-around (GAA) devices may not be interoperable with traditional design processes and tools, major investments in developing software and verification would be anticipated. As semiconductor innovations advance, gate-all-around (GAA) devices will inevitably grow more and more significant. The comprehensive examines of gate-all-around (GAA) devices, encompassing their applications, benefits, problems, and operational mechanisms have done in this chapter. Instead of comprehensive examines of various designs of gate-all-around (GAA) devices and functionalities of and their potential influence on the future of semiconductor technology, and their merits and drawbacks have also discussed.

items.title: Fundamentals of Memristors
items.abstract: Memristors have attracted significant attention as an emerging class of nonvolatile memory devices capable of addressing the growing limitations of conventional charge-based memory technologies. As modern computing systems demand higher data density, faster operation, and reduced energy consumption, memristors offer a promising alternative by storing information in programmable resistance states rather than electrical charge. Their simple metal–insulator–metal structure, nanoscale scalability, and low power operation make them strong candidates for future memory architectures, logic-in-memory systems, and neuromorphic computing platforms. This book chapter presents a comprehensive overview of the fundamentals of memristors, highlighting their operating principles, device characteristics, and expanding range of applications. Memristive behavior arises from the phenomenon of resistive switching, where a device undergoes reversible transitions between high-resistance and low-resistance states under an applied electric field. These transitions occur through well-defined physical stages, including the initial high-resistance state, the nucleation and growth of conductive filaments, the establishment of a stable low-resistance state, and the eventual rupture of these filaments that restores the device to its original state. Such processes capture the intrinsic memory and nonlinearity of memristors, forming the basis of their functionality. Different categories of memristors are discussed, along with dominant switching mechanisms such as electrochemical metallization and valence change processes, which are governed by ionic migration, redox reactions, and defect dynamics within the active layer. Material selection plays a critical role in determining memristor performance and reliability. This chapter examines commonly used electrode materials and a broad spectrum of resistive switching materials, including binary metal oxides, perovskite compounds, organic materials, and emerging two-dimensional systems. Key memory performance metrics—such as endurance, data retention, switching speed, energy consumption, variability across devices and cycles, and scalability—are analyzed to provide a realistic assessment of device robustness and manufacturability. To connect material-level phenomena with device and system behavior, multiscale modeling approaches are introduced, ranging from microscopic physical models to numerical techniques such as kinetic Monte Carlo and finite element methods, as well as compact models suitable for circuit and system-level simulations. Finally, the chapter discusses current challenges and future research directions, including variability control, long-term reliability, and large-scale integration. Overall, this chapter offers a detailed and balanced foundation for students and researchers seeking to understand memristor technology and its potential role in next generation memory and computing systems.

items.title: Evaluating Processing-In-Memory (PIM) Topologies for Graph Processing Workloads
items.abstract: Large-scale graph processing algorithms (e.g., PageRank, Breadth-First Search, Single-Source Shortest Path) are foundational to web search, social network analysis, bioinformatics, and recommendation systems. However, conventional CPU/GPU compute architectures struggle to process graph algorithms efficiently. Graph workloads are inherently memory-bound: they exhibit low compute-to-memory ratios, irregular access patterns, poor spatial and temporal cache locality, and severe pointer-chasing behaviors. On traditional von Neumann systems, up to 85% of total execution cycles are spent stalling on off-chip DRAM interconnects, leading to substantial energy waste. Processing-In-Memory (PIM) has emerged as a promising architectural paradigm to break the 'memory wall' by shifting compute primitives directly inside or adjacent to memory structures. However, PIM is not a monolith: hardware implementations range from fine-grained bank-level PIM (e.g., UPMEM DPU, Samsung FIMDRAM) to 3D-stacked logic-layer PIM (e.g., HBM/HMCC-style) and CXL-attached disaggregated near-memory accelerators. This paper presents a cycle-accurate architectural evaluation comparing three representative PIM topologies against a high-end server-grade multi-socket Xeon processor across four canonical graph benchmarks (BFS, PageRank, SSSP, Connected Components) operating on real-world and synthetic scale-free graphs (up to Scale 28). Using a gem5-based cycle-accurate simulation framework integrated with Ramulator2, our results demonstrate that 3D-stacked logic-layer PIM achieves an average 8.4x speedup and a 7.2x reduction in energy consumption over baseline CPU architectures by leveraging ultra-wide TSV bandwidth. Bank-level PIM achieves superior memory bandwidth (14.2x) but suffers from strict bank-to-bank inter-processor communication overheads during global graph traversal phases. We synthesize these architectural trade-offs into a quantitative design guideline matrix for next-generation graph processing hardware.
items.venue: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews

items.title: Electrostatic charge model for dual-layer oxide thin-film transistors
items.abstract: A simple electrostatic two-equation model for dual-layer thin-film transistor (TFT) operation is developed. The model distributes electrostatic charge between the top and bottom semiconductor layers, and the resulting transfer and mobility curves accurately simulate experimental dual-layer a-IGZO/a-IZO TFT operation. The model further provides an analytic expression that maps charge confinement in the high-mobility a-IZO bottom semiconductor layer with the a-IGZO top-layer thickness and the conduction-band offset. By considering both a-IGZO/a-IZO layer charge partition and competing thickness-dependent oxygen vacancy trap density effects, the model suggests an optimal a-IGZO layer thickness of 9–12 nm. Importantly, this general electrostatic model extends to most dual-layer TFT systems and calculates how the top semiconductor layer TFT turn-on voltage changes sharply with the conduction band offset and layer thickness.

items.title: Dynamic Voltage Scaling and Adaptive Body Bias for Energy-Efficient Ultra-Low Voltage CMOS VLSI Systems under Process Variations
items.abstract: The development of ultra-low voltage (ULV) CMOS circuits for the Internet of Things (IoT), wearable electronics, wireless sensor networks, implantable biomedical devices, and edge computing has increased due to the increasing need for dependable and energy-efficient Very Large-Scale Integration (VLSI) systems. Sub-threshold and near-threshold operation dramatically lowers dynamic power consumption, but also degrades circuit performance and reliability by increasing propagation delay, leakage current, and sensitivity to process and temperature changes. This research suggests a hybrid adaptive power optimization system that combines Dynamic Voltage Scaling (DVS) and Adaptive Body Biasing (ABB) to address these issues. The suggested method simultaneously regulates the supply voltage based on workload needs and dynamically modifies the transistor body bias in accordance with process corners and temperature conditions. CMOS logic circuits, such as an inverter, NAND gate, NOR gate, and complete adder developed in 45 nm CMOS technology using the Cadence Virtuoso Analog Design Environment, are used to assess the suggested framework. Multiple process corners (TT, SS, FF, FS, and SF), supply voltages between 0.25 V and 0.5 V, and temperatures between −20°C and 125°C are all simulated. Robustness against manufacturing-induced process changes is assessed using Monte Carlo analysis. Average power, leakage power, propagation delay, Power-Delay Product (PDP), and Energy-Delay Product (EDP) are used to evaluate performance. The results show that the suggested ABB-DVS architecture increases robustness, lowers leakage power, boosts energy efficiency, and offers a scalable solution for next-generation low-power CMOS VLSI systems.
items.venue: International Journal of Science and Engineering Science Research

items.title: Divide and conquer: Scalable performance and energy in MCM GPUs
items.abstract: Multi-chip-module (MCM) GPUs offer a promising path to scale compute capability beyond monolithic designs by integrating multiple chiplets on a common package. However, the impact of disaggregation on performance scalability and energy consumption remains underexplored. The design space grows rapidly across dimensions such as SMs per chiplet, chiplet count, and interconnection network. The inter-chiplet network is particularly critical, as it determines whether additional compute resources translate into performance gains. This limited understanding leaves industry and research without clear guidance on the performance and energy trade-offs of MCM GPU scaling. In this work, we investigate whether distributing compute and memory capability across multiple chiplets offers a more scalable alternative to concentrating resources. We quantify their effects on performance, energy, and efficiency and examine how inter-chiplet topology influences scalability at different system sizes. Our results demonstrate that a 16 chiplet Torus configuration with 256 SMs delivers a remarkable $2.40\times$ performance improvement over a state-of-the-art MCM architecture with the same compute capability, while simultaneously reducing energy consumption by $4.45\times$. These substantial gains provide evidence that disaggregation is a first-order architectural factor and will be critical to unlocking the performance and energy-efficiency potential of next-generation GPUs.

items.title: Discrete electron storage and retention in single α-MoO3 nanocrystals
items.abstract: The development of high-density, energy-efficient nonvolatile memory (NVM) devices can benefit from the integration of novel charge-trapping materials with nanoscale performance. Here, we demonstrate the synthesis of orthorhombic-phase α-MoO 3 nanoparticles (NPs), achieved via solution processing, and their incorporation as discrete High-k charge trapping sites within a Metal-Oxide-High-k-Oxide-Semiconductor (MOHOS) architecture employing ultrathin Al 2 O 3 tunnel and blocking layers. Conductive Atomic force microscopy (cAFM) and Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) were used to directly correlate mapping of both topography and local electrical behavior at the single-NP level. cAFM I-V curves over individual MoO 3 NPs revealed charge trapping/detrapping with threshold shifts around 1 V. KPFM confirmed localized electrostatic potential shifts corresponding to the storage of ∼10-30 electrons per NP, with independent transport-based (cAFM) and electrostatic (KPFM) estimates agreeing to within a factor of two. By combining discrete trapping scalability and low-power operation, single MoO 3 NP capacitor geometry delivers reliable reversible storage. These single-node charge states provide a materials-level basis for discrete-trap memory with potential for multi-level storage.

items.title: Dielectric Modulated Extended Source DG‐TFET–Based Label‐Free Biosensor
items.abstract: The tunnel field-effect transistor (TFET) is a gated, reverse-biased p-i-n junction device that operates based on the quantum mechanical band-to-band tunneling (BTBT) mechanism. This work presents a label-free biosensor based on an extended source double-gate (ESDG) dielectric-modulated TFET (DM-TFET) architecture, simulated using Sentaurus Technology Computer-Aided Design device tools. Nanogap cavities are strategically introduced near the source and drain regions by selectively etching portions of the fixed HfO₂ dielectric layer. This design enables the immobilization of a high concentration of biomolecules, significantly enhancing the interaction between the analyte and the sensing region. The sensitivity (Sn) of the proposed biosensor is evaluated under various conditions, specifically focusing on nanogaps that are fully filled with biomolecules. The analysis considers both neutral and charged environments, including positively and negatively charged biomolecules. Additionally, the impact of a wide range of dielectric constants (k) on sensor performance is systematically studied. This comprehensive evaluation reveals the influence of the dielectric environment and biomolecular charge on the sensor's electrostatic behavior and sensitivity. Device performance parameters such as subthreshold swing, transfer characteristics, energy band diagrams, and I ON /I OFF ratio are analyzed for uncharged biomolecules, with k varying from 1 to 12. Additionally, the effect of steric hindrance is considered by evaluating the sensitivity for four distinct nanogap fill profiles: increasing, decreasing, concave, and convex—each with varying k values. The sensitivity of the proposed ESDG-DM-TFET biosensor is also benchmarked against existing FET- and TFET-based biosensors reported in the literature, demonstrating enhanced performance.

items.title: Design, Stability Improvement, and Scaling of a 4-Transistor Static Latch for Digital Compute-in-Memory
items.abstract: Abstract As data-driven applications grow in importance, several concerns have emerged regarding cloud computing. While cloud computing still offers superior performance, issues such as latency, security, and limited internet availability prevent many applications from adopting modern algorithms. Recently, edge computing has therefore gained traction. In edge computing, the computation is performed entirely on the local device, circumventing the need for internet access and cloud connectivity. Many edge devices are battery-powered and have only a limited power budget. Edge computing therefore focuses on extremely power-efficient operation. Memory movement represents a significant contribution to overall power use. A common method to reduce this overhead is Compute-in-Memory (CIM). While CIM research was initially predominantly driven by analog computing concepts, many advantages of digital computation can also be leveraged for CIM, making digital CIM an attractive alternative. One disadvantage of digital CIM lies in its comparably large memory footprint. In this work, we extend our prior work, which presented a novel standard cell-compliant static latch that can be placed alongside digital logic [1]. The bitcell achieves latching behavior with only four transistors and offers a 73% smaller footprint compared to a standard latch. Our prior work focused on fault mechanisms of the bitcells, as well as the implications of using the cell in system level, given comparably high error rates. In this work, we reiterate our previous findings and investigate the use of backgate biasing to improve system stability. We perform simulations that show improvements of 2.25x and 15x in static noise margin (SNM) and data retention, respectively. Additionally, we perform silicon measurements also indicating improvements in cell stability. To investigate the scaling potential, we transfer the design to a design-rule-clean layout in a commercial 12 nm finFET technology. We finally draw a comparison between the 22 nm implementations from our original work and the 12 nm implementation, indicating that moving to finFET technologies can also improve cell stability.

items.title: Decoupling Thermal and Electronic Effects of Metal Contacts in Bilayer MoS2 Transistors
items.abstract: Contact resistance remains a primary bottleneck in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor field-effect transistors (FETs), yet the concurrent influence of metal work function, adhesion, and deposition temperature obscures the underlying mechanisms. Here, using bilayer MoS2 as a model system, we systematically benchmark four metals (In, Bi, Ti, Pd) and discover that the metal melting point, which sets the deposition thermal budget, is strongly correlated with interface integrity. Low-melting-point metals (Bi, In) preserve an intact van der Waals gap (≈0.3 nm), whereas high-melting-point metals (Ti, Pd) damage the interface and collapse the gap to ≈0.19 nm (Pd) or destroy it entirely (Ti), as revealed by high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM). Despite Fermi-level pinning rendering all devices n-type, Pd outperforms Ti in contact resistance, underscoring the primacy of interface quality over work function alignment. Remarkably, Bi, despite its higher melting point and work function than In, delivers the lowest contact resistance (≈0.14 kΩ·μm) and highest on-state current (≈525 μA·μm-1 at Lch = 100 nm), which we attribute to its semi-metallic band structure that suppresses metal-induced gap states. This work establishes a design rule of contact metals for n-type MoS2 FETs: low work function, low deposition temperature, and low density of states, which is expected to extend to other 2D semiconductor nanoelectronics and integrated circuits.

items.title: Data-Driven Modeling and Circuit-Aware Optimization of Gate-All-Around Multi-Bridge Channel FETs
items.abstract: Aggressive semiconductor scaling toward sub-3 nm technology nodes requires advanced device optimization frameworks capable of efficiently exploring high-dimensional electrostatic design spaces while preserving physics accuracy and circuit-level applicability. Conventional Technology Computer-Aided Design (TCAD) based optimization requires thousands of simulations, limiting scalability for sub-3 nm device design. This work proposes a physics-driven hybrid machine learning and multi-objective evolutionary optimization framework for electrostatic parameter optimization of sub-3 nm Gate-All-Around Multi-Bridge Channel FET (GAA MBCFET) devices targeting ultra-low-power IoT hardware. The framework integrates calibrated TCAD simulation, hybrid surrogate learning using XGBoost and Random Forest, and cellular multi-objective evolutionary optimization to enable fast design exploration under circuit-aware constraints. The hybrid surrogate achieves improved prediction fidelity (RMSE ≈ 0.47, R 2 up to 0.94) while reducing TCAD simulation requirements by ~78% and optimization runtime by ~65%. Device-level optimization achieves subthreshold swing of 57.6 mV/dec, ~22% DIBL reduction, ~40–45% leakage reduction, ~28–32% ON current improvement, and ~30–35% transconductance improvement. Multi-objective optimization improves Pareto hypervolume by ~32–38% with ~35% faster convergence. Circuit-level validation using a sub-3 nm GAA MBCFET SAR ADC demonstrates ~15–22% switching delay reduction and ~35–45% standby power reduction under low-voltage IoT operation. The proposed framework enables physics-consistent, data-driven, and application-aware optimization for next-generation sub-3 nm semiconductor and IoT edge computing platforms.
items.venue: Journal of Circuits, Systems and Computers

items.title: Can Organic and Oxide Semiconductors Do More Than Coexist? Functional Heterointerfaces for Hybrid Thin‐Film Transistors
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Organic and oxide semiconductors differ fundamentally in their transport physics, interfacial chemistry, mechanical behavior, and processing requirements, yet these differences also make them functionally complementary. Integrating the two material classes, however, remains challenging because of their distinct surface chemistries, deposition conditions, thermal budgets, and interfacial stability. Beyond the question of whether such dissimilar materials can simply coexist, a more important issue is whether their integration can create functions unavailable to either material alone. This review demonstrates how carefully engineered organic‐oxide heterointerfaces can transform material dissimilarity into a functional advantage, enabling sensing, memory, nonlinear signal processing, and computation. We classify hybridization at the circuit, channel, and interface‐layer levels and connect each architecture to its underlying charge‐injection, transfer, trapping, recombination, tunneling, and fluctuation mechanisms. Lateral and vertically stacked circuits exploit the natural polarity matching between p‐type organic and n‐type oxide semiconductors, whereas directly coupled or interlayer‐mediated channels enable ambipolar, anti‐ambipolar, negative‐transconductance, Gaussian‐like, and sigmoidal responses. Hybrid contact, dielectric, passivation, and charge‐storage layers further regulate injection barriers, molecular organization, photogating, and carrier retention. By linking hybrid architecture and interface coupling to device transfer functions and target applications, this review presents organic‐oxide heterointerfaces as a design platform for thin‐film transistors and heterojunction devices.

items.title: Bandgap Reference Circuits for AI Hardware
items.abstract: Bandgap reference (BGR) circuits play a critical role in ensuring power stability and precision in modern artificial intelligence (AI) hardware, including Tensor Processing Units, Neural Processing Units, and Graphics Processing Units. However, as semiconductor technology scales to sub-7-nm FinFET and gate-all-around transistors, process variations and device mismatches introduce random voltage offsets, which can degrade model accuracy, power efficiency, and computational reliability in deep learning accelerators. To mitigate these challenges, advanced layout techniques such as common-centroid transistor placement, matched resistor arrays, and dummy structures are employed, along with digital trimming, adaptive biasing, and curvature compensation, to enhance voltage accuracy and thermal stability. Furthermore, designing BGR circuits for AI applications involves a trade-off between area, accuracy, and power dissipation. High-precision BGR circuits with low-temperature coefficient designs improve voltage stability but increase circuit complexity and power consumption, making them unsuitable for battery-operated edge AI and Internet of Things devices. Conversely, low-power BGR circuits, optimized for wearables, smart sensors, and edge computing, focus on minimal leakage currents and efficient biasing techniques, sometimes at the cost of accuracy and robustness against supply variations. However, high-performance AI accelerators in cloud data centers require ultra-low drift and high-stability BGR circuits, often consuming additional silicon area due to compensation circuits. This chapter explores the challenges of design trade-offs in AI-focused BGR circuits, highlighting strategies for designing and optimizing power efficiency and computational reliability in emerging AI architectures. This chapter provides a detailed analysis of the BGR circuits for AI and machine learning applications, offering a comprehensive understanding of the topic. It also compares state-of-the-art BGR circuits, highlighting their respective advantages and disadvantages.

items.title: An Enhanced CMOS Analog Predistortion Linearizer to Independently Fine-Tune the AM-AM and AM-PM of CMOS PA
items.abstract: This work presents a K/Ka–band two-way parallel combined CMOS power amplifier (PA) employing an enhanced analog predistortion (APD) linearizer with dedicated AM-AM and AM-PM correction networks. The proposed APD utilizes diode-connected transistors for AM-AM correction and a cold-FET (CFET)-based AM-PM compensation network to simultaneously mitigate gain and phase distortions. As a proof of concept, the PA circuit is fabricated in a 65-nm CMOS process with a total area of 0.81 mm2. The linearized PA achieved a saturated power ($P_{\text {sat}}$) > 18 dBm, with peak power-added efficiency (PAE) > 24% across the band. In addition, with APD-ON, the AM-AM and AM-PM distortions are greatly compensated with less than 1 dB gain peaking at 23 & 25 GHz and$OP_{\text {1dB}}$at 25 GHz, respectively. In addition, with 256-quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), a 400-MHz bandwidth, and a 9.2 dB peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) signal, a linear-average output power of 15 dBm yielded an error vector magnitude (EVM) of -25 dB (5%). In contrast, the adjacent channel leakage ratio (ACLR) of −39.5 dBc is achieved at 25 GHz.
items.venue: IEEE Transactions on Circuits & Systems II Express Briefs

items.title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Technique for Advanced Systems Design
items.abstract: Through automation, intelligent decision-making, and increased efficiency across a range of industries, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are revolutionizing system design. These technologies optimize system performance through predictive analytics, data-driven insights, and self-learning mechanisms. The artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation minimizes human intervention, whereas machine learning (ML) algorithms continuously refine system processes, enhancing accuracy and adaptability in fields such as healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and cyber security. One of the most transformative aspects of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) is their capability to enhance scalability and flexibility in system architecture. Real-time data processing is made possible by edge computing and cloud-based artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, which lower latency and increase responsiveness. Additionally, artificial intelligence (AI)-powered security systems strengthen cyber security by detecting anomalies, preventing cyber threats, and adapting to evolving risks in real time. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are revolutionizing VLSI design by automating complex tasks like placement, routing, and floor planning, drastically reducing design cycle times and enhancing power, performance, and area (PPA) metrics. Machine learning (ML) algorithms learn from historical data to optimize floor planning, transistor sizing, and routing, often exceeding manual efforts in efficiency. Artificial intelligence (AI) reduces the number of iterations required to achieve timing closure, leading to faster turnaround times (TAT). Artificial intelligence (AI) tools predict potential failure points and automatically generate test vectors, enhancing functional coverage and reducing manual debugging efforts. Self-learning, flexibility, and transparency will be the main focuses of artificial intelligence (AI)-integrated system design in the future. Explainable artificial intelligence (AI), which offers clear insights into artificial intelligence (AI)-driven decision-making, will be essential in enhancing responsibility and trust. Quantum artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to revolutionize problem-solving, offering immense computational power for complex simulations and optimizations. Moreover, ethical artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks and regulations will become increasingly important in addressing concerns related to bias, fairness, and responsible artificial intelligence (AI) usage. The basis of system design will be rewritten as artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies develop further, initiating access to the development of highly effective, intelligent, and autonomous systems. Innovation will be increased by its integration with cutting-edge technologies like blockchain, quantum computing, and the Internet of Things. The smooth integration of real-time data processing, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation, and ethical artificial intelligence (AI) principles will shape system architecture in the future and promote a more intelligent, safe, and sustainable digital ecosystem.

items.title: AI‐Driven VLSI
items.abstract: With advancing technology, very-large-scale integration (VLSI) is leading the way with the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and quantum computing into day-to-day applications. The integration of VLSI and AI has enabled revolutionary improvement in semiconductor technology, providing intelligent, high-speed, and low-power computing systems. Traditional VLSI design processes are typically constrained by manual optimization methodologies, larger design complexity, and vast resource utilization. The application of AI, in the guise of ML and deep learning (DL), has introduced automation to essential phases of VLSI design like circuit layout, optimization, testing, and verification. AI has been a need to propel electronic design automation (EDA), advancement, productivity, and precision in many aspects of the design process, with the increased complexity of new chip designs. AI-based techniques enhance power, performance, and area (PPA) trade-offs, reduce design iterations, and improve fault detection mechanisms, leading to higher yield and reduced time-to-market. Furthermore, AI predictive analytics in chip production optimizes defect detection and process control for better chip reliability and efficiency. AI models analyze vast amounts of historical design data and prior layouts to predict optimal floor plans and placements, minimizing congestion, reducing interconnect delays, and lowering power consumption. This chapter focuses on AI utilization in VLSI design, its application areas in EDA, and challenges in AI-based VLSI systems. On the basis of the review of recent AI techniques, upcoming trends, and illustrations, the book presents an exhaustive account of the combination of VLSI and AI and establishes a base for future innovation and research in smart semiconductor design.

items.title: Zero-Rate-Output Instability Phenomena in MEMS Gyroscopes With and Without Quadrature Nulling
items.abstract: This work investigates instability phenomena in amplitude modulated gyroscopes with sub $0.1~^{\circ }$ /hr bias stability and $0.03~^{\circ }$ / $\surd $ hr angle random walk. A predictive model is developed for the dependence of the zero-rate output (ZRO) on temperature for both the condition of uncompensated quadrature, and, notably, also for the case of quadrature nulled by an automatic loop with electromechanical electrodes. The model verification requires an accurate calibration of various parameters: other than the usual ones (resonance, quality factor, split value...), the work also includes a temperature characterization of the feedthrough capacitances and of quadrature, on dozens of samples. The model predicts ZRO variations in closed-loop quadrature to depend more on scale-factor changes and drive-sense feedthrough, rather than on quadrature or phase changes, which are instead known main contributors in absence of quadrature null. Experiments are taken both as ZRO vs temperature curves and as Allan deviations in controlled conditions: results confirm some of the model suggestions, but highlight additional phenomena, not captured by the model, like stability dependence on drive amplitude, and Random Telegraph Noise (RTN). [2026-0058]

items.title: Wafer-Scale Estimation of Thermal Stability With Magneto-Optical Measurement System for STT-MRAM
items.abstract: The magnetic anisotropy field of perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA) films is an important magnetic characteristic directly linked to data retention for Spin Transfer Torque Magnetoresistive Random Access Memory (STT-MRAM). To measure the fullwafer characterization, we develop a polar magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) measurement system incorporating a unique electromagnet with a temperature-controlled chuck and stage. The validity of this system is confirmed by correlation with the conventional technique. The spatial resolution of the system is demonstrated to 20 μm, which is on the order of millimeters with a conventional inline MOKE tool. We also measured the uniformity of magnetic anisotropy across the full wafer at 150 °C and estimated the temperature stability of patterned MTJ. The magneto-optical measurement system is expected to be promising for inline inspection of device characteristics.

items.title: WSe2-FETs: Device Architectures, Progress in Doping Strategies, Contact Engineering, Reliability Challenges, and Exciting Prospects for Next-Generation Low-Power Nanoelectronics
items.abstract: Sub-10 nm nanoelectronics scaling demands channel materials combining superior electrostatic control, high mobility, and low power consumption. Tungsten diselenide ( ${\mathrm{WSe}}_{{2}}\text {)}$ has emerged as a premier 2-D candidate due to its tunable bandgap, atomic thickness, and ambipolar transport. This review systematically examines recent WSe 2 field-effect transistor advancements across five core domains: architectures, doping, contact engineering, reliability, and applications. Advanced configurations, including dual-gate FETs, vertically stacked complementary FETs (CFETs), and steep-slope variants, significantly enhance scalability and energy efficiency. Surface charge transfer (SCT) and substitutional doping enable stable unipolar operation while preserving gate control. Contact optimization via van der Waals (vdW) interfaces and alloyed electrodes effectively mitigate Fermi-level pinning (FLP) and reduces contact resistance ( ${\mathrm{R}}_{\text {C}}\text {)}$ . Interfacial passivation with h-BN and plasma treatments robustly suppresses charge trapping and threshold voltage hysteresis. Finally, WSe 2 -FETs are positioned for transformative roles in low-power CMOS, flexible electronics, biosensors, neuromorphic computing, and optoelectronics, alongside key commercialization pathways.

items.title: Unveiling Search‐Robust One‐Shot Learning Operation in FeTFT‐Based Ternary Content‐Addressable Memory
items.abstract: With the rapid growth of data‐centric artificial intelligence (AI), ternary content‐addressable memory (TCAM) has emerged as a promising platform for parallel in‐memory search. Here, we systematically investigate how the gate‐dielectric material and structural design of metal–ferroelectric‐metal–insulator–semiconductor (MFMIS) ferroelectric thin‐film transistors (FeTFTs) affect TCAM search operation and long‐term robustness. By comparing ZrO 2 (11 nm), ZrO 2 (8 nm), and HfO 2 (8 nm) gate dielectrics, we decouple the effects of material substitution, thickness scaling, and equivalent‐oxide‐thickness (EOT)‐matched behavior. All devices show proper initial TCAM operation, with ZrO 2 8 nm exhibiting the highest initial sensing performance owing to its larger read current. Under repeated search cycling, however, ZrO 2 11 nm proves the most robust, while HfO 2 8 nm suffers the most severe degradation—governed by competition between electron trapping and donor‐like state creation rather than conventional ferroelectric fatigue. One‐shot classification simulations using experimentally extracted bit error rate (BER) trends confirm that device‐level degradation directly translates into accuracy loss, with ZrO 2 11 nm retaining the highest accuracy. Increasing the memcapacitor area ratio enlarges the memory window but degrades sensing response due to added parasitic capacitance and RC delay. These findings establish gate‐dielectric and interface design guidelines for search‐robust FeTFT‐based TCAM.

items.title: U.S.-Vietnam Semiconductor Cooperation: Progress, Constraints, and Pathways Forward
items.abstract: executive summary: This article examines U.S.-Vietnam semiconductor relations since 2023, arguing that despite alignment under the two states' comprehensive strategic partnership (CSP), cooperation has yet to produce meaningful structural upgrading of Vietnam's position in the global semiconductor value chain. main argumentThe 2023 U.S.-Vietnam CSP marked a major upgrade in bilateral relations, with semiconductors identified as a central pillar of future cooperation. Yet progress to date has fallen short of initial expectations. This gap stems from two interacting factors. First, despite the upgrade, the U.S. has maintained a cautious approach toward Vietnam with policy incoherence and mixed signals that undermine momentum for deepening high-tech collaboration. This landscape has been further complicated by foreign and trade policy shifts under the Trump administration that have disrupted key cooperation mechanisms and increased uncertainty for U.S. firms. Second, and more fundamentally, Vietnam's domestic ecosystem continues to face structural constraints, including inadequate infrastructure, workforce shortages, and constraints in the business environment. These limitations weaken Vietnam's ability to attract and sustain high-value semiconductor cooperation. The CSP provides an important political framework but achieving its semiconductor ambitions will depend on credible policy support, firm-level confidence, and Vietnam's capacity to address domestic bottlenecks. policy implications • Vietnam should prioritize domestic capacity building as this remains the major challenge for deeper cooperation in the semiconductor sector. Without stronger infrastructure, a deeper talent pool, and a more predictable business environment, Vietnam will struggle to attract high-value and high-tech investment. Deepening engagement with U.S. firms and academic institutions is also crucial to anchor cooperation at the market level. • The U.S. should align its policy tools with the strategic logic of the CSP. The continuation of Vietnam's nonmarket economy status, restrictive export-controls, and high tariff pressures send mixed signals, weakening business confidence and limiting the momentum created by upgrading the partnership. • Both sides should prioritize advanced packaging and workforce development as practical areas of cooperation. These areas match Vietnam's current comparative advantages while supporting U.S. supply chain diversification, allowing cooperation to move gradually from low-value manufacturing toward more knowledge-intensive semiconductor activities.

items.title: Transition-Region Co-Optimization for Enhanced dV/dt Ruggedness in 4H-SiC MOSFETs
items.abstract: Under high-speed switching conditions, silicon carbide (SiC) metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) are susceptible to reliability failures induced by high dV/dt stress, which has emerged as a critical bottleneck limiting their high-frequency and high-efficiency applications. This article presents a systematic investigation of the failure behavior and underlying physical mechanisms of 1200 V 4H-SiC mosfet s under high dV/dt conditions. Transient electric-field concentration across the thin gate oxide in the transition region is identified as the primary trigger of dV/dt -induced failure, based on double-pulse testing combined with thermal emission microscope, focused ion beam, and scanning electron microscopy failure analyzes. Further technology computer aided design (TCAD) transient simulations reveal that both an excessive thin-gate-oxide length and dynamic incomplete-ionization effects contribute to severe transient gate-oxide electric-field intensification during fast voltage ramping. Based on these insights, a co-optimization strategy centered on electric-field redistribution is proposed and experimentally validated by shortening the thin-gate-oxide length and reducing the surface doping concentration in the transition region. The optimized device can operate reliably at dV/dt exceeding 330 V/ns, with no failure observed even under the extreme condition of $\boldsymbol {R}_{\boldsymbol {g}}$ = 0 $\boldsymbol {\Omega }$ , representing more than a threefold improvement over the original device. Furthermore, continuous-pulse stress tests demonstrate stable gate leakage current after 2.5 × 10 6 high-speed switching cycles under dV/dt stress above 300 V/ns, indicating no observable gate-oxide degradation. Large-scale statistical measurements on 1200 V devices confirm that key static parameters, including threshold voltage, on-resistance, and breakdown voltage, remain unchanged, while high-temperature reverse-bias testing at ${\text{175}}\; ^{\circ }{\text{C}}$ for 1000 h verifies that the proposed optimization does not compromise long-term static reliability.

items.title: Transfer-Aware Kernel Placement on Modern Ryzen APUs
items.abstract: Modern Ryzen accelerated processing units (APUs) expose multiple on-die accelerators, such as GPUs and NPUs, whose full utilization requires placement decisions that account for both compute capability and shared-DRAM behavior. In unified-DRAM APUs, the CPU, GPU, and NPU share system DRAM, while each accelerator incurs a different cost to make operands and results visible through the memory system. This letter presents a transfer-aware kernel-placement framework that measures per-accelerator compute and transfer costs and applies a residency-depth cost model to decide placements at compile time for concurrent heterogeneous execution. Evaluation on two Ryzen AI APUs and large language model (LLM)-derived GEMM/GEMV workloads shows that the best placement target changes with transfer-cost amortization and differs across devices and APUs. Compared with a greedy policy that assigns each operation class as a whole to its lowest-cost device, the proposed placement reduces execution time by 18.69% on average on the AI350% and 17.95% on average on the AI365, reaching up to an additional $1.65\times $ speedup in GEMM-dominant scenarios.

items.title: Track-Structure-Induced Ion-Energy Dependence of Single-Event Upsets in a 65-nm DICE SRAM
items.abstract: With the widespread adoption of flip-chip packaging and the increasing complexity of integrated circuit structures, high-energy heavy ions have become increasingly important in ground-based single-event effects (SEEs) evaluation. This work experimentally and numerically investigates the ion-energy dependence of single-event upset (SEU) sensitivity in a commercial 65-nm dual-interlocked storage cell (DICE) SRAM. SEU cross sections were measured using 209Bi and 181Ta ions under comparable linear energy transfer (LET) conditions. Despite the comparable LET values, 209Bi consistently induces significantly larger SEU cross sections than 181Ta, with the difference approaching one order of magnitude. To interpret the experimental observations, a modified G4SEE-based Monte Carlo model incorporating a dual-sensitive-volume criterion was developed to reproduce the dual-node upset behavior of the DICE SRAM. The simulations show that higher-energy ions generate a larger fraction of energetic $\delta $ -rays, resulting in a broader lateral ionization profile and a higher probability of simultaneous charge collection by a sensitive-node pair. Additional simulations with different physics configurations indicate that Coulomb scattering and nuclear reactions contribute negligibly to the simulated SEU cross sections, suggesting that the observed ion-energy dependence is primarily governed by differences in the direct-ionization track structure. These results indicate that LET alone is insufficient to characterize SEU sensitivity in redundancy-hardened SRAMs and highlight the importance of explicitly considering ion energy and track structure in SEE evaluation and radiation-hardness assurance.

items.title: Toward a Unified Memristive Edge Platform for Sensing, Security, and Neuromorphic Computing
items.abstract: Memristive devices are increasingly considered for next-generation edge hardware because their conductance dynamics can support nonvolatile memory, sensing, stochastic security primitives, and energy-efficient computing. However, the device requirements of these functions are not identical: sensing requires stimulus-responsive transduction, hardware security benefits from entropy and device uniqueness, whereas neuromorphic computing generally requires controllable multilevel states and bounded variability. This paper presents an application-driven comparison of representative metal-oxide, two-dimensional, nanowire/diffusive, and flexible memristive device families across these competing requirements. A qualitative cross-functional benchmark is introduced to assess functional suitability and integration readiness, identifying HfOx devices as a balanced technology candidate rather than a u niversally optimal solution. Using a forming-free, multi-bit Pd/Ti/HfO2/Pd ReRAM device as an experimentally grounded computing case study, the paper proposes a regime-engineered, crossbar-based platform in which sensing-, security-, and computing-oriented sub-arrays share a common HfO2 material and process foundation while retaining function-specific interfaces and operating conditions. The resulting framework provides device-to-system design guidance for developing secure, multifunctional, and locally intelligent edge systems.
items.venue: IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Very Large Scale Integration of System-on-Chip

items.title: Thickness-dependent performance evaluation of ferroelectric HfO 2 gate for 20 nm NCFETs
items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a systematic simulation-based analysis of impact the ferroelectric layer thickness t fe of HfO 2 impacts the electrical performance of ferroelectric, negative capacitance field-effect transistors (NC-FETs) compared to that of a conventional dielectric-based metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET). Performance was simulated over the full range from 6–10 nm. To assess device behavior, the capacitance-matching principle established in Landau–Khalatnikov’s model of polarization has been utilized using Silvaco TCAD software. The electrical performances have then been evaluated using a common set of both AC and DC figures of merit, including threshold voltage ( V th ); subthreshold swing ( SS ); drain-induced barrier lowering ( DIBL ); drain current ratios ( I on /I off ); off state leakage current ( I off * ); gate capacitance ( C gg * ); and peak transconductance ( g m,max ). Results show that HfO 2 integrated gates consistently outperform conventional dielectric MOSFETs, with two distinct performance optima identified; a local optimum at 6 nm in the large-thickness regime (6–10 nm) and a global optimum at 2 nm across the entire 0.5–10 nm investigation range. A systematic thickness scaling study into the less than 5 nm range identifies 2 nm as the global optimum, where V th = 0.45 V; SS = 65.4 mV dec −1 ; DIBL = 0.05 V/V; I on /I off = 5.75 × 10 12 ; I off = 5.06 × 10 −17 A; C gg = 2.87 fF μ m −1 ; and g m,max = 1.18 mS. The near-thermionic SS of 65.4 mV dec −1 approaches but does not achieve the fundamental 60 mV dec −1 thermal limit, consistent with the planar single-gate architecture employed in this study. Further scaling below 2 nm will result in rapid performance degradation due to ferroelectric domain degradation and enhancement of the depolarization field. These results may be used to prescribe numerical guidelines for thickness scaling of ferroelectric HfO 2 NC-FET devices as they are developed for next-generation applications.

items.title: Thermal-Aware Write Management on 3-D NAND Flash Solid-State Drives
items.abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and multimedia applications, solid-state drives (SSDs) are required to support intensive data-access activities, including model training, data collection, inference, and multimedia processing. Although 3-D nand flash significantly improves storage density by vertically stacking multiple layers of memory cells, its highly compact structure hinders heat dissipation and makes it susceptible to localized heat accumulation during peak workloads. When the temperature exceeds a predefined safety threshold, the system activates dynamic thermal throttling (DTT) mechanisms to maintain data integrity, which can significantly degrade system performance. To address this issue, our research proposes a thermal-aware write management scheme for SSD writes that prevents DTT activation and maintains stable performance under peak workloads. When burst read/write requests arrive, the current state of the SSD is analyzed to derive a safe energy budget for each thermal node. The conventional dynamic and static wear-leveling mechanisms are temporarily suspended, and incoming write requests are redirected to relatively cooler and spatially distributed regions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed scheme effectively reduces the maximum operating temperature while maintaining stable write performance across multiple real-world workloads from the Storage Networking Industry Association (SNIA) IOTTA trace suite.

items.title: Thermal Evaluation and Cost-Effective Optimization of Hybrid Three-Level Si/SiC ANPC Converters to Expand the Power Capacity Limitation
items.abstract: Hybrid Si/SiC converters offer a favorable balance between performance and cost and are promising for renewable energy applications. However, their power capacity is fundamentally limited by thermal constraints, and a systematic approach to expand this limit in a cost-effective manner is still lacking. This article investigates the power-capacity limitation of hybrid Si/SiC three-level active neutral-point clamped (ANPC) converters through a quantitative electrothermal analysis. The power loss distribution and junction-temperature characteristics of Si IGBTs and SiC mosfets are analyzed under different switching frequencies, load conditions, and power factors, enabling the identification of dominant thermal bottlenecks.
