As a result, the LFN properties of all IAZO TFTs follow the classical 1/f noise model well over 1 ∼ 1000 Hz. LFN analysis reveals that the origin of LFN shifts from carrier number fluctuations (Δ N ) to mobility fluctuations (Δ μ ) for stacked SiO 2 + HfO 2 insulator structures with varying HfO 2 thicknesses. When the HfO 2 thickness is 15 nm, the origin of LFN can be attributed to the carrier number with correlated mobility fluctuation (Δ N −Δ μ ). According to Δ N −Δ μ model, the calculated interfacial trap density ( N t ) is 5.9 × 10 19 cm −3 eV −1 , significantly lower than that of IAZO TFTs using a single-layer SiO 2 insulator (1.12 × 10 20 cm −3 eV −1 ). This demonstrates that high-quality gate insulator stacks can reduce the trap density near the insulator/channel interface, thereby enhancing device performance. Meanwhile, Hooge’s parameter ( α H = 1.1 × 10 −2 ) of IAZO TFT with HfO 2 gate insulator was extracted from the LFN measurement. Therefore, LFN enables quantitative understanding of the physical mechanisms of interface trap states and defects, thereby revealing their intrinsic transport characteristics and guiding device optimization.
items.venue: Journal of Physics D Applied Physics

items.title: AI for Science with GPT-6 Astra: Thermal Design and Electrothermal Analysis of 2D CFET
items.abstract: Thermal optimization of 2D CFET inverters requires testing structural proposals against their electrical costs. We examine these research tasks using an AI agent workflow within a supplied electrothermal model. At 12 nm, Astra selects a redistributed source-interconnect geometry, while a coordinating agent proposes a substrate-directed heat-removal path. The combined design reduces peak temperature rise by 1.67 K at fixed metal volume and 20 μW. A subsequent metal-resistance sensitivity gives about 0.6-K inverter cooling alongside a 2% nFET on-current loss. Effective contact-length scaling further shows that lower temperature can accompany higher thermal resistance when current falls. Reproduction identifies agreeing implementations and retains a 104.95-K failure for diagnosis. These results show that an AI scientist workflow can propose thermal structures, test them under common constraints, and quantify their electrical cost.

items.title: A reliability assessment methodology for repurposed smartphones: current to temperature dependency as a probable indicator
items.abstract: This paper presents a methodology for the reliability assessment of embedded computers built from repurposed smartphone motherboards, a key enabler for circular economy strategies. While reuse strategies like repurposing extend product lifespans and reduce waste, their adoption is hindered by the lack of adapted reliability assessment methodologies. Traditional approaches, designed for linear economies, rely on detailed component-level data and component-specific measurements—both impractical for reused systems due to information opacity and system integration constraints. We propose a system-level reliability assessment methodology tailored to circular economy constraints, focusing on measurable indicators like electrical current consumption. An accelerated life test was conducted on 30 repurposed Fairphone 2 motherboards under combined thermal and computational stress for 1344 h. Despite the absence of failures or measurable degradation—a key limitation of this study—current consumption exhibited a temperature-dependent power-law trend with high inter-device variability (exponent m=2.4−4.6). The exponent m emerges as a potential decision criterion for reuse as it reflects macroscopic system behaviour. It however requires further results for validation because this study does not establish a correlation between m and degradation. This work bridges the gap between circular economy goals and reliability engineering, offering a scalable approach for assessing reused electronics. Future research will explore aggressive acceleration methods to validate current consumption as a reliability indicator and identify underlying degradation mechanisms.

items.title: A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW OF NANODCAL FOR FIRST-PRINCIPLES QUANTUM TRANSPORT SIMULATIONS
items.abstract: First-principles quantum transport simulations play a central role in the design and understanding of nanoscale electronic, spintronic, and optoelectronic devices. Among the available computational platforms, nanoDCAL (Nanodevice Calculator) has emerged as a specialized and powerful tool that integrates density functional theory (DFT) with the non-equilibrium Green’s function (NEGF) formalism within a localized atomic orbital framework. This review provides a systematic overview of the theoretical foundations, numerical implementation, input architecture, and representative applications of nanoDCAL, based on its official user reference documentation and reported benchmark studies. Emphasis is placed on the unique capabilities of nanoDCAL for two-probe device simulations, spin-dependent transport, spin–orbit coupling, and photocurrent calculations in low-dimensional materials. The strengths, limitations, and perspectives of nanoDCAL are discussed in comparison with other widely used quantum transport packages, highlighting its relevance for next-generation nanoelectronic and spintronic device research.
items.venue: Journal of Thu Dau Mot University

items.title: RAVEN-3.5D: Rapid Architecture Validation Enabling NoC-based 3.5D Multi-CPU/GPU Chiplet Systems
items.abstract: Advanced processors leverage 3.5D Integration to deploy stacks of 3D chiplets on an interposer. The architecture of such processors is complex as the chiplets need to be dimensioned, taking into account area and power, while ensuring that they can be assembled to make modular systems, such as the re-use of AMD's CCD chiplets in multiple products. As the cost for advanced packaging technology drops, it will migrate to lower-end systems, but the academic and open-source communities are not yet ready for studying such systems. Indeed, there are currently no openly available platforms to explore complex multi-chiplet, heterogeneous (CPU/GPU) architectures, particularly with appropriate high-bandwidth 3.5D NoCs, cache coherency and the ability to prototype at the RTL level. We present Raven-3.5D, a platform which can quickly generate the full RTL for these systems. The user specifies the system topology (number of chiplets, their composition, the global NoC topology, etc.) in a simple YAML file, and our platform generates the full RTL and software configuration. To program these systems, we present a lightweight software flow based on OpenCL which can compile applications to run on multi-core CPUs and multi-GPUs. We present two case-studies (i) focused on a footprint-constrained system (ii) a system design based on three re-usable chiplets. The full research platform is available as open-source and we believe it will be of great benefit to an interdisciplinary research community.
items.venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems, Volume 1
